        .From Live Session Week 01; lecturer screenshots (Folder: '1.9. Live Session')
            .Cardiopulmonary II (See [CP2_PatientClientManagementModel])
                -Focus on specific screening, examination, and interventions for patients with primary and secondary cardipulmonary disfunctions

            .Symptoms REPE
                ↓
                x
                ↓
                Assessment/Examination
                ↓
                Re-assessment (go back to x or advance)
                Intervention

            .Impairments → Intervention → Re-assessment (did it work?)
                -Poor aerobic endurance assessed on 6 MWT → perform aerobic endurance training 3x/wk for 4 weeks → improved 6 MWT distance
                -(+) lung consolidation via auscultation → perform drainage techniques x 1 session → (-) lung consolidation via auscultation
                -Poor chest expansion with thoracic excursion measurement via circumference → perform inhalation/ventilatory muscle training techniques 2x per week for 4 weeks → Improved chest expansion with +1 cm gain
            .Screening in Physical Therapy
                Red Flags — referral out, treat and refer, or treat
                Vitals
                Open ended questions
                Medical chart review
                Bilateral Symptoms, Constitutional Symptoms, Etc
                Palpitations reported
                Pain patterns and referrals
            .Chart Review
                Obtain important information about the patient
                Diagnosis, date of event, patient history
                Medications
                Lab values
                Surgeries or procedures
                Imaging
                Hospital course
                Family history of home environment
            .Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Screening Procedures
                DDx chest pain
                Dyspnea — pulmonary vs cardiac origin, red flag?
                Syncope
                Fatigue
                Cough
                Pain in LE
                Rib pain, neck pain, chest wall pain pulmonary of origin
            .Remember!
                Screening for referral is based on
                    PMH - What they told you
                    Clinical presentation - What you saw
                    Associated signs and symptoms - What you asked about
            .Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Physical Therapy Examination
                History and interview
                    IE: pt. reports chest pain, ask what makes it worse or better, when did it start, etc.
                Systems review and associated CVP presentation
                    IE: Integumentary: edema and wound in LES — vascular insufficiency, CHF, kidney disease
                Inspection and Observation
                    -Posture, breathing rate and rhythm, color, pallor, accessory mm. hypertrophy, pt. position, lines/ tubes/ drains, etc, palpation of chest wall or peripheral circulation, temperature
                Exam techniques
                    Heart and lung sounds, chest wall motion, etc.
                DC planning — reserved for acute care setting
            .Mechanical vs Non-Mechanical Examples
                Shoulder / arm pain
                    MI vs shoulder impingement vs radicular neck pain
                Neck Pain
                    Tumor vs cervical joint dysfunction
                Back pain
                    AAA vs lumbar joint dysfunction

        Module 1: Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Screening & Examination Part 1

        Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Screening in Physical Therapy

        .Screening in Physical Therapy
            What components included in the screening process?
                • Take vital signs
                • Review the pain body chart
                • Review medications and their potential side effects against current signs and symptoms
                • Watch for red flag histories, risk factors, and associated signs and symptoms
                • Always ask a broad, open-ended question
                • Conduct the medical chart review
            Define a “Red Flag”
                Be alert to the following red flags of "systemic illness":
                    • Gradual onset with no known cause
                    • Gradual, progressive, cyclical onset
                    • Constant / intense pain
                    • Symptoms unrelieved by rest or change in position
                    • Bilateral symptoms
                        • Pigmentation changes
                        • Edema
                        • Rash
                        • Clubbing/nail bed changes
                        • Weakness
                        • Numbness/tingling
                        • Burning
                    • Constitutional symptoms
                        • Fever
                        • Diaphoresis
                        • Night sweats
                        • Pallor
                        • Fatigue
                        • Nausea
                        • Vomiting
                        • Diarrhea
                        • Dizziness/syncope
                        • Weight loss
                        ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                        Red Flag-Vital Signs 
                            • Correlate unusual vital signs with other signs and symptoms, such as: 
                                • Pallor 
                                • Perspiration 
                                • Fatigue 
                                • Palpitations
                                    • Irregular heartbeats lasting for hours; > six episodes per minute 
                                    • Especially with SOB, chest pain, dizziness, lightheadedness 
                                    • +Family history of sudden cardiac death 
                                    • Personal history of heart disease 
                                    • Clients who are neurologically unstable as a result of a recent CVA, head trauma, spinal cord injury, or other central nervous system insult often exhibit new arrhythmias  during the period of instability
                    Other Associated Signs and Symptoms
                        • Headache
                        • Visual changes
                        • Bowel/bladder
                        • Unusual vital signs
                        • Warning signs of cancer
                        • Dyspnea
                        • Orthostatic hypotension
            What 3 questions must you ask as you screen a patient in Physical therapy?
                (From videos)
                    Are there any red flag symptoms here?
                    Is there anything that's saying a vascular issue versus a radicular lumbar issue?
                    Do I treat or refer this patient out?
                ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                (From .pdf)Ask yourself these questions:
                    1.Refer the patient out (outside scope of PT practice)
                    2.Diagnose and treat (within scope of PT practice)
                    3.Treat and refer out (alert medical team to concerns)

        .MSK vs Red Flag or Underlying Pathology
            Thorough history and physical exam
            VITALS
            Can be a puzzle, but should be aware of alerting S and Sxs
            Explain as MSK vs Disease processes when a patient presents with
                Bilateral Lower Extremity Swelling
                Back pain, fever, night sweats, fatigue, nausea
                Dyspnea, orthostatic hypotension, headache
                Shoulder pain, unintentional weight loss, night pain, night sweats

        .Red Flags of Systemic Illness 
            Gradual onset with no known cause
            Gradual, progressive, cyclical onset
            Constant/intense pain
            Symptoms unrelieved by rest or change in position
            Bilateral symptoms
            Constitutional symptoms

            What are some examples of a systemic illness may lead to these symptoms that may alert a referral out?
                (See 'Red Flags above::systemic illness')

        .Precautions/Contraindications to Therapy
            Resting heart rate 120 to 130 bpm Γ(Açò NO! es Blood Pressure)
                Anemic individuals may have increased normal resting pulse that should be monitored
                    Γ 20 o 30 bpm per dalt de lo normal
                Γ normal resting heart rate for adults (HR) 60 to 100 (60-100) beats per minute (bpm)
            Resting systolic pressure 180 to 200 mm Hg
                Γ Hypertensive crisis: Systolic over 180 and/or diastolic over 120. 
            Resting diastolic pressure 105 to 110 mm Hg
                Γ Entre Stage 2 = at least 90 mm Hg i Hypertensive crisis (no arriba): diastolic over 120.
            Marked dyspnea
            Loss of palpable pulse or irregular pulse with symptoms of dizziness, nausea, or SOB
            Palpitations
            -----------------------------------------------
            (Γ)('FIVE MAIN PRESSURE RANGES')
                From CP1 (ΓI put it here for reference) (Why so many versions ¿?)
                    • Normal: Less than 120/80 mm Hg;
                        ¦Els llimits de les carreteres espanyoles (fora de població), del mínim al màxim
                    • Elevated: Systolic between 120-129 and diastolic less than 80;
                        ¦Si pases 10 km a 129 (putja de 9 en 9, no de 10 en 10), multat!
                    • Stage 1: Systolic between 130-139 or diastolic between 80-89;
                    • Stage 2: Systolic at least 140 or diastolic at least 90 mm Hg;
                    • Hypertensive crisis: Systolic over 180 and/or diastolic over 120.

        .Pain Assessment
            Where is pain of cardiac origin felt?
                ✗(See Folder: 'REF Constants MIX::Referred Pain')
            Where is pain of diaphragmatic origin felt?
                -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                -Pain of cardiac and diaphragmatic origin is often felt in the shoulder because the heart and the diaphragm are supplied by the C5, C6 spinal segment
                ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                Common Patterns of Pain Referral
                    Diaphragmatic irritation → Shoulder, low back
                    Heart → Shoulder, neck, upper back, TMJ

        .Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Screening Specifics 
            Chest pain assessment
            Dyspnea of cardiac vs pulmonary origin

        .Let’s Practice
            Describe what screening components would give you the MOST information to treat, treat and refer, or refer out. 
                1.Neck pain, upper quadrant symptoms, or thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) vs Cardiovascular problem or a thoracic aneurysm
                    Vital sign and symptoms assessment
                2.Chest pain from MI vs. thoracic radicular symptoms
                    Vital sign and symptoms assessment
                3.Low back pain vs. abdominal aortic aneurysm
                    Palpation and auscultation
                4.Altered mental status due to respiratory alkalosis
                    Chart review of ABGs

        .Medical Chart Review
            .Medical Chart Review 1
                Why is the medical chart review critical for the PT. in both, the outpatient and inpatient setting?
                    Γ Red Flags to protect the patient and yourself for litigation

            .Medical Chart Review 2
                Acute illness 
                    • Medically stable
                    • Sedation
                    • Mechanical ventilation status
                    • Mental status changes
                Diagnosis and date of event
                    • What and when? Chronic, acute, acute on chronic
                PmHx & SocHx
                    • Where else can you find this information if it is not in the chart?
                        • Obtain as much information from:
                        • Medical chart review
                        • Family 
                        • Social worker
                        • Caregivers at previous place of residence 
                        • Confirm as much as you can with patient, and ensure not 
                        infringing upon HIPPA guidelines 
                Medications mmm.MiniGuideLookingForMeds
                    • What medications will you look for in the chart that may alert you that there could be treatment limitations?

            .Goals of Cardiopulmonary PT
                • Think of some ways we can reach the below goals in the acute CVP patient.
                • Improve or redistribute ventilation 
                • Increase the effectiveness of the cough mechanism and promote airway clearance
                • Prevent postoperative pulmonary complications
                • Improve the strength, endurance, and coordination of the muscles of ventilation
                • Maintain or improve chest and thoracic spine mobility
                • Correct inefficient or abnormal breathing patterns and decrease the work of breathing
                • Promote relaxation and relieve stress
                • Teach the person how to deal with episodes of dyspnea
                • Improve a patient’s overall functional capacity for daily living, occupational, and recreational activities
                • Aid in bronchial hygiene; prevent accumulation of pulmonary secretions

            .Discharge Planning
                • Crucial part of the physical therapist’s role in the acute care setting
                • Role shifting and expanding from providing interventions to acting as a consultant and offering recommendations
                • At evaluation, determination of patient’s rehabilitation potential bears on discharge disposition
                • Patient works with discharge planner in acute care
                • Involved in securing durable medical equipment

                Assess current level of function vs prior level of function
                ↓
                Report activity tolerance and rehabilitation potential to determine next level of care
                    Home with no needs, home PT or outpatient
                    Skilled nursing facility
                    Acute rehabilitation or Inpatient Rehabilitation
                ↓
                Detailed home set up and family support

                .Richmond Agitation & Sedation Scale ('Richmond Agitation & Sedation Scale.png') (!!E.Grade & Doc)
                    Score | Classification (RASS)  
                        - +4 | Combative  
                          - Overtly combative or violent; immediate danger to staff  
                        - +3 | Very agitated  
                          - Pulls on or removes tube(s) or catheter(s) or has aggressive behavior toward staff  
                        - +2 | Agitated  
                          - Frequent non-purposeful movement or patient-ventilator dyssynchrony  
                        - +1 | Restless  
                          - Anxious or apprehensive but movements not aggressive or vigorous  
                        - 0 | Alert and calm  
                          - Spontaneously pays attention to caregiver  
                        - -1 | Drowsy  
                          - Not fully alert, but has sustained (more than 10 seconds) awakening, with eye contact, to voice  
                        - -2 | Light sedation  
                          - Briefly (less than 10 seconds) awakens with eye contact to voice  
                        - -3 | Moderate sedation  
                          - Any movement (but no eye contact) to voice  
                        - -4 | Deep sedation  
                          - No response to voice, but any movement to physical stimulation  
                        - -5 | Unarousable  
                          - No response to voice or physical stimulation  
                    Source:  
                        https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0207174.t001

                        - No pushing or pulling (e.g., no pushing up from a chair or opening heavy doors).

                        - No lifting one arm above your head (you can lift both arms above your head at the same time).
                        - No reaching behind your back (e.g., no tucking in your shirt, putting your wallet in the back pocket, pulling your trousers up from the back, or reaching behind for hygiene purposes).

            ..Cardiac Terms
                .Mini Menú
                    Afterload Γ(about force ejection)
                    Preload Γ(about stretching)
                    End Diastolic Volume
                    End Systolic Volume 
                    Stroke Volume (SV) = EDV-ESV
                    Frank-Starling Law
                    Ejection Fraction
                    HFpEF
                    HFrEF

                .Afterload Γ(about force ejection)
                    The amount of pressure that the heart needs to exert to eject the blood during ventricular contraction
                        ¦Despues de la carrega, disparar (la força del tir)
                .Preload Γ(about stretching)
                    The initial stretching of the cardiac myocytes prior to systole
                .End Diastolic Volume
                    The filled volume of blood within the ventricle prior to contraction 
                .End Systolic Volume 
                    Residual volume of blood remaining in the ventricle after ejection
                .Stroke Volume (SV) = EDV-ESV
                .Frank-Starling Law
                    -Defines the relationship between length and tension in the heart, where the end-diastolic volume determines end-diastolic length of ventricular muscle fibers and is proportional to tension generated during systole, as well as to cardiac output, stroke volume, and stroke work.
                .Ejection Fraction
                    Total volume of blood ejected/End Diastolic Volume (SV/EDV) or amount of blood in the ventricle prior to ejection
                        ¦Lo esguitat / lo que hi hava = ¿?
                .HFpEF
                    Diastolic Heart Failure
                .HFrEF
                    Systolic Heart Failure

    ////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

        PT 2201 Cardiopulmonary 1 Prep/ 
        Supplementary Materials  


        Blood Flow through the Heart:  
        Review the following image to better understand how blood flows through the heart and into systemic 
        circulation via the aorta. You should be able to name all the different structures here, as well as direction 
        of flow within and through each of these structures.  


        Electrical Conduction through the Heart: 
        Review the following to better understand the electrical conduction through the heart. You will see it is 
        initiated via the SA node, then travels through the atrium and into the ventricles. This will match the ECG 
        reading you will learn in the initial modules of PT 2201. 


        Mechanics of Breathing 
        In the image below you should be able to understand and explain the mechanics of breathing, including 
        terms such as, muscles of inspiration, elastic recoil on expiration, atmospheric pressure vs intrapleural 
        pressure, and gas exchange.  
   

        Pulmonary System 
        The pulmonary system is the lungs, their airways, and their vascular network.  

         
        Structure 
        The upper respiratory tract is the nose, pharynx, and larynx.  Pictured is the lower respiratory trach. The 
        section in green in the conduction zone and moves air in and out of the lung, The blue zone e is the 
        respiration zone where actual gas exchange occurs.  

           
        Alveoli 
        This is where gas exchange occurs at the lung. The oxygen enters the lung tissue and carbon dioxide is 
        removed from the lung and back to the air to be exhaled.  

         
        Lung volumes  
        Below is the tracing of lung volume found in a normal pulmonary function test and definition of each 
        volume measured.  


        ERV:  Expiratory reserve volume; maximal volume that can be expired from a resting expiration.
        FRC: Functional residual capacity; volume of gas in lungs at resting expiratory level.
        IC: Inspiratory capacity; maximal volume that can be inspired from resting expiratory level.
        IRV: Inspiratory reserve volume; maximal volume that can be inspired from end-tidal inspiratory level.
        TLC: Total lung capacity; volume of gas in lungs at end of maximal inspiration
        VC: Vital capacity; maximal volume that can be expired after maximal inspiration
        MVV:  Maximal voluntary ventilation; the amount of air that can be moved in and out of the lungs during a given time period.
        RV: Residual volume; the volume of air contained in the lungs after a maximal expiration.
        TV: Tidal Volume; amount of air that moves in or out of the lungs with each respiratory cycle.


        Vital Signs 
        The below charts show normal vital signs for adults and what are abnormal vital signs.  
        Normal Vital Signs in Adults 
        Heart Rate 60-100 beats per 
        minute 

        < 60 bradycardia 
        > 100 tachycardia 

        Respiratory Rate 12-18 breaths per 
        minute 

        < 10 bradypnea 
        > 20 tachypnea  
        Blood Oxygen 95-100% < 90% hypoxia 

        
        Terms to know 
        Terms related to measures of cardiovascular function 
        BP: blood pressure; BP=COTPR or BP=(SVHR) TPR; reported as SBP/DBP 
        DBP: diastolic blood pressure - measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart rests between 
        beats or when the heart is filling with de-oxygenated blood to move through the heart.  
        SBP: systolic blood pressure - measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart beats or when 
        blood is released into systemic circulation from the left ventricle.  
        CO or Q: cardiac output; CO=Heart RateStroke Volume; measured in mL/min or the total amount of 
        blood the heart pumps in a minute 
        ECG: Electrocardiogram; recording of electrical signals of the heart. The ECG reading will contain waves 
        and intervals that match the electrical conduction through the heart as depicted above.  
        HR: heart rate; measured as the number of beats in a minute. 
        SV: stroke volume; measured in mL and is the total amount of blood pumped from the left ventricle 
        during each heartbeat. 
        TPR: total peripheral resistance or the level of resistance in the vascular/arterial system; measured as the 
        amount of force exerted on the arteries in circulating blood. 
     

        Terms related to measures of pulmonary function 
        FVC: forced vital capacity; maximal volume that can be expired after maximal inspiration  
        FEV1: forced expiratory volume in 1 sec; maximal volume that is expired in the first sec  
        FEV1/FVC: ratio of the FEV1 to FVC; low values can indicate COPD  
        PFT: Pulmonary Function Test; include measurement of lung volumes, FVC, maximum voluntary 
        ventilation 
        RR: respiratory rate; number of breaths per minute 
        TV: tidal volume; volume of air inspired by lungs in each breath  
        VE: Minute ventilation; Amount of air inspired by lungs in one minute  

         
        Terms related to measures of exercise prescription 
        FITTE Principle: Mnemonic for elements of exercise prescription; F(requency), I(ntensity), T(ime), T(ype), 
        E(njoyment)  
        HRmax: maximum heart rate during exercise, in beats per minute  
        HRreserve: difference between maximum heart rate and resting heart rate 


        MET: Metabolic Equivalent; standard unit for quantifying intensity of aerobic exercise relative to the 
        resting metabolic rate; equal to 3.5 mL of oxygen intake per kg body mass per minute   
        RPE: Rating of Perceived Exertion; scale for measuring an individual’s perceived work effort during 
        exercise  
        VO2: volume of oxygen inspired in Liters per minute  
        VO2max: maximum capacity of volume of oxygen inspired during aerobic exercise, in liters per minute  
        VO2reserve: difference between maximum oxygen intake and resting oxygen intake  
         

        Terms related to cardiovascular dysfunction 
        CAD: coronary artery disease OR blockage in the coronary arteries 
        CHF: Congestive Heart Failure 
        CKD: Chronic Kidney Disease  
        DVT: Deep vein thrombosis  
        HF: Heart Failure 
        HTN: hypertension or high blood pressure 
        Hypotension: low blood pressure 
        MI: myocardial infarction or heart attack 
        PAD: peripheral arterial disease 
        PVD: peripheral venous disease 
 

        Terms related to pulmonary dysfunction 
        COPD: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disorder 
        Obstructive: a group of pulmonary diseases characterized by presence of airflow obstruction that is 
        attributable to either chronic bronchitis or emphysema with difficulty with expiration (getting air out of 
        the lungs) 
        PE: Pulmonary Embolism; a blood clot that is in the lungs 
        Restrictive: a group of pulmonary diseases in which there is reduced lung compliance and difficulty with 
        lung expansion and inspiration (getting air into the lungs)  
         

        Terms related to oxygenation status and blood gases 


        Acidemia: condition that causes an increase in hydrogen ions in the blood, resulting in a decrease in 
        pH. It can also be defined as abnormally high blood acidity, which can be caused by an increase in acidic 
        substances or a decrease in alkaline substances. This means that the serum pH is lower than normal, 
        with arterial pH less than 7.35 
        Alkalemia: also known as alkalosis, occurs when the concentration of hydrogen ions in the blood 
        decreases, resulting in an increase in pH. This means that the serum pH is higher than normal, with 
        arterial pH greater than 7.45 
        Hypoxia: low level of oxygen in the tissues of the body 
        Hypoxemia: low levels of oxygen in the blood 
        Hyperoxemia: partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) in arterial blood gas analysis is higher than 100 mmHg 
        Hypercarbia/Hypercapnia:  high level of carbon dioxide in the blood, above the normal range of 35–45 
        mmHg 
        Hypocarbia/Hypocapnia:  low level of carbon dioxide in the blood, below the normal range of 35–45 
        mmHg 
        Hyperventilation: rapid or deep breathing in the presence of low oxygen, causes CO2 levels to drop 
        Hypoventilation:  shallow or slow breathing, CO2 levels rise 
        PaO2: Pressure of oxygen in the arterial blood 
        SaO2: Saturation of oxygen on hemoglobin measured from arterial blood 
        SpO2: Saturation of oxygen on hemoglobin measured with a pulse oximeter 
    

        Terms related to lab values 
        ABG: Arterial Blood Gases 
        CBC: Complete Blood Cell Count  
        HCT: Hematocrit; % of red blood cells in plasma 
        Hb: Hemoglobin; the primary molecule for transportation of oxygen in the blood 
        Plt: Platelets  
        RBC: Red Blood Cell 
        WBC: White Blood Cell

..Course Introduction
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    ..Course Description 
        This course is a continuation of PT 2201 Cardiopulmonary Part I with primary focus on physical therapy management of the cardiopulmonary patient throughout the continuum of care.  The primary goal is to develop competency in the assessment and treatment of cardiopulmonary dysfunction and pulmonary disease and complex medical conditions will be introduced with an emphasis on principles of exercise prescription and patient safety.  The material for this course is presented through online discussions, and synchronous online discussions of various course topics.  Out of class work includes study and reflection, completion of the assignments, readings and review of assigned materials, completion of necessary research, and group meetings for study or project completion.  Onsite laboratory sessions will develop requisite skills to apply or further enhance understanding of online materials.

    ..DPT Cardiopulmonary Course Sequence
        PT 2201
        Cardiopulmonary
        Physical Therapy 1

        PT 2202
        Cardiopulmonary
        Physical Therapy 2

        PT 2028
        Health and
        Wellness

        PT 2079
        Management of
        Medically Complex
        Patients

    ..Course Outcomes 
        On completion of this course, students will be able to:

        Apply the six components of the patient/client management model (Examination, Evaluation, Diagnosis, Prognosis, Intervention, Assessment of Outcome) to patients with cardiovascular and pulmonary dysfunction.
        Perform a screen for cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases and justify differential diagnosis based on cardiopulmonary data and assessment; identify the need for referral to other health care professionals as appropriate.
        Perform a cardiovascular and pulmonary an evaluation and identify appropriate treatment interventions related to findings.
        Perform cardiovascular and pulmonary interventions as related to identified impairments.
        Develop a treatment plan for patients with primary and secondary cardiopulmonary disorders reflecting the nature of the individual case based on client signs and symptoms.
        Identify the purpose, implications, and precautions of various life support monitoring equipment commonly used in the treatment of patients with cardiovascular and pulmonary disease.
        Apply appropriate evaluation and treatment in patient’s following cardiovascular and pulmonary surgical procedures and organ transplantation.
        Identify the role of the physical therapist and other members of the health care team in caring for patients with cardiovascular and pulmonary impairments.
        Discuss cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation models, and patients that are appropriate for participation.
        Identify the role of the physical therapist in cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation settings.
        Discuss and define hospital-based coding systems, patient code status and emergency response.

            Scope: This policy applies to all students, faculty members, and administrators engaged in the

            1. Purpose 
            The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for practical examinations 
            administered in the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) program. The use of practical 
            examinations as part of student assessment is critical in determining the student’s level 
            of competency with psychomotor skills, clinical reasoning, and decision making. This 
            policy reflects the academic standards outlined in the Commission on Accreditation in 
            Physical Therapy Education (CAPTE) Standards & Required Elements and the Physical 
            Therapy Code of Ethics, ensuring integrity, fairness, and professionalism in the 
            assessment process of rigorous physical therapy education. This policy also encourages 
            students to strive for academic excellence and mastery of the material, ensuring 
            adequate preparation to meet the demands of professional practice.  
            2. Policy 
            This practical examination policy is applicable to all skill-based practical examinations 
            throughout the DPT program. This document establishes the rules and procedures 
            regarding scheduling, student conduct, retake/remediation, and performance 
            expectations for practical examinations. This policy provides comprehensive guidelines 
            for the examination process; however, it does not encompass every possible scenario. 
            The program reserves the right to address situations that may arise on a case-by-case 
            basis, ensuring fairness, consistency, and adherence to the program’s academic 
            standards.

            1. Purpose 
            The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for written examinations administered in 
            the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) program. Periodic assessment of content knowledge 
            and clinical application via written examination is essential for teaching, learning, and 
            evaluation purposes. This policy reflects the academic standards outlined in the Commission 
            on Accreditation in Physical Therapy Education (CAPTE) Standards & Required Elements and 
            the Physical Therapy Code of Ethics, ensuring integrity, fairness, and professionalism in the 
            assessment process of rigorous physical therapy education. This policy also encourages 
            students to strive for academic excellence and mastery of the material, ensuring adequate 
            preparation to meet the demands of professional practice.  
            2. Policy 
            This written examination policy is applicable to all major written examinations throughout 
            the DPT program.  This document establishes the rules and procedures regarding 
            examination retake/remediation, scheduling, and student conduct for major written 
            examinations. 
            3. Definitions 
            Major examination: Any written examination or quiz administered to a student in a 
            proctored environment.  
            4. Major Written Examination Retake/Remediation 
            There is no opportunity for retake or formal remediation of written examinations. 
                   4.1      Course instructors may present different opportunities for students to demonstrate

            5. Examination Scheduling 
            5.1. The course instructor will provide the date and time of each written examination in

            Examinations scheduled during non-class time should remain between 10:00 AM –

            Exceptions to the examination schedule may be made for students with an approved

            The length of time provided to complete an examination should not exceed the 
            scheduled class time.  
            5.3.1. All students are expected to begin the major examinations at the designated 
            start time scheduled by the course instructor. 
            5.3.2. Students are expected to refer to the course syllabus and/or Canvas 
            materials to confirm the examination start time. 
            5.3.3. Failure to begin the examination within 15 minutes of the designated start

    ..Health and Wellness Statement
        Your Well-being Matters: Graduate school and college in general can be an exciting and challenging time for students. Taking time to care for yourself and seeking appropriate support can help you achieve your academic and professional goals. You are encouraged to maintain a healthy lifestyle by eating a balanced diet, exercising regularly, avoiding drugs and alcohol, getting enough sleep, and taking time to relax.  

        It can be helpful to remember that we all benefit from assistance and guidance sometimes, and many resources are available to support your well-being while you are at Pitt.  If you or anyone you know experiences overwhelming academic stress, persistent complicated feelings, and/or challenging life events, you are strongly encouraged to seek support. In addition to reaching out to friends and loved ones, consider connecting with a faculty member you trust for assistance connecting to helpful resources. The University Counseling Center is also here for you. 

        As a student in the hybrid option, you can call the Student Assistance Program at 877-567-8327 at any time to connect with a clinician.  

        If you or someone you know is feeling suicidal, please call the University Counseling Center at any time at 412-648-7930. 

        National Suicide Hotline 

        If the situation is life-threatening, please call 911 or 988.  “988” is a suicide hotline recently launched in the US.  It works the same as “911,” but dialing or texting “988” will connect a person directly to the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You do not have to be suicidal to reach out to 988.  The trained counselors can help you through whatever mental health challenges you are experiencing.

        .Patient Client Management Model As Related to Cardiopulmonary Physical Therapy  
            Here you will start to familiarize yourself with the patient client management model as it relates to cardiopulmonary physical therapy. You will notice some content that you have already learned in the previous course, and now see how that information can be utilized to being to perform physical therapy examination and screening procedures, development of a plan of care and performance of chosen interventions for your cardiopulmonary patient.

            ..Introduction to Cardiopulmonary PT II
                ('01 files-654bb66d643cb.m4a')
                    Screening
                    Examination
                    Interventions
                ('02 files-61697827ec44a.m4a')
                    Patient Client Management [CP2_PatientClientManagementModel]
                        1º.DIAGNOSIS
                            -Both the process and the end result of evaluating examination data, which the pyhiscal therapist organizes into defined clusters, syndromes, or catergories to help determine the prognosis (including the plan of care) and the most appropriate intervention strategies. 
                        2º.PROGNOSIS (Including Plan of Care)
                            -Determination of the level of optimal improvement that may be attained through intervention and the amount of time required to reach that level. The plan of care specifies the interventions to be used and their timing and frequency.
                        3º.INTERVENTION
                            -Purposeful and skilled interaction of the physical therapist with the patient/client and, if appropriate, with other individuals involved in care of the patient/client, using various physical therapy procedures and techniques to produce changes in the condition that are consistent with the diagnosis and prognosis.  The physical therapist conducts a re-examination to determine changes in patient/client status and to modify or redirect intervention.  The decision to re-examine may be based on new clinical findings or on lack of patient/client progress. The process of re-examination also may identify the need for consultation with or referral to another provider.
                        4º.OUTCOMES
                            -Results of patient/client management, which include the impact of physical therapy interventions in the following domains: pathology/pathophysiology (disease, disorder, or condition); impairments, functional limitations, and disabilities; risk reduction/prevention; health, wellness, and fitness; societal resources; and patient/client satisfaction. 
                        5º.EXAMINATION
                            -The process of obtaining a history, performing a system review, andand selecting and adminstering tests and measures to gather data about the patient/client. The initial examination is a comprehensive screening and specific testing process that leads to a diaganostic classification.  The examination process also may identify possible problems that require consultation with or referral to another provider. 
                        6º.EVALUATION
                            -A dynamic process in which the physical therapist makes clinical judgments based on data gathered during the examination.  This process also may identify possible problems that require consultation with or referral to another provider.

..1.0. Module Introduction
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
                                      
    .Module Introduction
        Module 1 will cover physical therapy screening and examination of the cardiovascular and pulmonary system. This module will cover the defining characteristics of cardiovascular and pulmonary screening and examination. You will begin to learn the ins and outs of screening and exam with a focus on cardiovascular and pulmonary specific findings. This module will lead into next module that will give more specific screening and exam techniques with findings.  This module will expose you to procedures that will act as a foundation for all the other modules, in addition to lab-based materials that will be practiced in the immersions.  

    .Learning Objectives
        Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to:
            Apply the use of the Hypothesis-Oriented Algorithm for Clinicians for evaluation, and re-examination in patients with cardiopulmonary dysfunction. 
            Describe and administer the six components of the patient/client management model (Examination, Evaluation, Diagnosis, Prognosis, Intervention, Assessment of Outcome) to patients with cardiopulmonary dysfunction.  
            Give rationale for the selection of evaluative tools in the management of the cardiopulmonary patient. 
            Assess and develop a subsequent plan for inpatient (acute care, rehab, skilled nursing), outpatient, home, and community-based on screening and evaluation outcomes. 
            Describe and choose appropriate cardiovascular and pulmonary screening and examination procedures to justify differential diagnosis based on cardiopulmonary data and assessment; identify the need for referral to other health care professionals as appropriate.

            are the primary determinants to assess patient readiness for mobility and response to activity, 
            these values need to be corroborated with other patient findings. Although recommendations are  
            provided for various conditions, individual patient vital signs and co-morbidities should guide 
            clinical decision making. Any questions of medical stability should be discussed with the 
            healthcare team. It is recommended to read the introduction prior to going to any other section of 
            this document for important contextual information.

                 .PHARMACOLOGY

            Introduction
            The purpose of obtaining vital signs (VS) is to detect and monitor physiologic states and assess 
            activity responses to aid in exercise prescription. VS determine patient risk for adverse events, such 
            as cardiovascular episodes and syncope. Compared to outpatient settings, hospitalized patients 
            present more often with abnormal or labile VS and are at a higher risk of immediate events 
            requiring acute care physical therapists to assess and monitor VS with greater frequency. Assessing 
            pulse rate (PR), respiratory rate (RR), temperature, and blood pressure (BP) are essential 
            components of a systems review in a physical therapy (PT) examination.1 Additionally, tissue 
            oxygenation, measured by pulse oximetry, is necessary to assess hypoxemia. Physical therapists 
            should correlate current VS values with other data points such as symptoms, baseline VS, 
            medication schedule, lab values, and comorbidities when making decisions about patient care.
            Normal Values:
            • Values presented are for adults
            • Baseline health and fitness influence VS, particularly PR and BP
            Frequency of VS Monitoring:
            • VS at rest help determine readiness for PT intervention, in conjunction with other findings
            • VS during PT interventions and recovery assess hemodynamic and oxygenation responses and 
            stability
            • PT providers (physical therapists and physical therapist assistants) should follow the institution 
            policy and procedures regarding activity
            • PT providers should monitor VS for adverse reactions, especially during medication 
                  adjustments, transfusions, or other procedures
            • Critical Care: (refer to Vital Sign Interpretation in the Intensive Care Unit for more details)
            • Intensive care units (ICU) involve more specialized monitoring and invasive treatments that 
            cannot be handled safely in the general wards/floors
            • VS should be assessed continually during PT interventions in the ICU
            Accuracy of Measurement:
            • Accuracy of VS measurement and documentation is of extreme importance, but education on 
            techniques is beyond this guideline’s scope
            • Poor technique can cause inaccurate BP measurement2
            • The Academy of Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Physical Therapy offer several videos 
            • (#VitalsAreVital) to guide PT providers and students to perform VS accurately
            • VS are dynamic measurements that can be influenced by many factors
            • Caffeine, smoking, stress, agitation/delirium, and other factors can contribute to an elevated 
            PR, RR, and BP
            • Medications and administration timing can influence VS
            • BP is exceptionally dynamic; interpretation in the context of trends is best
            • Documentation should include the patient position, extremity, or activity during VS 
            measurement (i.e. sitting, supine, rest, mobility)

           


            6

            Vital Sign Interpretation for General Adult Population
            Blood Pressure (BP)
            •      Blood pressure (BP) = Cardiac Output (CO) x Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR)
            • CO = Stroke Volume (SV) x Heart Rate (HR) 

            Other organizations (International Society of Hypertension, American College of Physicians, American 
            Academy of Family Physicians, 8th Joint National Committee) not listed in this table have guidelines  
            regarding hypertension categories. Refer to these references for additional evidence.150-152
            •      Hypotension: < 80 mmHg SBP; < 60 mmHg DBP4,5 
            •      Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP): Average pressure of the blood in the arteries during a cardiac cycle;            
            can serve as an indicator of perfusion to vital organs
            • MAP = [SBP + (2 x DBP)]/36 
            •      Normal MAP:  70 - 110 mmHg7-9 
            • MAP < 60 mmHg can result in ↓ perfusion of vital organs 
            • Consult with the medical team if MAP < 65 mmHg to determine appropriateness of activity
            • Low values can be a sign of stroke, internal bleeding, sepsis, etc. 
            • High values can be a sign of kidney failure, heart failure, etc.
            •       Pulse Pressure (PP) = SBP - DBP 
            • Normal PP range: 40 - 60 mmHg10
            • PP outside of the normal range is a significant factor in the development of heart disease
            • Low or “narrowed” (< 25% SBP) can be a sign of heart failure (HF) (low SV), aortic valve 
            stenosis, blood loss, etc.10
            • Chronic elevation (> 59 mmHg) can be a sign of arterial resistance, HF, ↑ SBP, aging, etc.7,1
            BP - Clinical Considerations
            • Assess for BP trends as normal fluctuations occur (e.g. nocturnal or postprandial dipping)12 
            • SBP ↑ with hypervolemia and ↓ with hypovolemia
            •      Normal Exercise Response
            • SBP ↑ in a linear fashion, 10 mmHg per Metabolic Equivalent (MET) until physiologic maximum 
            (dampened response in patients on beta blockers)13 (Refer to Pharmacology Section for more  
            details) 
            • Monitor BP post PT intervention until returns to baseline
            •     Hypertension (HTN)
            • HTN is generally asymptomatic, so symptoms should not drive the need for VS assessment
            • Monitor for the following symptoms: headaches; visual impairments; confusion; pounding in 
            chest, neck, or ears
            • In most cases, there is no known cause
            • Potential causes: hypercalcemia; thyroid diseases; full bladder; sympathetic stimulation; stress/
            anxiety; white coat HTN; hypervolemia11,14
            • Cardiovascular risk ↓ with ↓ BP, but dosage amounts of antihypertensive medications may be 
            associated with ↑ adverse effects, including ↑ fall risk15

            (mmHg)
            Normal < 120 and < 80
            High-normal/Elevated/
