    .The Importance of Vital Signs 
        • If you only have time for one thing 
            • Take the vital signs…they are called vital for a reason! 
        Red Flag-Vital Signs 
            • Correlate unusual vital signs with other signs and symptoms, such as: 
                • Pallor 
                • Perspiration 
                • Fatigue 
                • Palpitations
        -----------------------------------------------
        All vital signs should be DOCUMENTED 
            • Pulse 
            • Respirations 
            • Pulse oximetry (O2 saturation) 
            • Skin temperature 
            • Core body temperature (oral or ear) 
            • Blood pressure 
            • Pain

    .Precautions/Contraindications to Therapy (!!E).Lv1 (!!P)
        • Resting heart rate 120 to 130 bpm
            Γ HR normal: 60-100; 20 més de lo normal
            • Anemic individuals may have increased normal resting pulse that should be monitored 
        • Resting systolic pressure Γ(SBP) 180 to 200 mm Hg
            Γ Blood Pressure Hypertensive crisis: Systolic over 180 and/or diastolic over 120
            ¦A 180 km del motor a tope (sustolic del motor), denúncia
        • Resting diastolic pressure Γ(DBP) 105 to 110 mm Hg
            Γ Blood Pressure Stage 2: Systolic at least 140 or diastolic at least 90 mm Hg
            ¦ 10 per damunt de Stage 2
        • Marked dyspnea 
        • Loss of palpable pulse or irregular pulse with symptoms of dizziness, nausea, or SOB
            ¦Es maretja, gomita, i s'anfuega; es mor i ja no the puls (el simtomes del borratxo)
        -----------------------------------------------
        (Γ)('FIVE MAIN PRESSURE RANGES')
            From CP1 (ΓI put it here for reference) (Why so many versions ¿?)
                • Normal: Less than 120/80 mm Hg;
                • Elevated: Systolic between 120-129 and diastolic less than 80;
                • Stage 1: Systolic between 130-139 or diastolic between 80-89;
                • Stage 2: Systolic at least 140 or diastolic at least 90 mm Hg;
                • Hypertensive crisis: Systolic over 180 and/or diastolic over 120.
            From CP2 in this slide
                • Normal: 120/80 mmHg or less
                • Pre-hyper-tension: 120-139 and/or 80-90 mmHg;
                • Hypertension Stage 1 (High Blood Pressure): 140-159 and/or 90-99 80-89 mmHg;
                • Hypertension Stage 2 (High Blood Pressure): 160 and/or 100 mmHg;
                • Hypertensive Crisis (Emergency State): 180 and/or 110 mmHg.

    .Heart Palpitations (!!E).Lv1 (!!P)
        • Irregular heartbeats lasting for hours; > 6 episodes per minute 
        • Especially with SOB, chest pain, dizziness, lightheadedness 
        • + Family history of sudden cardiac death 
        • Personal history of heart disease 
        • Clients who are neurologically unstable as a result of a recent CVA, head trauma, spinal cord injury, or other central nervous system insult often exhibit new arrhythmias during the period of instability

    .Examples of “Medical Referrals” Associated with Vitals and Palpations (!!E).Lv1 (!!P)
        • Persistent low-grade (or higher) fever, especially associated with constitutional symptoms, most commonly sweats but also unintended weight loss, malaise, nausea, vomiting. 
        • Any unexplained fever without other systemic symptoms, especially in the person taking corticosteroids or otherwise immunosuppressed. 
        • Weak and rapid pulse accompanied by fall in BP (pneumothorax)

    .Pain Assessment
        .Direct Pressure and Shared Pathways ('Direct Pressure and Shared Pathways')
            -Pain of cardiac and diaphragmatic origin is often felt in the SHOULDER because the heart and the diaphragm are supplied by the C5 C6 spinal segment Γ('heart & diaphragm C5 C6.jpg') (!!E)
        .Common Patterns of Pain Referral Γ('Y:\XTemp\Assignatures\700 BIBLIOTECA VISUAL\03 DPT\REF Constants MIX\Referred Pain\')
            Site of Lesion → Referral Site 
                Diaphragmatic irritation → Shoulder, low back 
                Heart → Shoulder, neck, upper back, TMJ

        .Pain Assessment - Examples (!!E).Lv1
            • Neck pain, upper quadrant symptoms, or thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) vs CV problem or a thoracic aneurysm 
                • Vital sign and symptoms assessment 
            • Chest pain from MI vs. thoracic radicular symptoms 
                • Vital sign and symptoms assessment 
            • Low back pain vs. abdominal aortic aneurysm 
                • Palpation and auscultation 
            • Altered mental status due to respiratory alkalosis 
                • Chart review of ABGs

    -This lecture will cover the general screening process in physical therapy for patients with cardiovascular and pulmonary dysfunction with a focus on understanding what the screening process means in terms of red flags and clinical decision making to refer a patient out other healthcare professionals when concerns are present.

    .The Acute Care Patient
        • Acute illness 
            • Need more finite information to proceed with care 
            • Medical stability 
            • Determine pertinent information 
        • May be unable to perform thorough history or medical status assessment due to: 
            • Sedation 
            • Mechanical ventilation 
            • Mental status changes
            • Γ Pain
        ----------------------------------------
        • Obtain as much information from: 
            • Medical chart review 
            • Family 
            • Social worker 
            • Caregivers at previous place of residence 
            • Confirm as much as you can with patient, and ensure not infringing upon HIPPA guidelines

    .Diagnosis and Date of Event 
        • Need to know PRIMARY and SECONDARY DIAGNOSES 
        • Date of event determines acuteness

    .Patient History
        Relevant social history
            Self-abusive social habits (excessive drinking of alcohol, smoking, use of illicit drugs) can affect cardiopulmonary system
        Other medical problems and past medical history
            Other medical problems may have a bearing on evaluation and treatment 
                Ex: patient with extensive cardiac history, but in hospital for abdominal surgery
        Risk factors for heart disease (!!E).Lv3
            HTN
            smoking
            elevated cholesterol
            family history
            stress
            sedentary lifestyle
            older age
            obesity
            diabetes 

    .Medications 
        • Provides insight about patient’s present or recent past medical history 
        • Important to be aware of side effects of medications 
        • Refer to Joint Vital Sign Booklet pages 24-31 ¿?

    .Risk of DVT (!!E.Grade & Doc) (!!E).Lv2
        Clinical Characteristic → Score
            -Active cancer (patient either receiving treatment for cancer within the previous 6 months or currently receiving palliative treatment) → 1 
            -Paralysis, paresis, or recent cast immobilization of the lower extremities → 1 
            -Recently bedridden for ≥ 3 days, or major surgery within the previous 12 weeks requiring general or regional anesthesia → 1 
            -Localized tenderness along the distribution of the deep venous system → 1 
            -Entire leg swelling → 1 
            -Calf swelling at least 3 cm larger than that on the asymptomatic side (measured 10 cm below tibial tuberosity) → 1 
            -Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg → 1 
            -Collateral superficial veins (non-varicose) → 1 
            -Previously documented deep vein thrombosis → 1 
            -Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis → -2
            ---------------------------------------------------------------------
            Clinical probability simplified score 
                DVT "likely" → 2 points or more 
                DVT "unlikely" → Less than 2 points 
                ---------------------------------------------------------------------
                • Wells criteria for the prediction of deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
                • Wells scoring system for DVT:
                    -2 to 0: low probability
                    1 to 2 points: Moderate probability
                    3 to 8 points: high probability 

    .Oxygen Therapy and Other Respiratory Treatment 
        • Use of supplemental O2 should be noted along with method of delivery 
        • Know amount of O2 being delivered 
        • Correlate with ABGs 
        • Note other respiratory treatments (aerosols, bronchodilator treatments, incentive spirometers)

    .Surgical Procedures 
        • Understanding of specific surgical approaches and procedures is important 
        • Extent of surgery predicts activity performance impairments 
        • Post-operative restrictions and risks

        Hospital course 
        Nutritional intake 
        Home Environment and Family Situation

    .Never Hesitate
        • To speak to the physician/medical team for clarification 
            • Post-operative restrictions and protocols 
            • Lab values 
            • Procedures and out of bed status 
        • Collaborate with nursing 
        • Always use your clinical judgement, as you should know specific risks vs. benefits of your intervention

    .Key Terms and Concepts
        1. Purpose of Medical Chart Review 
            • Extract pertinent information for a patient database. 
            • Develop an optimal treatment plan based on the obtained information. 
        2. Importance of Real-Time Information 
            • Acute care settings provide real-time patient data. 
            • Enables thorough screening before physical therapy engagement. 
        3. Obtaining Information Beyond the Chart 
            • Patient history and direct interviews supplement medical records. 
            • Focus on information crucial for treatment appropriateness. 
        4. Critical Information from Medical Chart 
            • Primary and secondary diagnoses determination. 
            • Date of events, especially for acute situations. 
            • Social habits impact on cardio-pulmonary systems. 
            • Risk factors for cardiovascular disease. 
            • Medication details for treatment implications. 
        5. Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Symptoms 
            • Evaluation based on chart information. 
            • Monitoring vitals, lab values, and recent events. 
            • Assessment of cardiovascular and pulmonary-related surgeries, procedures, and treatments. 
        6. Laboratory Data 
            • Importance in cardio-pulmonary dysfunction assessment. 
            • Significance of deviations from normal values. 
        7. Venous Thromboembolism Risk 
            • Assessing likelihood during initial patient assessment. 
            • Utilizing assessment tools and chart information. 
        8. Oxygen Use and Respiratory Treatments 
            • Noting supplemental oxygen details. 
            • Understanding respiratory treatments impact on exercise. 
        9. Surgical Approaches and Procedures 
            • Knowledge of anatomy and surgical history. 
            • Impact on physical therapy diagnosis and treatment planning. 
        10. Electrocardiogram (ECG) and Imaging 
            • ECG for heart muscle and rhythm assessment. 
            • Reviewing radiological reports for cardiovascular and pulmonary imaging. 
        11. Vital Signs and Clinical Course 
            • Monitoring vital signs for trends and baselines. 
            • Physician and caregiver notes for clinical insights. 
        12. Additional Chart Review Areas 
            • Nutritional intake and its impact on treatment. 
            • Home situation insights for post-acute planning. 
            • Discussion with medical team for unclear or missing information. 

            Questions and Answers (!!Q)
                Q1: Why is real-time information crucial in acute care settings? 
                    • A1: Real-time data allows for thorough patient screening before physical therapy engagement, ensuring safety and appropriateness of treatment.
                Q2: How does social history impact the evaluation of a patient's cardio-pulmonary system?
                    • A2: Social habits like excessive drinking or smoking can affect the cardio-pulmonary system, influencing rehabilitation and treatment planning. 
                Q3: What role does medication play in the patient screening process?
                    • A3: Understanding current medications provides insights into potential treatment limitations, signs, and symptoms related to the medication.
                Q4: Why is it essential to review both primary and secondary diagnoses?
                    • A4: Primary diagnoses may lead to admission, but secondary diagnoses, like pneumonia postoperatively, may guide physical therapy referral and treatment. 
                Q5: How does knowledge of surgical approaches impact physical therapy planning?
                    • A5: Understanding surgical details helps define physical therapy diagnosis, identify limitations, and plan appropriate therapeutic procedures. 
                Q6: What information can be inferred from laboratory data in cardio-pulmonary dysfunction?
                    • A6: Laboratory data provides insights into the seriousness of dysfunction based on deviations from normal values. 
                Q7: Why is it important to monitor vital signs for trends?
                    • A7: Trends in vital signs help track improvement or decline, establishing baselines for assessing clinical progress. 
                Q8: How does discussing unclear chart information contribute to patient safety?
                    • A8: Ensures a comprehensive understanding of the patient's status, allowing for informed decisions on treatment cancellation, postponement, or cautious proceeding.
                ----------------------------------------------------------
                Clinical Judgment and Conclusion
                    -Always apply clinical judgment when synthesizing patient information. As a physical therapist, your expertise is crucial for ensuring patient safety and making informed decisions regarding the appropriateness of physical therapy sessions. Communicate effectively with the medical team to address any uncertainties and provide optimal care for the patient. 

        Medical Chart Review 
            • Definition: Extracting pertinent information from the patient's medical record to develop a comprehensive database. 
            • Example: Reviewing lab values, imaging reports, and physician notes to understand the patient's current health status. 
        Acute Care Settings 
            • Definition: Healthcare settings where patients with acute illnesses receive real-time information for immediate decision-making. 
            • Example: Hospitals with electronic medical records (EMR) providing up-to-date patient information. 
        HIPAA Standards 
            • Definition: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act standards ensuring patient data confidentiality. 
            • Example: Safeguarding patient information during chart reviews and interviews. 
        Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Findings 
            • Definition: Identifying cardiac and respiratory-related information in the medical chart. 
            • Example: Recognizing symptoms, procedures, and diagnostic tests related to cardiovascular and pulmonary health. 
        Laboratory Data 
            • Definition: Information obtained from various diagnostic tests. 
            • Example: Reviewing cardiac enzymes, blood lipids, and arterial blood gases for cardio-pulmonary dysfunction assessment. 
        Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) 
            • Definition: Increased risk for blood clot formation in veins. 
            • Example: Assessing likelihood of DVT (Deep Vein Thrombosis) during initial patient assessment. 
        ECG (Electrocardiogram) 
            • Definition: Recording of heart's electrical activity. 
            • Example: Analyzing ECG data for myocardial injury, hypertrophy, and rhythm disturbances. 
        Radiological Reports 
            • Definition: Documentation of imaging studies. 
            • Example: Reviewing chest radiographs, CT scans, and MRI reports for cardiovascular and pulmonary imaging. 

            Questions and Answers (!!Q)
                Q1: Why is a medical chart review essential in acute care settings? 
                    A1: A medical chart review is crucial in acute care settings to gather real-time information, enabling a thorough screening of patients before engaging in physical therapy. It ensures the therapist is aware of the patient's current medical status, allowing for informed treatment decisions. 
                Q2: What role does HIPAA play in the medical chart review process? 
                    A2: HIPAA standards are essential to maintaining patient confidentiality during the chart review. Therapists must adhere to these standards to safeguard sensitive patient information obtained during the screening process. 
                Q3: How can laboratory data aid in assessing cardio-pulmonary dysfunction? 
                    A3: Laboratory data, including cardiac enzymes, blood lipids, and arterial blood gases, provides valuable insights into the severity of cardio-pulmonary dysfunction. Deviations from normal values help determine the seriousness of the dysfunction.
                Q4: Why is it important to know a patient's home situation during screening?
                    A4: Understanding the patient's home environment and family situation provides insights into their premorbid function. This information helps set realistic treatment goals, assess the need for post-acute rehabilitation, and ensures a safe transition to home care.

        Purpose of Medical Chart Review in Acute Care Settings 
            • Obtain real-time patient information. 
            • Enable thorough screening before physical therapy. 
        Key Components of Chart Review 
            • Primary and additional diagnoses. 
            • Medication history and cardiovascular risk factors. 
            • Cardiovascular and pulmonary findings, including imaging and lab values. 
        Importance of HIPAA Compliance 
            • Safeguarding patient confidentiality during information extraction. 
        Clinical Considerations in Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Screening 
            • Recognition of symptoms and procedures. 
            • Utilization of ECG, radiological reports, and laboratory data. 
            • Assessment for venous thromboembolism (VTE). 
        Beyond the Chart: Interviewing and Clinical Judgment 
            • Obtaining information during patient interviews. 
            • Using clinical judgment to synthesize patient information. 
            • Discussing concerns with the medical team for collaborative decision-making.

        11:27

        ↑---------------------------------------------------------------------

    -This lecture will cover aspects of screening the cardiovascular and pulmonary systems and will give you insight into signs and symptoms that will lead you into either immediate medical referral or further investigation of underlying cardiovascular and pulmonary pathology. The information you obtain in the cardiovascular and pulmonary screen will allow you to identify areas that may require further examination and will lead into the next content areas of cardiovascular and pulmonary examination procedures.

    .Cardiovascular Screening
        .Screening for Cardiovascular Causes of Chest, Breast, Rib Pain
            Risk factors 
                Gender 
                Age 
                Ethnicity 
            Clinical presentation 
                Pain precipitated by exercise 
                Cardiac pain patterns 
                Absence of 3 P’s (!!E).Lv1
                    Plural Pain
                        Exacerbated by respiratory movements
                    Palpation Pain
                        Pain on palpation is typically associated with musculoskeletal disorders
                    Position Pain
                        -Pain that occurs with changes in position of the neck, trunk, or shoulder and indicates musculoskeletal origin instead of a cardio pulmonary issue
                    ¦Si la Pleura, palpita, cambia de posició
        
        .Differential Diagnosis of Chest Pain (!!E).Lv1
            Table 16-2 Differentiation of non-anginal discomforts from angina 
                -1.Stable angina → Non-anginal discomfort (chest wall pain) 
                -2.Relieved by nitroglycerin (30 sec to 1 min) → Nitroglycerin generally has no effect 
                -3.Comes on at the same heart rate and blood pressure and is relieved by rest (lasts only a few minutes) → Occurs any time; lasts for hours 
                -4.Not palpable → Muscle soreness, joint soreness, evoked by palpation or deep breaths 
                -5.Associated with feelings of doom, cold sweats, shortness of breath → Minimal additional symptoms 
                -6.Often seen with ST-segment → No ST-segment depression

        .Angina or Myocardial Infarction ('Angina or Myocardial Infarction')
            -Angina and/or myocardial infarction (MI) can appear as arm and shoulder pain that can be misdiagnosed as arthritis or other musculoskeletal pathologic conditions.

        .Dyspnea Γ(shortness of breath) (!!E).Lv1
            • Can be cardiac or pulmonary in origin 
            • Can be related to activity, exertion or body position 
            • Severity of dyspnea is related to extent of disease 
            • Dyspnea on exertion (DOE) 
                • Often the result of left ventricle dysfunction, failure to clear all blood from lungs resulting in pulmonary congestion and SOB
            ---------------------------------------
            • Extreme dyspnea includes: 
                • Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND) and orthopnea 
                • PND and sudden, unexplained episodes of SOB often accompany heart failure 
            • Dyspnea relieved by specific breathing (pursed-lip breathing) or by specific body position (leaning forward on arms) generally related to pulmonary disease rather than cardiac
            --------------------------------------------
            .Dyspnea - Red Flags (!!P) 
                • Patients with known cardiac involvement who develop progressively worse dyspnea need referral to physician 
                • Patients who cannot climb a single flight of stairs without feeling moderately or severely winded should have referral to physician 
                • Patients who are awakened at night or experience shortness of breath when lying down, need referral to physician 

        .Syncope Γ(fainting)
            • Sudden loss of consciousness accompanied by an inability to maintain postural tone 
            • Can be related to reduced oxygen delivery to brain 
            • Cardiac and non-cardiac causes 
            • Related to side effects of medications (eg. vasodilators)
            ----------------------------------------------------------
            Red Flags (!!P)
                • Medical referral recommended for unexplained syncope, especially in presence of heart or circulatory problems or if risk factors for heart attack or stroke are present 

        .Fatigue
            • Can be related to cardiac dysfunction 
            • Fatigue of cardiac nature often accompanied by associated symptoms 
            • Fatigue beyond expectations during or after exercise is red flag, especially with no other explanation (!!P)
        
        .Cough 
            • Usually associated with pulmonary disease, but can be pulmonary complication of cardiac disease 
            • Cough, especially at night, can be associated with heart failure and/or a side effect of calcium channel blockers 
            • Left ventricular dysfunction, mitral valve dysfunction resulting in pulmonary edema or left ventricular heart failure may also result in cough

        .Cyanosis ('Cyanosis') (!!E).Lv3
            • Suggests inadequate blood oxygen levels 
            • Most often associated with cardiac and pulmonary problems 
            --------------------------------------------
            • Central cyanosis 
                • oxygen levels reduced in arterial blood 
                -----------------------------------------
                Caused by: 
                    Lung disease 
                    Congestive heart disease 
                    Abnormal hemoglobin
            • Peripheral cyanosis 
                • normal blood oxygenation but decreased or slow blood flow
                -----------------------------------------
                Caused by: 
                    Heart failure 
                    Venous obstruction 
                    Cold environment 

        .Edema
            • An accumulation of fluid 
            • Cardiac vs. Non-cardiac causes of edema may indicate a red flag and medical referral (!!P)

        .Lower Extremity Pain
            • Pain in limb, pelvis, or buttock may be result of ischemia related to PVD 
            • Deep vein thrombosis after surgery may develop and will present with an enlarged, warm, and painful leg 

        .Vascular Causes of Lower Quadrant Pain – Red Flag (!!P)
            • Vascular pain is often throbbing in nature and exacerbated by activity. With atherosclerosis, a lag time of 5 to 10 minutes occurs between when the body asks for increased oxygenated blood and when symptoms occur because of arterial occlusion. 
            • The client is older, often with a personal or family history of heart disease. 
            • Other risk factors include hyperlipidemia, tobacco use, and diabetes. 

    .Pulmonary screening
        .Screening for Pleuropulmonary Causes of Chest, Breast or Rib Pain
            Past medical history
                Cancer
                    DDX Ex: Neck Pain vs. Pancoast Tumor
                Recent pulmonary infection
                Recent accident or hospitalization
            Clinical presentation (!!P)
                • Red Flags: Pain exacerbated by deep breathing and activity or a productive cough with bloody or rust-colored sputum
                • Pain is localized or worsens with coughing, deep breathing, respiratory movements.
                • Pain is relieved by restricting expansion of the chest wall

        .Underlying Pleuropulmonary Condition
            Auto-splinting or lying on the involved side to reduce pain, and pain that worsens with recumbency (supine position)
            MSK Pain vs. Pleuropulmonary Pain
                Assess for the 3 p’s Γ(Absence of: pleuritic, positional, and palpable)
                MSK → Symptoms do not increase with pulmonary movements
                Pleuropulmonary → Symptoms increase with pulmonary movements and cannot be reproduced with palpation
            ---------------------------------
            Underlying Pleuropulmonary Condition (!!E).Lv2
                1. Increased symptoms occur with recumbency 
                2. Increased chest pain with exercise can also be a sign of asthma 
                3. Presence of associated signs and symptoms such as persistent cough, dyspnea (rest or exertional), or constitutional symptoms 
                4. Chest pain with sudden drop in blood pressure or symptoms such as dizziness, dyspnea, vomiting, or unexplained sweating while standing or ambulating for the first time after surgery, an invasive medical procedure, assault, or accident involving the chest or thorax
            
        .Immediate Medical Attention (!!P)
            • Abrupt onset of dyspnea with weak and rapid pulse and fall in BP (pneumothorax or Pulmonary embolism) 
            • Symptoms of inadequate ventilation or carbon dioxide retention 
            • Red flag symptoms in a patient with a history of CA (especially lung CA)

        .Guidelines for Physician Referral (!!E).Lv1
            • Pain referred from the pulmonary system: 
                • aggravated by respiratory movements 
                • aggravated by supine position (may be pleuritic in origin b/c abdominal contents push up against the diaphragm) 
            • Shoulder or chest pain that subsides with auto-splinting (lying on painful side) 
            • Presence of persistent cough, dyspnea at rest, fever, pallor, new productive cough

    .Final Questions
        • After the screening, find a “final question” that works for you. Here are a few examples: 
            • Are there any other symptoms anywhere else in your body that we haven’t talked about yet? 
            • Is there anything else you would like to tell me? 
            • Is there anything else you think I should know? 
            • Is there anything else you think is important about your condition that we haven’t discussed yet?

    .Remember 
        • Screening for referral is based on 
            1. PMH - What they told you 
            2. Clinical presentation - What you saw 
            3. Associated signs and symptoms - What you asked about

    .Cardiovascular & Pulmonary Screening - Key Terms and Concepts
        Cardiovascular Screening 
            • Definition: The process of assessing a patient's risk factors and clinical presentation for cardiovascular disease. 
            • Example: Evaluating age, gender, and clinical symptoms related to chest pain. 
        Modifiable Factors 
            • Definition: Factors that can be changed or controlled to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. 
            • Example: Lifestyle choices such as obesity, diabetes, and smoking. 
        Muscle Disorders 
            • Definition: Conditions affecting the musculoskeletal system, often associated with pain related to changes in neck, trunk, or shoulder position. 
            • Example: Pain exacerbated by specific movements indicating muscle origin. 
        Angina 
            • Definition: Chest pain or discomfort caused by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle. 
            • Example: Chest pain with exertion, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin, associated with other symptoms like cold sweats. 
        Dyspnea 
            • Definition: Shortness of breath, a symptom that can arise from cardiac or pulmonary origin. 
            • Example: Difficulty breathing during exertion or specific body positions, common in heart failure patients. 
        Cyanosis 
            • Definition: Bluish discoloration of the skin, indicating inadequate blood oxygen. 
            • Example: Skin turning blue due to poor blood oxygenation in cardiac or pulmonary problems. 
        Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) 
            • Definition: Blood clot formation in deep veins, potentially requiring immediate medical referral. 
            • Example: Swelling, warmth, and pain in a limb post-surgery, indicating a potential DVT. 
            ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (!!Q)
            Q1: How does a physical therapist differentiate cardiac pain from muscle-related pain? 
                A1:
                    -Cardiac pain, like angina, is relieved by rest and nitroglycerin, associated with specific cardiac patterns.
                    -Muscle-related pain can be localized with movement assessment, exacerbated by neck or shoulder motion. 
            Q2: What are red flags indicating the need for immediate medical referral during screening? 
                A2:
                    Syncope: Loss of consciousness with postural tone loss. 
                    Severe Fatigue: Beyond normal expectations, especially during or after exercise. 
                    Edema: Sudden or continuous swelling, especially in ankles, abdomen, and hands. 
            Q3: How can a physical therapist recognize symptoms of vascular disease during screening?
                A3: Vascular pain is throbbing, exacerbated by activity, and has a 5-10 minute relief time. Older patients with heart disease history and risk factors like smoking may exhibit vascular pain. 
            Q4: When should a therapist refer a patient with new-onset dyspnea for immediate medical attention?
                A4: Immediate referral is needed if dyspnea is associated with symptoms like cyanosis, fatigue, cough, or chest pain, indicating potential cardiac or pulmonary issues.

        Cardiovascular Screening
            • Identifying risk factors: age, gender, ethnicity. 
            • Modifiable factors: obesity, diabetes, smoking. 
            • Clinical presentation: chest pain patterns, angina symptoms. 
        Muscle Disorders and Pain Differentiation 
            • Differentiating muscle-related pain from cardiac origin. 
            • Assessing pain with movements to isolate muscle-related issues. 
        Dyspnea and Associated Symptoms 
            • Recognizing dyspnea as a symptom of cardiac or pulmonary origin. 
            • Understanding symptoms related to exertion, body position, and activity. 
        Red Flags for Immediate Referral 
            • Syncope, severe fatigue, sudden edema. 
            • Recognizing signs requiring urgent medical attention. 
        Vascular Disease Screening 
            • Throbbing pain with activity and relief time. 
            • Differentiating vascular pain from musculoskeletal sources. 
        Pulmonary Screening 
            • Assessing past medical history for cancer, infections, or recent hospitalization. 
            • Identifying red flags: pain worsened by breathing, coughing, or respiratory movements. 
        Interview Process and Information Gathering 
            • Importance of comprehensive information during screening. 
            • Asking specific questions to trigger relevant patient information. 
        Screening Referral Considerations
            • Decision-making based on past history, clinical presentation, and associated signs. 
            • The vital role of screening referrals in physical therapy practice.

4.Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Physical Therapy Examination
    ..1.5. Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Physical Therapy Examination
        ..('PT 2202_Mod 1_Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Physical Therapy Examination.pdf')
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!E.f)

    -This lecture will cover the cardiovascular and pulmonary examination and evaluation. It will detail the important components of the examination, along with the specific cardiovascular and pulmonary findings. You will also be given detail on how examination findings can lead to appropriate PT diagnosis, prognosis, and development of a plan of care. This lecture will lead into the subsequent lectures in this module where you will be given further detail on how to perform specific examination techniques. 

    .Elements of Patient/Client Management ('Elements of Patient-Client Management') [CP2_Elements of Patient-Client Management]
        Γ Açò ve de PM1
        Examination
        Referral/Consultation
        Evaluation
        Diagnosis
        Prognosis
        Intervention
        Outcomes
        Fig. 16.1. The elements of patient management leading to optimal outcomes. Screening takes place anywhere along this pathway.

    .History/Interview 
        Gather important information: 
            1. Medical chart review 
            2. Present complaint 
            3. History of medical problems 
            4. Report of symptoms 
            5. Risk factors 
            6. Perception and understanding of the problem 
            7. Family situation 
            8. Readiness to learn 
            9. Goals for rehabilitation (both occupational and leisure)

    .Guide to PT Practice ('Guide to PT Practice')
        General Demographics
        • Age
        • Gender
        • Race/ethnicity
        • Primary language
        • Education
        ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        Social History
            • Cultural beliefs and behaviors
            • Family and caregiver resources
            • Social interactions, social activities, and support systems
        Employment/Work (Job/School/Play)
            • Current and prior work (job/school/play), community, and leisure actions, tasks, or activities
        Growth and Development
            • Developmental history
            • Hand dominance
        Living Environment
            • Devices and equipment (eg, assistive, adaptive, orthotic, protective, supportive, prosthetic)
            • Living environment and community characteristics
            • Projected discharge destinations
        General Health Status (Self-Report, Family Report, Caregiver Report)
            • General health perception
            • Physical function (eg, mobility, sleep patterns, restricted bed days)
            • Psychological function (eg, memory, reasoning ability, depression, anxiety)
            • Role function (eg, community, leisure, social, work)
            • Social function (eg, social activity, social interaction, social support)
        Social/Health Habits (Past and Current)
            • Behavioral health risks (eg, smoking, drug abuse)
            • Level of physical ﬁtness
        Family History
            • Familial health risks
        Medical/Surgical History
            • Cardiovascular
            • Endocrine/metabolic
            • Gastrointestinal
            • Genitourinary
            • Gynecological
            • Integumentary
            • Musculoskeletal
            • Neuromuscular
            • Obstetrical
            • Prior hospitalizations, surgeries, and preexisting medical and other health-related conditions
            • Psychological
            • Pulmonary
        Current Condition(s)/Chief Complaint(s)
            • Concerns that led the patient/client to seek the services of a physical therapist
            • Concerns or needs of patient/client who requires the services of a physical therapist
            • Current therapeutic interventions
            • Mechanisms of injury or disease, including date of onset and course of events
            • Onset and pattern of symptoms
            • Patient/client, family, signiﬁcant other, and caregiver expectations and goals for the therapeutic intervention
            • Patient/client, family, signiﬁcant other, and caregiver perceptions of patient’s/client’s emotional response to the current clinical situation
            • Previous occurrence of chief complaint(s)
            • Prior therapeutic interventions  
        Functional Status and Activity Level
            ``• Current and prior functional status in self-care and home management, including activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL)
            • Current and prior functional status in work (job/school/play), community, and leisure actions, tasks, or activities
        Medications
            • Medications for current condition
            • Medications previously taken for current condition
            • Medications for other conditions
        Other Clinical Tests
            • Laboratory and diagnostic tests
            • Review of available records (eg, medical, education, surgical)
            • Review of other clinical ﬁndings (eg, nutrition and hydration)

    .Sample Questions for Cardiac Symptoms (!!E).Lv2.practical
        Stable angina
            Non-anginal discomfort AKA Chest Wall Pain
        -------------------------------------------------------- 
            Relieved by nitroglycerin (30 sec to 1 min)
                Nitroglycerin generally has no effect 
            Comes on at the same heart rate and blood pressure and is relieved by rest (lasts only a few minutes)
                Occurs any time; lasts for hours 
            Not palpable
                Muscle soreness, joint soreness, evoked by palpation or deep breaths 
            Associated with feelings of doom, cold sweats, shortness of breath
                Minimal additional symptoms 
            Often seen with ST-segment depression
                No ST-segment depression

    .Systems Review 
        -Brief examination of all systems that would affect the ability of the patient to “initiate, sustain, and modify purposeful movement for the performance of actions, tasks or activities that are important for function” 
            1. CP system → heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and presence of edema 
            2. MSK system → gross symmetry, gross ROM, gross strength, height, and weight 
            3. NM system → gross movement involving balance, gait, locomotion, transfers, and transition as well as motor control and motor learning 
            4. Integumentary system → pliability (texture), presence of scar formation, skin color, and skin integrity

    .Physical Examination 
        Box 16-1 Guide categories for tests and measures 
            • Aerobic capacity/endurance 
            • Anthropometric characteristics 
            • Arousal, attention, and cognition 
            • Assistive and adaptive devices 
            • Circulation (arterial, venous, lymphatic) 
            • Cranial and peripheral nerve integrity 
            • Environmental, home and work (job/school/play) barriers 
            • Gait, locomotion, and balance 
            • Integumentary integrity 
            • Motor function (motor control and motor learning) 
            • Neuromotor development and sensory integration 
            • Orthotic, protective, and supportive devices 
            • Pain 
            • Posture 
            • Prosthetic requirements 
            • Range of motion (including activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living) 
            • Reflex integrity 
            • Self-care and home management (including activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living) 
            • Sensory integrity 
            • Ventilation and respiration/gas exchange 
            • Work (job/school/play), community, and leisure integration or reintegration (including instrumental activities of daily living) 
        From American Physical Therapy Association: Guide to Physical Therapist Practice, ed 2 Baltimore, 2003, APTA. 

    .Inspection/Observation 
        • Observation, key component in cardiopulmonary patients 
        • General appearance 
            • level of consciousness, body type, posture, skin tone, external monitoring 
        • Facial characteristics 
            • expression, effort to breathe 
        • Evaluation of neck 
            • activity of neck musculature during breathing; appearance of jugular veins; presence of hypertrophy or adaptive shortening 
        • Evaluation of chest 
            • resting and dynamic
        ------------------------------------------------------
        • The sternocleidomastoid muscles often hypertrophy in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease owing to increased work of the accessory muscles to assist with breathing.
        ------------------------------------------------------
        • Posture and body type 
            • Example: 
                • The increased size of the abdomen in obesity (or pregnancy) restricts the full downward movement of the diaphragm during inspiration and restricts lung tissue at rest, therefore creating a restrictive effect on the lung.
        ------------------------------------------------------
        • Chest wall observation 
            • deformities or changes that may impact lung expansion
        ------------------------------------------------------
        • Patient position of comfort ('Patient position of comfort') (!!E).Lv3
            • Example: 
                1. Semi-Fowler’s Position 
                    - best for patients with Heart Failure 
                    - Elevated bed and lying down improves ventilation 
                2. Professorial Position 
                    - used by COPD patients 
                    - helps stabilize thorax 
                    - assists accessory muscles to breathe more efficiently
        --------------------------------------------------------
        • Jugular venous distention (JVD) ('Jugular venous distention')
        --------------------------------------------------------
        Take note of a patient’s lines, drains, and tubes during initial inspection. 
            • Identify those which are present 
            • Determine how lines/drains/tubes will be managed or impact your PT plan
        ---------------------------------------------------------
        • Phonation, cough, cough production 
        • Appearance of extremities 
        • Observation of fingers, toes, calves of legs 
        • Digital clubbing – chronic tissue hypoxia

    .Inspection/Observation of Breathing (!!E).Lv2.practical
        • Breathing Patterns: 
            • Apnea 
                • absence of ventilation 
            • Bradypnea 
                • slow rate, regular rhythm 
            • Tachypnea 
                • fast rate, shallow depth, regular rhythm 
            • Cheyne-Stokes Γ('Real-life video of cheyne-stokes breathing.mp4') Γ('Types of Respirations Examples.mp4')REPE
                • increasing then decreasing depth, period of apnea interspersed, seen in critically ill 
            • Apneustic Γ('Types of Respirations Examples.mp4')REPE
                • slow rate, deep inspiration followed by apnea, irregular rhythm, brainstem disorders 
            • Orthopnea 
                • difficulty breathing when lying down 
            • Hyperventilation 
                • fast rate, increased depth, regular rhythm
                    Γ(Hyperventilation vs. Dyspnea = increased depth)
            • Dyspnea
                • rapid rate, shallow depth, regular, accessory muscle use
                    Γ(Dyspnea vs. Tachypnea = accessory muscle use)

    .Table 16-5 Guidelines for evaluating cough and secretions ('evaluating cough and secretions')
        Cough
            Characteristics Associated
                Features Interpretation
        --------------------------------------------------------------------
        1.Nonspecific
            Sore throat, runny nose, runny eyes
                Acute lung infection; tracheobronchitis
        2.Productive
            Preceded by an earlier, painful, nonproductive cough associated with an upper respiratory tract infection
                Lobar pneumonia
        3.Dry or productive   
            Acute bronchitis
                Bronchopneumonia
        4.Paroxysmal; mucoid or bloodstained sputum
            Flu-like syndrome
                Mycoplasma or viral pneumonia
        5.Purulent sputum
            Sputum formerly mucoid
                Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis
        6.Productive for more than 3 months consecutively and for at least 2 years
                Chronic bronchitis
        7.Foul-smelling, copious, layered purulent sputum
            Long-standing problem
                Bronchiectasis
        8.Blood-tinged sputum
            Month long
                Tuberculosis or fungal infection
        9.Persistent, nonproductive
                Pneumonitis, interstitial fibrosis, pulmonary infiltrates
        10.Persistent, minimally productive
            Smoking history, injected pharynx
                “Smoker’s cough”
        11.Nonspecific; minimal hemoptysis
            Long-standing
                Neoplastic disease
        12.Nonproductive
            Long-standing; dyspnea
                Mediastinal neoplasm
        13.Brassy
                Aortic aneurysm
        14.Violent cough
            Sudden; onset at the same time as signs of asphyxia; localized wheezing
                Aspiration of foreign body
        15.Frothy sputum
            Worsens in supine position; dyspnea
                Heart failure, pulmonary edema
        16.Hemoptysis
            Sudden; simultaneous dyspnea; pleural effusion
                Pulmonary infarct

    .Endurance and/or Functional Assessment (!!E).Lv2.practical
        • Determine patient’s response to activity 
            • Going from supine, sitting, standing, some type of ADL, and ambulation 
            • Measure HR, rhythm (ECG), BP, symptoms, heart/lung sounds before and after 
            • Abnormal response – very rapid rise with increased workload, very flat rate of rise, decrease 
            • Heart rhythm – assess regularity, final interpretation should be done with ECG; assessing for arrhythmias 
        • Aerobic testing 
            • 6 Minute Walk Test (6MWT) 
            • Graded treadmill testing 

    .Endurance and/or Functional Assessment ('Summary of normal responses to activity')
        • BP measurement 
            • Arterial BP is general indicator of function of heart as a pump (systolic/diastolic) 
            • Accuracy in measurement is critical to the correct interpretation of BP 
        • Evaluation of oxygen saturation 
            • Should be evaluated in patients with heart failure, pulmonary HTN, pulmonary disease 
        ``• Other S and Sxs of CV inadequacy: (!!E).Lv1.practical
            • Angina (variant, pre-infarction) 
            • Pericarditis 
            • Mitral valve dysfunction 
            • Bronchospasm 
            • Esophageal spasm 
            • Shortness of breath 
            • Palpitations 
            • Dizziness 
            • Fatigue
        ----------------------------------------------------------------
        Table 16-12	Summary	of Normal Responses	to Activity (!!E.V) (!!E).Lv2 (!!P)
            Physiological
                Variable Response to Increased Work
                    Response to	Endurance Activity
            ----------------------------------------
            Heart rate (HR)
                Gradual rate of rise with increase in workload
                    Remains the same with continuation of the activity past steady state (first few minutes)
            Systolic blood pressure (BP)
                Gradual rate of rise with increase in workload
                    Remains the same with continuation of the activity past steady state (first few min)
            Diastolic blood pressure
                ±10 mm Hg with any activity
                    ±10 mm Hg with any activity
            SpO2
                Stays the same or increases
                    Stays the same or increases
            Respiratory rate (RR)
                Gradual increase with workload, rapid rate of rise after anaerobic threshold
                    Stays the same

    .What is next? 
        After completion of full cardiopulmonary examination, PT develops a clinical judgment based on the data 
            Decision about interventions and plan of care
            Develops a PT diagnosis 
        Re-examination 
            Formal process of selecting tests/measures to evaluate progress and modify or redirect interventions

    .Plan of Care 
        • Treatment duration and frequency
        • Planned Interventions 
        • Goals 
        • Acute Care Specific: 
            • Equipment recommendations 
            • Discharge destination regarding PT needs 
                • Home without any needs 
                • Home physical therapy 
                • Outpatient physical therapy 
                • Acute rehabilitation 
                • Skilled nursing facility 
                • Extended care facility

    .PT Role in Discharge Planning 
        • What is discharge planning? 
            • The development of a discharge plan for a patient prior to leaving the hospital 
        • Discharge decisions are multidisciplinary and based on PT, OT, case manager or social worker, MD and other various healthcare professional's input 
        • PT plays the role of functionally assessing the patient to make appropriate and safe discharge destination recommendations or placement 
            • Home with No further need vs Homecare PT 
            • Skilled Nursing (short term care) 
            • Acute rehabilitation 
            • Outpatient 
            • Extended care facility (no therapy services, need full time care)

    .Discharge Planning
        • Patient’s life context and prior level of function (PLOF) 
        • Patient’s current function and disability 
        • Patient’s desires and needs 
        • Patients' ability to participate in their care

    .Discharge Destination and POC 
        • Discharge destination may drive plan of care 
        • Treatment interventions focus, goals, duration, frequency for Acute Rehab vs. SNF vs. Homecare vs Outpatient

    .Cardiovascular & Pulmonary PT Examination
        Examination Process 
            • Definition: A systematic process in physical therapy involving patient history, system review, tests, and measures to gather data for clinical judgment. 
            • Example: Assessing cardiovascular and pulmonary aspects to determine appropriate interventions. 
        Prognosis 
            • Definition: Determining the predicted level of optimal function to guide the development of a care plan. 
            • Example: Estimating the expected outcome of a patient's recovery based on the examination findings. 
        Outcome Measures 
            • Definition: Objective tools used to evaluate patient functional status, allowing for goal setting and tracking progress. 
            • Example: Five Times Sit to Stand test measuring aerobic capacity and function. 
        Discharge Planning 
            • Definition: Part of the PT plan of care involving decisions about the patient's discharge destination based on examination data. 
            • Example: Considering home setup, assist levels, and patient preferences for a safe and effective transition post-treatment. 
            -----------------------------------------------------------------------
            Questions and Answers (!!Q)
                Q1:What is the role of PT diagnosis in the examination process?
                    A1: PT diagnosis involves determining the impact of the condition on function, guiding the selection of interventions. It is distinct from medical diagnosis and aids in clinical decision-making.
                Q2:Why is discharge planning crucial in the cardio-pulmonary examination?
                    A2: Discharge planning considers the patient's life context, prior level of function, and preferences to decide the most appropriate destination post-treatment, influencing the PT plan of care. 
                Q3:How does the PT use outcome measures in the examination process?
                    A3: Outcome measures are objective tools to evaluate patient functional status, aiding in goal setting and tracking progress. They help determine the effectiveness of interventions. 
        
        1. Examination Process (!!E).Lv2.practical
            • Patient history, system review, tests, and measures. 
            • Clinical judgment, diagnosis, and prognosis. 
            • Continuous re-examination and plan of care updates. 
        2. Patient History and Interview 
            • Gathering information beyond the medical chart. 
            • Importance of effective communication and rapport. 
            • Sample descriptors and questions for assessing cardiac symptoms. 
        3. System Review 
            • Brief examination of major systems affecting movement. 
            • Assessment of communication, affect, cognition, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, neuromuscular, integument. 
        4. Physical Examination 
            • Inspection and observation of general appearance, posture, skin tone. 
            • Assessment of neck and chest, evaluating accessory muscle use. 
            • Palpation procedures for cardiovascular and pulmonary abnormalities. 
            • Auscultation methods for heart and lung sounds.
        5. Functional Assessment 
            • Determining patient response to activity through vital signs, ECG, and auscultation. 
            • Identifying abnormal blood pressure responses. 
            • Monitoring symptoms and modifying exercise prescriptions. 
        6. Outcome Measures 
            • Utilizing measures like Five Times Sit to Stand for goal setting. 
            • Tracking progress and functional status. 
        7. Plan of Care 
            • Clinical judgment based on examination data. 
            • Interventions, treatment duration, and frequency. 
            • Goals and continuous re-examination. 
        8. Discharge Planning 
            • Considering home setup, assist levels, and patient preferences. 
            • Deciding discharge destination based on examination findings. 
            • Influencing the PT plan of care. 
        9. Patient Education 
            • Providing education on signs and symptoms. 
            • Enhancing patient understanding of their condition. 
        10. Recommended Discharge Destinations 
            • Acute rehab, skilled nursing facility, home care, outpatient. 
            • Tailoring interventions based on the recommended destination. 
        Remember, the examination is a dynamic process, and continuous assessment and communication with the patient are essential for effective cardiovascular and pulmonary physical therapy.

        Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Screening and Exam Activity
            ('PT 2202_Mod 1_Live Session_CV and Pulmonary Screening and Exam Activity.pdf', SOLUTON: 'PT 2202_CVP Screening and Exam_Ans Key PDF.pdf')
                Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Screening and Examination Activity    
                    Read the following questions and complete as a group: 
                        1. Give an example of each of the following in terms of a CV and Pulmonary Finding: 
                            a. Refer the patient out (outside scope of PT practice) 
                            b. Diagnose and treat (within scope of PT practice) 
                            c. Treat and refer out (alert medical team to concerns)
                            ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                            ``-Below answers can vary, but make sure they have an observation, test/measure, vital sign, etc., along with symptom presentation for each. Feel free here to give some clinical feedback from your experience. Example of Tx and Refer, as this can be the most difficult: pt dx BLE Morton’s neuroma, but patient has s and sx of vascular disease, including pitting edema, B symptoms, possibly mention ABI assessment and measuring – this would be a “treat and refer” where patient can have a POC developed to improve vascular sxs, but also needs a vascular consult/workup)

                        2. You are approaching a patient in the outpatient setting. Name a single observation you may see right away that could indicate a pulmonary dysfunction may be present.
                            -Central or peripheral cyanotic signs, wearing O2, coughing, breathing rhythm and RR are
                            not normal. 

                        3. Describe the difference between dyspnea that is of cardiac vs pulmonary in origin. 
                            -Dyspnea, or the feeling of being short of breath, can be a symptom that comes from a cardiac or pulmonary origin and may be related to activity, exertion, or body position. For example, in a patient with heart failure, it may be difficult for them to breath when they are lying flat, and they may need to elevate their upper body when lying down. Dyspnea on exertion can be a result of a cardiac problem, specifically left ventricular dysfunction because of pulmonary congestion that results from a back of fluid in the lungs and results in shortness of breath.

                        4. Let’s say you have a patient that has cardiac origin dyspnea or SOB, what may you see if you add supplemental oxygen, and how may you educate the staff that it is NOT a pulmonary issue?
                            -No change in SpO2, remains breathless. Explain to staff this is CV issue where blood flow does not appear to be adequate to provide O2 not only to the periphery but to the lungs to function adequately. If it was solely an oxygenation issue at that time the SpO2 likely could change with addition to O2.

                        5. A patient presents to the outpatient setting with back pain and BLE radiculopathy. What signs and symptoms may you discover that make you think that this is more of a vascular issue and how would you convey that to the patient and referral back to PCP?
                            -Vascular pain is often throbbing in nature and exacerbated by activity. With atherosclerosis, a lag time of 5 to 10 minutes occurs between when the body asks for increased oxygenated blood and when symptoms occur because of arterial occlusion. Here you can talk about pain that is mechanical vs non-mechanical in nature. 

                        6. Explain DDx of neck pain vs a Pancoast tumor in terms of patient history, clinical presentation and other factors that require further investigation.
                            Also, the lung may be a location of CA for one who has a history of smoking that may require further investigation. An example for a DDx that would require use of pulmonary screening would be a patient referred to PT neck and shoulder pain, and the patient may have a history of smoking along with new cough and SOB. You could decide to perform lung auscultation as they have been complaining of new onset shortness of breath. In the upper lobe you discover an absent breath sound which may be indicative of bronchogenic tumor or mass, namely a Pancoast tumor, which would mean a medical referral is required.

        Medical Chart Review Activity

                Medical Chart Review Activity  
                    -Review the Following Medical Chart. Discuss all the important components you will review, and any concerns you may see in this chart. Also, review some areas of information where you would need further data, missing components or need to consider when seeing this patient. Plan for how you will initiate your patient screen and evaluation.  

                        Name: Saul Goodman 
                        Admission: 9/10/2022 
                        DOB: 10/20/1954 
                        Admitting Diagnosis: Chest Pain, NSTEMI

                        Patient Profile:  Spanish as primary language, retired/disabled, Ht: 166 cm, weight: 55 kg, 
                        smoker 50 ppd 

                        Allergies: latex, Vicodin  

                        H&P: patient was admitted to the ER with chest pain, unrelieved by NG. Patient reported the chest pain was constant and unrelieved by rest. It started this morning and has lasted for 4 hours before it became unbearable and radiated into the L arm. The patient was admitted to the cardiac ICU for further monitoring where ECG revealed ST segment changes. Patient was in a hypertensive emergency, and BP normalized from 230 systolic to 124 systolic with IV labetalol 15mg. The patient was immediately treated with unfractionated heparin with bolus dosing and a continuous infusion and is now stable. Patient denied fever, chills, sick contact. Patient does now have mild crackles bilaterally on physical exam. Otherwise, low suspicion for infection however ordered CXR to confirm.  

                        PmHx: Diabetes II, COPD, CAD, HTN, HFpEF, Schizophrenia, Anxiety disorder
                            Γ HFpEF is a type of heart failure where the heart pumps normally (preserved ejection fraction) but has difficulty filling with blood properly (diastolic dysfunction)

                        PsHx: Stent Placement 2003 LAD, R TKA March 2022 

                        Physical Exam: 
                            Constitutional: NAD, laying in bed, appears comfortable, however drowsy post-op 
                            Eyes: clear sclera 
                            ENMT: moist mucous membranes 
                            Head/Neck: no appreciable JVD 
                            Respiratory/Thorax: mild crackles bilaterally, adequate air movement, no increased Work of

..2.0. Module Introduction
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    Module Introduction
        Module 2 will continue to cover physical therapy screening and examination of the cardiovascular and pulmonary systems. This module will get into more depth regarding specific screening and examination tools that will allow you to discover red flags that require referral to other medical professionals, determine the severity of the cardiovascular and pulmonary dysfunction, and discover impairments associated with cardiovascular and pulmonary disease that can be addressed by specific physical therapy interventions. This module will continue to expose you to procedures that will act as a foundation for all the other modules, in addition to lab-based materials that will be practiced in the immersions.  

    Learning Objectives
        Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to:
            Apply the use of the Hypothesis-Oriented Algorithm for Clinicians for evaluation, and re-examination in patients with cardiopulmonary dysfunction. 
            Describe and administer the six components of the patient/client management model (Examination, Evaluation, Diagnosis, Prognosis, Intervention, Assessment of Outcome) to patients with cardiopulmonary dysfunction. 
            Give rationale for the selection of evaluative tools in the management of the cardiopulmonary patient. 
            Assess and develop a subsequent plan for inpatient (acute care, rehab, skilled nursing), outpatient, home, and community-based on screening and evaluation outcomes. 
            Describe and choose appropriate cardiovascular and pulmonary screening and examination procedures to justify differential diagnosis based on cardiopulmonary data and assessment; identify the need for referral to other health care professionals as appropriate.

            .Capillary Refill Time Test (CRTT)
                • Purpose: 
                    • Screen for poor peripheral circulation
                • Procedure: 
                    • Have the patient seated with hands at heart level (upper) or in long sitting (lower) 
                    • Depress nail bed for 5 seconds so they blanch or turn white 
                    • Time and note when the color returns 
                    • Positive findings for poor circulation include: 
                        a. Finger ≥ 3 seconds 
                        b. Toe ≥ 5 seconds
            -----------------------------------

                • Brachial Pulse
                • Temporal Pulse
                • Carotid Pulse
                • Femoral Pulse
                • Popliteal Pulse
                • Tibialis Posterior Pulse
                • Dorsalis Pedis Pulse

                    .Grading strength of pulses ('All Body Pulses.png') (!!E.Grade & Doc)
                        Grade 0 - absent 
                        Grade 1+ - palpable but diminished 
                        Grade 2+ - palpable and brisk (normal) 
                        Grade 3+ - increased 
                        Grade 4+ - increased and bounding

    .Cardiac Palpation Sites
        • Purpose: 
            • Assess for visible pulsations outside of the norms 
        • Procedure: 
            • Supine with bed elevated to 30 degrees OR Left lateral decubitus position 
            • Palpate all areas with pads of fingers, followed by heel of hand 
        • Findings: 
            • Thrills ➔ Murmur 
            • Heaves ➔ Cardiac Hypertrophy 
            • Pain ➔ MSK origin 
            • Deformities ➔ pectus carinatum('') or pectus excavatum('')
        -------------------------------------------------------- ('.Cardiac Palpation Sites')
        1. Aortic Area
            • 2nd R intercostal space 
        2. Pulmonary Area 
            • 2nd L intercostal space 
        3. Right Ventricular Area 
            • 3-5th intercostal space, L sternal border 
        4. Left Ventricular Area 
            • 4-5th intercostal space, medial to midclavicular line 
        5. Apical Region

        • Assess the integrity of valve closure as related to the cardiac cycle, heard as a “lub” “dub”

    .Heart Sounds – Procedure ('Heart Sounds Procedure') Γ('Normal Heart Sounds - MEDZCOOL.mp4')
        1. Patient in supine with HOB at 30 degrees with the patient relaxed and breathing normally 
        2. Place the diaphragm of the stethoscope over each of the 4 valvular regions with light pressure 
        3. Listen for S2 “dub” at the aortic and pulmonic area 
        4. Listen for S1 “lub” over the tricuspid or mitral region
