    .Apical Pulse ('Apical Pulse')
        • Apex of heart, 5th ICS midclavicular line 
            • Very accurate measure of heart rate 
            • Palpated or auscultated

    .Edema – Limb Circumference ('Edema – Limb Circumference') 
        • Purpose 
            • Measure limb girth in the light of edema 
            • Compare R vs. L 
            • Procedure 
                • Lower extremity 
                    • Measure circumference at Knee joint or tibial tubercle(''), then repeat 10 cm above 
                • Upper extremity 
                    • Measure circumference at styloid process(''), then repeat 10 cm above 

    .Edema - Pitting ('')
        • Purpose
            • Determine the extent of the pitting edema
        • Procedure
            • Apply digital pressure of or 15-30 sec over bony prominence
            • Release and determine soft (pitting) vs. indurated (non-pitting) edema
            • Grade edema based on depth and record time to for tissue normalization
            • Edema resolving > 40 sec suggestive of heart failure (!!E.Grade & Doc)

    .Carotid Artery('') Auscultation 1
        • Purpose: 
            • Screen for possible carotid artery blockage 
        • Procedure: 
            1. Patient seated or supine with head turned slightly away from examiner 
            2. Place stethoscope bell at each site and perform steps 3-4 at each: 
                • Angle of jaw, Carotid bifurcation(''), Base of neck, Subclavian artery 
            3. Patient inhales, exhales, then holds breath for 15 sec 
            4. Listening occurs during and immediately after exhalation 
        • Findings 
            • (+) carotid, systolic bruit, is a blowing or swishing sound
                Γ('Carotid Bruit Sound..mp4') 

    .Carotid Artery Auscultation 2 ('Carotid Artery Auscultation')
        Base of jaw 
        Carotid Bifurcation 
        Base of Neck 
        Subclavian Artery

    .Abdominal Aorta('') Palpation ('Abdominal Aorta Palpation')
        • Purpose: 
            • Screen for possible presence of abdominal aortic aneurysm('') 
        • Procedure 
            1. Patient supine with knees bent 
            2. Examiner places index fingers pointing toward the head, just above the umbilicus and lift of midline. You can use 2 or 1 hand based on preference. 
            3. Press down firmly to locate the pulsating aorta 
            4. Palpate for size, location and pulsation 
        • Findings 
            • Normal width ~ 2.5 cm (1 inch or ~2 fingertips) 
            • (+) AAA Wide pulsation (≥4 cm) or large lateral pulsation

    .Abdominal Aorta Auscultation ('Abdominal Aorta Auscultation')
        • Purpose 
            • Screen for possible presence of abdominal aortic aneurysm 
        • Procedure 
            1. Patient supine with knees bent and examiner on right side 
            2. Examiner places the stethoscope just above the umbilicus and left of midline 
        • Findings 
            • (+) AAA with sounds of bruits or swishing in the presence of a wide pulse
                Γ('Aortic Regurgitation Murmur Sound.mp4')

    .Cardiovascular Examination (!!E).Lv2.practical
        Cardiovascular Active Examination 
            • Definition: Specific procedures following patient history, investigating cardiovascular system health. 
            • Example: Assessing color, temperature, and circulation to reveal abnormalities in blood flow and vascular health. 
        Peripheral Pulses 
            • Definition: Assessment of pulses at various sites to indicate distal blood flow. 
            • Example: Weak femoral pulses suggesting peripheral vascular disease. 
        Heart Sounds 
            • Definition: Auscultation to assess integrity of valve closure during the cardiac cycle. 
            • Example: S1 and S2 heart sounds representing mitral/tricuspid and aortic/pulmonic valve closures. 
        Edema Measurement 
            • Definition: Quantifying swelling in limbs to monitor cardiovascular-related conditions. 
            • Example: Pitting edema indicating chronic or prolonged swelling. 

    .Cardiovascular Examination Procedures 
         Questions and Answers (!!Q)
            Q1:What does color assessment in cardiovascular examination reveal? 
                A1: Color can indicate reduced blood flow (pale/white or blue) or increased blood flow (redness) Γ(infection), providing insights into the cardiovascular system's health. 
            Q2:How is the capillary refill test performed, and what does it assess?
                A2: The test involves depressing the patient's nail bed for 5 seconds, with a normal refill time of 2 seconds. A positive finding (>3 seconds) suggests poor circulation, aiding in peripheral vascular disease diagnosis. 
            Q3:Why is the apical heart rate considered accurate, and where is it located? 
                A3: The apical heart rate is obtained at the apex of the heart (5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line), providing an accurate measure due to proximity to the source of heart sounds. 

    .N/A 1 Step.3_CT.CP2_ExaminationOrder_1º (!!E).Lv2.practical
        1.Observation and Inspection 
            • Assess color, temperature, and circulation. 
            • Evaluate abnormalities in blood flow and vascular health. 
        2.Peripheral Pulses Assessment 
            • Obtain radial, brachial, femoral, popliteal, tibialis posterior, and dorsalis pedis pulses. 
            • Grade pulses on a scale and correlate findings with distal blood flow. 
        3.Palpation of Cardiac Region 
            • Palpate various regions corresponding to the heart's anatomy. 
            • Identify abnormal sensations, thrills, or heaves during palpation. 
        4.Auscultation of Heart Sounds 
            • Listen to heart sounds (S1 and S2) with a diaphragm over aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid, and mitral valve areas. 
            • Differentiate normal and abnormal heart sounds. 
        5.Assessment of S3 and S4 Sounds 
            • Auscultate at the apex for early ventricular filling sounds (S3) and ventricular wall vibration during atrial contraction (S4). 
            • Recognize associations with heart conditions. 
        6.Heart Murmurs and Friction Rub 
            • Distinguish between innocent and abnormal heart murmurs. 
            • Identify pericardial friction rub as a sign of pericarditis. 
        7.Carotid Artery Auscultation 
            • Perform auscultation at jaw, carotid bifurcation, base of the neck, and subclavian artery. 
            • Detect systolic bruits indicating possible carotid issues. 
        8.Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Screening 
            • Palpate abdominal aorta for size, location, and pulsation. 
            • Listen for bruits indicating a possible aneurysm. 
        9.Edema Measurement 
            • Use circumferential measures to quantify edema in upper and lower limbs. 
            • Monitor for changes and assess baseline measures. 
        10.Supine Position Assessments 
            • Perform supine assessments for carotid artery, abdominal aortic aneurysm, and edema. 
            • Ensure relaxation of abdominal wall for accurate findings. 
        -Remember, a comprehensive cardiovascular examination involves a combination of visual inspection, palpation, and auscultation to gather information crucial for diagnosis and treatment planning. 

    .Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)
        Definition: 
            -An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) refers to the abnormal dilation or bulging of the abdominal aorta, the major blood vessel that supplies blood to the abdomen, pelvis, and legs. This condition occurs when a weakened area of the aortic wall allows the vessel to balloon outward, creating a potentially life-threatening situation.

        Clinical Significance for Physical Therapy: 
            1.Emergency Awareness: 
                • An AAA can lead to a medical emergency if it ruptures, causing severe internal bleeding. 
                • Physical therapists need to be vigilant for signs of AAA, especially if patients present with associated symptoms such as sudden and severe abdominal or back pain. 
            2.Screening and Assessment: 
                • Physical therapists may play a role in screening for AAA in patients with risk factors, such as older age, male gender, smoking history, and a family history of AAA. 
                • During assessment, palpation of the abdominal aorta may reveal signs of an aneurysm, such as a wide pulsation or abnormal lateral pulsation 
            3.Referral and Communication: 
                • Recognizing potential signs of AAA requires prompt referral to a medical professional for further diagnostic testing, such as ultrasound or CT scan. 
                • Effective communication with healthcare providers is essential to ensure timely diagnosis and intervention. 
            4.Exercise Prescription and Precautions: 
                • Physical therapists need to consider exercise prescription carefully for patients with known AAA or those at risk. 
                • Certain exercises, especially those involving straining or heavy lifting, might pose a risk of aneurysm rupture. Therapists should tailor exercise programs to ensure patient safety. 
            5.Post-Surgical Rehabilitation: 
                • Patients who undergo surgical intervention for AAA repair may require rehabilitation postoperatively. 
                • Physical therapists can contribute to recovery by designing exercise programs to improve cardiovascular health, strength, and overall function. 
            6.Patient Education: 
                • Educating patients about the signs and symptoms of AAA, especially if they have risk factors, empowers them to seek timely medical attention. 
                • Encouraging lifestyle modifications, such as smoking cessation and blood pressure control, can contribute to AAA prevention. 

        Conclusion: 
            -While physical therapists are not primary diagnosticians for AAA, they play a crucial role in early recognition, referral, and post-surgical rehabilitation. Awareness of AAA signs, risk factors, and appropriate communication with the healthcare team contribute to comprehensive patient care and safety.

    .General Observation & Inspection
        Signs and symptoms of respiratory distress 
            Cough
            hemoptysis
            Γ-----------------
            chest pain related to pleuritic pain
            dyspnea
            Γ------------------
            wheezing
            ease of phonation 
        Inspect thorax 
            Chest shape 
            Movement with inspiration and expiration 
        Respiratory pattern 
            Depth 
            Ratio of inspiration to expiration (1:2 is normal) 
            Sequence of chest wall movement during inspiration and expiration 
            Presence of accessory mm use 
        Look for presence of: 
            Digital clubbing ('Digital Clubbing')
            Supplemental O2 
            Surgical incisions leading to shallow breathing

    .Surface Anatomy of the Lungs ('Surface Anatomy of the Lungs')

    .Tracheal Shift ('')
        • Purpose 
            • assess for the presence of a tracheal shift 
        • Procedure 
            • examiner would palpate the position of the trachea with their index finger 
        • Findings 
            • mass effect of a large pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or intrathoracic mass will shift the mediastinum away from the primary abnormality 
            • collapse of a lung caused by bronchial obstruction will shift the mediastinum toward the primary abnormality

    .Chest Wall Motion ('Chest Wall Motion') [CP2_Chest Wall Motion] (See [CP2_Chest Wall Motion/Expansion])
        • Purpose: 
            • Note symmetry, superior, A/P & Lat motion 
        • Procedure: 
            • Place thumbs while slightly gathering the skin at the following positions: 
                1. Anterior at mid sternum - upper lobe 
                2. Anterior at xiphoid (thumbs horizontal) - right middle lobe and left lingula 
                3. Posteriorly at T8 level - lower lobe motion 
        • Findings: 
            • Normal: 3-5 cm expansion from midline 
            • reduction in expansion or movement bilaterally in those with COPD 
            • non-symmetrical movement in those with a unilateral lung collapse 
            • unilateral delay suggests atelectasis, pneumonia, post-operative guarding or poor chest wall muscle function

    .Diaphragmatic Motion ('Diaphragmatic Motion')
        • Purpose: 
            • Asses the integrity and capability for the diaphragm to engage in inspiration 
        • Procedure: 
            • Palpate the diaphragm with thumbs over the costal margin and thumb tips meeting at the xyphoid 
            • Ask the patient to take a deep breath 
            • Examiner’s hands should move equally apart, with circumferential diameter increasing by 2 to 3 inches at the end of inspiration 
        • Findings: 
            • Unequal, little or no movement 
            • Normal = 2-3 inches (5.1-7.6 cm) separation

    .Tactile Fremitus ('') Γ('Tactile Fremitus.mp4') Γ('Tactile Fremitus_ Cups Demonstration.mp4')
        • Purpose 
            • Assess areas of increased or decreased fremitus 
        • Procedure 
            1. Place palms or ulnar boarder of hand surface between spinous process and scapula 
            2. patient is asked to repeat “99” as the examiner notes bilateral differences 
            3. examiner will place their hands by moving in the ordered fashion as depicted here to compare side to side and region to region 
        • Findings 
            • (+) increased to decreased fremitus or sound transmission during contralateral comparison 
            • warrants further investigation, as may have consolidation or poor ventilation in area

    .Mediate Percussion ('Mediate Percussion') Γ('Percussion Technique.mp4')
        • Purpose: 
            • Evaluate changes in lung density by sounds produced 
            • Be aware of other areas outside the lungs, such as organ tissue or bowel regions 
        • Procedure: 
            • middle finger of one hand place flat on the patient’s chest wall along the IC space 
            • examiner’s other hand is used to strike the middle finger on the chest well 
        • Findings: 
            • sounds can be described as resonant, hyper-resonant, tympanic, dull or flat 
            • Abnormal or normal based on the anatomic location 

    .Normal Resonance Pattern of the Chest ('Normal Resonance Pattern of the Chest')
        • Areas of dullness → red circles 
        • Areas of tympany → small blue dots

    .Lung Sounds - Purpose ('Lung Sounds Purpose')
        • Process of listening to the sounds of air passing through the tracheobronchial tree and alveolar spaces during breath cycle 
        • Confirmation of chart findings, percussion and/or tactile fremitus findings, and reassessment tool 
        • Perform over entire lung space, at least one breath in each bronchopulmonary segment 
        • Lung sounds increase in areas of increased tissue density 
            • Ex. Consolidation-lung tissue becomes firm and solid due to exudates

    .Lung Sounds - Procedure ('Lung Sounds Procedure')
        • Patient in sitting with anterior and posterior thorax exposed 
        • Patient is instructed to perform deep breathing through the mouth when the stethoscope is placed against the skin at each location 
        • The examiner should move in a cephalocaudal fashion by first placing the stethoscope diaphragm in the rib interspace beginning on the left side of C7 
        • Auscultate in one location, move across midline, and auscultate the same level for one full breath per location 
        • Move down, auscultate, and cross midline again 
        • Remain medial to the scapular border

    .Lung Sounds – Normal Findings ('Lung Sounds Normal Findings') ('')Difícil d'entendre
        • Bronchial/Tracheal 
            • Loud tubular sounds over the trachea and manubrium 
            • Pause will be heard from inspiration and expiration 
            • Equal inspiratory and expiratory phase 
        • Bronchovesicular 
            • Softer vs. bronchial, and in 2nd intercoastal space 
            • No pause between inspiration and expiration 
        • Vesicular sounds 
            • Soft rustling sounds over more distal airways in the peripheral lung fields 
            • Inspiration longer than expiration

    .Lung Sounds – Abnormal Findings (!!E).Lv2.practical
        Bronchial heard where vesicular sounds should be 
            • Fluid or secretion 
        Decreased breath sounds 
            • Hypoventilation or severe congestion 
        Absent breath sounds 
            • Collapsed lung or severe consolidation 
        Wheeze/Rhonchi 
            • Continuous sound with constant pitch and varying duration 
            • Airway obstruction from bronchoconstriction or retained secretions with expiration 
            • Present with inspiration indicates significant obstruction 
        Stridor (!!P)
            • extremely high-pitched wheeze with upper airway obstruction heard both inspiration and expiration 
            • medical emergency 
        Crackles/Rales 
            • Discontinuous sound of 
            • bubbling or popping sound with presence of fluid or sudden open/closing of airway

    .Adventitious Breath Sounds Γ Table
        Adventitious breath sounds 
            Nomenclature
                Respiratory cycle when heard 
                    Probable cause
                        Quality
                            Pathological causes examples
        ------------------------------------------------
        Continuous
            Wheezes (rhonchi)
                Frequently on EX, can be on IN (if severe obstruction) 
                    Airway obstruction
                        High or low pitched
                            Bronchospasm or secretions narrowing the airway 
        Discontinuous
            Crackles (rales)
                More commonly on IN
                    -Restrictive or obstructive disease, sudden opening of closed airways, movement of secretions during inspiration and expiration 
                        Bubbles bursting
                            Atelectasis, pulmonary edema, fibrosis, pleural effusion, pneumonia, CHF 
        Pleural Rub Γ('Pleural Rub Sounds.mp4')
            Continuous or discontinuous 
                IN or EX
                    Pleural inflammation
                        Rubbing of leather or sandpaper Together

    .Errors of Auscultation to Avoid (!!E).Lv2.practical
        Errors
            Correct technique
        --------------------------------------------------------
        Listening to breath sounds through the patient's gown
            Placing bell or diaphragm directly against the chest wall 
        Allowing tubing to rub against bed rails or patient's gown 
            Keeping tube free from contact with any objects during auscultation 
        Attempting to auscultate in a noisy room
            Turning television or radio off 
        Interpreting chest hair sounds as adventitious lung sounds 
            Wetting (mojar) chest hair before auscultation if thick 
        Auscultating only the "convenient" areas
            Asking alert patient to sit up rolling comatose patient onto side to auscultate posterior lobes

    .Voice Transmission Tests
        • Purpose: 
            • To discover if consolidation is present in the lungs 
        • Procedure: 
            1. Place the stethoscope over the area of the lung that may be impaired and perform the following: 
                • Egophony → Patient says E, positive finding when A is heard ¦EA Sports Games
                • Bronchophony → Patient says 99, positive finding when sound heard loudly 
                • Whispered Pectoriloquy → Patient whispers, positive finding when whisper heard loudly 
            2. Compare side to side and region to region 
        • Findings: 
            • See above for positive findings within each procedure 
            • Louder sounds over areas of consolidation (mucus) 
            • Softer sounds over areas of hyperinflation, like COPD

    .Pulmonary Examination
        Key Terms and Concepts: 
            1. Respiratory Distress: 
                • Definition: A state where the patient experiences difficulty in breathing, often characterized by symptoms like cough, chest pain, hemoptysis, wheezing, and breathlessness during speech. 
                • Example: Wheezing in quiet breathing may suggest an underlying respiratory issue. 
            2. Chest Wall Inspection: 
                Anterior, Posterior, Right Lateral, Left Lateral 
                    • Definition: Examination of the chest shape and movement during inspiration and expiration, checking for abnormalities like kyphosis, scoliosis, or chest deformities. 
                    • Example: Assessing for abnormal chest structure that may impede breathing. 
            3. Tracheal Shift Assessment: 
                • Definition: Palpation of tracheal position to identify shifts away or toward midline, indicating disproportionate intrathoracic pressures or lung volumes. 
                • Example: A shift away may indicate a mass effect like a large pleural effusion. 
            4. Chest Wall Motion: 
                • Definition: Evaluation of chest wall movement to detect reduced or excessive motion associated with obstructive or restrictive lung conditions. 
                • Example: Unilateral delay may suggest atelectasis or pneumonia.

        Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
            Q1: What signs indicate respiratory distress during observation?
                • A1: Signs include cough, chest pain, hemoptysis, wheezing, and breathlessness during speech. 
            Q2: Why is tracheal shift assessment important?
                • A2: It helps identify disproportionate intrathoracic pressures or lung volumes, indicating conditions like pleural effusion or lung collapse.
            Q3: What is the significance of chest wall motion assessment in physical therapy?
                • A3: It reveals how well the chest wall moves during breathing, providing insights into lung conditions such as COPD or restrictive disorders. 

        I. General Observations and Inspection Step.3_CT.CP2_ExaminationOrder_2º
            • Observing signs of respiratory distress: 
                • Dry vs. productive cough
                • Pleuritic chest pain
                • Hemoptysis
                • Wheezing
                • Ease of phonation 
            • Inspecting chest shape and movement: 
                • Anterior, posterior, right lateral, left lateral 
                • Assessing for abnormalities and breathing ease
        II. Tracheal Shift Assessment 
            • Procedure: 
                • Palpate tracheal position
                • Identify shifts away or toward midline
            • Interpretation: 
                • Shift away: Mass effect (pleural effusion)
                • Shift toward: Lung collapse or bronchial obstruction
        III. Chest Wall Motion Assessment 
            • Purpose: 
                • Evaluate chest wall movement. 
            • Procedure: 
                • Palpate upper, middle, and lower chest regions. 
                • Note symmetry and amount of movement. 
            • Interpretation: 
                • Unilateral delay: Atelectasis, pneumonia. 
        IV. Additional Tests: Egophony, Bronchophony, Whispered Pectoriloquy 
            • Purpose: 
                • Assess voice transmission for abnormal lung regions. 
            • Procedure: 
                • Perform tests over suspected impaired lung areas. 
                • Evaluate sound transmission during phonation or whispering. 
            • Interpretation: 
                • Abnormal findings may indicate conditions like consolidation or mucus presence. 
        V. Lung Sounds and Percussion 
            • Auscultation: 
                • Normal breath sounds (bronchial, broncho-vascular, vesicular). 
                • Abnormal sounds (wheezing, stridor, crackles). 
            • Percussion: 
                • Evaluate changes in lung density. 
                • Distinguish normal, dull, and tympanic sounds. 
        VI. Voice Transmission Testing 
            • Egophony: Assess for "A" sounds during "E" pronunciation. 
            • Bronchophony: Evaluate loudness of spoken sounds (e.g., "99"). 
            • Whispered Pectoriloquy: Assess loudness of whispered sounds. 

        Conclusion: 
            -Pulmonary examination is crucial in physical therapy to identify respiratory distress and assess chest wall motion. 
            -Observations, tracheal shift assessment, and additional tests provide valuable information for diagnosing and treating various lung conditions. Auscultation, percussion, and voice transmission testing enhance the comprehensive evaluation of pulmonary function.

7.Other Systems Examination Procedures

    .Abdominal Quadrants ('Abdominal Quadrants')

    .Deep Palpation 
        • Purpose 
            • Allow patient to feel comfortable with deeper palpation prior to organ testing 
            • Assess for size, location, consistency and mobility of organs 
        • Procedure 
            • Patient supine with head on pillow, arms at sides, and knees bent and supported by pillows 
            • Examiner to place 4 fingertips flat on the abdomen and depress 5-8 cm or 2-3 inches 
            • Circle fingers in a rotary motion, then move to next area 
            • Assess all abdominal quadrants 
        • Findings: 
            • Tenderness, masses, enlargement of organs, tissues or muscles

    .Liver Palpation – Purpose & Procedure 
        • Purpose 
            • Assess for size, location, consistency and mobility of the liver to determine masses or tenderness 
        • Procedure 
            • Patient supine with head on pillow, arms at sides, and knees bent and supported by pillows and examiner on the right 
            • Place left hand under the patient’s back parallel to the lowest ribs 
            • Place 4 fingers of right hand in the RUQ, parallel to the midline, and index finger in line with costal margin 
            • Ask the patient to deeply inhale, then push down firmly with the right hand while the left hand remains as a posterior support 
        • Findings
            • Normal 
                • smooth, firm edge of liver may be felt by right hand or not being able to palpate the liver 
            • Positive/Abnormal 
                • Edge of liver extending beyond 1-2 cm indicates enlargement 
                • Differentiate between heart failure related liver failure vs. metastatic liver findings 
                    • Heart Failure: enlarged, soft, smooth and tender 
                    • Metastases: enlarged, hard, irregular, nodular, non-tender
            
    .Kidney Palpation – Purpose & Procedure 
        • Purpose 
            • Assess for size, location, consistency and mobility of the kidney to determine masses or tenderness 
        • Procedure 
            • Patient supine with head on pillow, arms at sides, and knees bent and supported by pillows and examiner on the right or left 
            • Place left hand under the patient’s back and other hand on top of the abdomen below the costal margin 
            • Press the two hands firmly together
        • Findings 
            • Normal 
                • Smooth, rounded, lower pole of the kidney 
                • May not be able to palpate 
            • Positive/Abnormal 
                • Enlarged kidney, nodules, tenderness 
            • Left side inferior pole of the kidney can rarely be palpated versus the right side 
                • As the left kidney is positioned slightly upper than the right kidney due to the asymmetry within the abdominal cavity caused by the liver. 

    .Other Types of Physical Therapy Examinations
        .Key Terms and Concepts: 
            1. Deep Palpation of the Abdomen:
                • Definition: A technique involving the use of deep palpation skills to assess abdominal organs for tenderness, masses, enlargement, and mobility. 
                • Example: Deep palpation aids in evaluating the size, location, and consistency of organs. 
            2. Bimanual Liver Palpation: 
                • Definition: A detailed procedure for palpating the liver using a bimanual technique, assessing for normal or abnormal findings. 
                • Example: Liver palpation is crucial to identify abnormalities related to cardiovascular and pulmonary complications. 
            3. Kidney Palpation: 
                • Definition: Palpation of the kidneys to assess for size, location, consistency, and mobility, aiding in the detection of masses or tenderness. 
                • Example: Kidney palpation is relevant in patients demonstrating kidney-related impairments or as a risk factor for cardiovascular disease. 

        .Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
            Q1: Why is deep palpation of the abdomen important in physical therapy? 
                • A1: Deep palpation helps assess tenderness, masses, and mobility of abdominal organs, providing valuable information about the patient's condition.
            Q2: What are the steps involved in bimanual liver palpation?
                1. Patient in supine position. 
                2. Examiner on the right side. 
                3. Left hand under the patient's back for support. 
                4. Right hand with four fingers over the liver. 
                5. Index finger follows the angle of the lower ribs. 
                6. Ask the patient to deeply inhale while pushing down firmly. 
            Q3: How does kidney palpation differ from liver palpation?
                • A3: In kidney palpation, the hands are pressed firmly together, aiming to feel the organ in the posterior region. It is normal not to palpate the kidney. The right side's inferior pole is more palpable than the left. 

        .Summarized Information: (!!E)
            I. Deep Palpation of the Abdomen: 
                • Procedure: 
                    • Patient supine, knees bent, and resting on pillows. 
                    • Examiner uses four-finger technique with rotary motion. 
                    • Assess tenderness, masses, and organ characteristics. 
            II. Bimanual Liver Palpation: 
                • Procedure: 
                    • Patient supine with head on pillows, arms and knees supported. 
                    • Examiner on the right side. 
                    • Left hand under the patient's back for support. 
                    • Right hand with four fingers over the liver. 
                    • Instruct the patient to inhale deeply while pushing down firmly. 
                • Findings: 
                    • Normal: Smooth, firm edge felt. 
                    • Abnormal: Enlargement, tenderness, irregularity, or abnormal tissue density. 
            III. Kidney Palpation: 
                • Procedure: 
                    • Patient supine with the examiner on the right side. 
                    • Left hand under the patient's back, and the other hand on the abdomen below the coastal margin. 
                    • Press the hands firmly together and feel for the kidney, best felt in the posterior region. 
                • Findings: 
                    • Normal: Smooth, rounded kidney felt, especially the lower pole. 
                    • Abnormal: Enlargement, nodules, tenderness.

            .Conclusion: 
                -Deep palpation of the abdomen, bimanual liver palpation, and kidney palpation are essential techniques in physical therapy. These examinations provide valuable insights into organ conditions, aiding in the assessment of cardiovascular, pulmonary, and kidney-related impairments. Regular practice enhances proficiency in these skills, contributing to a comprehensive patient evaluation.

    .Kidney (!!F)
        .Role of the Kidney in the Human Body: 
            -The kidneys are vital organs in the human body, playing crucial roles in maintaining homeostasis and overall health. Some key functions include: 
                1. Filtration of Blood: 
                    • The primary function is to filter waste products, excess fluids, and electrolytes from the blood to form urine. 
                2. Fluid and Electrolyte Balance: 
                    • Regulation of the body's fluid balance and electrolyte levels, including sodium, potassium, and phosphate. 
                3. Blood Pressure Regulation: 
                    • The kidneys release renin, an enzyme that regulates blood pressure by influencing the balance of sodium and water. 
                4. Erythropoiesis Regulation: 
                    • Production of erythropoietin, a hormone that stimulates the production of red blood cells in the bone marrow.

        .Hormones Affecting the Kidneys: 
            1. Renin:
                • Released by the kidneys to regulate blood pressure. 
            2. Erythropoietin: 
                • Stimulates red blood cell production in response to low oxygen levels. 
            3. Calcitriol: 
                • An active form of vitamin D produced by the kidneys, important for calcium and phosphate absorption in the intestines.

        .Possible Diseases Affecting the Kidneys:
            1. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): 
                • Gradual loss of kidney function over time. 
            2. Acute Kidney Injury (AKI): 
                • Sudden and temporary loss of kidney function, often due to severe infection, dehydration, or other factors. 
            3. Polycystic Kidney Disease (PKD): 
                • Genetic disorder causing the formation of fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys. 
            4. Kidney Stones: 
                • Hard deposits that form in the kidneys, often causing pain and obstruction. 

        .Causes of Kidney Diseases: 
            1. Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 
                • Prolonged high blood pressure can damage the kidneys over time. 
            2. Diabetes: 
                • Uncontrolled diabetes is a leading cause of kidney disease, impacting the small blood vessels in the kidneys. 
            3. Infections: 
                • Severe infections, if left untreated, can lead to kidney damage or failure. 
            4. Genetic Factors: 
                • Inherited conditions, such as polycystic kidney disease, can contribute to kidney disorders.

        .Impact of Cardiovascular Dysfunction on the Kidneys:
            1. Reduced Blood Flow: 
                • Cardiovascular issues, such as heart failure or atherosclerosis, can lead to reduced blood flow to the kidneys, impairing their function. 
            2. Increased Renal Artery Resistance: 
                • Hypertension and atherosclerosis can increase resistance in the renal arteries, affecting the kidneys' ability to filter blood. 
            3. Fluid Retention: 
                • Heart failure can lead to fluid buildup in the body, putting additional strain on the kidneys to regulate fluid balance. 
            4. Activation of Renin-Angiotensin System: 
                • Cardiovascular problems may stimulate the renin-angiotensin system excessively, leading to elevated blood pressure and potential kidney damage.

        -In summary, the kidneys are integral to maintaining various physiological processes in the body. Cardiovascular dysfunction can significantly impact kidney function, highlighting the interconnectedness of these two vital systems in maintaining overall health. Regular monitoring and management of cardiovascular health are essential to prevent or mitigate potential kidney-related  complications. 

    .Liver (!!F)
        .Liver Functions 
            1. Metabolism: 
                • Carbohydrate Metabolism: Regulates blood glucose levels by storing or releasing glycogen. 
                • Fat Metabolism: Synthesizes and processes fats for energy storage. 
            2. Detoxification: 
                • Converts harmful substances, like drugs and toxins, into water-soluble compounds for excretion. 
            3. Protein Synthesis: 
                • Produces blood-clotting factors, albumin, and other proteins essential for maintaining blood volume and pressure. 
            4. Storage: 
                • Stores essential vitamins (A, D, E, K) ¦(KEDA) and minerals. 
                • Acts as a reservoir for blood. 
            5. Bile Production: 
                • Secretes bile, crucial for digestion and absorption of fats in the small intestine. 

        .Hormones Affecting the Liver: 
            1. Insulin: Regulates glucose storage and utilization. 
            2. Glucagon: Stimulates the release of glucose from the liver. 
            3. Cortisol: Influences carbohydrate, protein, and fat metabolism.
                ¦Cagar insulina al sol 

        .Possible Liver Diseases:
            1. Hepatitis: 
                • Causes: Viral infections (Hepatitis A, B, C), alcohol, toxins. 
                • Impact: Inflammation of the liver, affecting its normal functions. 
            2. Cirrhosis: 
                • Causes: Chronic alcoholism, viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease. 
                • Impact: Scarring and fibrosis, leading to impaired liver function. 
            3. Fatty Liver Disease: 
                • Causes: Obesity, diabetes, excessive alcohol consumption. 
                • Impact: Accumulation of fat in liver cells, leading to inflammation. 
            4. Liver Cancer (Hepatocellular Carcinoma): 
                • Causes: Chronic viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, alcohol abuse. 
                • Impact: Uncontrolled cell growth in the liver. 
            5. Hemochromatosis: 
                • Causes: Genetic disorder leading to excessive iron absorption. 
                • Impact: Iron accumulation in the liver, causing damage. 

        .Reasons for Liver Diseases:
            1. Viral Infections: Hepatitis viruses (A, B, C) directly attack liver cells. 
            2. Alcohol Abuse: Chronic alcohol consumption leads to inflammation and cirrhosis. 
            3. Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD): Linked to obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. 

        .Impact of Cardiovascular Dysfunction on the Liver:
            1. Congestive Heart Failure (CHF): 
                • Impact: Reduced blood flow to the liver, leading to congestion and impaired function. 
                • Complication: Hepatic congestion and hepatomegaly. 
            2. Ischemic Heart Disease: 
                • Impact: Reduced oxygen supply to the liver, affecting its metabolic functions. 
                • Complication: May contribute to liver dysfunction and damage. 
            3. Portal Hypertension: 
                • Impact: Increased pressure in the portal vein, affecting blood flow through the liver. 
                • Complication: Can lead to conditions like cirrhosis. 
            4. Coagulation Abnormalities: 
                • Impact: Liver dysfunction can affect clotting factor synthesis, leading to bleeding disorders.

        .Conclusion: 
            -The liver plays a pivotal role in maintaining metabolic homeostasis, detoxification, and synthesis of essential proteins. Various diseases, influenced by viral infections, alcohol abuse, or metabolic disorders, can compromise liver function. Cardiovascular dysfunction can impact the liver through reduced blood flow, contributing to conditions such as hepatic congestion and impaired coagulation. Understanding the interplay between liver function and cardiovascular health is crucial for comprehensive patient care. Regular monitoring and lifestyle modifications are essential in preventing and managing liver-related complications.

        .Case 1
            -The patient is a 62-year-old female who was admitted to the intensive care unit with a diagnosis of bilateral lower lobe pneumonia. The chart review reveals a history of smoking and chronic bronchitis. 
            -The chest radiograph demonstrated infiltrates at the bases of the lungs.
            -A PT Consult is received.

            Questions
                1.Just based on what you see here what are your top concerns?
                    -Possible considerations - lower lobe pneumonia leading with consolidation leading to areas of reduced ventilation. This patient has a high risk of atelectasis associated with chronic underventilation in the lower lobes, low SpO2, changes in pH/ABGs, and other possible concerning factors. If in the ICU the patient likely is very ill and may even possibly be mechanically ventilated. It would be important to possibly also know viral vs bacterial, but with the consolidation just in the lower lobes you may think more bacterial pneumonia, as viral would have more lung regions affected, but this is not always the case. The history of smoking and chronic bronchitis also can mean that the patient may have general poor health and possibly have other co-morbidities associated with heart health.
                2.Think about the PT examination. What components would be included for this patient and why? The examinations should address your top concerns, and also propose some findings based on the case.
                    -This patient would require careful monitoring of vitals, especially BP and SpO2. General
                    observations of the patient may reveal signs of respiratory distress with reduced depth and
                    pattern of expiration an inspiration, they may possibly be hyperventilating and/or have
                    increased accessory muscle use in light of the restrictive lung condition with impacted bilateral
                    lower lobes. The patient will also have some form of supplemental oxygen.
                    Possible Answers and explanation/findings:
                        -Tracheal deviation IF there is an associated lung collapse.
                        -Chest wall expansion with poor bilateral expansion in the lower lobular region along with an expansion of <3-5 cm from midline. If was unilateral lobe, then would see a delay or reduced expansion in the affected lung region vs the unaffected lung.
                        -Tactile fremitus with an increased or decreased fremitus or sound transmission compared to the upper/mid lobes. The increased vs decreased will be dependent on the thickness and severity of the consolidation.
                        -Mediate percussion with a dull sound is heard over the dense areas of consolidation
                        -Voice transmission testing with increased vs decreased transmission over the areas of consolidation, which is dependent on the thickness or vicious nature of the secretions.
                        -Lung sounds with bronchial sounds where vesicular should be in the lower/outer lobe region, which can indicate the presence of secretions. Crackles on inspiration over the lower lobes where the secretions are located, especially if they are loose or less viscous. There may also be absent or decreased breath sounds over the areas of consolidation depending how thick and viscous the secretions are in the area
                3.Based on your findings would you treat, treat and refer, or refer out completely.
                    N/A

        .Case 2
            -A 65-year-old female was admitted to the hospital 2 days ago with complaints of acute chest pain and SOB. She has a hx of HTN, obesity and lives a sedentary lifestyle. She also a 50 pk per year smoking history.
            -As you approach the acute care room what may be the initial observations you need to make?
                You would make some cardiovascular and pulmonary observations, such as:
                    -Signs of respiratory distress, thorax inspection, respiratory depth and pattern, or any presence of digital clubbing as an indicator of chronic oxygen deprivation
                    -Color of the patient to check for presence of pallor vs redness
                    -General appearance, such as, level of consciousness, appearance of accessory mm use, jugular vein
                    -Appearance of chest wall shape and size
                    -Body habitus and the location of adipose tissue, as the patient is obese and with increased adipose tissue in the abdominal or neck region can impact lung function
                    -Presence of edema, which could indicate poor peripheral vascular health and/or poor heart function/compliance

            .Questions
                1.What pertinent history would you ascertain before performing a physical exam (from medical chart review and patient)?
                    -It would be important obtaining as much information from the chart prior to entering the patient room, such as:
                        -Diagnosis and date of event, as with acute chest pain and hx of HTN it would important to know if a final dx of angina vs MI was obtained
                        -ECG outcomes and any other cardiac dx testing, imaging studies (patient may have had a cardiac cath) that can assist in determining what may be going on at the level of the heart
                        -Lab values, such as, CBCs, coagulation profiles, ABGs, troponins
                        -Medications, those the patient is currently on and those the patient takes regularly
                        -Vital signs
                        -In the patient room you it will be important to clarify any outstanding questions you may have on patient medical history and current hospital course, as well as, social history and family environment/home situation to make an appropriate DC rec
                2.What CV physical examination findings may you expect at rest, with mobility, and recovery?
                    -The patient is sedentary, obese and a smoker with high BP, therefore monitoring vitals closely will be of utmost importance, and this patient may have high BP and HR at rest and with mobility, along with possibly dyspnea, SOB and reduced SpO2. At rest heart sounds would be assessed, and if the patient had a recent MI or has the presence of heart failure heart sounds may be abnormal with presence of S3 or S4 sound with poor ventricular health and may have a murmur present based on the turbulent nature of blood flow through the heart.
                3.If this patient was in the outpatient setting seeing you for a dx of “Shoulder Pain,” what CV examination techniques would you need to obtain prior to proceeding to evaluate the orthopedic issue?
                    -Angina and/or myocardial infarction (MI) can appear as arm and shoulder pain that can be misdiagnosed as arthritis or other musculoskeletal pathologic conditions, therefore, it would be important to take your BP and HR assessment and look for any other signs of heart related symptoms, such as chest pain, sweating, SPB, etc

        .Case 3
            -A patient is admitted to the hospital with complaints of progressive DOE along with increased sputum production over the last week. He has a history of COPD, emphysema and cor pulmonole. He is referred to PT.

            Questions
                1.What questions would you ask regarding his DOE?
                    • Can you climb a single flight of stairs without SOB?
                    • Does is resolve with rest?
                    • Is it associated with a cough?
                    • Is it relieved by changes in body position, such as, leaning on arms or pursed lip breathing?
                    • Does SOB come on suddenly and does it happen at night or in a lying down position?
                2.Prior to initiating a functional assessment what observations would you expect to see? 
                    With the COPD you may see increased hypertrophy of the accessory muscles and a barrel chest.
                    With dyspnea and sputum production the patient may have increased RR and reduced depth of
                    breathing, possibly even appear to be hyperventilating. Due to the chronic condition of COPD
                    there may be the presence of pallor and/or digital clubbing due to reduced oxygen status
                3.After initial assessment you find:
                    RR 24
                    HR 84
                    BP 150/60
                    Decreased lower costal expansion; use of accessory mm
                    Decreased breath sounds in the bases of the lungs and wheezes
                    O2 sats 90% on 2 L of O2
                    6-minute walk test 250 meters
                        (Γ)Normal Values for the 6-Minute Walk Test
                            - Healthy Adults:
                              - Males:  
                                - Average distance: 500–700 meters (approximately 1,640–2,300 feet).

                              - Females:  
                                - Average distance: 400–600 meters (approximately 1,310–1,970 feet).
                              - These values vary based on age, height, weight, and activity level.

                            - Age-Specific Norms (Approximate):
                              - 20–29 years: ~700 meters.

                              - 40–49 years: ~600 meters.
                              - 50–59 years: ~550 meters.
                              - 60–69 years: ~500 meters.
                              - 70+ years: ~400–450 meters.
                4.What concerns do you have for this patient based on this assessment?
                    The presence of decreased lower costal expansion; use of accessory mm, decreased breath
                    sounds in the bases of the lungs and wheezes mean that the patient has lung involvement,
                    which may be a product of his R sided heart failure leading to pulmonary edema. His O2 sats
                    90% on 2 L of O2 along with a very low distance on the 6 MWT indicates very poor exercise
                    tolerance and status.

        .Case 4
            -A 60 yo male patient presents to you in outpatient PT with a diagnosis of R shoulder pain. The patient has little information available to you in his chart, but you are able to find some information, including: factory worker for 35 years (still working, but now on the office side), history of prostate cancer 15 years ago where he underwent localized radiation (non-malignant), smoking (unsure if has quit yet), alcoholism (but has not had a drink for over 5 years) and had a previous bout with this shoulder pain about 6 months ago (you see he saw his PCP for it, and had an  x-ray that was clear and was given pain medications only) He presents to you in a seated position in the waiting room, you notice he has been coughing quite a bit while sitting there. You walk him back to the exam room….

            Questions
                1.Just based on what you see here what are your top concerns?
                    This patient has many concerning red flags that would need to be addressed prior to proceeding
                    with the should examination. While R should pain isn’t necessarily the referral side for angina or
                    MI, it still cannot be ruled out, and based on his history of smoking you would need to perform a
                    vitals exam. One large concern here is the history of working in a factory, smoking, alcoholism,
                    and cancer, which is coupled with this cough. It would be important to tease out all this
                    information and also assess if there is any neck pain involved, and/or if the current pain is
                    mechanical in nature, as with this history you would want to screen out for any red flags related
                    to malignancy in the lung region
                2.Think about the PT examination.  What components would be included for this patient and why? The examinations should address your top concerns, and also propose some findings based on the case.
                    The screening of the pulmonary and cardiac system would be important, as for reasons stated
                    above to determine MSK vs pleuropulmonary issues, and this then would lead into possibly a
                    more thorough examination, such as, heart sounds, breath sounds, chest expansion, and
                    mechanical/position examination techniques to determine any sinister pathological process.
                    Let’s propose you determine that the patient has been coughing but is not sick otherwise, has
                    pain with deep breathing, reduced chest wall expansion on the right upper chest, and
                    reduced/absent breath sounds in the R upper chest region. You were unable to reproduce the
                    shoulder pain with any mechanical movements, and he expressed some presence of neck pain
                    on the R.
                3.Based on your findings would you treat, treat and refer, or refer out completely?
                    Based on the findings proposed above I would refer out to the patient’s PCP and not treat the
                    patient at this time due to the lung findings. I would want to have the patient worked up for any
                    possible lung pathology that would not be able to be treated within the PT scope of practice at
                    this time, and have the patient return when medically cleared.

..2.6. Module 2 Quiz (!!Q)
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    Question 1
    The optimal position for auscultation of the lung sounds is which of the following? 
      Supine 
      Side lying 
      Sitting 
      Prone 

      Sitting
        For auscultation of the lung sounds, the optimal position is for the patient to be sitting to permit auscultation of the entire lung space, including both the anterior and posterior chest wall. 

    Question 2 (!!F)
    Wheezes are described by which of the following auscultated sounds? 
      Soft, low-pitched sounds heard primarily during inspiration 
      Discontinuous adventitious lung sounds similar to brief bursts of popping bubbles 
      An abnormal sound similar to two pieces of leather or sandpaper rubbing together 
      Continuous adventitious lung sounds with a constant pitch and varying duration 

      Continuous adventitious lung sounds with a constant pitch and varying duration
        Wheezes are continuous adventitious lung sounds with a constant pitch and varying duration. They are most frequently heard on exhalation and are associated with airway obstruction. 
     
    Question 3
    Which of the following conditions would transmission of lung sound increase? 
      An increase in lung tissue density such as consolidation. 
      A decrease in lung tissue density 
      Shallow breaths are taken. 
      The distance between the airway and the stethoscope is increased such as obesity. 

      An increase in lung tissue density such as consolidation.
        A pathological condition in the lungs can change the transmission of the sounds. An increase in lung tissue density causes increased sound transmission.
     
    Question 4
    Egophony is BEST described by which of the following in a patient with emphysema dominant COPD? 
      The said phrase “99” is heard more loudly than normal 
      The said phrase “E” is heard much softer than normal as “A.” 
      Whispered words are heard more loudly than normal 
      The said phase “E” is heard more loudly than normal as “A.” 

      The said phrase “E” is heard much softer than normal as “A.” 
        Egophony is having the patient say “E” and what is auscultated is “A.” In an emphysema patient the auscultated “A” is much more softer than normal due to hyperinflation from emphysema disease. 

    Question 5 (!!F)
    Auscultation at the "lower left sternal border", approximately the fourth to fifth intercostal spaces, describes the area where which of the following heart sounds is heard? 
      Aortic area 
      Pulmonary area 
      Tricuspid area 
      Mitral area 

      Tricuspid area
        The tricuspid area is located at the lower left sterna border, approximately the fourth to fifth intercostals space.
     
    ``Question 6 (!!F)
    Which of the following heart sounds, when heard early in diastole, is a diagnostic sign of congestive heart failure? 
      S1 
      S2 
      S3 
      S4 

      S3
        A third heart sound (S3) occurs early in diastole while the ventricle is rapidly filling (immediately following S2). It is a key diagnostic sign for congestive heart failure.

    Question 7
    Lung sounds auscultated in the latter half of inspiration that are commonly associated with pulmonary edema are BEST described as which of the following?
      Wheezes 
      Crackles 
      Bronchovesicular 
      Pleural Rub 

      Crackles
        Crackles are discontinuous adventitious lung sounds that sound like a brief burst of popping bubbles. Peripheral airways can collapse owing to atelectasis, pulmonary edema, fibrosis, or compression from pleural effusion, and often crackles auscultated with these pathological conditions in the latter half of inspiration.

    Question 8
    Which of the palpation techniques assists in the confirmation of consolidation in an area of the lung?
      Palpation of the mediastinum for tracheal shift 
      Palpation of chest wall movement or asymmetry 
      Palpation of fremitus (vibration) when the patient says “99” 
      Palpation of the anterior chest wall with the thumb tips meeting and the xiphoid 

      Palpation of fremitus (vibration) when the patient says “99” 
        Fremitus is defined as the vibration that is produced by the voice or by the presence of secretions in the airways and is transmitted to the chest wall and palpated by the hand. When fremitus is increased, the suspicion of consolidation is supported.

    Question 9
    A patient who presents with back pain and upon assessment of palpating the abdominal aortic region you find a 4 cm width abdominal aorta pulsation and with this you would continue to treat the back, but still refer back to the PCP. 
      True 
      False

      False 
        This patient is an immediate referral back, possibly even to the ED due to the nature of the pulsation, especially if this is unknown. This could be unstable and lead to increased mortality if left untreated. 

    Question 10
    When performing liver palpation you feel a positive test with the liver extending 1-2 cm past where it normally would be felt. You feel a hard irregular boarder that is non-tender. This is indicative of heart failure related liver dysfunction. 
      True 
      False 

      False
        Heart Failure related:
            enlarged, soft, smooth and tender.
        Metastases realted:
            enlarged, hard, irregular, nodular, non-tender.

    .Module Introduction
        Module 3 will cover cardiovascular and pulmonary physical therapy interventions. This module will cover how the examination and evaluation findings can lead into specific treatment interventions that can address specific cardiovascular and pulmonary impairments.  We will delve into treatment plan development and modification for those with primary and secondary cardiopulmonary disorders in all physical therapy settings. This module will expose you to procedures that will act as a foundation for all the other modules, as well as lab-based materials that will be practiced in the immersions.  This module will also cover some aspects of discharge planning for the physical therapist in the acute care setting, as that is a large part of the plan of care and treatment plan development that we will consider throughout this module.  

    .Learning Objectives
        Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to:
            Apply the use of the Hypothesis-Oriented Algorithm for Clinicians for intervention selection & re-examination in patients with cardiopulmonary dysfunction.
            Describe and administer the six components of the patient/client management model (Examination, Evaluation, Diagnosis, Prognosis, Intervention, Assessment of Outcome) to patients with cardiopulmonary dysfunction.
            Develop a treatment plan and select appropriate interventions for patients with primary and secondary cardiopulmonary disorders reflecting the nature of the individual case based on client signs and symptoms, and consider the various settings:  inpatient (acute care, rehab, skilled nursing), outpatient, home, and community.
            Modify physical therapy intervention and plan of care when a patient exhibits signs of intolerance.
            Identify the role of the physical therapist and other members of the health care team when recommending, selecting, and performing interventions on patients with cardiopulmonary impairments.
            Design and administer an intervention plan including, but not limited to:  percussion, breathing exercises, positioning, strengthening, postural drainage, conditioning (aerobic exercise), relaxation techniques, energy conservation, suctioning, cough techniques, patient and family education.

8.Introduction to the Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Physical Therapy Plan of Care
    ..3.2. Introduction to Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Physical Therapy Plan of Care
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    .('Intro to CVP Physical Therapy POC.pdf')
        .Elements of Patient/Client Management ('Elements of Patient-Client Management') (See [CP2_Elements of Patient-Client Management])

        .(Eval.)Evaluation 
            • Synthesis of all information: 
                • Eval.1.Patient history 
                • Eval.2.Medical chart review 
                • Eval.3.Interview of with patient and family 
                • Eval.4.Systems review 
                • Eval.5.Physical examination

        .PT Diagnosis 
            • Classification into a practice pattern 
            • Primary dysfunctions to guide the therapist toward interventions that should be addressed initially 
            • Examples of cardiovascular/pulmonary related PT practice patterns: 
                • 6A: Primary prevention/risk reduction for cardiovascular/pulmonary disorders 
                • 6B: Impaired aerobic capacity/endurance associated with deconditioning 
                • 6C: Impaired ventilation, respiration/gas exchange, and aerobic capacity/endurance associated with airway clearance dysfunction 
                • 6D: Impaired aerobic capacity/endurance associated with cardiovascular pump dysfunction or failure 
                • 6E: Impaired ventilation and respiration/gas exchange associated with ventilatory pump dysfunction or failure 
                • 6F: Impaired ventilation and respiration/gas exchange associated with respiratory failure

        .Prognosis
            • Plan of care is developed based on the prognosis 
            • Typically, statement is included in plan of care

        .Plan of Care 
            • Plan of care includes the following: 
                1. Overall goals stated in measurable terms that indicate the predicted level of improvement in functioning 
                2. A general statement of interventions to be used 
                3. Proposed duration and frequency 
                4. Anticipated discharge plans

        .Intervention 
            Int.1. Aimed at treatment of impairments 
            Int.2. Must re-assess the patient to determine impact 
            Int.3. Must match examination findings and goals 
            Int.4. Improve patient outcomes 
            Int.5. Once complete evaluation is performed, design intervention plan aimed at: 
                Int.5.1. Improved secretion clearance 
                Int.5.2. Improve ventilation & breathing patterns 
                Int.5.3. Improved exercise tolerance or functional activity tolerance 
                Int.5.4. Postural re-training for improved ventilation 
                Int.5.5. Relaxation & Energy Conservation 
                Int.5.6. Chest wall mobility 

        .Cardiovascular & Pulmonary Plan of Care
            1. Understanding Cardiovascular & Pulmonary Plan of Care Key Terms and Concepts: 
                • Plan of Care: A comprehensive strategy outlining interventions and expected outcomes for cardiovascular and pulmonary conditions. 
                • Diagnosis: The physical therapist's classification of the patient's primary dysfunction for targeted interventions. 
                • Prognosis: Prediction of the patient's optimal function level and the estimated duration for improvement. 
                • Practice Patterns: Defined categories from the APTA guide, aiding therapists in selecting interventions. 

                Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                    1. What is the purpose of a Plan of Care?
                        • Answer: The Plan of Care guides interventions to achieve optimal outcomes for cardiovascular and pulmonary patients. 
                    ``2. How does PT diagnosis differ from medical diagnosis? 
                        • Answer: PT diagnosis focuses on functional limitations, guiding the therapist to specific interventions, unlike medical diagnoses.
                    3. Why is Prognosis crucial in a Plan of Care?
                        • Answer: Prognosis predicts optimal function levels and sets the expected duration for improvement, aiding in goal-setting. 

            2. Components of Plan of Care 
                Key Terms and Concepts: 
                    • Overall Goal: Measurable target indicating the predicted level of improvement in functioning. 
                    • Interventions: Specific strategies addressing the primary dysfunctions, e.g., airway clearance or ambulation. 
                    • Duration and Frequency: Proposed time and frequency of treatment.
                        How can I understand and learn how to apply this in practice? (!!)
                    • Discharge Plans: Anticipated plans post-treatment, often applied in hospital or acute care settings. 

                Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                    1. Why is an Overall Goal crucial in the Plan of Care?
                        • Answer: It provides a measurable target, outlining the predicted level of improvement in the patient's functioning. 
                    2. What are Discharge Plans, and why are they important?
                        • Answer: Discharge Plans anticipate post-treatment steps, ensuring a smooth transition and preventing relapse. 
                    3. Tailoring Interventions for Cardiovascular & Pulmonary Conditions 

                Key Terms and Concepts: 
                    • System-specific Interventions: Targeting impacted areas, e.g., airway clearance or functional endurance improvement. 
                    • Ambulation with Intensity Parameters: Enhancing functional endurance through guided ambulation. 
                    • Functional Limitations: Impact of the condition on the patient's daily functioning.

                    Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                        1. How are interventions tailored for Cardiovascular & Pulmonary conditions?
                            • Answer: They address specific dysfunctions, such as airway clearance or improving functional endurance through guided ambulation. 
                        2. What is the significance of targeting Functional Limitations?
                            • Answer: Understanding how the condition affects daily functioning helps tailor interventions for optimal outcomes. 
                        4. Next Steps in Cardiovascular & Pulmonary Plan of Care 

                Key Terms and Concepts: 
                    • Detailed Intervention Development: Delving into specifics in developing treatment interventions. 
                    • Cardio-Pulmonary Physical Therapy Plan of Care: Comprehensive strategy combining examination findings, diagnosis, prognosis, and targeted interventions.

                    Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                        1. What is the focus of the next lectures in Cardiovascular & Pulmonary Plan of Care? 
                            • Answer: The next lectures will delve into the specifics of developing treatment interventions for cardiovascular and pulmonary conditions. 
                        2. How is the Cardio-Pulmonary Physical Therapy Plan of Care formulated?
                            • Answer: It combines examination findings, diagnosis, prognosis, and targeted interventions for a comprehensive approach.

9.Acute Cardiovascular & Pulmonary Physical Therapy Intervention
    ..3.3. Interventions for Acute Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Conditions
