    .('Interventions for Acute CP Conditions.pdf')
        .Physical Therapy & the Hospitalized Patient 
            N/A

        .Loss of Function 
            • Multiple factors contribute to loss of function 
                • Prolonged hospitalization 
                • Acute inflammation 
                • Severity of illness 
                • Marginal baseline function 
                • Exposure to corticosteroids 
                • Neuromuscular blockers 
                • Prolonged immobilization 
                • Length of stay 

        .Acute Cardiopulmonary Conditions 
            • Disease in which O2 transport system fails to meet immediate demand 
            • Acute cardiopulmonary dysfunction is often associated with: 
                • Ischemic CVD 
                • COPD 
                • Postoperative pulmonary complications 
                • HTN 
                • DM 
                • Obesity

        .Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Effects of Immobilization 
            • Cardiovascular: 
                • Increased basal heart rate 
                • Decreased max heart rate 
                • Decreased max oxygen uptake 
                • Orthostatic hypotension 
                • Increased risk VTE 
                • Decreased total blood volume 
                • Decreased Hemoglobin concentration 
            • Pulmonary
                • Decreased vital capacity 
                • Decreased residual volume 
                • Decreased PaO2 
                • Impaired ability to clear secretions 
                • Increased ventilation-perfusion mismatch

        .Conditions Associated with Acute Cardiopulmonary Dysfunction 
            Conditions
                Practice Pattern
                    Associated clinical findings
            ------------------------------------
            -C1.Conditions: Obesity, cigarette smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia Type 2 diabetes 
                Practice Pattern 6A: Primary prevention/risk reduction for cardiovascular/pulmonary disorders 
                    Associated clinical findings: Hypoventilation, atelectasis, CO2 retention, resting SBP >140 mm Hg
            -C2.Conditions: Prolonged immobilization, sedentary lifestyle 
                Practice Pattern 6B: Impaired aerobic capacity/endurance associated with deconditioning 
                    Associated clinical findings: Elevated resting heart rate, early fatigue, dyspnea on exertion
            -C3.Conditions: Cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, acute bronchitis, pneumonia, lung abscess, asbestosis, inhalation burns, asthma, pulmonary fibrosis 
                -Practice Pattern 6C: Impaired ventilation, respiration/gas exchange, and aerobic capacity/endurance associated with airway clearance dysfunction 
                    -Associated clinical findings: Cough productive of more than 30 mL of secretions per 24 hours, fever, shortness of breath, hypoxemia, CO2 retention, respiratory acidosis, decreased FEV1
            -C4.Conditions: Congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease, diseases of aortic and mitral valves, cardiomyopathy, endocarditis, shock, peripheral arterial disease, congenital heart anomalies 
                -Practice Pattern 6D: Impaired aerobic capacity/endurance associated with cardiovascular pump dysfunction or failure 
                    -Associated clinical findings: Shortness of breath, jugular venous distension, S3 heart sound, crackles on auscultation, decreased ejection fraction, cyanosis, dependent edema, claudication
            -C5.Conditions: Chest trauma, Guillain–Barré syndrome, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, muscular dystrophy, post– polio syndrome, emphysema, burns to upper body, Parkinson disease 
                -Practice Pattern 6E: Impaired ventilation and respiration/gas exchange associated with ventilatory pump dysfunction or failure 
                    -Associated clinical findings: Paradoxical breathing, inability to cough, dyspnea, reduced peak expiratory flow rate, reduced tidal volume and peak inspiratory pressure
            -C6.Conditions: Acute respiratory distress syndrome, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, sepsis 
                -Practice Pattern 6F: Impaired ventilation and respiration/gas exchange associated with respiratory failure 
                    -Associated clinical findings: Hypoxemia, abnormal chest radiograph, increased resting respiratory rate, mechanical ventilation required, fever, hypoxemia

        .Goals of Cardiopulmonary PT 
            • Improve or redistribute ventilation 
            • Increase the effectiveness of the cough mechanism and promote airway clearance 
            • Prevent postoperative pulmonary complications 
            • Improve the strength, endurance, and coordination of the muscles of ventilation 
            • Maintain or improve chest and thoracic spine mobility 
            • Correct inefficient or abnormal breathing patterns and decrease the work of breathing 
            • Promote relaxation and relieve stress 
            • Teach the person how to deal with episodes of dyspnea 
            • Improve a patient’s overall functional capacity for daily living, occupational, and recreational activities 
            • Aid in bronchial hygiene; prevent accumulation of pulmonary secretions

        .Examples of Cardiopulmonary Treatment Options 
            • Airway clearance 
                • Manual or mechanical procedures that facilitate mobilization of secretions from airways 
                • Postural drainage, percussion, vibration 
                • Cough techniques 
                • Suctioning 
            • Breathing strategies, positioning and facilitation 
                • Therapeutic positioning techniques and ventilatory movement strategies 
                • Positioning for dyspnea relief and positions for improved ventilation 
            • Breathing Exercises 
                • Pursed lip breathing, paced breathing, inspiratory holds, stacked breathing 
                • Diaphragmatic breathing 
                • Thoracic mobilization techniques

        .Physical Therapy & Mechanical Ventilation 
            • Improved outcomes in patients who are mechanically ventilated and receive PT treatment 
            • Special Considerations for Mechanically Ventilated Patients 
                • Goal of ventilated patients is to return to spontaneous breathing 
                • Weaning: process of discontinuing mechanical ventilation 
                • Combination of mechanical ventilation and medications leads to complications 

        .Special Considerations for Mechanically Ventilated Patients 
            • Intervention considerations 
                • Airway clearance 
                • Inspiratory muscle strengthening 
                • Diaphragmatic facilitation 
                • Breathing strategies 
                • Optimizing communication with other health care professionals 
                • Special attention to preoperative teaching for prevention of pulmonary complications 

        .Exercise/Mobilization 
            • Exercise in form of both endurance and strength training should be used in acute care setting to prevent and treat 
            negative neuromuscular and cardiopulmonary sequelae of critical illness 
            • Goal of endurance 
                • maximize independence and efficiency when patient performs ADLs 
            • Consider all indications and contraindications to mobilization in the acute care patient
            ----------------------------------------------------
            • Components of exercise: intensity, duration, frequency, and modes 
                • Monitor HR, BP, RR, SaO2 
                • Intensity: Borg rate of perceived exertion, monitor levels of SOB, complaints of angina 
                • Duration: amount of time patient can tolerate activity 
                • Frequency: multiple short intervals of exercise followed by rest is tolerated better in acute care 
                • Modes of exercise: Functional activities are commonly used in acute care 

        .Abnormal Responses to Exercise (!!P)
            Abnormal responses to exercise (per 1 MET level)
                Heart rate increases more than 20 to 30 bpm above resting heart rate
                Heart rate decreases below resting heart rate
                Systolic blood pressure increases more than 20 to 30 mm Hg above resting level
                Systolic blood pressure decreases more than 10 mm Hg below resting level, diziness, nausea/vomiting
                Oxygen saturation drops below prescribed level
                Patient becomes short of breath or respiratory rate increases to a level not tolerated by the patient
                ECG changes, chest pain
                Nonverbal/nonvital signs of possible exercise intolerance:
                    Color changes
                    Diaphoresis
                    Increased accessory mm use
                    Agitation, nonverbal signs of pain

        .Functional Mobility Training 
            • Bed Mobility 
            • Transfers 
            • Ambulation 
            • Gait belt is warranted 
            • Note resting vital signs 
            • Cessation of activity warranted by abnormal responses to HR, blood pressure, SpO2, or fatigue by the patient 
            • Progression of this activity is based on the patient’s response

        .Maintaining Patient Safety 
            • Must monitor patients closely to determine how the patient is responding to patient interventions 
            • Start with low-level exercise and progress slowly, monitoring patient’s response 
            • May need to add AD for safety and balance control 
            • Room set up to reduce number of obstacles prior to getting oob

        .Patient Education 
            • Patient and caregiver education is essential 
            • Decreases length of stay, decreases patient anxiety, increases quality of life, increases adherence with medical advice 
            • Must assess learner to determine areas of need and learning style & cognitive status

        .Discharge Planning 1
            • Crucial part of the physical therapist’s role in the acute care setting 
            • Role shifting and expanding from providing interventions to acting as a consultant and offering recommendations 
            • At evaluation, determination of patient’s rehabilitation potential bears on discharge disposition 
            • Patient works with discharge planner in acute care 
            • Involved in securing durable medical equipment

        .Discharge Planning 2
            • Assess current level of function vs prior level of function 
            • Report activity tolerance and rehabilitation potential to determine next level of care 
                • Home with no needs, home PT or outpatient 
                • Skilled nursing facility 
                • Acute rehabilitation or Sub-acute rehabilitation facility 
            • Detailed home set up and family support

        .Decision Tree for Discharge Planning ('Decision Tree for Discharge Planning')
            -Per a Ruperta: desorganitzat
                -DISCHARGE DESTINATION
                    -Can the patient return home once medically stable for discharge from the Acute Care Setting?
                        -Accessibility of the home Stairs, with or without railings Location of bedroom and bathroom
                        -Family or social support available Realistic and appropriate, proportional to amount of assistance required
                -Is there potential for the patient to return home?
                -Can the patient tolerate three hours of therapy daily?
                -Acute Rehabilitation Facility
                -Subacute Rehabilitation Facility

                -PT not indicated
                -Extended Care Facility or Skilled Nursing Facility
                -Basic Care Facility

                    -At wheelchair level→wheelchair and seating system, ramp, sliding board, bedside commode (drop arm), shower/tub bench, hospital bed (with trapeze)
                    -At ambulatory level→wheelchair and seating (for distances), assistive device (cane, crutches, walker), hospital bed (with trapeze), bedside commode, shower/tub bench
                -Re-evaluate for rehabilitation potential if patient status or available support changes
                -Is further PT indicated?
                -Can the patient get in and out of the house?
                -Outpatient PT until discharge
                -Home PT

        .Interventions for Acute Cardiopulmonary Conditions
            1. Understanding Acute Cardiovascular & Pulmonary Interventions Key Terms and Concepts: 
                • Acute Cardio-Pulmonary Conditions: Diseases or states where the oxygen transport system fails to meet immediate demands. 
                • Functional Loss Factors: Acute inflammation, severity of illness, exposure to corticosteroids, and prolonged immobilization. 
                • Hospital-Related Impairments: Changes in physical, cognitive, and emotional functioning due to hospitalization. 

                Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                    1. What characterizes Acute Cardio-Pulmonary Conditions?
                        • Answer: Conditions where the oxygen transport system fails, often resulting in significant periods of bed rest and associated adverse effects. 
                    2. What factors contribute to Functional Loss in hospitalized patients?
                        • Answer: Acute inflammation, severity of illness, exposure to corticosteroids, neuromuscular blockers, and prolonged immobilization. 

            2. Impact of Immobilization on Cardiovascular & Pulmonary Systems
                Key Terms and Concepts: 
                    • Effects on Systems: Impact on cardiovascular, respiratory, musculoskeletal, central nervous, and metabolic systems. 
                    • Deleterious Effects: Weakening, contractures, altered sensation, cognitive changes, and reduced bone density.

                Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                    1. How does Immobilization impact the Musculoskeletal System?
                        • Answer: It leads to weakness, contractures, and poor contraction. 
                    2. Why is Physical Therapy crucial in countering the effects of Immobilization?
                        • Answer: Physical therapy plays a vital role in mobilizing patients, preventing serious effects on various systems.
                
            3. Conditions Associated with Acute Cardio-Pulmonary Dysfunction 
                Key Terms and Concepts: 
                    • Common Conditions: Cardiovascular diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases, postoperative pulmonary complications, and complications of hypertension, diabetes, and obesity.
                    • Clinical Findings: Hypoventilation, electrolyte imbalances, and carbon dioxide retention.

                Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                1. Name a common condition associated with Acute Cardio-Pulmonary Dysfunction.
                    • Answer: Obesity, associated with clinical findings like hypoventilation, electrolyte imbalances, and carbon dioxide retention. 
                2. What is the importance of reviewing Clinical Findings in acute conditions?
                    • Answer: It helps tailor interventions to specific patient needs.

            4. Goals and Interventions for Acute Cardio-Pulmonary Patients 
                Key Terms and Concepts: 
                • Goals: Maximizing independence, improving function, and enhancing quality of life. 
                • Interventions: Airway clearance techniques, therapeutic positioning, breathing exercises, patient education, and monitored functional mobility. 

                Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                    1. What are the goals related to Cardio-Pulmonary Physical Therapy patients?
                        • Answer: Maximizing independence, improving function, and enhancing quality of life. 
                    2. Name an intervention for optimizing oxygen transport.
                        • Answer: Airway clearance techniques, therapeutic positioning, breathing exercises, and monitored functional mobility.

            5. Therapeutic Interventions for Acute Care Patients
                Key Terms and Concepts: 
                    • Mechanically Ventilated Patients: Require sedative and analgesic drugs, leading to complications like neuromuscular weakness and delirium. 
                    • Weaning Process: Coordinating physical therapy interventions to facilitate the transition from mechanical ventilation.

                Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                    1. What complications may arise in Mechanically Ventilated Patients?
                        • Answer: Complications include neuromuscular weakness, delirium, and impaired physical function. 
                    2. Why is the Weaning Process critical for patients on mechanical ventilation?
                        • Answer: It minimizes complications, reduces ICU stay, and prevents atrophy in inspiratory muscles.

            6. Exercise in the Acute Care Setting
                Key Terms and Concepts: 
                    • Endurance Training: Maximizing independence in activities of daily living (ADLs). 
                    • Components of Exercise: Intensity, duration, frequency, and mode. 

                Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                    1. What is the goal of Endurance Training in the Acute Care Setting?
                        • Answer: Maximizing independence in performing ADLs. 
                    2. How is Exercise monitored in the Acute Care Setting?
                        • Answer: Monitoring heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and using the RPE or dyspnea scale. 

            7. Functional Mobility Training and Patient Education 
                Key Terms and Concepts: 
                    • Functional Mobility Training: Initiated as soon as the patient can roll bilaterally and maintain vital parameters. 
                    • Patient Education: Essential for decreasing length of stay, reducing anxiety, and increasing adherence to medical advice.

                Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                    1. When is Functional Mobility Training initiated in the Acute Care Setting?
                        • Answer: As soon as the patient can roll bilaterally and maintains vital parameters. 
                    2. Why is Patient Education crucial in the Acute Care Setting?
                        • Answer: It decreases length of stay, reduces anxiety, and increases adherence to medical advice. 
                    
            8. Discharge Planning and Patient-Centered Care 
                Key Terms and Concepts: 
                    • Discharge Planning: Anticipating patient's needs for the next level of care. 
                    • Patient-Centered Care: Involving the patient in decision-making for optimal outcomes.

                Questions and Answers: (!!Q)
                    1. What is the role of Discharge Planning in Acute Cardio-Pulmonary Care?
                        • Answer: It anticipates the patient's needs for the next level of care and involves patient-centered decision-making.
                    2. Why is Patient Involvement crucial in Discharge Planning? 
                        • Answer: Patient involvement ensures decisions align with their preferences and leads to optimal outcomes.

            In conclusion, a comprehensive understanding of acute cardiovascular and pulmonary interventions is crucial for physical therapy students to provide effective care in the acute care hospital setting.

10.Airway Clearance Techniques
    ..3.4. Airway Clearance Techniques

    .('Airway Clearance Techniques.pdf')
        .Airway Clearance Techniques
            • Manual or mechanical procedures that facilitate mobilization of secretions from airways 
            • Optimal airway clearance choice based on pathophysiology and symptoms, stability of medical status, patient’s adherence 
            • Patient examination before, during, and after treatment provides information to judge patient tolerance and treatment effectiveness 
            • Goals: optimize airway patency, increase ventilation and perfusion matching, promote alveolar expansion, increase gas exchange
                (Γ)patency
                    Definition: The condition of being open, unobstructed, or free from blockages, especially in reference to a bodily passage or channel.
                    Synonym: Openness

        .Devices Used for Airway Clearance - Table 17-3 Summary of devices used for airway clearance

        .High Frequency Chest Wall Oscillation Devices 
            • Positive pressure air pulses are applied to the chest wall via inflatable chest or air pulse generator 
            • Oscillations cause transient flow increases in airways, loosening mucus, and producing cough like shear forces 
                • Decreased viscoelasticity of mucus 
                • Helps sputum expectoration 
                • Improve airflow in low lung volumes

        .High Frequency Chest Wall Oscillation Device - The Vest ('The Vest')

        .Positive Expiratory Pressure Devices 
            • Allows more air to enter the peripheral airways via collateral channels 
            • The pressurized air goes behind secretions to prevent alveoli from collapsing 
                • Face-mask or mouthpiece 
                • One-way valve 
                • Manometer 
            • Benefits: 
                • Gives independence to patients with COPD and other pulmonary disorders 
                • Improves compliance 
                • Decreases hospital length of stay

        .TheraPEP - Example of Positive Expiratory Pressure Device ('TheraPEP')

        .Vibratory Positive Expiratory Pressure 
            • A controlled vibration system which produces positive expiratory pressure and cyclic oscillation of airways during expiration 
                • Improves lung function and oxygenation 
                • Facilitates mucus expectoration 
            • Flutter device is gravity dependent while acapella can be used in any position 
                • Patients must be able to generate sufficient airflow  to cause vibration of steel ball in flutter 
                • Acapella comes in high flow and low flow

        .Vibratory Expiratory Pressure Devices - Acapella and Flutter ('Acapella and Flutter')

        .Mechanical Percussor ('Mechanical Percussor')
            • Variable speeds 
            • Provides gentle mechanical vibrations to remove secretions 
            • Less frequently used in hospital setting 

        .Mechanical Insufflator ('Mechanical Insufflator')
            • Uses positive pressure to deliver maximal inhalation, followed abruptly by a switch to negative pressure in the upper airway 
            • This aims at simulating the airflow changes that occur during a cough, thereby assisting sputum production 
            • Found to be most effective for patients with neuromuscular disease

        .Additional Airway Clearance Devices 
            • Oral high frequency oscillation device('')
                • Improves clearance of CO2 
                • Used when conservative measures fail 
            • Intrapulmonary percussive ventilation device('')
                • Combines aerosol inhalation and internal thoracic percussion via mouthpiece 
            • Cornet device('')
                • Vibratory positive expiratory pressure device to improve mucus expectoration and oxygenation 

        .Postural Drainage ('Postural Drainage')
            • Assumption of one or more body positions that allow gravity to assist with draining secretions from each lung segment 
                • “Good lung down” 
            • Positions can be modified to address precaution or relative contraindication 
            • Positioning requires adjustable bed, pillows, blanket rolls 
            • Priority given to treating most affected lung segment first 
            • Encourage deep breathing and coughing 
            • Most appropriate for mucus producing conditions, especially cystic fibrosis

        .Postural Drainage – Procedure 
            1. Begin any treatment session using auscultation techniques to determine area(s) of need. 
            2. Bronchodilators, mucolytic agents, water, or saline may be nebulized and inhaled before postural drainage to decrease thickness of sputum thereby enhancing secretion removal 
            3. Prior to beginning a treatment session review and choose technique(s) to enhance drainage 
                • Alone without hands on techniques OR add 
                • Percussions or vibrations over chest wall to further loosen mucus 
            4. Perform postural drainage by properly positioning patient while simultaneously performing technique(s) to enhance drainage from the lung area of interest 
                • STOP to allow significant coughing to occur. 
                • STOP the manual technique 3-5 minutes per lobe to auscultate again 
                • Re-do this portion of treatment until auscultation produces maximally reduced pathological breath sounds 
            5. After treatment position patient in bed in the same position that was most useful in drainage for 5-10 mins or longer if tolerated 

        .Percussion and Vibration ('Percussion and Vibration')
            • Percussion 
                • Chest percussion aimed at loosening retained secretions (manually or mechanically) 
            • Vibration 
                • Performed manually or mechanically and utilized in postural drainage positions to clear secretions

        .Clinical Tips Regarding Percussion ('Clinical Tips Regarding Percussion')
            Right Cupped Hand
            Wrong Flat Hand
            Manual Percussion
            Manual Vibration 

        .Chest Vibration Vest ('')

        .Precautions and Relative Contraindications for Postural Drainage ('Trendelenburg position') (!!P)
            Box 17-1 Precautions and relative contradictions for postural drainage 
                Precautions
                    • Pulmonary edema 
                    • Hemoptysis 
                    • Massive obesity 
                    • Large pleural effusion 
                    • Massive ascites 
                Relative contraindications
                    • Increased intracranial pressure 
                    • Hemodynamically unstable 
                    • Recent esophageal anastomosis 
                    • Recent spinal fusion or injury 
                    • Recent head trauma 
                    • Diaphragmatic hernia 
                    • Recent eye surgery

        .Precautions and Relative Contraindications for Percussion and Vibration (!!P)
            Box 17-2 Precautions and Relative Contraindications for Percussion and Vibration
                Precautions
                    • Uncontrolled bronchospasm 
                    • Osteoporosis 
                    • Rib fractures 
                    • Metastatic cancer to ribs 
                    • Tumor obstruction of airway 
                    • Anxiety 
                    • Coagulopathy 
                    • Convulsive or seizure disorder 
                    • Recent pacemaker placement 
                Relative Contraindications
                    • Hemoptysis 
                    • Untreated tension pneumothorax 
                    • Platelet count below 20,000 per mm3 
                    • Unstable hemodynamic status 
                    • Open wounds, burns in thoracic area 
                    • Pulmonary embolism 
                    • Subcutaneous emphysema 
                    • Recent skin grafts or flaps on thorax 

        .Cough Techniques and Assists 
            • Effective cough consists of four stages 
                1. Inspiration 
                2. Closure of glottis 
                3. Abdominal and intercostal muscle contraction 
                4. Forceful expulsion of air 
            • Surgical patients: instruct in splinting 
            • Ineffective cough can lead to retained secretions, atelectasis, hypoxemia, and respiratory failure

        .Instructions for Teaching Effective Cough 
            • Position patient for allowing trunk extension and flexion 
                • seated or side lying usually recommended 
            • Maximize inspiratory phase with spinal extension and opening of the chest wall 
            • Maximize intrathoracic and intra-abdominal pressure with forward flexion of the spine while performing the cough 
                • May instruct patient to perform a self abdominal thrust at end of cough 
            • Orient patient to timing and trunk movements prior to performance

        .Splinting During Coughing ('Splinting During Coughing')

        .Huff and Cough Technique
            • Helps loosen secretions and may induce a cough 
            • Good for post surgical patients 
            • Steps: 
                1. Sit up straight with chin tilted slightly up and mouth open. 
                2. Take a slow deep breath to fill lungs 
                3. Hold breath for two or three seconds. 
                4. Open the mouth and force the air out of your lungs with the mouth open as if trying to fog up a mirror 
                5. Repeat this maneuver two more times and then follow with one strong cough to clear mucus from the larger airways. 
                6. Do a cycle of four to five huff coughs as part of your airway clearance.

        .Active Cycle Breathing (See 'Active Cycle Breathing') ('26 Active Cycle Breathing.png')
            • Consists of a series of maneuvers performed by patient to emphasize independence in secretion clearance and thoracic expansion
                Breathing control 20/30 seconds ↓
                    3-4 deep breaths ↓
                        Breathing control ↓
                            3-4 deep breaths ↓
                                Breathing control ↓
                                    Huffing followed by cough if needed ↑

        .Manual Hyperinflation and Airway Suctioning ('Manual Hyperinflation and Airway Suctioning')
            • Suctioning is performed routinely for intubated patients to facilitate the removal of secretions and stimulate the cough reflex 
            • Patients with artificial airways can be instructed in huffing and cough assist techniques 
            • Suction catheter can reach only to level of mainstem bronchi 
            • Suctioning should be the last resort 
            • Lavage can be used to stimulate reflexive cough

        .Airway Clearance Techniques   
            Key Terms and Concepts 
                1. Airway Clearance Techniques: 
                    • Definition: Manual or mechanical procedures facilitating the mobilization of secretions from the Airways. 
                    • Examples: Postural drainage, percussion, effective cough, suctioning. 
                2. Goals of Airway Clearance: 
                    • Optimizing Airway Patency: Ensuring clear air passages. 
                    • Increasing Ventilation and Perfusion: Enhancing gas exchange. 
                    • Matching Alveolar Expansion: Promoting optimal lung function. 
                3. Devices for Airway Clearance: 
                    • High-Frequency Chest Wall Oscillation Device (HFCWD): 
                        • Example: The Vest. 
                        • Usage: Positive pressure air pulses via a vest to loosen mucus. 
                    • Positive Expiratory Pressure Device: 
                        • Example: The Therapy. 
                        • Usage: Increases air entering Airways, aiding secretion clearance. 
                    • Vibratory Positive Expiratory Pressure Devices: 
                        • Examples: Flutter, Acapella. 
                        • Usage: Controlled vibrations aid in mucus expectoration. 
                    • Mechanical Percussor: 
                        • Usage: Provides gentle vibrations to mobilize secretions. 
                    • Mechanical Insufflator: 
                        • Usage: Positive pressure followed by negative pressure to induce coughing. 

                    Questions and Answers (!!Q)
                        Q1. What are airway clearance techniques? 
                            A1: Airway clearance techniques are procedures, either manual or mechanical, that help mobilize secretions from the Airways, aiding in effective breathing. 
                        Q2. Name a device for airway clearance in cystic fibrosis. 
                            A2: The Vest, a High-Frequency Chest Wall Oscillation Device (HFCWD), is commonly used for patients with cystic fibrosis.
                        Q3. What is the purpose of positive expiratory pressure devices? 
                            A3: Positive Expiratory Pressure Devices aid in increasing air entering peripheral Airways, promoting collateral channels for secretion clearance. 
                        Q4. How does vibratory positive expiratory pressure help? 
                            A4: Devices like Flutter and Acapella provide positive expiratory pressure and oscillations, facilitating mucus expectoration. 
                        Q5. Explain the mechanism of a mechanical percussor. 
                            A5: Mechanical percussors use variable-speed vibrations against the chest wall to loosen and mobilize retained secretions.

                Summary 
                    • Airway clearance techniques are crucial for patients with impaired mucociliary transport or excessive pulmonary secretions. 
                    • Devices such as HFCWDs, positive expiratory pressure devices, vibratory devices, and mechanical percussors aid in secretion mobilization. 
                    • Postural drainage involves specific body positions to use gravity for secretion drainage. 
                    • Percussion and vibration techniques enhance drainage by providing additional force. 
                    • Cough techniques like effective cough, huffing, and active cycle breathing promote independent secretion clearance. 
                    • Suctioning is reserved for patients unable to clear secretions independently and requires specialized training.

            Remember, patient assessment and individualization of techniques are crucial for successful airway clearance.

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
11.Breathing Strategies & Training Interventions
    ..3.5. Breathing Strategies and Training Interventions
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    .('Breathing Strategies & Training Interventions.pdf')
        -------------------------------------- Breathing Strategies
        .Therapeutic Positioning Techniques and Ventilatory Movement Strategies 
            • Assist with progression from dependence to independence in mobility and breathing 
                • Indicated for patients who have weakness of the diaphragm 
                • Inspiratory effort breathing with upper extremity movement 
                • Expiration effort breathing with upper extremity movement 
                • Progress breathing techniques to functional activity 

        .Patient Positioning for Improved Ventilation 
            • Position of one’s body can greatly influence breathing and movement 
            • Position of body greatly influences ventilation and respiration 
                • Use of prone positioning is beneficial for improved oxygenation

        .Positioning for Dyspnea Relief ('Positioning for Dyspnea Relief')
            • Arms supported allows the accessory breathing muscles to act on the rib cage allowing more expansion for inspiration

        .Pursed-Lip Breathing 
            • Indications 
                • Dyspnea, wheezing (rest or exertion) 
                • Decreases patient’s symptoms of dyspnea 
                • Slows respiratory rate and decrease airway collapse in pts with COPD 
            • Procedure 
                1. Inhale through the nose with the mouth closed for several seconds 
                2. Exhale slowly over 4 to 6 seconds through pursed lips 
                3. Increase ratio from 1:2 to 1:6 (but should not be forced) 
                4. Progress by having the patient practice PLB while standing or with exercising 
            • Consideration: 
                • Not perform forceful abomination contraction with expiration

        .Paced Breathing 
            • Low endurance, DOE, fatigue, anxiety, tachypnea 
            • Patient controls breathing during activity 
            • “breath in at the beginning of activity and out at the end” 
            • Great with low endurance patients 
            • Can be used with PLB or diaphragmatic techniques 
            • Counting steps to coordinate inspiration and expiration 
                • “in” 1, 2 “out” 1,2,3,4

        -------------------------------------- Γ .Diaphragmatic Breathing (DB)
        .Diaphragmatic Breathing ΓAKA belly breathing or abdominal breathing
            • Indicated for hypoxemia, tachypnea, atelectasis, anxiety, pulmonary secretions, and other conditions with diaphragmatic weakness 
            • Improve diaphragm’s involvement in inhalation 
                • IE: reduce chest breathing & facilitate belly breathing 
            • Used to manage dyspnea, reduce atelectasis, increase oxygenation 
            • Facilitate outward motion of abdominal wall while reducing upper rib cage motion during inspiration

        .Sniffing 
            • Indications: 
                • Ensure patient knows how to activate the Diaphragm 
            • Procedure 
                • Place fingers below the xyphoid process 
                • Sniff in several times 
                • Observe abdominal and/or lower costal expansion with each sniff 
                • Progress by having patient gradually prolong the sniff

        .Diaphragmatic Controlled Breathing – Procedure ('DB Procedure')
            1. Explain to the patient the goals of DB 
            2. Position the patient in a sitting or supine position with the trunk supported in slight flexion 
                • NOTE: slight posterior tilt facilitates the diaphragm, while anterior tilt will facilitate upper chest breathing 
            3. Place the dominant hand over the upper abdominal region 
            4. Place the non-dominant hand over the mid-sternal region 
            5. Instruct the patient to breath through the nose and direct the air so the dominant hand rises with inspiration 
                • Little to no movement in non-dominant hand

        .Diaphragmatic Breathing Facilitation Techniques 
            • Counterpressure ('Counterpressure')
                • Allow for patient to feel the pressure and biofeedback of the clinician's pressure 
                • As a means for providing resistance as a progression to DCB 
                • Procedure: 
                    • Place your hand over your patient’s dominant hand and apply resistance or pressure 
                    • Instruct the patient to breath into your hand and push against the pressure
            • Quick Stretch/muscle energy technique ('Quick Stretch')
                • If the patient is having difficulty activating the diaphragm to full capacity or coordinating diaphragmatic activation at inspiration 
                • Procedure: 
                    • Best performed in supine with patient’s knee bent 
                    • Place your hand over the patient’s mid abdomen 
                    • Instruct the patient to perform DB a few times 
                    • Prior to inspiration apply a quick stretch or “Scoop” up and under the thorax 
                    • Then instruct the patient breath into your hand 
                        • NOTE: you may perform the scoop over the patient’s hand or directly over the abdomen
            • Lower costal expansion ('Lower costal expansion')
                • Best performed in sitting 
                • Place your hands or the patient’s hands over the patient’s anterolateral rib cage 
                • Instruct the patient to breath into the hands 
                • This will also facilitate diaphragmatic motion 
                • Considerations: 
                    • May also perform this with a belt around the lower costal region 
                    • Ensure the patient has relaxed shoulders to not use accessory muscles

        .Upper Chest Inhibition Technique ('Upper Chest Inhibition Technique')
            • Inhibiting the upper chest can help a patient recruit the diaphragm during inhalation and reduce accessory muscle use 
            • Used only after implementation of other techniques 
            • Procedure: 
                1. The patient is positioned in supine 
                2. therapist’s arm is placed on the upper chest and their other hand on the mid abdominal region 
                3. Have the patient perform a few respiratory cycles 
                4. When the patient inhales, the therapist applies pressure to the upper chest to resist expansion. 
                    • The therapist may apply a quick stretch to the diaphragm if needed prior to inhalation 
                5. Instruct the patient to breath into your hand on the abdominal region 

        -------------------------------------- .Γ Segmental Breathing 
        .Segmental Breathing 
            • Encourages expansion of specific part of the lung that has been under ventilated 
            • Prevent lung collapse/shut down 
            • Indicated for asymmetrical chest wall expansion with absence of breath sounds, localized lung consolidation, asymmetrical posture, area of collapsed lung 
            • Followed by inspiratory training to allow for expansion and ventilation to the newly ventilated lung area 

        .Segmental Breathing – Procedure ('Segmental Breathing – Procedure')
            1. Identify the area of emphasis via examination 
                • IE: reduced expansion in left lower lobe of lung with chest expansion assessment – treat left lower lobe region 
            2. Place the patient in the best position to access that lung region & most comfortable for the patient 
            3. Place your hand over the chest wall overlying the area of emphasis 
            4. Instruct the patient to breathe in deeply through the nose trying to direct airflow toward your hand while you apply 
            a counter pressure with your hand 
            5. Gradually decrease your pressure as the patient inspires to allow for expansion of that area 
            6. Instruct the patient to hold that breath for 2-3 seconds at the end of inspiration, then exhale 
            7. Have the patient use their own hand or belt as HEP

        .Segmental Breathing – Procedure Example ('Segmental Breathing – Procedure Example')

        .Segmental Breathing Belt Assist Procedure 
            • Lateral basal expansion (left side) 
                1. The belt is placed around the left lateral basal region, and the shorter end continued around the the right side and held with the right hand 
                2. The other end should be crossed over the thighs and fixed under the right thigh 
                3. The patient performs a breath cycle and at the end of the breath out the patient should pull the belt firmly and breath into the belt against the resistance 
                4. At full inspiration the pressure is released, and the expansion is maintained for a moment before expiration

        -------------------------------------- .Γ Inspiratory Training Interventions
        .Inspiratory Training 
            Indications: 
                Prevent complications of poor ventilation and mobilize secretions with improved cough 
                Performed post-DB and segmental breathing to allow for improved airflow to newly opened lung regions 
                Indicated for patients with signs of dec diaphragm and intercostal muscle strength/endurance 
            Inspiratory muscle training 
                Same theory as skeletal muscle training 
                Principles of overload (low load over longer time), specificity and reversibility
                Ensure patient can correctly use muscles of inhalation 
                    2 parts 
                        • Strengthening 
                        • Endurance 

        .Diaphragmatic Strength vs. Endurance 
            Training Prescription 
                • Strength training 
                    1. Assess diaphragmatic strength (fair or reduced) via palpation 
                    2. Therapist places hand just below rib cage on both sides of thorax 
                    3. Before patient initiates inspiration, the therapist gives a small amount of resistance to the diaphragm 
                    4. Continue this pressure through the inspiratory phase & no resistance on exhalation 
                    5. Progression – when patient can breathe comfortably for 15 mins without accessory mm use may add further resistance manually or with weights over abdomen with inspiration 
                • Endurance 
                    • Use time dependent deep breathing exercises for 2-3 daily sessions up to 30 mins

        .Incentive Spirometry ('Incentive Spirometry ')
            • Often used post-op 
            • Key is to perform with long slow breaths upon inspiration and PLB upon expiration as needed 
            • Increased ventilation and help mobilize secretions 
            • Perform up to 10x per hour as able – should assess patient’s ability prior to prescribing 

        .Inspiratory Holds and Stacked Breathing
            Indications 
                Ventilate poorly ventilated areas 
                Improve cough capabilities for airway clearance 
                Hypoventilation, atelectasis, ineffective cough 
            Inspiratory Holds 
                -Involves prolonged holding of breath at maximum inspiration 
                -The patient is instructed to hold his or her breath at the height of inspiration for 2 to 3 seconds, followed by relaxed exhalation 
            Stacked Breathing 
                Series of deep breaths that build on top of previous breath without expiration (i.e. stacked breaths) 
                Each inspiration is accompanied by a brief inspiratory hold 

        .Breathing Strategies and Training Interventions in Acute Care 
            Key Terms and Concepts 
                1. Breathing Strategies: 
                    • Definition: Techniques to improve ventilation and lung function. 
                    • Examples: Diaphragmatic breathing, segmental breathing, pursed lip breathing. 
                2. Therapeutic Positioning Techniques: 
                    • Purpose: Assist patients in progressing from dependence to independence and mobility. 
                    • Examples: Prone positioning, lateral positioning, sitting with trunk support. 
                3. Ventilatory Movement Strategies: 
                    • Objective: Enhance breathing efficiency and recovery after exercise. 
                    • Examples: Specific body positions during breathing, inspiratory and expiratory movements. 
                4. Inspiratory Effort Facilitation: 
                    • Technique: Instructing patients to breathe in during shoulder flexion, abduction, and external rotation.
                    • Purpose: Opens up the chest wall to facilitate inspiratory effort. 
                5. Exhalation Facilitation: 
                    • Technique: Instructing patients to breathe out during shoulder extension, adduction, and internal rotation. 
                    • Purpose: Aids in effective exhalation. 

                    Questions and Answers (!!Q) 
                        Q1. How do therapeutic positioning techniques assist in patient progression? 
                            A1: Therapeutic positioning techniques, such as prone positioning and sitting with trunk support, help patients transition from dependence to independence and improve mobility. 
                        Q2. What is the purpose of inspiratory effort facilitation? 
                            A2: Inspiratory effort facilitation involves instructing patients to breathe in during specific movements, such as shoulder flexion, to open up the chest wall and enhance inspiratory function. 
                        Q3. Why is segmental breathing important? 
                            A3: Segmental breathing targets poorly ventilated areas, aiding in lung expansion and improving cough capabilities. It's beneficial for patients with hypoventilation or ineffective cough. 
                        Q4. Explain the technique of pursed lip breathing. 
                            A4: Pursed lip breathing involves inhaling through the nose and exhaling slowly through pursed lips. It's effective in reducing respiratory rate, promoting better airway patency, and assisting patients, especially those with COPD. 
                        Q5. When might inspiratory holds be used in acute care? 
                            A5: Inspiratory holds are used to promote lung expansion and improve cough capabilities. They are indicated for patients experiencing hypoventilation, atelectasis, or ineffective cough.

            Summary 
                • Breathing Strategies encompass techniques like diaphragmatic breathing, segmental breathing, and pursed lip breathing. 
                • Therapeutic Positioning Techniques aid in patient progression from dependence to independence, including prone positioning and sitting with trunk support. 
                • Ventilatory Movement Strategies involve specific body positions during breathing, enhancing efficiency, and aiding recovery after exercise. 
                • Inspiratory Effort Facilitation focuses on instructing patients to breathe during specific movements to open up the chest for improved inspiration. 
                • Exhalation Facilitation involves guiding patients to exhale during particular movements, aiding in effective exhalation. 
                • Inspiratory Holds, Stack Breathing, and Sustained Breathing are global ventilatory training interventions used to improve lung function, especially after segmental breathing interventions. 

        Remember, a personalized approach and continuous assessment are essential in implementing these strategies in the acute care setting.

12.Other Exercise Interventions for the Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Patient
    ..3.6. Other Exercise Interventions for the Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Patient
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    .('Other Exercise Interventions for CVP pt.pdf')
        .Relaxation Exercises 
            • Promotion of relaxation may be the primary component to a cardiopulmonary intervention 
            • You may instruct the patient on deep breathing using the diaphragm in supine or sitting 
            • Emphasize the inhalation and also may add relaxing music or surroundings

        .Thoracic Mobilization Techniques ('Thoracic Mobilization Techniques.png')
            • Simple thoracic mobilization techniques to increase the ability of the thorax to expand during breathing 
            • Examples: 
                • Vertical towel roll in supine to improve anterior chest mobility, may incorporate upper extremities 
                • Quadruped unilateral thoracic rotation 
                • Thoracic extension over the chair 
                • Side lying thoracic rotation with inhalation & exhalation

        .Postural Training and Strengthening ('Postural Training and Strengthening')
            • Scapular stabilization program 
                • Example: Bilateral scapular adduction with inhalation upon opening and exhalation upon return to midline 
            • Wall slides 
                • Inhalation on rise, exhalation on return

        .Extremity and Trunk Exercises 
            • Extremity and trunk movements can be performed with breathing to enhance chest mobility 
            • Can be performed after DB, segmental breathing, postural drainage to enhance ventilation and chest mobility 
            • Great for patients who had periods of immobility
            -------------------------------------------------------
            • Chest mobilization with total pattern exercise ('Extremity and Trunk Exercises')
                • Patient exhales with seated flexion and inhales with seated extension 
                • Patient inhales with lateral side bending, and exhales upon return to midline
            -------------------------------------------------------
            • Cane exercise for chest mobilization ('Extremity and Trunk Exercises 2')
                • Inhale with bilateral shoulder flexion using cane, then exhale with bilateral shoulder extension with cane 
                • With cane overhead patient exhales as they rotate trunk, then inhale as they return to midline

        .Functional Mobility Training Considerations 
            • Remove any auditory, visual or tactile breathing cues 
            • Walking 
                • Use inspiration: expiration ratio of 1:2 
                • Example: breath in 2 steps, breath out 4 steps 
                • Find a comfortable pattern 
            • Stair climbing 
                • Initially instruct patient to climb stairs during expiration, stop, then inspire, climb as you expire and so on 
                • Progress to ratio of 1:2

        .Physical Therapy Exercise Interventions for Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Patients   
            Key Terms and Concepts 
                1. Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Patient: 
                    • Definition: Individuals with conditions affecting the heart or lungs. 
                    • Examples: COPD, post-thoracic surgeries, thoracic spine injuries. 
                2. Relaxation Techniques: 
                    • Purpose: Facilitate slower and methodical breathing. 
                    • Examples: Pursed lip breathing, diaphragmatic breathing, integrated relaxation components. 
                3. Thoracic Spine and Rib Cage Mechanics: 
                    • Importance: Vital role in breathing mechanics and ventilatory support. 
                    • Considerations: Reduced mobility can lead to decreased oxygenation. 
                4. Thoracic Mobilization Techniques: 
                    • Methods: Use of vertical tower roll, quadruped position, and sideline positioning. 
                    • Benefits: Enhances anterior chest mobility and opens the chest for improved breathing. 
                5. Scapular Stabilization Exercises: 
                    • Purpose: Improve posture and open the chest wall. 
                    • Examples: Wall slides, standing shoulder external rotation with breathing integration. 
                6. Total Pattern Extremity and Trunk Exercises: 
                    • Definition: Movements aimed at large patterns to enhance chest mobility. 
                    • Examples: Seated flexion and extension, lateral side bending with cane, coordinated extremity and trunk movements.

                Questions and Answers (!!Q)
                    Q1. How do relaxation techniques benefit patients with cardiovascular and pulmonary conditions? 
                        A1: Relaxation techniques, like pursed lip breathing and diaphragmatic breathing, aid in slowing down breathing patterns, promoting oxygenation, and serving as an adjunct to other interventions, such as endurance training. 
                    Q2. What role does the thoracic spine play in breathing mechanics? 
                        A2: The thoracic spine's mobility and the rib cage's appropriate action are crucial for ventilatory support. Reduced mobility can lead to decreased oxygenation, especially in patients with injuries, surgeries, or poor posture affecting the thoracic region. 
                    Q3. Can you explain the significance of scapular stabilization exercises in respiratory interventions? 
                        A3: Scapular stabilization exercises help improve posture, leading to the opening of the chest wall. This enhances breathing mechanics and allows for improved chest expansion, vital for patients with cardiovascular and pulmonary conditions. 
                    Q4. How are total pattern extremity and trunk exercises beneficial for functional carryover? 
                        A4: These exercises involve large movement patterns, promoting airflow during inhalation and exhalation. Coordinated extremity and trunk movements are essential for functional carryover, especially in patients with periods of immobility. 
                    Q5. Why is it important to integrate breathing strategies into functional activities like walking or stair climbing? 
                        A5: Integrating breathing strategies into functional activities ensures the application of proper inspiratory and expiratory ratios. This not only improves ventilatory status but also promotes a return to prior levels of function in daily activities. 

            Summary 
                • Cardiovascular and pulmonary patients benefit from a holistic approach, including relaxation techniques, thoracic mobilization, scapular stabilization exercises, and total pattern extremity and trunk exercises. 
                • The thoracic spine's role in breathing mechanics and rib cage mobility is critical for optimal oxygenation. 
                • Scapular stabilization exercises enhance posture, leading to improved chest expansion and breathing mechanics. 
                • Functional carryover is achieved through coordinated extremity and trunk movements, emphasizing large patterns that promote airflow. 
                • Integrating breathing strategies into functional activities ensures a seamless transition from mechanical aspects to practical application in daily life.

            Remember, individualized exercise interventions and continuous assessment are crucial for optimizing outcomes in cardiovascular and pulmonary patients.

        INSTRUCTIONS 
            You will be given a list of cardiopulmonary exam findings and choose a treatment(s) to give that patient based on those findings.
                challenge, try to progress some of the chosen interventions, such as adding strengthening 
                components, functional activity with new breathing patterns, etc.

            1.Hypertrophy of accessory muscles, dyspnea on exertion, digital clubbing, reduced costal expansion lower lobes 
                What would you choose as your treatment and why?
                    -Based on the patient presentation you may consider a chronic pulmonary condition like COPD. 
                    -Interventions may include pursed lip breathing with increased time spent in exhalation, then progress this by adding it to functional training like ambulation, stairs, etc. Activity pacing with possible need for AD for UE support and information on tripoding position to maximize the use the accessory muscles especially considering the reduced lower costal expansion possibly indicating hyperinflated lungs. Some may attempt DB training, but this may not be possible is the disease has progressed to flatten the diaphragm, so assessing diaphragmatic function via sniffing would be indicated prior to initiating this intervention. 

            2.Reduced unilateral right mid and lower chest expansion, absent breath sounds right lower lobe, crackles mid right lobe. 
                What would you choose as your treatment and why?
                    Based on this patient presentation you may consider a diagnosis of right lower lobe atelectasis due to pneumonia and chronic hypoventilation in the region, which has caused the lung to shut down but also with that you may have continued consolidation/mucus production. Initially it would be best to treat the presence of crackles if they are related to mucus consolidation to clear the region for next stages of treatment, clearance techniques may include coughing and postural drainage targeting the treatment area. Then treatment may consist of any of the segmental breathing interventions targeting the area of hypoventilation where reduced chest expansion was discovered, inspiratory training for overall lung expansion (incentive spirometry, stacked breathing, inspiratory holds), and coughing retraining if indicated.

            3.Dyspnea with ambulation 50 feet, barrel chested posture, breath sounds normal, digital clubbing, increased accessory muscle use, increased respiratory rate with rest and further increase with exertion. 
                What would you choose as your treatment and why?
                    This patient would be appropriate for aerobic conditioning, activity pacing, pursed lip breathing and relaxation techniques to improve functional endurance levels. You may even consider additions of scapular stabilizer strengthening with breathing retraining techniques in order to work on postural strengthening that would be considered with a patient with this postural abnormality.

            4.(+) tactile fremitus and egophony L lower lobe, (+) crackles L lower lobe, weak cough, reduced SpO2 at rest 
                What would you choose as your treatment and why?
                    This patient likely is suffering from an area of localized mucus consolidation in the L lower lobe, and due to the weak cough, they are unable to clear this mucus, so postural drainage would be indicated with possible need for percussion and/or vibration. Instruction on an effective cough would be indicated as well and may include some inspiratory training interventions to improve cough force along with huff and cough technique to keep airway open for clearance. Once the mucus is cleared inspiratory training, diaphragmatic breathing, and/or segmental breathing to target the newly ventilated lung region would be a great progression.

..3.8 Module 3 Quiz (!!Q)

    .Question 1
    Which of the following factors that contribute to functional losses in a hospitalized patient does a physical therapist have the MOST influence to improve? 
      Acute inflammation 
      Severity of illness 
      Prolonged immobilization 
      Marginal baseline function 
      
      Prolonged immobilization
        Prolonged immobilization or bed rest can be greatly affected by a physical therapist who advocates for early mobilization in a hospital setting. Acute inflammation, severity of illness, and marginal baseline function are factors for which a physical therapist can intervene but are less likely influenced as much as prolonged bed rest.

    Question 2
    Which of the following medical interventions is best administered prior to initiating an airway clearance technique, like postural drainage, to improve secretion mobility and clearance? 
      Optimal pain control 
      Inhaled bronchodilator 
      Inhaled antibiotics 
      Intravenous anticoagulants 
      
      Inhaled bronchodilator
        Inhaled bronchodilator medications are given prior to the airway clearance procedure enhances the overall intervention outcome. Inhaled antibiotic medications will have better deposition into the lung if they are given following the airway clearance procedure. 

    Question 3
    Which of the following conditions is a primary indication for airway clearance procedures? 
      Dry, nonproductive cough 
      Dyspnea with exertion 
      Excessive pulmonary secretions 
      Acute inflammation of the lungs 
      
      Excessive pulmonary secretions
        Indications for airway clearance procedures include impaired mucociliary transport, excessive pulmonary secretions, and ineffective or absent cough. While airway clearance may reduce dyspnea due to improved lung surface areas available for oxygenation, it is not a primary indicator for the intervention.  

    Question 4
    A patient experiencing dyspnea my lean forward on supported hands. Which of the following statements provides the BEST rationale for why this position relieves dyspnea? 
      Respiratory muscle length is shortened. 
      Intra-abdominal pressure is reduced. 
      Improved respiratory accessory muscle action on the rib cage. 
      Provides a position of rest for the patient. 
      
      Improved respiratory accessory muscle action on the rib cage.
        With the arms supported, the accessory breathing muscles can act on the rib cage and the thorax, allowing more expansion for inspiration. When the patient leans forward on supported hands, the intra-abdominal pressure rises and thus pushes the diaphragm up in a lengthened position. The improved length–tension relationship (optimal muscle length) provides the diaphragm an increased strength of contraction.

    Question 5
    Which of the following breathing exercises would BEST facilitate air flow into poorly ventilated areas? 
      Pursed-lip breathing 
      Paced breathing 
      Inspiratory hold technique 
      Diaphragmatic controlled breathing 
      
      Inspiratory hold technique
        An inspiratory hold technique involves prolonged holding of the breath at maximum inspiration. It can improve the flow of air into poorly ventilated regions of the lungs.

    Question 6
    Which of the following techniques would be BEST employed if after repeated instruction and trials, the patient is unable to understand and perform diaphragmatic breathing? 
      Stacked breathing 
      Counterpressure 
      Unilateral costal breathing 
      Inspiratory hold technique 
      
      Counterpressure
        If the desired breathing pattern is not achieved using the diaphragmatic controlled breathing technique, counterpressure can be applied by the clinician to provide manual biofeedback for the patient to better understand how to activate the diaphragm. 

    Question 7
    Which of the following breathing exercise techniques would enhance fast-twitch glycolytic muscle fibers of the diaphragm in a patient with good strength? 
      ✗Three quick sniffs through the nose with slow relaxed exhalations 
      Deep breathing using diaphragmatic breathing for 30 minutes, two to three times per day 
      Manual resistance applied to the diaphragm through the inspiratory phase. 
      Reduces the number of sniffs to one at an increasingly slower pace 
      
      Manual resistance applied to the diaphragm through the inspiratory phase. 
        Diaphragmatic weakness is attributed to fast-twitch glycolytic fibers, so strengthening versus endurance exercises are indicated. Manual resistance, using weights on the abdomen, or use of mechanical devices such as a piece of pipe add resistance or overload to stimulate the muscle to generate a force against resistance.
 
    Question 8
    If a patient is demonstrating excessive use of accessory muscles during breathing, which of the following breathing strategies would be MOST appropriate to implement with the patient? 
      Pursed-lip breathing (!!F)
      Paced breathing 
      Upper chest inhibiting technique 
      Inspiratory hold technique 
      
      Upper chest inhibiting technique 
        Upper chest inhibiting technique helps to reduce the use of accessory muscles during breathing and enhances the use of the diaphragm for breathing. 
  
    Question 9
    Which of the following conditions would be considered a contraindication to a Trendelenburg position for postural drainage of the lower lobes of the lungs? 
      Congestive heart failure 
      Pleural effusions 
      Pneumothorax 
      Pneumonia
      
      Congestive heart failure
        Contraindication to a Trendelenburg position for postural drainage would include congestive heart failure, cardiomyopathy, increased intracranial pressure, esophageal reflux, recent head trauma, and recent eye surgery.
 
    Question 10
    A physical therapy plan of care in the acute care setting includes the following, EXCEPT: 
      Recommended discharge destination 
      Possible medical equipment needs 
      Duration and frequency of treatments 
      Patient’s medical diagnosis 
      
      Patient’s medical diagnosis 
        While it may be mentioned in the assessment, the medical diagnosis is not an integral part of the PT plan of care.

    .Module Introduction
        Module 4 will be presented in 2 units. The first unit will cover therapeutic interventions for prevention of cardiovascular disease and interventions for those with known cardiovascular disease.  Individuals with CV disease can be seen in a variety of different outpatient settings including an outpatient PT clinic, a formal cardiac rehabilitation program or even in the home health setting.  This module will also review emergency responses, as this will be an important component to working with any patient suffering from a cardiovascular event. The second unit you will review cardiovascular, pulmonary, and other system examination procedures in preparation for your onsite lab immersion. In this module you will review the previous examination and screening lectures along with preparing for the lab immersion by reviewing the schedule and lab manual.

    .Learning Objectives
        Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to:
            Apply the use of patient/client management model for evaluation, intervention selection, and re-examination for the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease. 
            Select the appropriate interventions for patient who require prevention of cardiovascular disease and interventions for those with known primary and secondary cardiopulmonary disorders. 
            Modify physical therapy intervention and plan of care when a patient exhibits signs of intolerance. 
            Identify the role of the physical therapist and other members of the health care team when recommending, selecting, and performing interventions on patients with known cardiovascular disease. 
            Perform a screen for cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases and justify differential diagnosis based on cardiopulmonary data and assessment; identify the need for referral to other health care professionals as appropriate.
            Discuss and define hospital-based coding systems, patient code status and emergency response. 
            Apply the use of the Hypothesis-Oriented Algorithm for Clinicians for evaluation selection, and re-examination in patients with cardiopulmonary dysfunction.
            Give rationale for selection of evaluative tools in management of the cardiopulmonary patient. 
            Modify physical therapy examination technique when a patient exhibits signs of intolerance. 
            Screen for cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases and justify differential diagnosis based on cardiopulmonary data and assessment; identify the need for referral to other health care professionals as appropriate.

                What is Cardiac Rehabilitation?
                • An individualized and personalized treatment plan, including 
                evaluation and instruction on physical activity, nutrition, 
                stress management, and other health related areas 
                • An important part of the treatment of your specific heart 
                problem. If you have one of the following diagnoses you 
                may be eligible to participate 
                » Heart Attack
                » Angina 
                » Cardiac surgery, such 
                as coronary bypass  
                or valve surgery

                » Coronary artery 
                angioplasty or stents
                » Heart failure
                » Heart transplantation 

                • Generally covered by most health insurance companies 
                but check your plan to determine copays or other 
                requirements. Contact your local Cardiac Rehabilitation 
                facility to inquire what programs are available for patients 
                who do not have insurance

                Cardiac Rehabilitation
                An Individualized Supervised Program For You

                Benefits of Cardiac Rehabilitation:
                • Live longer and lessen your chances for another 
                heart attack
                • Control heart disease symptoms such as chest 
                pain or shortness of breath
                • Stop or reverse damage to your blood vessels in 
                your heart
                • Lessen the physical and emotional effects of 
                heart disease
                • Improve your stamina and strength, getting you 
                back to your usual activities, including work, 
                hobbies, and regular exercise 
                • Improve your confidence and well-being

                This information is prepared and presented as a service to you from the American Association of Cardiovascular and 
                Pulmonary Rehabilitation (AACVPR). To find the nearest Cardiac Rehabilitation Center visit www.AACVPR.org

                Cardiac Rehabilitation Offers:
                • Assessment of your personal  
                risk factors for heart and blood 
                vessel disease
                • Beginning and maintaining a 
                personalized exercise plan that 
                works for you 
                • Psychological/stress assessment 
                and counseling

                • Education and support to make 
                healthy lifestyle changes such as:
                » Maintaining a healthy weight
                » Heart healthy eating
                » Avoiding tobacco and 
                environmental smoke
                • Opportunity to meet and share 
                stories with other patients like you

                • Monitoring and better control of:
                » Blood pressure
                » Lipids /cholesterol
                » Diabetes
                • Improved communication with 
                your doctor and other healthcare 
                providers about your progress 
                following your cardiac event

                Recent scientific studies have shown that people who complete a cardiac 
                rehabilitation program can increase their life expectancy by up to five years.

        .Primary Prevention 
            • Active intervention for risk factors that cause cardiovascular disease 
            • Candidates 
                • individuals who are at moderate or high risk of developing cardiovascular disease and with family histories of CVD 
                • high prevalence of modifiable risk factors 
            • Two problems with primary prevention 
                • compliance 
                • lack of payment for services
            --------------------------------------------------
            • Risk factors affected by primary prevention 
                • high cholesterol, aerobic capacity, exercise tolerance, weight, resting BP, glucose, well-being, stress tolerance 
            • Components of primary prevention program 
                • Therapeutic exercise—aerobic and resistance 
                • Dietary counseling 
                • Stress management or biofeedback 
                • Smoking cessation 
                • Pharmacological management 
                • Education and self-management techniques  

        .Guidelines for Risk Assessment - Box 18-1 Guidelines to risk assessment (!!E).Lv1
            .Hypertension
                Goal:
                    <140/90 mm Hg
                    <130/85 mm Hg if renal insufficiency or heart failure present
                    <130/80 mm Hg if diabetic 
                Initiate drug therapy if lifestyle modification is ineffective

                    Goal: At least 30 minutes if moderate intensity (40% to 60% of max.) activity, most days of the week 
                    Flexibility exercises and resistance training (if appropriate) should also be included

                        LDL <160 mg/dL if ≤ 1 risk factor for CHD present

                        > 150 mg/dL or is HDL is:

                            < 50 mg/dL for women
