        .Rehabilitation of Patients with Documented Cardiovascular Disease 1 
            Coordination, Communication, Documentation
                Patient-related instruction
                     Procedural Interventions
                        Therapeutic exercise 
                            • Functional training in self-care and home management, including activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IDAL) 
                            • Functional training in work (job/school/pay), community, and leisure integration or reintegration, including IADL, work hardening, and work conditioning 
                            • Manual therapy techniques, including mobilization/manipulation 
                            • Prescription, application, and, as appropriate, fabrication of devices and equipment (assistive, adaptive, orthotic, protective, supportive, or prosthetic) 
                            • Airway clearance techniques 
                            • Integumentary repair and protective techniques 
                            • Electrotherapeutic modalities 
                            • Physical agents and mechanical modalities

        .Rehabilitation of Patients with Documented Cardiovascular Disease 2 
            • Patient populations
            • May have a primary or secondary cardiovascular disorder 
            • Rehabilitation programs 
            • Rehabilitation should be a multidisciplinary program of education, exercise, behavioral change 
            • Rehabilitation is organized into progressive phases of programming from Phase I (acute care) to Phase 4 (supervised community setting)

        .Types of Cardiac Rehab Programs 
            • Rehab of patients with cardiovascular disorders 
                • Can occur in any physical therapy setting 
            • Cardiac rehab 
                • Can be provided by a number of medical professionals including physical therapists and exercise physiologists 
            • Formal Cardiac Rehab Program 
                • Formal multidisciplinary program in outpatient, includes exercise, education and lifestyle modification, covered by Centers for Medicare and Medicaid

        .Phases of Cardiac Rehabilitation (!!E.Grade & Doc) (!!E).Lv3
            Phase I
                Acute or hospital phase 
                This phase begins when a patient is considered to be medically stable after the CV event 
            Phase II
                Early outpatient phase / Intensive Monitoring 
                Begins after discharge and lasts 6 to 12 weeks
            Phase III
                Training or maintenance phase Begins at end of 
                Phase II; patients exercise in larger groups 
            Phase IV
                -Disease prevention program 
                -Individuals are at high risk for infarction because of risk factors; also includes those who continue to want to be seen in a supervised environment

        .Acute Care Phase (Phase I)
            • Early mobilization of acute coronary patient to activity reduces complications and improves mortality rate 
            • Early mobilization has become a well-established practice 
            • Poor candidates for rehabilitation (!!P) (!!E).Lv1
                • Overt CHF, unstable angina pectoris, hemodynamic instability, serious arrhythmias, conduction defects, impaired function of other organ systems 
                • Uncontrolled hypertension 
                • Other diseases or illnesses that preclude exercise

        .Management of CV Patients During the Acute Phase 1 
            • Evaluation of physiological responses to self-care and ambulation 
            • Provision of feedback to the IP team of physicians and nurses about patient’s response to activity 
            • Provision of safe guidelines for activity progression 
            • Patient and family education on disease and self-monitoring, physical activity progression

        .Management of CV Patients During the Acute Phase 2 
            • Initial assessment/examination 
                • Conducted when patient is considered stable 
                • Chart review 
                • Patient–family interview 
                • Physical examination 
                • Activity (self-care) and ambulation evaluation (ADL monitor) 
                • Ambulation activity

        .Management of CV Patients During the Acute Phase 3 (!!E).Lv3
            • Activity program guidelines 
                1. Indications for an unmodified program 
                    • Patients who demonstrate appropriate hemodynamic, ECG, and symptomatic responses to self-care and ambulation evaluation 
                2. Indications for a modified program 
                    • Program is modified for persons designated as “complicated” 
                3. Indications for withholding a program 
                    • Criteria that exclude patients from participation until instability improves

        .McNeer Criteria for Complicated MI (!!P) (!!E).Lv1
            • Poor ventricular function 
            • Significant ischemia with low-level activity 
            • Cardiogenic shock 
            • Ventricular tachycardia and/or fibrillation 
            • Second or third degree atrioventricular (AV) block 
            • Persistent sinus tachycardia (HR >100 at rest) 
            • Persistent systolic hypotension (systolic BP <90mm Hg at rest) 
            • Pulmonary edema

        .Management of CV Patients During the Acute Phase 4 (!!P) (!!E).Lv1 
            • General precautions 
                • Before each activity session, the patient’s status should be reassessed 
            • Relative contraindications to continuing exercise 
                • Unusual heart rate increase >50 bpm increase 
                • BP indicative of hypertension SBP >210 or DBP >110 mmHg 
                • Drop in systolic blood pressure drop of 10 mmHg SBP 
                • Symptoms with activity of
                    angina
                    excessive dyspnea
                    excessive fatigue
                    mental confusion
                    dizziness
                    severe leg claudication
                    signs of pallor
                    cold sweat
                    ataxia
                    changing heart sounds with activity
                    changing lung sounds with activity
                    ECG abnormality

            • Education 
                • Amount and type of information given to patient and family depend on their characteristics 
                • Information should be organized in a packet 
                • Keep instructions simple 
                • All team members should coordinate educational materials in 
                • Education plan should be specific to the individual and address risk factors 
            • Information that should be included in patient education: 
                • Disease process and prognosis 
                • Individual’s risk factors and recommendations 
                • General activity guidelines and home exercise program 
                • Role of exercise 
                • Medications 
                • Nutrition and prescribed diet 
                • Self-monitoring techniques 
                • What to do in an emergency 
             Information typically provided by the Physical Therapist

        .Management of CV Patients During the Acute Phase 5
            • Other components of the acute phase 
                • Diet and nutrition 
                    • Individual counseling is provided by a dietician with input from the physician 
                • Psychological and behavioral rehabilitation 
                    • Most patients experience fear, anxiety, depression, and/or anger 
                    • Psychologists, specialized clinical nurse practitioners, social workers are examples of team members
            ---------------------------------------------------------------
            • Outcome measures 
                • Due to limited hospital stay in the acute phase, outcomes expected are based on the functional limitations or disabilities 
            • Discharge planning 
                • Review of general activity guidelines, exercise prescription, dietary, medications, symptoms 
                • Referral to outpatient rehabilitation 
                • Low-level symptom-limited exercise test
            ----------------------------------------------------------------
            • Self management of symptoms 
            • Patient knowledge of factors associated with condition 
            • Aerobic capacity or exercise tolerance or endurance 
            • Ability to perform physical tasks related to self-case and home management 
            • Physiologic response to increase oxygen demand 
            • Symptoms associated with increased oxygen demand 
            • Level of assistance/supervision required for task performance safety with all activities

        .Rehabilitation for Patients with Known Cardiovascular Disease   
            Key Terms and Concepts 
                1. Primary Prevention Rehabilitation: 
                    • Definition: Wellness programs aimed at preventing cardiovascular diseases before manifestation. 
                    • Examples: Therapeutic exercise, dietary counseling, and smoking cessation. 
                2. Candidates for Primary Prevention: 
                    • Description: Individuals with risk factors before the disease manifests. 
                    • Considerations: Lack of long-term compliance, high prevalence of risk factors. 
                3. Components of Primary Prevention: 
                    • Inclusions: Therapeutic exercise, dietary counseling, smoking sensation. 
                    • Screening Tools: Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire (PAR-Q), guidelines from organizations like the American Heart Association. 
                4. Rehabilitation of Patients with Cardiovascular Disease: 
                    • Goal: Improve functional mobility and address impairments in physical therapy setting. 
                    • Phases: Multidisciplinary approach, four phases including inpatient and disease prevention. 
                5. Cardiac Rehabilitation Programs: 
                    • Types: Home health, outpatient, inpatient. 
                    • Phases: Acute care (Phase One), early outpatient, training or maintenance, disease prevention.

                Questions and Answers (!!Q)
                    Q1. Why is primary prevention crucial for cardiovascular diseases? 
                        A1: Primary prevention is vital due to the high prevalence of risk factors like smoking and high cholesterol. It addresses lifestyle modifications before disease manifestation, impacting long-term outcomes positively. 
                    Q2. What are the components of a primary prevention program? 
                        A2: Components include therapeutic exercise, dietary counseling, and smoking cessation. Screening tools like PAR-Q ensure the safety of individuals before engaging in exercise programs. 
                    Q3. How does the rehabilitation of patients with known cardiovascular disease differ from primary prevention? 
                        A3: Rehabilitation focuses on improving functional mobility and addressing impairments. It involves a multidisciplinary approach, education on risk factor reduction, exercise, and behavioral changes. 
                    Q4. What are the four phases of cardiac rehabilitation? 
                        A4: The phases include inpatient (Phase One), early outpatient, training or maintenance, and disease prevention. Each phase has specific goals and criteria for progression. 
                    Q5. Why is the acute care phase (Phase One) crucial in cardiac rehabilitation? 
                        A5: Phase One involves early mobility post-cardiac insult, reducing complications, and improving mortality rates. Physical therapists play a vital role in assessing safety, mobilization, and educating patients. 

            Summary 
                • Primary prevention focuses on lifestyle modifications before cardiovascular diseases manifest, incorporating exercise, dietary counseling, and smoking cessation. 
                • Rehabilitation for known cardiovascular patients involves a multidisciplinary approach, addressing impairments and improving functional mobility. 
                • The four phases of cardiac rehabilitation include inpatient, early outpatient, training or maintenance, and disease prevention. 
                • Physical therapists play a crucial role in the acute care phase (Phase One), assessing safety, mobility, and educating patients for a smooth transition to subsequent phases. 
                • Continuous monitoring, education, and coordination with the healthcare team are essential components for successful cardiac rehabilitation. 

            -Remember, individualized care and ongoing assessment are key to optimizing outcomes for patients with cardiovascular diseases during rehabilitation.

        .Post Acute Phase Rehabilitation 1
            • Center for Medicare/Medicaid Services and National Coverage Determination (NCD) defines cardiac rehabilitation as: 
                • consisting of comprehensive, long term programs involving medical evaluation, prescribed exercise, cardiac risk factor modification, education, counseling 
            • Aim is to reduce subsequent CV-related morbidity and mortality
            ---------------------------------------------------------------
            EXERCISE → EDUCATION → BEHAVIOR CHANGES

        .Post Acute Phase Rehabilitation 2
            NCD 20-10 provides coverage guidelines for Medicare beneficiaries 
            Patient who do not have a place to attend for rehabilitation or do not qualify, still qualify for outpatient rehabilitation

        .Candidacy for Cardiac Rehabilitation 
            • Traditionally, patient groups include: 
                • complicated/uncomplicated MI, heart failure, angioplasty, heart transplant, stable angina, post-bypass, or valve replacement 
            • Referred groups have expanded to include individuals with comorbid conditions, poor ejection fraction, cardiomyopathy, serious arrhythmias 
            • Current covered groups under CMS NCD: 
                • MI within past 12 months, CABG, stable angina, PTCA, heart or heart lung transplant, valve repair 
                • chronic stable heart failure recently added

        .Home Based Cardiac Rehabilitation 
            • Candidates for home based CR 
                • heart disease & uncomplicated hospital course (low-risk) and considered to be 
                • unable to travel to the program 
            • Extensive discharge instructions regarding self-monitoring techniques, exercise guidelines, dietary management, medications, 
                • keep an accurate daily activity log 
                • weekly telephone call by a member of the rehabilitation team

        .Rehabilitation/Secondary Prevention in the Outpatient Setting 
            The rehabilitation team
                Interdisciplinary approach 
            Program components 
                Should include all aspects of secondary prevention of CVD 
                Risk factor assessment and interventions aimed to reduce

        .Members of the Cardiac Rehabilitation Team 
            Medical Director
                A responsible for overall effectiveness and safety of the program 
            Program Coordinator
                oversees all team personnel and facilities 
                develops & revises policy, procedures, and budgets 
                selects needed equipment; and responsible for coordinating and supervising staff. 
                Physical therapist, registered nurse, or exercise physiologist
            Exercise Training Professional
                -knowledgeable in exercise physiology, pathology, exercise training techniques, monitoring equipment, arrhythmia recognition, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and Advanced Cardiac Life Support 
                -Physical therapist, RN, or exercise physiologist 
            Dietician
                A professional knowledgeable in nutrition assessment and counseling and experienced in dietary planning and modification
            Behavioral Specialist
                skilled in behavioral evaluation and counseling
                coping mechanisms, family patterns of interaction, and available community resources
                psychologist or medical social worker usually fits this position. 
            Vocational Counselor
                -referral source to the program to assist the individual in a return to work, or in counseling and referral for training for a different career.

        .Efficacy of Cardiac Rehabilitation 
            • Exercise rehabilitation has made positive impact on: 
                • Risk factors 
                • Functional capacity 
                • Cardiovascular efficiency 
                • Cardiac mortality rate 
            • No evidence from RCT of an independent effect of exercise in the prevention of recurrent coronary events in patients recovering from MI, coronary bypass surgery, angina pectoris 
            • Many individuals are not referred who would benefit

        .Initial Assessment 
            • Ventricular function as it relates to functional abilities
            • Thorough medical history 
            • Patient–family interview 
            • Physical examination 
            • Exercise test or a 6-minute walk test to determine target HR 
            • Blood chemistry panel

        .General Management Strategies 
            • Maintenance of safe and effective risk reduction program is important to establishing treatment - monitoring guidelines 
            • Treatment monitoring guidelines are specific to the patient

        .Stratification for Risk of Event (!!P) (!!E).Lv2
            Lowest risk
                Moderate risk
                    Highest risk
            -----------------------------
            1St.Γ LV
                No significant LV dysfunction (EF>50%)
                    Moderately impaired LV function (EF = 40% to 49%)
                        Decreased LV function (EF<40%)
            2St.Γ ANGINA & DYSRHYTHMIA - DURING EXERCISE
                No resting or exercise-induced complex dysrhythmia
                    Signs/symptoms, including angina at moderate levels of exercise (5 to 6.9 METs or in recovery)
                        Survivor of cardiac arrest or sudden death 
            3St.Γ CAD INTERVENTIONS
                Uncomplicated MI, CABG, angioplasty, atherectomy, or stent 
                    Moderate risk is assumed for patients who do not meet the classification of either highest risk or lowest risk. 
                        Complex ventricular dysrhythmia at rest or with exercise
            4St.Γ CHF & ISCHEMIA
                Absence of CHF or signs/symptoms indicating postevent ischemia 
                        MI or cardiac surgery complicated by cardiogenic shock, CHF, and/or signs/symptoms of postprocedure ischemia 
            5St.Γ HEMODYNAMICS RESPONSES TO EXERCISE
                Normal hemodynamics with exercise or recovery
                        -Abnormal hemodynamics with exercise (especially flat or decreasing systolic blood pressure or chronotropic incompetence with increasing workload)
            6St.Γ ANGINA
                Asymptomatic, including absence of angina with exertion or recovery 
                        Signs/symptoms, including angina pectoris at low levels of exercise (<5.0 METs) or in recovery
            7St.Γ FUNCTIONAL/EXERCISE CAPACITY
                Functional capacity ≥ 7.0 METs(a)
                        Functional capacity <5 METs
            8St.Γ DEPRESSION
                Absence of clinical depression
                        Clinically significant depression
            9St.Γ RISK FACTORS
                Lowest risk classification is assumed when each of the risk factors in the category is present. 
                        Highest risk classification is assumed with the presence of any one of the risk factors included in this category. 
            
            -CABG, coronary artery bypass graft; CHF, congestive heart failure; EF, ejection fraction; LV, left ventricle; METs, metabolic equivalent table; MI, myocardial infarction. 
            -(a)If measured functional capacity is not available, this variable is not considered in risk stratification process.

        .Methods and Tools for Daily Assessment of Risk (!!E).Lv3
            -Box 18-4 Recommended methods and tools for daily assessment of risk for exercise 
            -Pre-exercise assessment should include patient interview regarding recent signs/symptoms and medication adherence. Risk also is assessed with following clinical measures: 
                • Continuous or intermittent ECG monitoring 
                • Telemetry or hardware monitoring 
                • Quick look using defibrillator paddles 
                • Periodic rhythm strips 
                • BP 
                • HR (palpated) 
                • Symptoms and evidence of effort intolerance 
                • Rating of perceived exertion (RPE)

        .Interventions Utilized in the Outpatient Cardiac Rehabilitation Setting: 
            • Therapeutic exercice 
            • Aerobic training, resistance training, flexibility training, circuit training 
            • Patient instruction/education 
            • Coordination/communication

        .Recommendations for Aerobic Training (!!E).Lv2
            • Aerobic Exercise Prescription: 
                • Mode – functional and fun 
                • Intensity — establishing a target heart rate, use RPE or dyspnea scale to gauge 
                • Duration – interval training of 2-5 mins, build to continuous 30-45 mins 
                • Frequency – higher frequency to make true CV changes, 5-7d/wk

        .Formulas for Predicted and Target HRs (!!E.eq)
            Table 18-11 Formulas for calculating predicted and target heart rates(a) 
                A → General population → 220 - age = PMHR 
                B → Fit individuals older than 40 → 205 – age = PMHR 
                C → Karvonen method → THR = RHR + 40% to 60% (Max HR-RHR) 

                -HR, heart rate; MHR, maximum heart rate; PMHR, predicted maximal heart rate; RHR, resting heart rate. 
                -(a)Formulas A and B should not be used when the true maximal heart rate can be determined or the patient is taking medications that would affect the resting and exercise heart rate (e.g., β-blocking medications).

        .Recommendations for Aerobic Training ('Recommendations for Aerobic Training')
            • HIIT training may also be implemented 
            • alternating bouts of moderate and vigorous intensity exercise

        .Intensity (!!E).Lv2
            Moderate Intensity 
                • Relative scale: 5 or 6 on a scale of 0 to 10 
                • Example: brisk walking Γ(Fast walking, Caminada voraç, Caminada ràpida, Caminata rápida)
            Vigorous Intensity 
                • Relative scale: begins at a 7 to 8 on a scale of 0 to 10 
                • Example: running or jogging
            ---------------------------------------- ↓
            Talk Test 
                -As a rule of thumb, a person doing moderate-intensity aerobic activity can talk, but not sing, during the activity. 
                -A person doing vigorous-intensity activity cannot say more than a few words without pausing for a breath.

            Table 18-12 Angina and dyspnea rating scales 
                5-Grade angina scale
                    0 = No angina
                    1 = Light, barely noticeable
                    2 = Moderate, bothersome
                    3 = Severe, very pre-infarction pain

                5-Grade dyspnea scale
                    0 = No dyspnea
                    1 = Mild, noticeable
                    2 = Mild, some difficulty
                    3 = Moderate difficulty, but can continue
                    4 = Severe difficulty, cannot continue

        .Recommendations for Resistance Training (!!E).Lv2
            • Resistance exercise training 
                • 30-50% 1RM with 8-10 reps each mm group 
                • allowed 5 wks post MI, 8 weeks post bypass, and 2 weeks post-PTCA, 
                • AHA and AACVPR have guidelines for training
            -----------------------------------------------------------------------
            Box 18-7 Recommendations for resistance training 
                Pre-test:
                    To identify the load that should be performed, a 1 repetition maximum (1-RM) should be performed. 
                Training:
                    -Weights should be set at approximately 30% to 50% of the 1-RM. Perform one set of 8 to 10 repetitions for each major muscle group two to three times a week with a day of rest between each workout. 
                    -Specific considerations during resistance training: 
                        1. Exercise large muscle groups before small muscle groups. 
                        2. Raise weights slowly with controlled movements and return weights slowly with controlled movements. 
                        3. Exhale during the exertion phase of the lift, inhale during the return to rest position. 
                        4. Increase loads by 5 to 10 lb when 12 to 15 repetitions can be performed comfortably 
                        5. Minimize rest periods between exercises if trying to maximize endurance of muscles. 
                        6. Avoid straining; avoid sustained tight gripping; rating of perceived exertion (RPE) Should be between 11 and 13 (on scale of 20). 
                        7. Stop exercise in event of warning signs or symptoms such as dizziness, palpitations, unusual shortness of breath, or angina. (!!P)

        .Cardiac Rehabilitation Training Programs Considerations 
            • Program progression (!!E).Lv2
                • Increase duration first until patient reaches 20-30 minutes 
                • Increasing intensity of exercise - once duration achieved 
                • Changing mode of exercise to include upper or combined upper and lower extremity exercise 
            • Other considerations in planning exercise programs 
                • Altitude 
                • Cold vs Heat and humidity

        .Post Acute Phase Cardiac Rehabilitation
            Key Terms and Concepts
                1. Outpatient Cardiac Rehabilitation Program: 
                    • Definition: A program designed to limit the physiological and psychological effects of cardiac illness. 
                    • Objective: Reduce the risk of sudden death, control cardiac symptoms, stabilize or reverse atherosclerosis, and enhance psychosocial and vocational status. 
                2. Medicare Coverage Guidelines: 
                    • Guidelines: Provided by the American Association of Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Rehabilitation. 
                    • Eligibility: Medicare beneficiaries with specific cardiovascular diagnoses. 
                3. Patient Groups for Cardiac Rehabilitation: 
                    • Traditionally Included: MI, heart failure, angioplasty, heart transplant, stable angina, cabbage, or valve replacement. 
                    • Expanded Population: Comorbid conditions, poor ejection fraction, cardiomyopathy, serious arrhythmias. 
                4. CMS NCD Criteria: 
                    • Includes: Myocardial infarction, coronary artery bypass graft surgery, stable angina, percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty, heart or heart-lung transplantation, heart valve repair or replacement, stable chronic heart failure. 
                5. Home-Based Program: 
                    • Considerations: For patients unable to attend outpatient programs regularly due to travel distance. 
                    • Implementation: Extensive discharge instructions, weekly telephone calls, ECG information transmission. 

            Questions and Answers (!!Q)
                Q1. What is the primary objective of outpatient cardiac rehabilitation programs? 
                    A1: The primary objective is to limit physiological and psychological effects of cardiac illness, reduce the risk of sudden death, control cardiac symptoms, stabilize or reverse atherosclerosis, and enhance psychosocial and vocational status. 
                Q2. Who are traditionally included in patient groups for cardiac rehabilitation? 
                    A2: Traditionally included patients are those with myocardial infarction, heart failure, angioplasty, heart transplant, stable angina, cabbage, or valve replacement. The population has expanded to include individuals with comorbid conditions and serious arrhythmias. 
                Q3. What are the criteria for Medicare coverage according to CMS NCD? 
                    A3: Criteria include diagnoses such as myocardial infarction, coronary artery bypass graft surgery, stable angina, percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty, heart or heart-lung transplantation, heart valve repair or replacement, and stable chronic heart failure. 
                Q4. How is a home-based program implemented for cardiac rehabilitation? 
                    A4: Candidates for home-based programs receive extensive discharge instructions, weekly telephone calls, and the option to transmit ECG information. A follow-up session with the cardiac rehabilitation team is arranged, and monthly contacts are maintained for 6 to 12 months. 
                Q5. What considerations should be made when planning exercise programs for cardiac rehabilitation patients? 
                    A5: Considerations include altitude effects, exercise in cold environments, and exercise in heat and humidity. Each patient's exercise plan should be determined based on clinical status, functional capacity, personal needs, available facilities, equipment, and environmental factors.

            Summary 
                • Outpatient cardiac rehabilitation programs aim to limit the physiological and psychological effects of cardiac illness, reduce the risk of sudden death, and enhance psychosocial and vocational status. 
                • Medicare coverage guidelines, including CMS NCD criteria, provide eligibility for beneficiaries with specific cardiovascular diagnoses. 
                • Patient groups for cardiac rehabilitation have expanded to include those with comorbid conditions, poor ejection fraction, cardiomyopathy, and serious arrhythmias. 
                • Home-based programs offer an alternative for patients unable to attend outpatient programs regularly, with extensive discharge instructions, weekly telephone calls, and ECG information transmission. 
                • Exercise programs in cardiac rehabilitation should consider altitude effects, cold environments, and heat and humidity, with individualized plans based on clinical status, needs, and environmental factors.

    .('Other Cardiac Rehabilitation Considerations.pdf')
        .Education 
            • Early intervention 
            • Education about problem of CAD plays significant role in preventing further cardiovascular disease 
            • The outpatient setting 
            • Patient’s educational level should not be a limiting factor in achieving an understanding of disease and the rehabilitation process or risk factor modification 
            • Basic information should be provided to an individual and in a group format
            ----------------------------------------------------------
            • Diet and nutrition 
                • Should be designed to fit the person’s specific lipid abnormality, cultural background, lifestyle 
            • Weight loss 
                • Obesity is a significant risk factor for coronary artery disease 
            • Psychosocial recovery 
                • Anxiety, depression, or denial 
                • Social support

        .Lipid Values Indicative of Higher Risk
            Table 18-14 Lipid values indicative of higher risk 
                Total cholesterol (mg/dL) (>75th percentile)        >220        20 to 29 years old 
                                                                    >220        30 to 39 years old 
                                                                    >240        40 years or older 
                Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) (mg/dL)               >100 
                                                                    >175        Extremely high risk 
                High-density lipoprotein (HDL) (mg/dL)              <35 
                LDL:HDL                                             3:1 
                Triglycerides (mg/dL)                               >200

        .Risk Factor Adjustment Difficulties in Cardiac Patients (!!P) (!!E).Lv1
            -Patients with a combination of the following characteristics should be considered at higher risk for adjustment difficulties necessitating additional evaluation and support: 
                • Patients who: 
                    • live alone 
                    • do not have a confidant 
                    • recently divorced or widowed 
                    • socially isolated 
                    • multi-problem families 
                    • Smoke 
                    • Obese 
                    • have cultural or religious values that conflict with a philosophy of self-reliance and optimism 
                • Patients with: 
                    • low incomes 
                    • multiple chronic illnesses 
                    • without spiritual or religious comfort 
                    • history of mental health difficulties

        .Assessment and Outcomes Related to Psychosocial Concerns 
            Table 18-16 Assessment and outcomes related to psychosocial concerns 
                Assessment
                    -Staff should identify clinically significant levels of psychosocial distress using a combination of clinical interview and psychosocial screening instruments at program entry, exit, and periodic follow-up. 
                Outcomes
                    Clinical: 
                        -The patient should experience emotional wellbeing as evidenced by the absence of: 
                            1. Psychological distress indicated by clinically significant levels of depression, social isolation, anxiety, anger, hostility 
                            2. Drug dependency 
                            3. Excessive psychophysiology arousal
                    Behavioral: 
                        Program service should enhance the patient's ability to: 
                            1. Describe the recovery and rehabilitation process 
                            2. Develop realistic health-related expectations 
                            3. Assume responsibility for behavior change 
                            4. Demonstrate problem-solving capabilities 
                            5. Engage in physical exercise, meditation, and other relaxation techniques 
                            6. Demonstrate effective use of other cognitive-behavioral stress management skills 
                            7. Obtain effective social support 
                            8. Comply with psychotropic medications if prescribed 
                            9. Reduce or eliminate alcohol, tobacco, caffeine usage, or other nonprescription psychoactive drugs 
                            10. Return to meaningful social, vocational, and avocational roles
                    
        .Compliance 
            • Major problem in all cardiac rehabilitation centers 
            • Contributing factors 
                • duration of rehabilitation 
                • regimen complexity 
                • nature of side effects 
                • presence of symptoms 
                • social and environmental factors 
                • patient–therapist interaction

        .Benefits of Cardiac Rehabilitation 
            • Improvement in exercise tolerance 
            • Improvement in symptoms 
            • Improvement in blood lipids 
            • Reduction in cigarette smoking 
            • Improvement in psychosocial well-being and reduction of stress 
            • Reduction in mortality rate

        .Safety, Follow-up, and Discharge 
            • Safety in the outpatient cardiac rehabilitation setting 
                • Must be top priority 
                • Major cardiovascular events can occur such as sudden cardiac arrest 
                • Must be able to deal with cardiac arrest and other medical emergencies 
            • Follow-up assessment 
                • Should be performed and discussed with patient at least two times per month 
            • Criteria for discharge 
                • Reimbursement agencies request definitions of discharge criteria 
                • Rehabilitation goals and plans must be outcome-oriented 

        .Special Patient Populations 
            • Requires integration of clinical information and exercise physiology 
            • Patients with multisystem dysfunction may require special attention and individualized approach 
            • Require special considerations: (!!E).Lv3 
                • Women 
                • Elderly 
                • Patients with PAD, COPD, DM 
                • Patients who had a cerebrovascular accident 
                • Heart transplant 
                • Obesity 
                • Heart Failure

        .Facility Concerns 
            • Ideally facility has classroom space for group education, private counseling, and a library of educational materials 
            • Exercise space allow freedom of movement 
            • Easily accessible, pleasant, clean 
            • May be only cardiac rehabilitation or combined with sports medicine and/or pulmonary rehabilitation

        .Records and Documentation 
            • Provide method of retrieving information, evaluating value and validity of the rehabilitation process, analyzing cost effectiveness and a quality assurance 
            • Contents should include: (!!E).Lv3
                • Attending physician referral and authorization 
                • Pertinent medical data 
                • Initial cardiac rehabilitation evaluation Γ(for PTs)
                • Regular progress notes Γ(for PTs)
                • Monthly reports Γ(for PTs Maybe)
                • Monthly log records Γ(for PTs Maybe)
                • Discharge summary Γ(for PTs)

        .Medical and Legal Considerations
            • Legal problems stem from two aspects:
                • Adverse effects of medically prescribed exercise testing and fitness conditioning 
                • Consideration of disability pension and insurance benefits that may influence patient’s motivation

        .Charges to Patients and Third-Party Carriers 
            • Cardiac rehabilitation is not a major income producer in most facilities 
                • considered a part of the total cardiology care (product line) 
                • Medicare additionally requires that a physician directly supervises the program with emergency equipment available 
                • Staffing must consist of qualified personnel 
                • Some services are not covered (i.e., patient education)

        .Cardiac Rehabilitation Coverage
            • Covered Diagnoses 
                • Acute MI within 12 months 
                • CABG or PTCA 
                • heart transplant 
                • Stable angina 
                • HF with EF<35% (recently added in 2014) 
            • Duration 
                • 12 weeks or 26 sessions without individual review by a Medicare contractor 
                • contractor has the discretion to cover cardiac rehabilitation services beyond 18 weeks, but coverage must not exceed a total of 72 sessions

                Mechanisms of Beneficial Effects of Exercise Training and Cardiac Rehabilitation in Patients With Heart Failure
                    Lungs

                    Muscular

                    Vasal

                        ↓ Hypertension

        .Other Cardiac Rehab Considerations 
            Key Terms and Concepts 
                1. Educational Components in Outpatient Cardiac Rehabilitation: 
                    • Importance: Education on CAD as a secondary prevention measure. 
                    • Goal: Improved patient outcomes through increased understanding of the disease, rehabilitation process, risk factor modification, an psychosocial recovery. 
                    • Example: Group educational sessions covering basic information on cardiovascular disease. 
                2. Diet and Nutrition: 
                    • Significance: Essential for optimal long-term outcomes and prevention of future events. 
                    • Components: Education on diet, weight loss, and psychosocial recovery. 
                    • Example: Providing nutritional guidance tailored to each patient's needs. 
                3. Psychosocial Adjustment Risk Factors: 
                    • Identification: Screened through interviews and screening methods. 
                    • Program Services: Addressing psychosocial concerns through specialized interventions. 
                    • Example: Tailored program services based on identified psychosocial risk factors. 
                4. Patient Compliance: 
                    • Challenge: Only 20-50% of participants continue exercising after one year. 
                    • Factors: Complex and include the duration and complexity of the rehabilitation regimen, nature of symptoms, and social and environmental factors. 
                    • Role: Physician encouragement and support significantly impact compliance. 
                5. Benefits of Cardiac Rehabilitation: 
                    • Improvements: Exercise tolerance, symptom reduction, blood lipid improvement, reduced smoking, enhanced psychosocial well-being, stress reduction, and overall mortality reduction. 
                    • Importance: Integral in educating patients about the myriad benefits for motivation and program compliance. 
                6. Safety in Outpatient Cardiac Rehabilitation: 
                    • Priority: Ensuring safety to prevent major cardiovascular events. 
                    • Measures: Implementation of safety measures and personnel preparedness for emergencies. 
                    • Follow-up: Regular assessment, discussion of criteria for discharge, and readiness for unsupervised exercise programs. 
                7. Special Patient Populations: 
                    • Considerations: Individualized approach for populations with multisystem dysfunction. 
                    • Examples: Female patients with unique anginal symptoms like pain in the scapular region. 
                    • Challenges: Need for careful consideration and modification of exercise plans. 
                8. Cardiac Rehab Center: 
                    • Facility: Interdisciplinary team planning, monitoring programs, and providing education. 
                    • Ideal Setting: Includes a classroom, private counseling space, and a well-equipped exercise area. 
                    • Location: Can be hospital-based, satellite, or even at local gyms during different phases. 
                9. Sustainability Challenges: 
                    • Factors: Reimbursement, location, and facilities impact program sustainability. 
                    • Documentation: Thorough record-keeping, evaluation, and regular progress notes are crucial. 
                    • Legal Aspects: Adverse effects, disability pension considerations, and insurance benefits may pose challenges. 
                10. Covered Diagnoses and Duration: 
                    • Importance: Patient approval and detailed documentation for visit authorization. 
                    • Consideration: Medicare approval for up to 72 sessions, covering various diagnoses. 
                    • Example: Heart failure patients with an ejection fraction of less than 35% can be accepted.

            Questions and Answers (!!Q)
                Q1. Why is early education on CAD considered a secondary prevention measure? 
                    A1: Early education on CAD aims to prevent further cardiovascular disease and progression. It has been shown to improve long-term outcomes and patient compliance with rehabilitation programs. 
                Q2. What are some risk factors for psychosocial adjustment after a cardiac event? 
                    A2: Identified risk factors include previous experiences, premorbid health, misconceptions, and body concerns. Psychosocial concerns should be assessed through interviews and screening methods. 
                Q3. What are the challenges associated with patient compliance in cardiac rehabilitation programs? 
                    A3: Factors contributing to poor compliance include the duration and complexity of the rehabilitation regimen, nature of symptoms, social and environmental factors, and the patient-therapist interaction. Physician encouragement plays a significant role. 
                Q4. What are the benefits of cardiac rehabilitation, and why is it considered important? 
                    A4: Benefits include improved exercise tolerance, symptom reduction, better blood lipids, reduced smoking, enhanced psychosocial well-being, stress reduction, and an overall reduction in mortality. It is crucial for educating patients about these benefits to ensure motivation and compliance. 
                Q5. Why is safety a top priority in outpatient cardiac rehabilitation, and what measures should be in place? 
                    A5: Safety is crucial to prevent major cardiovascular events. Measures include regular assessment, discussions about criteria for discharge, and readiness for unsupervised exercise programs. Personnel must be prepared to deal with emergencies. 

            Summary 
                • Educational components in outpatient cardiac rehabilitation cover CAD prevention, diet, and psychosocial recovery. 
                • Psychosocial adjustment risk factors should be identified through interviews and screening methods, allowing tailored program services. 
                • Patient compliance challenges include complex factors, and physician encouragement significantly impacts adherence. 
                • Cardiac rehabilitation benefits encompass various aspects, emphasizing the importance of patient education for motivation and compliance. 
                • Safety measures, regular assessments, and readiness for unsupervised programs are paramount in outpatient cardiac rehabilitation. 
                • Special patient populations require individualized exercise plans, considering unique symptoms and challenges. 
                • The sustainability of cardiac rehabilitation programs faces challenges related to reimbursement, documentation, and legal aspects. 
                • Covered diagnoses and duration criteria impact patient approval and documentation for visit authorization. 
                • Heart failure patients with an ejection fraction of less than 35% can benefit from supervised cardiac rehabilitation, showcasing the multi-system impact of the disease.

16.Emergency Response Procedures
    ..4.6. Emergency Response Procedures (!!P)
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    .('Emergency Response Procedures.pdf')
        .Responding to Emergency Situations 
            • Demonstrate appropriate actions in event of clinical emergency. 
            • Provide information to expedite arrival of code response team. 
            • Identify appropriate positioning of patient in code situation. 
            • Identify protective measures to be taken in life threatening situations.

        .Emergency Procedures in Outpatient 
            1. Upon discovery of an individual in an emergency medical condition or state, the person finding the individual will begin assessment and support or alert a qualified employee to provide assessment and support. 
            2. The initial responder should request another staff member to contact the local Emergency Medical Service when necessary. 
            3. Support will be continued until the patient is alert and responsive or until EMS arrives and care is transferred to EMS 
            4. Patients and visitors should be cleared from the area.

        .Types of Emergency Situations in the Inpatient Setting (!!E.Grade & Doc) (!!E).Lv1
            • CONDITION A is Called when a patient is: 
                • cardiac or respiratory arrest requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation 
                • unresponsive 
                • without a pulse 
            • CONDITION C is called when a patient is: 
                • Pre-code to condition A 
                • unstable 
                • needs RAPID evaluation and/or treatment by medical team 

        .Pulseless Patient – Condition A 
            • Assess situation and establish unresponsiveness 
            • Call for assistance 
            • Begin CPR

        .Potential Crisis Situations - Condition C (!!P) 
            Respiratory: 
                Rate over 36 or less than 8/min 
                New onset of difficulty breathing 
                New pulse ox reading less than 85% 
                • unless patient has chronic hypoxemia 
            Heart Rate: 
                less than 40 or over 140/min with new symptoms, any rate over 160 
            Blood pressure 
                less than 80 or over 200 systolic over 110 diastolic with symptoms 
                • neuro change, chest pain, difficulty breathing

        .Crisis Situations-Condition C 
            • Acute neurologic change: 
                • Acute loss of consciousness 
                • New onset lethargy, difficulty walking 
                • Sudden collapse 
                • Seizure 
                • Sudden loss of movement (or weakness) of face, arm or leg

        .“Other” Emergencies- Condition C 
            • Chest pain 
            • Color change 
            • Suicide attempt 
            • Uncontrolled bleeding 
            • Bleeding into airway 
            • Unexplained agitation >10 min.

        .Procedure in an Emergency 
            • Dial appropriate emergency number if inside of a hospital 
            • Outside of hospital, dial 911 (activate the EMS) 
            • Identify type of emergency 
            • Identify yourself 
            • Provide patient location 
                • building, floor, wing, unit title

        .What to Do Until Team Arrives 
            • Take vitals 
            • Position patient 
            • Maintain BLS 
            • Apply AED (if appropriate)

        .What to Communicate to the Emergency Responders/Code Team 
            • Events leading to emergency 
            • Vital signs 
            • May need access to medical record 
                • medications 
                • allergies 
                • medical history

        .Review of Potential Life-Threatening Situations 
            • Seizures 
            • Pre-syncope and Syncope 
            • Falls 
            • Acute dyspnea 
            • Hypoglycemia

        .Seizures 
            • Ensure an open airway 
            • Prevent injury 
            • Notify appropriate personnel 
            • Observe and provide protection until emergency response team arrives. 
            • Do not restrain the victim during a seizure. 
            • Do not try to open the victim’s mouth or try to place any object between the victim’s teeth or in the mouth. 
            • It is not unusual for the victim to be unresponsive or confused for a short time after a seizure.

        .Pre-syncope 
            • Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness that results from global cerebral hypoperfusion. 
            • Many individuals with syncope have recurrent episodes. 
            • Vasovagal and orthostatic syncope are responsible for about 1/3rd of all syncope. 
            • Pre-syncope can last for a few seconds before onset of syncope. 
            • Associated signs and symptoms include: 
                • Pallor 
                • Sweating 
                • Lightheadedness 
                • Visual changes 
                • Weakness
            ------------------------------------------
            • Presents recognizable signs and symptoms 
            • Rapid first aid treatment could improve symptoms or prevent syncope from occurring 
            • presyncope of vasovagal or orthostatic origin, the priority is to assume a safe position such as sitting or lying down 
            • Individuals with syncope can be taught to recognize signs of presyncope and apply physical counter-pressure maneuvers: 
                • handgrip, arm tensing, abdominal muscle tensing, leg crossing with tensing, squatting, and neck flexion. 
                • May reduce symptoms of presyncope and prevent syncope

        .Pre-Syncope Counterpressure Maneuvers
            ('Pre-Syncope Counterpressure Maneuvers')
            ('Pre-Syncope Counterpressure Maneuvers 2')

        .Syncope 
            • Perform initial assessment 
            • Place patient in safe position 
            • Counterpressure maneuvers 
            • Monitor vitals 
            • Notify RN/MD 
            • Prevention and early recognition is key

        .Falls 
            • Ensure adequate airway and ventilation 
            • Stop any hemorrhage with pressure 
            • Immobilize cervical spine 
            • Notify appropriate personnel asap 
            • Assess patient from front to back for bleeding if patient is safe to move

        .Respiratory Distress 
            • Signs/Symptoms: 
                • Abnormal breathing (shallow, labored, noise) or respiratory rate 
                • Cyanosis 
                • Nasal flaring 
                • Decreased level of consciousness 
                • Restlessness 
            • If the patient has asthma, consider if patient requires assistance with bronchodilator/inhalers

        .Acute Dyspnea - Immediate Actions 
            • Maintain clear airway and place patient in comfortable breathing position. 
            • Observe and evaluate (vitals), suction if needed 
            • Notify appropriate personnel, call a code/911 if appropriate

        .Diabetic Emergencies - Hypoglycemia (!!P)
            • Hypoglycemia can manifest as a variety of symptoms, including: 
                • confusion 
                • altered behavior 
                • diaphoresis 
                • tremulousness 
            • If a diabetic has these symptoms, assume hypoglycemia exists 
            • If the person is unconscious, exhibits seizures, or is unable to follow simple commands or swallow safely, the first aid provider should call for EMS immediately.

        .Diabetic Emergencies (!!P)
            • Encourage the individual to swallow glucose (eg, tablets, liquid, gel). 
                • Reminder: levels are low (70 to 100 mg/dL) prior to exercise and the individual should be given a carbohydrate snack and postpone exercise hypoglycemia is corrected (typically about 20 to 30 minutes) 
            • Emergency services should be activated if symptoms do not resolve within 10 minutes or symptoms worsen 
            • It is reasonable to use dietary sugars as an alternative 
                • Orange juice (unsweetened, from concentrate), Jellybeans, Sucrose candy (Skittles), Mentos, Fructose (fruit leather), Whole milk

        .Emergency Response Procedures 
            Key Terms and Concepts 
                1. Immediate Responder Responsibilities: 
                    • Definition: The initial person responding to an emergency situation. 
                    • Insight: Required to ensure patient safety and initiate life-saving measures. 
                    • Example: Calling a code or 911, providing correct information, identifying patient positioning, and taking protective measures. 
                2. Outpatient Setting Challenges: 
                    • Importance: Independently handling emergencies due to limited resources. 
                    • Consideration: Knowing when to call 911, initiate CPR, and perform life-saving measures. 
                    • Example: Recognizing the need for immediate EMS support. 
                3. Inpatient Emergency Situations: 
                    • Distinction: Likelihood of higher acuity patients. 
                    • Conditions: Condition A (unresponsive without a pulse) and Condition C (patient becoming unstable). 
                    • Steps: Hospital emergency procedure for calling a code, assessing, calling for assistance, and initiating CPR. 
                4. Vital Signs in Condition C: 
                    • Significance: Monitoring vitals for potential crisis indicators. 
                    • Indicators: Abnormal respiratory rates, pulse ox readings, heart rates, and blood pressure changes. 
                    • Response: Initiating appropriate emergency measures based on vital signs. 
                5. Emergency Procedure Steps: 
                    • Steps: Dialing emergency number or activating the alert system, identifying the emergency type, providing patient location, and continuing vital sign monitoring. 
                    • Actions: Positioning the patient safely, initiating CPR, and applying AED if necessary. 
                    • Certification: Regular maintenance of BLS (Basic Life Support) certification. 
                6. Communication with Emergency Medical Team: 
                    • Information: Events leading to the emergency, vital signs, and relevant medical history. 
                    • Certainty: Providing accurate and concise information to assist the medical team. 

            Questions and Answers (!!Q)
                Q1. What are the responsibilities of an immediate responder in an emergency situation? 
                    A1: An immediate responder must know how to call a code or 911, provide correct information, identify patient positioning, and take protective measures in life-threatening situations. 
                Q2. How does the outpatient setting differ in handling emergencies compared to the inpatient setting? 
                    A2: In the outpatient setting, the therapist may need to work more independently. Recognizing the need to call 911, initiating CPR, and performing life-saving measures are crucial due to limited immediate resources. 
                Q3. What are the conditions considered in inpatient emergency situations? 
                    A3: Condition A involves an unresponsive patient without a pulse, while Condition C pertains to a patient becoming unstable. Both situations require knowledge of hospital emergency procedures. 
                Q4. Why is monitoring vital signs important in Condition C emergencies? 
                    A4: Abnormal vital signs, including respiratory rates, pulse ox readings, heart rates, and blood pressure changes, can indicate a potential crisis. Proper response measures depend on these indicators. 
                Q5. What steps should be followed in the emergency procedure, especially when calling for help? 
                    A5: Dial the appropriate emergency number, identify the emergency type, provide patient location, and continue vital sign monitoring. Position the patient safely, initiate CPR, and apply AED if needed. 
                Q6. Why is communication with the emergency medical team crucial during an emergency? 
                    A6: Accurate and concise communication regarding events leading to the emergency, vital signs, and medical history assists the medical team in providing effective care. 

            Summary 
                • Immediate responders play a crucial role in ensuring patient safety and initiating life-saving measures. 
                • Challenges in the outpatient setting include independently handling emergencies due to limited resources. 
                • Inpatient emergency situations include Condition A (unresponsive without a pulse) and Condition C (patient becoming unstable). 
                • Monitoring vital signs is essential in recognizing potential crisis indicators in Condition C emergencies. 
                • Emergency procedure steps involve calling the appropriate emergency number, identifying the emergency type, providing patient location, and continuing vital sign monitoring. 
                • Communication with the emergency medical team, providing accurate information, and maintaining BLS certification are vital for effective emergency response.

    .This activity will allow you to test your knowledge of primary versus secondary versus tertiary prevention related to cardiovascular disease. Participate in the following knowledge check activity to review primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.

    .Lesson 1 of 1
        1.Matching: Match to descriptor to the correct prevention.
            Interventions to prevent progression of the cardiovascular disease
            Does not reduce incidence or prevalence as the disease is present and progressed

..4.9. Module 4 (Unit 1) Quiz (!!Q)

    Question 1
    Overall, the goals of an inpatient cardiac rehabilitation program for a patient post-myocardial infarction include which of the following? 

    Assess patient safety during performance of activities anticipated in the home setting.
    Increase patient knowledge of the disease and management of the disease.
    Deliver optimal discharge instructions specific to a patient as a member of a cohesive team.
    All of the above

        The correct answer is: All of the above.
            Overall, the goals of inpatient cardiac rehabilitation are to assess for safety to perform activities in the home or the alternative care site after discharge from the hospital, and to increase patient knowledge of the disease and the management of the disease. In addition, the team members must function cohesively in preparing the patient for discharge.

    Question 2
    Which of the following factors should be considered when determining specific intensity parameters of an acute phase cardiac rehabilitation program?

    ECG findings only
    Heart rate
    Physician's preference
    Combination of ECG, hemodynamics, and symptoms

        The correct answer is: Combination of ECG, hemodynamics, and symptoms.
            It is the combination of all factors (hemodynamic, symptoms, and ECG findings) that must be considered in determining specific intensity parameters.
     
    Question 3
    Which of the following indicators would subsequently lead to withholding a program in the acute phase of cardiac rehabilitation? 

    Resting tachycardia (100 bpm)
    Large infarction clinically, stable after 2 to 3 days
    Angina at rest
    Blood pressure failing to rise with self-care activities
        
        Angina at rest
            The following criteria are used to exclude patients from participation in the activity program: (1) severe pump failure (shortness of breath, peripheral edema, diaphoresis or CXR, and falling blood pressure with activity), (2) recurrent malignant arrhythmias, and (3) angina at rest, second or third degree heart block, persistent hypotension, rapid atrial rhythm, and unstable angina pectoris
     
    Question 4
    Developing an exercise program that addresses the specific needs of the patient’s daily life and interests is BEST described by which of the following parameters of exercise? (!!F) 

    Mode
    Intensity
    Specificity
    Duration

        Specificity
            Specificity of training is related to the specific exercise needs of the patient’s regular daily needs and interests
     
    Question 5
    Which of the following factors should the physical therapist consider when prescribing frequency and duration of exercise for a patient in cardiac rehabilitation? 

    How long the patient has been disabled with the condition
    How much has the patient’s activity been reduced by the acute event
    The patient’s premorbid activity level and capability
    All of the above should be considered for the individualized program

        All of the above should be considered for the individualized program
            Exercise duration should be individualized and based on several factors: (1) length of disability, (2) reduced activity as a result of the acute event, and (3) premorbid activity level and neuromuscular capability.
     
    Question 6 (!!F)
    Which of the following progressions in exercise parameters would be MOST appropriate for a patient 2 weeks postoperative a coronary artery bypass graft who is currently walking on a treadmill for 20 minutes at 50% of maximal heart rate? 

    Increase the intensity of exercise to 60% of maximal heart rate.
    Increase the duration of exercise with the goal being at least 30 minutes
    Add resistive training exercise at 40% of one repetition maximum.
    Add low-intensity upper extremity exercise during treadmill walking.

        The MOST appropriate progression in exercise parameters for a patient 2 weeks postoperative from a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) who is currently walking on a treadmill for 20 minutes at 50% of maximal heart rate would be:

        Increase the duration of exercise with the goal being at least 30 minutes
            At 2 weeks into the cardiac rehabilitation, increasing the duration should be the first priority for a patient who is walking 20 minutes. Duration should be increased until the patient can exercise for at least 30 minutes, then intensity can be increased. A patient with a CABG should wait for 8 weeks with 3 weeks of continuous participation before resistive training is started.

    Question 7
    Which of the following environmental factors tends to increase peripheral resistance at rest and with exercise? 

    Altitude
    Cold temperature
    Heat
    Humidity

        Cold temperature
            Cold temperatures cause an increase in peripheral resistance at rest and with exercise. This peripheral vasoconstriction can subsequently cause an increase in arterial blood pressure and possibly create a situation for earlier ischemic changes with increased myocardial oxygen demands.

    Question 8
    In which of the following situations is NOT appropriate for a patient to be discharged from a cardiac rehabilitation program? (!!F)

    Anticipated goals and desired outcomes have been achieved.
    Patient declines to continue intervention.
    Patient is failing to attend scheduled appointments and not making progress.
    Patient was uncomfortable performing aerobic exercise on a treadmill

        Patient was uncomfortable performing aerobic exercise on a treadmill
            The patient may engage in other modes of aerobic exercise besides treadmill training, such as bike, and this would not be a reason for discharge. Key points for discharge include (1) the anticipated goals and desired outcomes have been achieved, (2) patient declines to continue intervention, (3) patient is unable to continue to progress toward goals because of medical or psychosocial complications, and (4) failure to make reasonable progress toward goals due to nonadherence to home program, failure to attend scheduled appointments, or lack of willingness or ability to participate in the program. 
     
    Question 9
    If a patient with type II diabetes presents with a blood glucose of 70 mg/dL prior to an exercise session in the physical therapy clinic, what is the suggested next step for this patient? 

    If the patient feels well, is adequately hydrated, then she or he can perform with low-intensity exercise.
    The patient should be given a 10- to 15-g carbohydrate snack and exercise should be postponed until hypoglycemia is resolved.
    Exercise is contraindicated and the patient should ingest a snack.
    The patient can begin to exercise, but blood glucose should be monitored every 15 minutes.

        The patient should be given a 10- to 15-g carbohydrate snack and exercise should be postponed until hypoglycemia is resolved.
            If blood glucose levels are low (70 to 100 mg/dL) prior to therapy, the individual should be given a 10- to 15-g carbohydrate snack and exercise should be postponed until hypoglycemia is corrected (typically about 20 to 30 minutes).
     
    Question 10
    Which of the following intervention would MOST likely be considered a primary prevention of cardiovascular disease? 

    Prevention of a 2nd cardiovascular episode
    Treatment designed to improve quality of life and reduce the symptoms after a disease or disorder has developed
    Dietary counseling for those with diabetes, weight management problems, and elevated cholesterol
    Interventions to prevent progression of the cardiovascular disease

        Dietary counseling for those with diabetes, weight management problems, and elevated cholesterol
            Specific components of a primary prevention program (active intervention for risk factors that cause cardiovascular disease) include (1) therapeutic exercise—aerobic and resistance, (2) dietary counseling for those with diabetes, weight management problems, and elevated cholesterol, (3) stress management or biofeedback, (4) smoking cessation, (5) pharmacological management for blood pressure, diabetes, or hypercholesterolemia, and (6) education and self-management techniques.
