        .Pulmonary Examination Techniques Skills Practice:
            .Auscultation of Lung Sounds
                •   Position patient in the sitting position.
                •   Place diaphragm of stethoscope directly against the skin.
                •   Give proper instructions, i.e., “Breathe in and out through your mouth”.
                •   Be sure that patient does not hyperventilate.
                •   Listen to lung sounds in at least 6 locations on both the anterior and posterior chest wall. Listen for quality of air exchange.
                •   Listen for one full breath in each location.
                •   Listen first at the apices, move stethoscope side to side, and compare each side.
                •   Note if sounds heard are normal (clear), abnormal or adventitious (noisy), diminished or absent (may be one-side only).
                •   Record findings.

                Critical Criteria:
                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Uses stethoscope appropriately.
                _________ Auscultates in appropriate areas.
                _________ Compares lung sounds bilaterally.          

            .Voice Transmission Tests
                •   Egophony- Patient says E, positive finding when A is heard (normal=muffled E sound)
                •   Bronchophony-Patient says 99, positive finding when sound heard loudly (normal=muffled /indistinguishable sound)
                •   Whispered Pectoriloquy: Patient whispers, positive finding when whisper heard loudly (normal=faint sound)

                Critical Criteria:
                _________ Uses stethoscope appropriately.
                _________ Auscultates in appropriate areas.
                _________ Compares lung sounds bilaterally.       

            .Mediate Percussion
                -Place non-dominant third finger in rib interspace and strike briskly with tip of dominant hand (index finger), strike twice with finger, compare audible sounds to contralateral sides
                Critical Criteria:

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Places non-dominant hand properly
                _________ Percusses with dominant hand properly.
                _________ Compares lungs bilaterally.          

            .Tactile Fremitus
                -Place ulnar hand surface over posterior thorax. Patient repeats ‘99’ and notes bilateral differences in vibration (increased or decreased)

                Critical Criteria:
                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Places hands correctly on patient 
                _________ Compares lungs bilaterally.          

            .Chest Wall Expansion:
                •   Patient in sitting
                •   Anterior at mid sternum - upper lobe
                •   Anterior at xiphoid (thumbs horizontal) - right middle lobe and left lingula 
                •   Posteriorly at T8 level - lower lobe motion

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Places hands correctly on patient 
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal motion

            .Diaphragmatic Breathing Assessment:  
                •   Patient in supine
                •   Palpate the diaphragm with thumbs over the costal margin and thumb tips meeting at the xyphoid while patient inhales deeply

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Places hands correctly on patient 
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal motion

            .Tracheal Deviation
                -Patient in sitting or standing, place finger over tracheal region

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Places hands correctly on patient 
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal motion

        .Cardiovascular Examination Techniques Skills Practice:
            .Cardiac Palpation Sites
                •   Patient in supine
                •   Use fingertips followed by heel of hand at the 4 cardiac palpation sites
                •   Abnormal findings of visible pulsations outside of the norm (cardiac) or chest wall deformities that may limit chest wall movements with respiration

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Places hands in correct locations on the chest wall
                _________ Modifies need for placement accordingly 
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal findings

            .Auscultation of Heart Sounds
                •   Locate the areas where you will listen to heart sounds.
                •   Position patient in supine 
                •   Listen to the heart sounds with the diaphragm of the stethoscope. 
                •   Bell is useful in picking up low pitched sounds (S3, S4, mitral stenosis).
                •   Assess your partner’s heart rate by taking the apical pulse (auscultate and palpate)
                •   Assess if the heart rate corelates with the radial pulse.
                •   Normal sounds:  S1 (lub-closure of mitral and tricuspid valves), S2 (dub-closure of aortic and pulmonic valves)
                •   Abnormal sounds:  S3 (heart failure, diastolic dysfunction), S4 (noncompliant/hypertrophic ventricle)

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Places stethoscope in correct locations on the chest wall
                _________ Modifies need for placement accordingly 
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal sounds
                _________ Assesses apical pulse with stethoscope and palpation method 

            .Carotid Artery Auscultation
                •   Patient seated or supine with head turned slightly away from examiner
                •   Place stethoscope bell at the four sites that follow the carotid artery
                •   Patient inhales, exhales, then holds breath for 15s & listening occurs during and immediately after exhalation
                •   Abnormal findings: systolic bruit, which is a blowing or swishing sound

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Place’s stethoscope in correct locations 
                _________ Modifies need for placement accordingly 
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal sounds

            .Abdominal Aorta Auscultation 
                •   Patient supine with knees bent and examiner on right side
                •   Examiner places the stethoscope just above the umbilicus and lift of midline (Image 8)
                •   Abnormal findings: bruits or swishing in the presence of a wide pulse

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Place’s stethoscope in correct location
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal sounds

            .Abdominal Aorta Palpation
                •   Examiner facing the patient’s head/shoulders 
                •   Place fingertips of both hands-on the abdomen with index fingers points toward the head, just above the umbilicus and lift of midline 
                •   Press down firmly to locate the pulsating aorta & palpate for size, location, and pulsation
                •   Normal findings: pulsation width ~ 2.5 cm (1 inch or ~2 fingertips)
                •   Abnormal findings: wide pulsation (≥4 cm) or large lateral pulsation

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Place’s stethoscope in correct location
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal palpation findings

            .Capillary Refill
                •   Limb at heart level, depress nail bed 5 seconds
                •   Positive findings for poor circulation include:  Finger ≥ 3 seconds; Toe ≥ 5 seconds 

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal palpation findings

        .Other Systems Examination Techniques Skills Practice:
            .Deep abdominal palpation
                •   Patient supine & examiner to place 4 fingertips flat on the abdomen and depress 5-8 cm or 2-3 inches 
                •   Circle fingers in a rotary motion, then move to next area 
                •   Assess all abdominal quadrants 
                •   Positive findings include tenderness, masses, enlargement of organs, tissues or muscles 

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Places hand on patient with correct finger placement
                _________ Depresses skin to the correct depth 
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal palpation findings

            .Bimanual Kidney palpation
                •   Patient supine & examiner on the right 
                •   Place left hand under the patient’s back and other hand on top of the abdomen below the costal margin 
                •   Press the two hands firmly together & to feel the organ in the posteriorly located hand
                •   Normal: Smooth, rounded, lower pole of the kidney or may not be able to palpate
                •   Positive/Abnormal: Enlarged kidney, nodules, tenderness
                •   Right side inferior pole & left side difficult to palpate 

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Places hands on patient in correct locations
                _________ Depresses skin to the correct depth 
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal palpation findings

            .Bimanual Liver Palpation
                •   Patient supine & examiner on the right 
                •   Place left hand under the patient’s back parallel to the lowest ribs
                •   Place 4 fingers of right hand in the RUQ, parallel to the midline, and index finger in line with costal margin 
                •   Patient to deeply inhale, then push down firmly with the right hand while the left hand remains as a posterior support
                •   Normal: smooth, firm edge of liver may be felt by right hand or not being able to palpate the liver
                •   Positive/Abnormal: Edge of liver extending beyond 1-2 cm indicates enlargement, tender, hard, and/or irregular 

                _________ Instructs patient in procedure 
                _________ Places hands on patient in correct locations
                _________ Depresses skin to the correct depth 
                _________ Notes normal vs abnormal palpation findings

        Part I: Cardiovascular Examination Procedures
            .Cardiac Palpation Sites

    .Part I: Cardiovascular Examination Procedures
        .1cpE.Cardiac Palpation Sites
            .Introduction 
                .Palpating the regions of the heart on the chest
                    quick screen to assess for any areas of abnormalities (means for differential diagnosis)
                        If feel thrills (Tremolors) or heaves (Arcadas)
                            would correspond with heart murmurs Γ(thrills) or cardiac hypertrophy Γ(heaves)
                        palpating over a region of the heart that corresponds with the structure can allow you to
                            associate that abnormality with that region
                                If pain is felt by the patient, you may consider
                                    a musculoskeletal type of pain.
                                If a deformity is felt, you could be feeling
                                    a chest wall structural abnormality such as pectus cranium('') or excavatum.

                .Procedure for Cardiac Palpation
                    1. Supine with bed elevated to 30 degrees OR left lateral decubitus position('') 
                    2. Palpate the following areas with pads of fingers, followed by heel of hand ('01 Finger pad and heel of hand palpation'): Γ('All About Heart Sounds.png')
                        a. Aortic Area at 2nd R intercostal space 
                        b. Pulmonary Area at 2nd L intercostal space 
                        c. Right Ventricular Area at 3-5th intercostal space, L sternal border 
                        d. Left Ventricular Area at 4-5th intercostal space, medial to midclavicular line or apical region 
                    3. Assess for Thrills, Heaves, Pain or Deformities

        .2cpE.Heart Sounds & Apical Heart Rate
            .Introduction 
                .Γ Initials for Assessing Heart Sounds
                    requires a quiet environment, a stethoscope with a diaphragm and a bell.
                        listen to the quality of heart valve closing during the movement of blood flow through the heart chambers.  
                            perform the auscultation in a systematic manner.
                                1. Heart sounds are assessed utilizing an auscultation method with the diaphragm of the stethoscope as the listening device.
                                    The diaphragm of the stethoscope is used to identify
                                        high-pitched sounds, while ¦Pla (baix) per a alt
                                    the bell is used to identify
                                        low-pitched sounds. ¦alt (la campana te altura) per a baix (low)
                                2. In listening to heart sounds you are assessing the normal S1 and S2 sounds produced by the closing of the valve
                                    which can be heard as “lub, dub.”  
                                        S1 Γ(lub) is best heard at the
                                            mitral and tricuspid valve
                                                signifying beginning of systole ¦L=aounta cap amunt 
                                        S2 Γ(dub) is best heard over the
                                            aortic and pulmonic valves
                                                signifying the end of systole. ¦D= Diastole
                                                Γ beginning of the diastole
                                4. A quality “lub, dub” should be heard and noted as S1 and S2.
                                    (See ' (!!Blind)
                                        CP2 Q&A.txt::mmm.HeartSounds_S3&S4
                                        CP2 Q&A.txt::mmm.HeartSounds_S3&S4_Mnemonic
                                        CP2.txt::mmm.Lub_Dub
                                        ')
                                    Abnormal heart sounds may include
                                        low pitched sounds
                                        extra sounds like
                                            “lub, dub, dub” defined as S3 ('S3 Heart Sound - MEDZCOOL.mp4')
                                            “la, lub, dub” defined as S4, ('S4 Heart Sound - MEDZCOOL.mp4')
                                        and/or murmurs Γ(High pitch = diaphragm). ('Holosystolic Murmur - Heart Sounds - MEDZCOOL.mp4')

                .Procedure for Assessing Heart Sounds [CP2_HeartSoundsProcd] (See [CP2_HeartSoundsEXAM1])
                    1. To initiate taking heart sounds it is important to ask patient consent & description of the technique.
                        This requires the examiner to place the stethoscope over 4 various areas of the chest wall around breast tissue 
                    2. The patient should be
                        in supine with the bed at 30 degrees of elevation with the head on a pillow.
                            If an adjustable bed is not available, then have the patient in supine as the next best option. 
                    3. Assess the 4 valves of the heart:
                        Please note that when you are placing your stethoscope in the following areas you should utilize light pressure.
                        -----------------------------------------------
                        -aortic (¦Comença per la esquerre com escrius i escriu una "A"), pulmonic, tricuspid, and mitral/apical ('02 valves skin location')
                            a. Aortic valve.
                                -First you will need to locate the second right intercostal space, just lateral to the patient’s sternal boarder.
                                    -Once located, place your stethoscope in the area and listen for quality and sounds of the “dub” or S2 sound (Image 2).  
                            b. Pulmonic valve.
                                -Here you will need to locate the second left intercostal space, just lateral to the sternal boarder.
                                -Once located, place your stethoscope in the area and listen for quality and sounds of the “dub” or S2 sound (Image 3). 
                            c. Tricuspid valve.
                                -Here you will need to locate the 4th – 5th intercostal space near the Γ(left) sternal boarder.
                                -Once located, place your stethoscope in the area and listen for quality and sounds of the “lub” or S1 sound (Image 4). 
                            d. Mitral Valve.
                                Now you will need to locate the 4th – 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line (baix de la mamella).
                                    How to find the midclavicular line
                                        -draw a ling dissecting the left clavicle in half, then take that line down to the noted intercostal region.
                                        -This is also known as the apex of the heart and could also be found below the patient’s nipple.
                                            -Once located, place your stethoscope in the area and listen for quality and sounds of the “lub” or S1 sound (Image 5). 
                
                .Locating the Apical Pulse ('03 Palpation of the Apical Pulse.png')
                    -It is important to note that the mitral valve is also where the apical heart rate can be found. So, while you are assessing the quality of the “lub” or S1 sound, you may also be able to take an apical heart rate by counting the beats per minute obtained in this area. The apical heart rate one of the most accurate measures of heart rate and heart rate quality. This can be auscultated (Image 5) OR palpated (Image 6).

        .3cpE.Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Palpation ('04 Palpation of Abdominal Aorta .png')
            .Introduction 
                -A patient with a suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm is a medical emergency, and screening for this is of utmost importance.
                -Patients may have a single symptom of back pain, and with this being able to examine the patient appropriately via palpation or auscultation techniques are required. 
            .Procedure for Palpating Abdominal Aorta 
                1. Examiner standing beside the patient and facing the patient’s head/shoulders 
                2. Examiner places fingertips of both hands-on the abdomen with index fingers points toward the head, just above the umbilicus and left of midline. You can use 2 or one hand based on preference (Image 7) 
                3. Press down firmly to locate the pulsating aorta Γ(7 cm) 
                4. Palpate for size, location, and pulsation 
                5. Normal findings are a pulsation width ~ 2.5 cm (1 inch or ~2 fingertips) 
                6. Abnormal findings for a (+) AAA are a wide pulsation (≥4 cm) or large lateral pulsation 
                    a. Width is the most important findings, not pulsation intensity

        .4cpE.Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Auscultation ('05 Auscultation of the Abdominal Aorta.png')
            .Introduction 
                -You may also use the stethoscope to assess for the presence of a AAA, and when taken with palpation you can even increase your sensitivity and specificity of the findings.
            .Procedure for Auscultating the Abdominal Aorta 
                1. Patient supine with knees bent and examiner on left side 
                2. Examiner places the stethoscope just above the umbilicus and left of midline (Image 8) 
                3. Abnormal findings for a (+) AAA are hearing bruits or swishing in the presence of a wide pulse

        .5cpE.Pitting Edema ('06 Pitting Edema.png') Γ(Foot)
            .Introduction 
                -Pitting edema is an indication of chronic and prolonged swelling, where the fluid is not being held within the vascular system but rather spending time in the interstitial spaces. This fluid can become fibrotic and thick, thus leading to a pitting effect when depression is applied to the skin. This type of edema can be common in CHF, DVT, liver failure or lymphedema. 
            .Procedure for Assessing Pitting Edema  
                1. Apply digital pressure of or 15-30s over bony prominence (Image 9) 
                2. Release and determine soft (pitting) vs. indurated (non-pitting) edema (Image 9)
                3. Grade edema based on depth and record time to for tissue normalization 
                4. Edema resolving > 40s suggestive of heart failure 

        .6cpE.Lower and Upper Extremity Limb Circumference ('07 Limb Circumference.png')
            .Introduction
                -Edema is an accumulation of fluid in the intercellular tissue that results from an abnormal expansion in interstitial fluid volume. The fluid between the interstitial and intravascular spaces is regulated by the capillary hydrostatic pressure gradient and the oncotic pressure gradient across the capillary. The accumulation of fluid occurs when local or systemic conditions disrupt this equilibrium, leading to increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, increased plasma volume, decreased plasma oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminemia), increased capillary permeability, or lymphatic obstruction. Edema can be associated with serious underlying cardiovascular pathology.  
            .Procedure for Assessing Lower and Upper Extremity Limb Circumference 
                1. Lower Extremity:
                    -Measure circumference at Knee joint or tibial tubercle, then repeat 10 cm above and 10 cm below, and repeat this according to the level of edema occurring in the distal and proximal regions over the entire the leg (Image 10) 
                2. Upper Extremity:
                    -Measure circumference at styloid process, then repeat 10 cm above, and repeat this according to the level of edema occurring in the distal and proximal regions over the entire the arm (Image 11) 
                3. Pre-mark your areas of measurement to standardize measurements 
                4. Assess right versus left side
            
        .7cpE.Capillary Refill of Lower and Upper Extremity ('08 Capillary Refill.png') Γ(Nails: big toe and finger)
            .Introduction 
                -Patients with cardiovascular dysfunction may have reduction in distal blood flow due to blockage in the peripheral vascular system in cases like PAD or reduced cardiac output in cases like heart failure. Assessing time to capillary refill is a quick and easy examination procedure that can assess distal blood flow. 
            .Procedure for Assessing Capillary Refill of Lower and Upper Extremity 
                1. Have the patient seated with hands at heart level (upper) or in long sitting (lower) 
                2. Depress nail bed for 5 seconds on the big toe (lower; Image 12) or distal finger (upper; Image 13) so they blanch or turn white 
                3. Time and note when the color returns 
                4. Positive findings for poor circulation include: 
                    a. Finger ≥ 3 seconds 
                    b. Toe ≥ 5 seconds 

        .8cpE.Carotid Artery Auscultation ('09 Carotid Artery Auscultation.png')
            .Introduction
                -Patients who have progressive vascular disease, HTN, or cardiac disease along with symptoms of lightheadedness or dizziness may require screening for carotid artery blockage.  
            .Procedure for Auscultating the Carotid Artery
                1. Patient seated or supine with head turned slightly away from examiner 
                2. Place stethoscope "bell" at each of the following sites, and at each site perform steps 3-5, then repeat at the next site, working your way down the pathway of the carotid artery: 
                    a. Angle of jaw (Image 14), Carotid bifurcation (Image 15), Base of neck (Image 16), Subclavian artery (Image 17) 
                3. Patient inhales, exhales, then holds breath for 15 seconds 
                4. Listening occurs during and immediately after exhalation 
                5. Findings for a (+) carotid blockage include hearing a systolic bruit, which is a blowing or swishing sound 

    Part II: Pulmonary Examination Procedures
        .9cpE.Tracheal Palpation ('10 Tracheal Palpation.png')
            .Introduction 
                -Assessing tracheal shift can assist the clinician in determining if there is a lung pathology present that could be impeding on the trachea to shift it away or toward the abnormality. The mass effect of a large pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or intrathoracic mass will shift the trachea away from the primary abnormality whereas collapse of a lung will shift the trachea toward the primary abnormality. 
            .Procedure for Palpating the Trachea 
                1. The patient should be positioned in sitting or standing and head at midline 
                2. The examiner should palpate the position of the trachea with their index finger (Image 18) 
                3. Note a shift of the trachea, and determine a shift away or toward the suspected abnormality

        .10cpE.Chest Wall Motion ('11 Chest Wall Motion.png')
            .Introduction 
                -Assessing chest wall motion can reveal how well the chest wall moves and give you information how well the chest wall moves to subsequently bring air into that lung region for oxygenation. Obstructive and restrictive lung conditions can lead to reduced or excessive motion in certain lung regions both bilaterally or unilaterally. For example, an overall reduction in expansion or movement bilaterally may be found in those with COPD who have the presence of hyperinflated lungs, or you may note excessive movement in the upper lobe region with increased accessory muscle use. Non-symmetrical movement may be found in those with a unilateral dysfunctional lung region or those with poor chest wall muscle function. A unilateral delay may suggest atelectasis, pneumonia, post-operative guarding. 
            .Procedure for Assessing Chest Wall Motion Γ('Lungs anatomy')
                1. The patient in sitting 
                2. The examiner will lightly place the hands over the chest wall area and thumb tips closely approximated 
                3. The examiner palms should draw the skin medially to gather any excess prior to deep inspiration and perform steps 4-5 and repeat at each of the following locations: 
                    a. Upper lobe: Examiner facing the patient anteriorly with thumbs and palms atop the clavicle at mid sternum, and fingers extended superiorly over the upper trapezius muscle (Image 19) 
                    b. Right Middle Lobe and Left Lingula(''): Examiner facing the patient anteriorly with thumbs at the xyphoid process with palms and fingers extended over the lateral mid-thorax (Image 20) 
                    c. Lower Lobe: Examiner facing the patient posteriorly with thumbs at the T8 spinous process and palms and fingers extended over the lateral lower thorax (Image 21) 
                4. Instruct the patient to deeply inspire 
                5. Note symmetry, superior, anterior-posterior, and lateral motion 
                    a. Normal: 3-5 cm expansion from midline (Image 19, 20, 21)

        .11cpE.Diaphragmatic Motion ('12 Diaphragmatic Motion.png')
            .Introduction 
                -The diaphragm plays a primary role in the inspiratory portion of the breath cycle, and when active it provides equal and upward and outward motion of the lower rib cage. Assessing diaphragmatic motion and action allows the clinician to determine the integrity and capability for the muscle to engage in inspiration. The extent of movement is important and in persons with underlying respiratory disease, excursion may be limited due inefficient breathing and the use of accessory muscles. 
            .Procedure for Assessing Diaphragmatic Motion 
                1. The patient should be in supine with their knees flexed and resting on pillows or a bolster 
                2. The examiner will palpate the diaphragm by placing the thumbs over the costal margin and thumb tips meeting at the xyphoid (Image 22) 
                3. Ask the patient to deeply inhale 
                4. The examiner’s hands should move equally apart, with circumferential diameter increasing by 2 to 3 inches at the end of inspiration (Image 22) 

        .12cpE.Lung Sounds ('13 Lung Sounds') ('14 Lung Sounds 2') [CP2_LS] (See [CP2_AuscultateLungSounds])
            .Introduction
                -Lung sounds are an auscultation technique that includes the process of listening to the sounds of air passing through the tracheobronchial tree and alveolar spaces.
                -Lung sounds can be defined as
                    normal or
                    abnormal/adventitious.  
                    --------------------------------------------------------------------
                    1. To assess lung sounds you will need your stethoscope and you will utilize the "diaphragm" for listening.
                    2. When auscultating you will be listening to the inspiratory and expiratory phase in the proximal and distal airways of the upper, middle and lower lung regions.
                    3. The most proximal airways, over the trachea and manubrium, will have a loud, tubular sound. These sounds are defined as "tracheal" or "bronchial sounds". This sound is heard as a longer expiratory phase then inspiratory phase with a pause in between the cycle.
                    4. The middle airways, located in the para-sternal region at the junction of the mainstem bronchi, will have a more medium pitched, rustling sound, defined as "bronchovesicular sounds". This sound will have an equal expiratory and inspiratory phase with no pause in between. 
                    5. Finally, in the more distal airways or peripheral lung segments, especially in the basilar or base regions, you will hear a soft, low pitched sound, defined as "vesicular sounds". This sound will have a longer expiratory phase then inspiratory phase.
                    6. If any of these sounds are found outside of their normal region, they could be considered abnormal. For example, bronchial breath sounds found in the lower lung regions may indicate consolidation.
                    7. Auscultation should be performed in a systematic manner, anteriorly and then posteriorly (or vice versa), listening to a at least one breath in each bronchopulmonary segment.
                        ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                        (Γ)
                            .
                                upper lung regions
                                    tracheal/bronchial sounds (loud, tubular sound)
                                        longer expiratory phase then inspiratory phase
                                            with a pause in between the cycle
                                middle lung regions (middle airways)
                                    bronchovesicular sounds (medium pitched, rustling sound)
                                        equal expiratory and inspiratory phase
                                            with no pause in between
                                lower lung regions (peripheral lung segments)
                                    vesicular sounds (soft, low pitched sound)
                                        longer expiratory phase then inspiratory phase
                            ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                            3.trachea and manubrium (tracheal/bronchial sounds)
                                loud, tubular sound
                                    name: tracheal or "bronchial sounds"
                                sound is heard as a longer expiratory phase then inspiratory phase REPE
                                    with a pause in between the cycle.
                            4.middle airways (at para-sternal region at the junction of the mainstem bronchi) (bronchovesicular sounds)
                                a more medium pitched, rustling sound, defined as "bronchovesicular sounds".
                                equal expiratory and inspiratory phase with no pause in between
                            5.more distal airways or peripheral lung segments, especially in the basilar or base regions (vesicular sounds)
                                soft, low pitched sound, defined as "vesicular sounds"
                                longer expiratory phase then inspiratory phase REPE
            .Procedure for lung sounds 
                1. To initiate taking lung sounds it is important to ask patient consent to place the stethoscope over the areas of their anterior and posterior chest wall, as this will require contact with the patient’s skin over the chest wall and breast region.
                2. Appropriately drape the patient when necessary. 
                3. The optimal position for auscultation of lung sounds is a seated position with their back and chest exposed, so ensure they are seated in a backless chair or on an examination table if they are able. Be sure to take precautions if the patient has poor sitting balance.  
                4. You will instruct the client to perform deep breathing through the mouth when the stethoscope is placed on the skin, and they should perform this activity with each placement of the stethoscope. Be sure to monitor the patient closely to make sure that they do not become dizzy from hyperventilation. 
                5. Starting at the posterior thorax place the stethoscope at the rib interspace left to the C7 spinous process. Then begin the process of the patient taking a deep breath. Then move the stethoscope across midline to assess the same region on the right side. You must assess bilaterally to see if there are any differences in sound between the right and left lung in the same region.
                6. Next move the stethoscope downward or inferior to the previous site for one breath assessment, then cross midline again. Repeat this downward and midline pattern until reaching the lower lung fields as the final assessment site.  Be sure to remain in rib interspaces, as to allow for full access to lung tissue and avoid sound impedance by the bony ribs. (Image 23)('13 Lung Sounds.png')
                7. Then you can auscultate the anterior thorax. Here you may initiate your listening over the trachea, which is not an area of lung assessment, but rather to just practice site for auscultating air sounds. 
                8. At the anterior thorax begin assessment on the left below the clavicle (Image 24)('14 Lung Sounds 2.png'), then repeat the process as stated previously to assess right and left lung fields proximal to distal.  
                9. The anterior thorax is a region where you may need to widen your locale of stethoscope placement in the middle lung regions, as there is increased amount of soft tissue here as well as impedance of sound from the heart. Therefore, place the stethoscope in a more lateral region of chest wall if needed. 
                10. Take note of the regions you are assessing, and ensure you are assessing for tracheal/bronchial, bronchovesicular and vesicular lung sounds in its dedicated region.
                11. If an abnormal sound is heard, then further evaluative measures can be taken to confirm findings.
     
        .13cpE.Voice Transmission Testing ('15 Voice Transmission Testing.png') [CP2_VoiceTransmissionTesting] (See [CP2_VoiceTransmissionTests])
            .Introduction 
                -Voice transmission testing is an auscultation method that can be utilized to discover abnormal lung regions. Lungs without pathology are filled with air, which does not transmit sound easily, therefore, when there is an area of impairments due to fluid or masses the sounds can be transmitted more clearly. There are 3 assessment techniques that can be utilized:  Egophony, Bronchophony, & Whispered Pectoriloquy.
            .Procedure for Egophony, Bronchophony, & Whispered Pectoriloquy 
                1. Have the patient in a seated position 
                2. Place the diaphragm of the stethoscope over the suspected lung region between the rib interspace (Image 25) 
                3. Instruct the patient to perform the following: 
                    a. Egophony: Patient says E, and a positive finding when A is heard
                    b. Bronchophony: Patient says 99, and a positive finding when sound heard clearly and loudly
                    c. Whispered Pectoriloquy: Patient whispers, and a positive finding when the whispered word is heard clearly and loudly
                4. Compare side to side and region to region
                5. General Findings: Louder sounds over areas of consolidation (mucus) & softer sounds over areas of hyperinflation, like COPD

        .14cpE.Mediate Percussion ('16 Mediate Percussion.png')
            .Introduction 
                -Mediate percussion evaluates changes in lung density by sounds produced via external vibrations applied to the chest wall over each of lung regions. Sounds produced can give you more information about the density of the tissue beneath the area of percussion and can be normal or abnormal based on the anatomical region being percussed. 
            .Procedure for Mediate Percussion of the Lungs 
                1. Have the patient in a seated position 
                2. The examiner should place the middle finger (Image 26) or 1-2 fingertips of the non-dominant hand flat on the patient’s chest wall between the each of the rib interspaces 
                3. Next, the examiner will strike the placed finger of the non-dominant hand with the fingertip of the dominant hand to produce a vibration (Image 27)
                4. Findings:
                    a. Resonant sound is heard over normal lung tissue, and is heard as a loud, low pitched, hollow sound that is long in duration ¦Loud Low
                    b. Dull sound is heard over dense tissue, such as consolidation or tumor/mass, and is heard as a medium, high pitched, thud-like sound of medium duration 
                    c. Tympanic sound is heard over hyperinflated lung regions, and is heard as a very loud, high or musical pitched sound of medium duration
                    ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                    (Γ)
                        .normal lung tissue
                            Resonant sound (indica hueco = tira i pega pedra en cova i resona VS. so viatja millor en sòlid)
                                loud, low pitched, hollow sound
                                    of long in duration
                        .consolidation or tumor/mass (dense tissue)
                            Dull sound 
                                medium, high pitched, thud-like sound
                                    of medium duration REPE
                        .hyperinflated lung regions
                            Tympanic sound
                                very loud, high or musical pitched sound
                                    of medium duration REPE

        .15cpE.Tactile Fremitus ('17 Tactile Fremitus.png')
            .Introduction 
                -Tactile fremitus is an examination technique that can assess the vibration of the chest wall via transmitted vocal sounds through the lung tissue. Fremitus is a palpable vibration of the chest wall transmitted from the phonating larynx and can be increased or decreased in specific locations based on tissue density in the region being palpated.  
            .Procedure for Tactile Fremitus of the Lungs 
                1. Have the patient in a seated position 
                2. The examiner will place palms or ulnar boarder (image 28) hand surface between spinous process and scapula 
                3. The patient is asked to repeat “99” as the examiner notes bilateral differences in the lung regions 
                4. The examiner will place their hands by moving in the ordered fashion to compare side to side and region to region 
                5. Positive findings include increased to decreased fremitus or sound transmission during contralateral comparison  
                    a. Increased fremitus may indicate an area of consolidation
                        Γ El so es transmitix millor cuan hi ha una massa
                    b. Decreased fremitus may indicate an increase in air or hyperinflation

        (Γ)Nuances (look for REPE, DIFF)
            .13cpE.Voice Transmission Testing
                b. Bronchophony: Patient says 99 Γ(in fremitus, 99 is also used), and a positive finding when sound heard clearly and loudly REPE.2
                c. Whispered Pectoriloquy: Patient whispers, and a positive finding when the whispered word is heard clearly and loudly REPE.2

    Part III: Other Systems Examination Procedures/ΓAbdominal & Visceral Palpation
        .16cpE.Deep Palpation ('18 Deep Palpation.png')
            Introduction 
                -Deep palpation of the abdominal region can be a useful to allow a clinician to assess organs that may be affected by cardiovascular and pulmonary disease. Deep palpation of the abdomen may aide as a precursor to specific organ testing, as it allows the patient to feel comfortable with deeper palpation along with allowing the examiner to assess any areas of tenderness. It also can allow the clinician to assess for size, location, consistency, and mobility of organs. 
            Procedure for Deep Palpation 
                1. Patient supine with head on pillow, arms at sides, and knees bent and supported by pillows 
                2. Examiner to place 4 fingertips flat on the abdomen and depress 5-8 cm or 2-3 inches (Image 28) 
                3. Circle fingers in a rotary motion, then move to next area 
                4. Assess all abdominal quadrants 
                5. Positive findings include tenderness, masses, enlargement of organs, tissues or muscles

        .17cpE.Kidney Palpation, Bimanual Technique ('19 Kidney Palpation Bimanual Technique.png')
            Introduction 
                -Kidney disease also can act as a risk factor or be a result of cardiovascular disease, so assessing the kidney may be indicated in some patients who demonstrate kidney related impairments. Palpating the kidney may allow you to assess for size, location, consistency, and mobility of the kidney to determine masses or tenderness.
            Procedure for Bimanual Kidney Palpation 
                1. Patient supine with head on pillow, arms at sides, and knees bent and supported by pillows and examiner on the right or left
                2. Place left hand under the patient’s back and other hand on top of the abdomen below the costal margin (Image 29)
                3. Press the two hands firmly together 
                4. As you are pressing the hands firmly together you are likely to feel the organ in the posteriorly located hand 
                5. Findings: 
                    a. Normal: Smooth, rounded, lower pole of the kidney or may not be able to palpate 
                    b. Positive/Abnormal: Enlarged kidney, nodules, tenderness 
                    c. left side inferior pole of the kidney can rarely be palpated versus the right side, as the left kidney is positioned slightly upper than the right kidney due to the asymmetry within the abdominal cavity caused by the liver

        .18cpE.Liver Palpation, Bimanual Technique ('20 Liver Palpation Bimanual Technique.png')
            Introduction 
                -Liver disease can lead to very serious cardiovascular and pulmonary complications, but also it may be a result of cardiovascular or pulmonary dysfunction. So, when there is concern for liver issues you may want to palpate the liver to assess for size, location, consistency, and mobility of the liver to determine masses or tenderness. You may not always be able to feel or palpate a normal liver, but abnormal findings can become apparent as disease progresses 
            Procedure for Bimanual Liver Palpation 
                1. Patient supine with head on pillow, arms at sides, and knees bent and supported by pillows and examiner on the right
                2. Place left hand under the patient’s back parallel to the lowest ribs 
                3. Place 4 fingers of right hand in the RUQ, parallel to the midline, and index finger in line with costal margin (Image 30) 
                4. Ask the patient to deeply inhale, then push down firmly with the right hand while the left hand remains as a posterior support 
                5. Findings: 
                    a. Normal: smooth, firm edge of liver may be felt by right hand or not being able to palpate the liver 
                    b. Positive/Abnormal: Edge of liver extending beyond 1-2 cm indicates enlargement, tender, hard, and/or irregular

    .Part IV: Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Treatment Interventions 
        .19cpE.Postural Drainage [CP2_PD] (See [CP2_PDP])
            Introduction 
                -Assumption of one or more body positions that allow gravity to assist with draining secretions from each lung segment. This treatment typically follows examination findings of consolidation in one or more lung regions via auscultation of breath sounds, voice transmission testing, tactile fremitus, and/or mediate percussion. 
            Procedure for performing postural drainage 
                1. Begin any treatment session using auscultation techniques to determine area(s) of need. 
                2. Bronchodilators, mucolytic agents, water, or saline may be nebulized and inhaled before postural drainage to decrease thickness of sputum, thereby enhancing secretion removal 
                3. Prior to beginning a treatment session review and choose technique(s) to enhance drainage 
                    a. Alone without hands on techniques OR add 
                    b. Percussions or vibrations over chest wall to further loosen mucus 
                4. Perform postural drainage by properly positioning patient to target the lung area of treatment (Image 31)('21 Postural Drainage.png'), while simultaneously performing technique(s) to enhance drainage from the lung area of interest 
                    a. STOP to allow significant coughing to occur. 
                    b. STOP after 3-5 minutes per lobe to use auscultation again 
                    c. Re-do this portion of treatment until auscultation produces maximally reduced pathological breath sounds 
                5. Post-treatment: 
                    a. position patient in bed in the same position that was most useful in drainage (Image 31) 
                    b. This pattern should be maintained 2 to 3x per day during treatment while consolidation or mucus is still being produced. In some cases, this means throughout life, especially with CF patients  
                    c. As part of the overall treatment plan patient should consistently utilize breathing techniques learned elsewhere in this course during daily life.
                -------------------------------------------------
                ('21 Postural Drainage.png')
                    Anterior upper segment (upper Babes)
                    Posterior apical segment

                    Left lingular
                    Anterior segments (lower lobes)

            .20cpE.Percussion Manual Procedure ('22 Percussion Manual Procedure.png') [CP2_PMP] (See [CP2_PM])
                1. Chest percussion is aimed at loosening retained secretions using your hands to percuss over the chest wall or using a mechanical device while a patient is in a postural drainage position.
                2. The clinician should apply percussion to the areas of the lung most involved. 
                3. Percussion involves clapping with cupped hands over the affected lung segment. This produces a hollow sound as the hand contacts the patient skin. (Image 32)  
                4. This should be performed at a rapid rhythm that may be 100-480 times per minute. 
                5. During percussion, it is important that the clinician has their hands cupped for patient comfort. They should not slap their hands on the patient with the hand flat.
                6. The clinician may have a thin layer of cloth between the patient and their hands during percussion to provide patient comfort.
            .21cpE.Vibration Manual Procedure ('23 Vibration Manual Procedure.png') [CP2_VMImm2] (See [CP2_VMImm1])
                1. Vibration may be used to assist with airway clearance while the patient is in a postural drainage position 
                2. The clinician applies vibration to the chest wall by using the palmar aspect of their hand and overlapping that hand with the other hand. (Image 33)  
                3. Once the hands are placed and pressed firmly on the chest wall the therapist will straighten their arms, and tense the muscles while creating a fine shaking motion over the chest wall. 
                4. During vibration the clinician may coordinate the treatment with the patients breathing and increase pressure on the thorax during expiration to assist with a more effective cough.
        
        .22cpE.Instructions for Effective Cough ('24 Effective Cough.png') [CP2_IEC] (See [CP2_EC])
            Introduction 
                -An effective cough consists of four stages: inspiration, closure of the glottis, abdominal and intercostal muscle contraction, and the forceful expulsion of air with opening of the glottis. An effective cough should maximize the function of each of these stages and a deficit in any of these areas will lessen the effectiveness of the cough. Take note of the inspiratory phase of the cough, and think of that as inspiration beyond tidal volume, as increase inspiration leads to increase air within the chest cavity leading to an increase in intrapulmonary pressure, which allows for a forceful expulsion of air into the lower pressure atmosphere.
                -It is important to teach a patient how to perform a cough. This is important in patients after surgery when pain may inhibit them from performing an effective cough. An ineffective cough can lead to retained sections, atelectasis, hypoxia, and respiratory failure.
             Procedure for producing an effective cough 
                1. Position patient allowing trunk extension and flexion, which is most preferable in a seated position, but you may use side-lying if required 
                2. Instruct the patient in how to obtain maximal inspiration, which may require initial verbal cues and positioning to open up the chest wall. This may take a few moments of practice to allow the patient to work on inspiratory holds, and master maximal inspiration. 
                3. Next have the patient perform maximal inspiration while performing slight spinal extension with cues to open the chest wall to bring air in (Image 33) 
                4. At end range or maximal inspiration, the patient should then flex forward while performing a forceful cough at end range (Image 34) 
                    a. May instruct patient to perform a self-abdominal thrust at end of cough to further increase intra-abdominal pressure 
                    b. In cough splinting, the patient is instructed to splint their incision by applying pressure over it with a pillow or blanket roll during the expiratory phase of the cough. This technique is often used in surgical patients to help them to get a more effective cough.

        .23cpE.Huff and Cough ('25 Huff and Cough') [CP2_HCImm2] (See [CP2_HCImm1])
            Introduction 
                -Huffing can be added to coughing as a means to help clear mucus when it is increasingly difficult for a patient, as it is a technique that can assist in keeping the upper airways open with a forceful cough.
            Procedure for instructing huff and cough 
                1. The patient should be sitting upright and straight with chin tilted slightly up and mouth open. 
                2. Instruct the patient to close the mouth and take a slow deep breath to fill lungs 
                3. Hold breath for two or three seconds. 
                4. Open the mouth and force the air out of your lungs with the mouth open as if trying to fog up a mirror (Image 35) 
                    a. Patient may also preform abdominal thrust with the huff-cough 
                5. Repeat this maneuver two more times and then follow with one strong cough to clear mucus from the larger airways.

        .24cpE.Active Cycle Breathing (See 'Active Cycle Breathing') ('26 Active Cycle Breathing.png')
            Introduction 
                -The active cycle of breathing consists of a series of maneuvers performed by the patient to emphasize independence in secretion clearance and thoracic expansion. This technique enables to patient to be more independent and less reliant on a caretaker for clearance of sections.
            Procedure for active cycle breathing 
                1. Breathing control where the patient performs diaphragmic breathing at normal tidal volume several times 
                2. Thoracic expansion exercises where the patient performs deep breathing 3-4 times REPE
                3. Return to Breathing control for 5 to 10 seconds, 
                4. Thoracic expansion exercises where the patient performs deep breathing 3-4 times REPE
                5. Followed by Breathing control 
                6. And lastly the patient tries a forced expiratory technique where they huff several times at mid to low lung volumes. (See Figure 2 for all steps)

        .25cpE.Pursed Lip Breathing ('27 Pursed Lip Breathing.png')
            Introduction 
                -Pursed lip breathing is commonly prescribed for those with increasing dyspnea and possible presence of wheezing at rest or with exertion. It allowsfor a direct line of air to the lungs for oxygenation via inhalation through the nose with a closed mouth, then a prolonged exhalation through a pursed mouth to allow for a quantity of air to be exhaled over time. This intervention can assist in decreasing a patient’s symptoms of dyspnea, generally slow respiratory rate and decrease airway collapse in patients, especially those with COPD.
            Procedure for instructing pursed lip breathing 
                1. Can be performed in any position 
                2. Instruct the patient to inhale through the nose with the mouth closed for several seconds (Image 36) 
                3. Then instruct the patient to exhale slowly over 4 to 6 seconds through pursed lips, but be sure to not perform forceful abomination contraction with expiration
                4. Inhalation to exhalation ratio should start at 1:2, then can progress to 1:6, but should not be forced 
                5. Progress by having the patient practice PLB while standing or with exercising

        .26cpE.Sniffing for Diaphragmatic Activation
            Introduction 
                -Sniffing can be performed quickly prior to initiating a diaphragmatic breathing intervention. Sniffing, while it can be used as an intervention alone, it can serve as a way to ensure the patient can activate the diaphragm. This may be especially useful for those with neurological insult that may render the diaphragm inactive or those with flattened diaphragms from lung hyperinflation or other postural abnormalities.
            Procedure for instructing sniffing 
                1. Place the patient in supine with pillows under their head and knees 
                2. The clinician should place fingers directly below the xyphoid process of the patient 
                3. Instruct the patent to sniff in through the nose several times 
                4. Observe abdominal and/or lower costal expansion with each sniff 
                5. Progress by having patient gradually prolong the sniff as a diaphragmatic training intervention. 

        .27cpE.Diaphragmatic Controlled Breathing ('28 Diaphragmatic Controlled Breathing.png')
            Introduction 
                -The diaphragm plays a primary role in the inspiratory portion of the breath cycle, and training it to become active in inspiration can be an important intervention in persons with underlying respiratory disease, where excursion may be limited or inhibited. Once you know the patient can activate the diaphragm you can then train diaphragm to become active with inspiration, and thus strengthen the diaphragm with a controlled breathing technique. To perform this intervention, you first should explain the goals of diaphragmatic breathing to the patient, that being to work on breathing that is directed at the abdominal region.
            Procedure for diaphragmatic controlled breathing 
                1. Position the patient in a sitting (Image 37) or supine (Image 38) position with the trunk supported in slight flexion with the patient’s knees bent over pillows or a bolster (NOTE: slight posterior tilt facilitates the diaphragm, while anterior tilt will facilitate upper chest breathing) 
                2. Instruct the patient to place the dominant hand over the upper abdominal region below the xyphoid process and the non-dominant hand over the mid-sternal region (Image 37 & 38) 
                3. Instruct the patient to breathe through the nose and direct the air so the dominant hand rises with inspiration 
                4. Little to no movement should be felt or observed in the non-dominant hand over the chest

        .28cpE.Diaphragmatic Facilitation Techniques 
            Introduction 
                -If the patient is having difficulty performing a diaphragmatic breathing technique the clinician may facilitate the muscles action with some hands-on techniques.  

                -Counterpressure is an intervention that may allow for patient to feel the pressure or biofeedback via a counterpressure force applied by the clinician over the diaphragm, but also it can serve as a means for providing resistance as a progression to diaphragmatic controlled breathing.  

                -Quick Stretch is an intervention that can be utilized if the patient is having difficulty activating the diaphragm to full capacity or coordinating diaphragmatic activation at inspiration. This intervention provides a quick manual stretch to the muscle fibers of the diaphragm, which will reflexively allow for diaphragmatic activation in response. This technique requires careful coordination with the patients breathing pattern, as you will apply the quick stretch right before inspiration is to occur. 

                -Lower costal expansion another hands-on technique used to promote diaphragmatic breathing. This technique is a nice home exercise for patients who need to increase repetitions and to continue to promote diaphragmatic breathing. This technique is meant to emphasize the lower costal expansion of the ribs, which in turn promotes activation of the diaphragm. This is best performed in sitting, therefore, places the patient is a more functional position. 

                -Upper chest inhibition is reserved for patients who continue to have upper chest and shoulder motions despite many attempts at facilitating the diaphragm. Inhibiting the upper chest can help a patient recruit the diaphragm during inhalation and reduce accessory muscle use and should only be used only after implementation of other techniques previously described.  

            .Procedure for diaphragmatic facilitation techniques 
                a. Counter Pressure ('29 Counter Pressure.png')
                    1. Position the patient in supine (Image 38) position with the patient’s knees bent over pillows or a bolster
                    2. Instruct the patient to place the dominant hand over the upper abdominal region below the xyphoid process and the non-dominant hand over the mid-sternal region
                    3. The clinician then places their hand over the patient’s dominant hand and applies resistance or pressure (Image 39) 
                    4. Instruct the patient to breath into your while you continue to apply pressure 
                b. Quick Stretch ('30 Quick Stretch') ('30b Quick Stretch.png')
                    1. Position the patient in supine position with the patient’s knees bent over pillows or a bolster 
                    2. Place your hand over the patient’s mid abdomen, below the xyphoid process 
                    3. Instruct the patient to perform diaphragmatic breathing a few times so you may feel and assess the expiration and inspiration timing
                    4. Then prior to performing step #5, you will inform the patient that you will be applying a quick stretch to the abdominal region during the next breath cycle
                    5. Prior to inspiration apply a quick stretch or “Scoop” up and under the thorax with a subsequent instruction for the patient breath into your hand (Image 40) 
                    NOTE: You may also perform the quick stretch over the patient’s hand for patient comfort as a modification (Image 41) 
                c. Procedure for Lower Costal Expansion ('31 Lower Costal Expansion')
                    1. Place the patient in sitting 
                    2. Instruct the patient to place their own hands over the anterolateral rib cage 
                    3. Instruct the patient to breath into their hands to facilitate diaphragmatic motion as the rib cage moves up and outward (Image 42) 
                    4. Other Considerations: 
                        a. Clinician may need to utilize their own hands to initiate and provide feedback (Image 43) 
                        b. May also perform this with a belt or theraband around the lower costal region for added resistance (Image 44) 
                        c. Ensure the patient has relaxed shoulders to not use accessory muscles 
                d. Upper Chest Inhibition Technique ('32 Upper Chest Inhibition Technique')
                    1. Have the patient is positioned supine with the patient’s knees bent over pillows or a bolster 
                    2. The clinician will place their arm over the upper chest and their other hand on the mid abdominal region (Image 45)
                    3. Have the patient perform a few respiratory cycles so you may feel and assess the expiration and inspiration timing 
                    4. When the patient inhales, the therapist applies pressure to the upper chest to resist expansion.   
                        a. The therapist may apply a quick stretch to the diaphragm if needed prior to inhalation 
                    5. Instruct the patient to breath into your hand on the abdominal region

        .29cpE.a.Segmental Breathing ('33 Segmental Breathing.png') ('33b Segmental Breathing.png')
            .Introduction 
                -Segmental breathing encourages expansion of specific part of the lung that has been under ventilated and can aide in prevention of lung collapse or shut down. This intervention is indicated for asymmetrical chest wall expansion with absence of breath sounds, localized lung consolidation, asymmetrical posture, and an area of a collapsed lung. This intervention is then followed by inspiratory training to allow for expansion and ventilation to the newly ventilated lung area expansion and ventilation to lung area that is not ventilated. 
                -Prior to choosing segmental breathing as an intervention, you will examine and identify the area of emphasis. For example, you may assess chest expansion and discover reduced expansion in left lower lobe of lung, you then confirm that there is absent or reduced breath sounds in that area to further confirm the area is not being ventilated adequately.  
            .Procedure for segmental breathing 
                1. Place the patient in the best position to access that lung region & most comfortable for the patient 
                2. Place your hand over the chest wall overlying the area of emphasis (Image 46) 
                3. Instruct the patient to breathe in deeply through the nose trying to direct airflow toward your hand while you apply a counter pressure with your hand 
                4. Gradually decrease your pressure as the patient inspires to allow for expansion of that area 
                5. Instruct the patient to hold that breath for 2-3 seconds at the end of inspiration, then exhale 
                6. Have the patient use their own hand (Image 47) or belt (Image 48) as HEP for facilitation and also to progress as added resistance
            .29cpE.b.Segmental breathing Belt Technique (Left basal) ('33c Segmental Breathing.png')
                1. The belt is placed around the left lateral basal region, and the shorter end continued around the right side and held with the right hand (Image 48) 
                2. The other end should be crossed over the thighs and fixed under the right thigh 
                3. The patient performs a breath cycle and at the end of the breath out the patient should pull the belt firmly and breath into the belt against the resistance 
                4. At full inspiration the pressure is released, and the expansion is maintained for a moment before expiration 

        .30cpE.Inspiratory Hold
            Introduction 
                -Inspiratory hold is an intervention aimed at global lung ventilatory training and allows for ventilation to poorly ventilated areas, improved cough capabilities for airway clearance and is indicated for patients who are experiencing hypoventilation, atelectasis, or ineffective cough. It is also an intervention that can be implemented post segmental breathing intervention, as it allows for ventilation to the newly opened lung areas. Inspiratory holds involve prolonged holding of breath at maximum inspiration. 
            Procedure for instructing inspiratory holds 
                1. Patient is in suping, sitting or standing 
                2. The patient is instructed to hold his or her breath at the height of inspiration for 2 to 3 seconds 
                3. The patient then performs a relaxed exhalation 

        .31cpE.Stacked Breathing  
            Introduction 
                -Staked breathing is an intervention aimed at global lung ventilatory training and allows for ventilation to poorly ventilated areas, improved cough capabilities for airway clearance and is indicated for patients who are experiencing hypoventilation, atelectasis, or ineffective cough. It is also an intervention that can be implemented post segmental breathing intervention, as it allows for ventilation to the newly opened lung areas. Inspiratory holds involve a series of deep breaths that build on top of previous breath without expiration. 
            Procedure for instructing stacked breathing 
                1. Patient is in suping, sitting or standing 
                2. The patient is instructed inspire once, hold that inspiration briefly, then inspire again on top of the previous inspiration
                3. The patient will continue this “stacking” or inspiration or breaths until maximum inspiratory levels can be reached and held for 2-3 seconds
                4. The patient then performs a relaxed exhalation

    .Heart Sounds
        -Auscultation of Heart Sounds & Check Off, you will be checked off on the below criteria before moving into the next section of this lab. This is out of 5 points for a lab grade. [CP2_HeartSoundsEXAM1] (See [CP2_HeartSoundsProcd])
            ■ Normal Sounds: S1 (lub-closure of mitral and tricuspid valves), S2 (dub-closure of aortic and pulmonic valves)
            ■ Abnormal Sounds: S3 (heart failure, diastolic dysfunction), S4 (noncompliant/hypertrophic ventricle)

                        ○ Aortic: LV Hypertrophy
            ○ Apical Pulse: found at the mitral valve, the most accurate measure of HR and quality
        ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
        What is Apical Heart Rate?
            The apical heart rate refers to the number of heartbeats per minute as measured by auscultating the apex of the heart. This method involves placing the stethoscope over the apex, typically located at the point of maximum impulse (PMI) in the fifth intercostal space along the midclavicular line, and counting the number of heartbeats heard within a specific time frame, usually one minute.

            Auscultating the apical pulse provides a direct assessment of the heart's rhythm and rate and is particularly useful in detecting irregularities such as arrhythmias or heart murmurs. The apical heart rate may differ from the radial pulse rate, which is palpated at the wrist, especially in conditions where there are disturbances in cardiac conduction or circulation.

            Healthcare professionals often use the apical pulse as part of a comprehensive cardiovascular assessment, particularly in clinical settings such as hospitals, clinics, or during physical examinations. Monitoring changes in the apical heart rate over time can help evaluate the effectiveness of treatment interventions, assess cardiovascular function, and identify any abnormalities requiring further evaluation or management.

    .Testing Format:
        -Each competency check is scheduled for 20 minutes. During the assessment one student will act as tester and one will act as patient. The tester will review the case description for a few minutes (2-3 minutes), conduct the testing scenario for 15 minutes, and then engage in a short debriefing session. You should be prepared to demonstrate all assessment and interventions covered in lab sessions 1 and 2, as you will need to be ready perform them related to the case you receive. Read the following points carefully:
            ● Chart review information, like lab values, ECG strip findings, surgical history, medical history, imaging, medications
            ● Identify key features of the chart review including history, medications. Also discuss the current findings and possible patient diagnosis.
            ● Discuss the lab value findings. Discuss the PT implications of the lab values and the EKG strip.
            ● Consider the patient’s history of present illness and hospital course. Identify precautions that the patient may have based on his current state.
            ● What would you include in your initial examination of this patient, including observation, inspection, and physical examination techniques?
            ● You will be asked to perform one examination technique pertinent to that case
            ● You will be asked to perform one intervention technique based on a single examination finding.
            ● Information specific to the examination and/or intervention technique
            ● Patient response & PT implications

        -Debriefing: Your instructor will briefly discuss key points and provide you with areas that went well and areas where performance could be improved. This will be brief and provide insight on your strengths and weaknesses noted during the lab practical session.
        -Scoring: Each case will have 6 associated tasks/questions, and the total points for the exam will be 30 points. Students must score at least 75% or equal to or greater than 22.5/30 to receive a passing grade on the competency check. If a student does not receive a passing score, the instructor will contact them by email to schedule a re-take.

        Scoring will be based on 6 key criteria:
            1. Identify key features of the chart review including history and medications, laboratory values and tests, medications. If present and applicable, discuss imaging and final dx.
            2. Discuss the lab values and EKG findings. Discuss the PT implications of the lab values and the EKG strip
            3. Consider the patient’s history of present illness and hospital course. Identify precautions that the patient may have based on his current state, post-operative status, etc.
            4. Describe what you include in your initial examination of this patient, including observation, inspection, and physical examination techniques.
            5. Perform an identified and appropriate cardiopulmonary examination procedure
            6. Perform an identified and appropriate intervention based on examination findings

        ----------------------------------------------------------- CASES
        Case Scenario 1: Cardiopulmonary Assessment
            Patient Background:
            - History: 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus type 2, and recent myocardial infarction (MI) two weeks ago.
            - Medications: Lisinopril, Metformin, Aspirin, and Metoprolol.
            - Laboratory Values: Elevated troponin levels, increased blood glucose levels, and elevated LDL cholesterol.

            - Final Diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome with heart failure.

            - Lab Values: Elevated troponin levels indicate recent myocardial damage. Increased blood glucose levels suggest poorly controlled diabetes.

            Explanation:

            - Patient History: Knowing the patient's recent hospital course and diagnosis helps in identifying precautions and tailoring interventions.
            
            - Examination: A thorough initial examination helps in identifying abnormalities and guiding treatment planning.
            
            - Procedure: Performing appropriate cardiopulmonary examination procedures ensures comprehensive assessment.
            
            - Findings and Intervention: Based on examination findings, tailored interventions are designed to manage symptoms, improve function, and minimize risks.

    .Auscultate lung sounds (Folder 'Heard Sounds') [CP2_AuscultateLungSounds] (See [CP2_LS])
        Auscultate lung sounds 
            ● Why: This involves listening to sounds produced by the lungs using a stethoscope. It helps in diagnosing conditions like pneumonia, bronchitis, asthma, or ﬂuid accumulation in the lungs (pulmonary edema).
                1. Position the patient in a seated position with their back and chest exposed. 
                2. Use a stethoscope with a diaphragm to listen to the sounds. 
                3. Start at the posterior thorax and place the stethoscope at the rib interspace left to the C7 spinous process. 
                4. Instruct the patient to take a deep breath through their mouth while the stethoscope is placed on the skin. 
                5. Move the stethoscope across the midline to assess the same region on the right side. 
                6. Move downward or inferior to the previous site for one breath assessment, then cross midline again. 
                7. Repeat this downward and midline pattern until reaching the lower lung ﬁelds as the ﬁnal assessment site. 
                8. Auscultate the anterior thorax by starting below the clavicle on the left side and repeating the process to assess the right and left lung ﬁelds proximal to distal. 
                9. Listen for normal or abnormal lung sounds in each bronchopulmonary segment. 
                10.If an abnormal sound is heard, further evaluation may be needed to conﬁrm ﬁndings.
            Note: The speciﬁc sounds heard during auscultation will depend on the patient's condition and any underlying respiratory issues.
