    .('Additional Cardiac and Vascular Procedures.pdf')
        Cardiac Ablation
        • Procedure to correct cardiac 
        arrhythmias 
        • Works by scarring or 
        destroying tissue in the heart 
        that triggers abnormal heart 
        rhythm 
        • Often completed with 
        catheters transfemorally but 
        can be done via median 
        sternotomy


        Pacemaker Implantation
        • Cardiac pacemaker
        • electronic pulse generator used to create an artificial action potential
        • Control of some types of cardiac arrhythmias
        • May be temporary measure or may be surgically implanted for permanent 
        function
        • General indications
        • SA node disorders, atrioventricular nodal disorders, tachyarrhythmias
        • Initiate myocardial depolarization by creating electrical voltage


        Pacemaker Implantation
        • Electrical conduction configurations are classified as unipolar or 
        bipolar
        • Cardiac pacing leads
        • Endocardial leads are placed inside the right atrium, right ventricle, 
        or both via transvenous route
        • Epicardial leads are attached directly to surface of right atrium or 
        right and left ventricle
        • Pacing lead is tolerant of repeated flexure
        • Clinician needs to know the type of pacemaker in order to understand 
        ECG tracing


        Pacemaker Implantation 
        A. dual chamber pacemaker
        B. dual lead AV pacemaker 
        (right-sided),
        C. biventricular pacemaker


        Pacemaker Implantation
        • Uniform communication 
        system is in place regarding 
        characteristics of particular 
        device
        • Generic pacemaker code, 
        NBG Code was developed 
        • Five positions make up the 
        code


        Precautions after Pacemaker Insertion
        • Sling for 24 hours to 1 week to be worn 
        on ipsilateral side of pacemaker 
        placement
        • No shoulder flexion and abduction > 90 
        degrees for 30 days
        • No shoulder extension past neutral
        • No lifting, pushing, pulling over 5 lbs.
        • Patient may be instructed to avoid use 
        of cane/walker on affected side
        • Patient may be instructed to use 
        handrails for guidance/balance only


        Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator 
        (ICD or AICD)
        Similar to pacemaker, but 
        designed to correct life-
        threatening arrhythmias

        Detects and corrects 
        arrhythmias

        Implanted into the patient 
        with or without a pacemaker

        Patients with left ventricular 
        ejection fraction (LVEF) of 
        <30% have a three to five 
        time increase in the 
        incidence of sudden death


        Surgical Interventions for Other Vascular 
        Disorders & Peripheral Vascular Interventions


        Carotid Endarterectomy
        • For patients with severe Carotid Artery Disease
        • Symptomatic patient with carotid artery stenosis 70% or 
        greater
        • Symptomatic patient with stenosis of 50% to 69% of the 
        carotid artery
        • Asymptomatic patient with stenosis of 60% or greater
        • Outcome – decreased risk of stroke
        • Use of stents may be indicated


        Endovascular Angioplasty
        • Newer procedure compared to carotid endarterectomy
        • Catheter inserted through femoral artery, through aortic 
        arch, and up to carotid artery
        • Remove plaque and place stents
        • Typically, bedrest 4 hours post procedure
        • Advantages- less invasive, less pain, early mobility, spares 
        SCM muscle, and faster recovery


        Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
        • Common risk factors for thoracic aortic 
        aneurysms include:
        • hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, 
        prior tobacco use, collagen vascular 
        disease, family history of aortic disease
        • Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAAs) classified 
        by location, size, shape, etiology
        • Indications for surgery
        • Aneurysms greater or equal to 5 cm or 
        with rapid aneurysm enlargement
        • Sudden change


        Abdominal Aortic Aneurysmectomy
        • Open approach or minimally 
        evasive (EAVR)
        • Aneurysms greater or equal to 5 
        cm or with rapid aneurysm 
        enlargement or sudden change 
        in pain
        • Patients at high risk for 
        pulmonary complications due to 
        incisional pain limiting cough and 
        deep breathing


        Endovascular Repair of AAA


        Peripheral Vascular Interventions
        • Type of intervention (surgical vs. percutaneous transluminal 
        angioplasty) is determined by:
        • Characteristics of a lesion (location, stenosis vs. occlusion, 
        length)
        • Pattern of arterial occlusion disease (multilevel vs. single level, 
        runoff status)
        • Patient demographics (gender, diabetes?)
        • Clinical situation (recurrent disease and indications)
        • Intraprocedural factors (initial hemodynamic response)


        Peripheral Vascular Interventions

        • Surgical bypass and arterial reconstruction interventions can be done on any 
        vessel
        • Common sites – femoral-popliteal region, aortofemoral region, infrapopliteal, 
        axillobifemoral

        Peripheral Vascular Surgery

        • Bypass procedures are typically WBAT
        • Amputations are NWB
        • Toe amputations usually require forefoot relief shoe for heel weight bearing only

        Weight bearing should be clarified by surgeon


        Peripheral Vascular Interventions
        • Exercise and mobility are important
        • Elevate affected extremity when sitting, assistive device may 
        be needed
        • Strongest predictor of successful outcome involves clinical 
        symptom of claudication
        • (+)claudication pain = better long-term outcomes and 
        fewer amputations (compared to patients with limb 
        threatening ischemia)

    .('Thoracic Organ Transplantation Part 1.pdf')
        History of Thoracic Organ Transplantation
        • Heart Transplant:
        • Early 1900s—Carrel and Guthrie 
        described techniques for 
        transplantation in animal models
        • 1950s—heterotopic transplantation 
        principal technique described but 
        orthotopic gaining favor
        • 1960s—determination of 
        immunosuppressive drugs to 
        increase survival
        • 1964—first cardiac transplantation 
        performed on human (animal to 
        human)
        • 1967—first human-to-human heart 
        transplant

        • Lung Transplant:
        • 1963—lung transplantation was 
        developing—first human lung 
        transplantation performed
        • 1970s and 1980s—improved 
        survival of transplant recipients 
        occurred
        • 1983—first successful single-lung 
        transplant


        Candidacy
        • Primary indication is progressive terminal cardiopulmonary disease 
        with limited life expectancy
        • Heart transplantations performed as a result of:
        • coronary artery disease
        • myocardial damage
        • cardiomyopathy
        • Lung transplantations performed as a result of: 
        • Emphysema & COPD 
        • Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
        • Failure of transplanted organ:
        • indication for heart and lung repeat transplantation


        Candidacy

        • Double lung transplant 
        increases survival rate to 65 
        years old
        • Reserved for younger patients 
        based on this data


        Indications for Heart Transplantation

        End-stage heart 
        disease

        • Hemodynamic 
        compromise due to 
        heart failure
        • Coronary artery disease
        • Cardiomyopathy
        • Refractory cardiogenic 
        shock

        NYHA class III–IV 
        despite maximal 
        therapy such as the 
        following:
        • Medication
        • Pacing (CRT)
        • Revascularization or 
        valve repair
        • Ventricular remodeling 
        procedure
        • Recurrent 
        hospitalization for heart 
        failure
        • Refractory ischemia 
        and EF <20%

        Poor quality of life

        • Intractable angina
        • Refractory arrhythmia
        • VO2max <10 
        mL/kg/min

        Other

        • Congenital heart 
        disease
        • Cardiac tumors


        Indications for Lung Transplantation

        COPD

        • BODE index of 7 
        to 10 and any of 
        the following:
        • Hx of acute 
        hypercapnia
        • Pulmonary 
        hypertension or 
        cor pulmonale
        • FEV1 of 20% and 
        DLCO of 20%

        Idiopathic 
        pulmonary 
        fibrosis
        • Evidence of usual 
        interstitial 
        pneumonitis and 
        any of following:
        • DLCO of 39%
        • 10% decrease 
        in FVC
        • <88% O2 
        saturation 
        during 6MWT
        • Honeycombing 
        on HRCT

        Cystic fibrosis

        • FEV1 of 30% and 
        any of following:
        • Increasing O2 
        requirements
        • Hypercapnia
        • Pulmonary 
        hypertension

        Idiopathic 
        pulmonary arterial 
        hypertension
        • Persistent NYHA 
        class III or IV
        • 350 meters or 
        declining 6MWT
        • Failing therapy 
        with epoprostenol
        • Cardiac index of 
        0.2 L/min/m2
        • Right atrial 
        pressure 15 mm 
        Hg

        Sarcoidosis

        • NYHA class III or 
        IV and any of 
        following:
        • Hypoxemia at rest
        • Pulmonary 
        hypertension
        • Right atrial 
        pressure 15 mm 
        Hg


        Medical Aspects of Evaluation
        • Starts with primary physician who must consider
        1. health status of the patient vs the average time spent on the waiting list
        2. balance between disclosing all available medical treatments and 
        offering the end-stage treatment of transplantation
        • When referral to transplant center occurs:
        • Input from multiple transplantation team members
        • Laboratory testing, presence of contraindications, social issues, patient 
        adherence to medical management and general health
        • If put on waiting list – must re-evaluate every 6 months for status changes


        Laboratory Tests and Procedures
        • Required examination and 
        assessment for transplant 
        candidacy or waitlist placement

        Absolute Contraindications for Heart and 
        Lung Transplant
        Cardiac transplantation Lung transplantation
        Absolute contraindications Absolute contraindications
        • Systemic illness with a life expectancy <2 years despite HT, including
        • Active or recent solid organ or blood malignancy within 5 years (e.g
        leukemia, low grade neoplasms of prostate with persistently elevated 
        prostate-specific antigen)
        • AIDS with frequent opportunistic infections
        • Systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoid, or amyloidosis that has multisystem 
        involvement and is still active
        • Irreversible renal or hepatic dysfunction in patients considered for only HT
        • Significant obstructive pulmonary disease (FEV1 <1 L/min)
        • Fixed pulmonary hypertension
        • Pulmontary artery systolic pressure >60 mm Hg
        • Mean transpulmonary gradient > 15mm Hg
        • Pulmonary vascular resistance >6 Wood units

        • Active malignancy within the past 2 years
        • Continued abuse of alochol, tobacco, or narcotics
        • Infection with the human immunodeficiency virus
        • Significant chest wall or spinal deformity
        • Hepatitis B antigen posivity
        • Hepatitis C with histologic evidence of liver disease
        • Limited ability to comply with medical regimen
        • Untreatable psychiatric condition with inability to comply with regimen
        • Absence of consistent support system

        .PT Examination of Transplant Candidates (!!E).Lv1
            • Chart review, inspection, vital signs, musculoskeletal exam, functional assessment, 6-Minute walk test, sit to stand test)
            • Lung transplantation candidate
                • need to assess efficacy of airway clearance techniques
            • Assessment of aerobic capacity/endurance with exercise and activity
            • Test results serve as basis for prescribing a program and provide useful information to the transplantation team
            • Patient may be referred to outpatient PT, cardiac or pulmonary rehab
            • Exercise may be contraindicated in patients with primary pulmonary hypertension as it may aggravate the condition

        Transplant List Acceptance
        • If accepted, medical profile is placed on national patient 
        waiting list for organ transplantation
        • Waiting list compiled by United Network of Organ Sharing 
        (UNOS); computerized matching and ranking of donor-
        recipient
        • Factors affecting ranking—tissue match, blood type, length 
        of time on list, immune status, distance between potential 
        recipient and donor


        Heart
        • Status 1A Æ50 days 
        • Status 1B Æ78 days 
        • Status 2 Æ309 days

        Lung
        • Recipients 12 years or younger 
        are ranked first by ABO blood 
        status
        • Other candidates are provided 
        a Lung Allocation Score (LAS)
        • score from 0 to 100 and are 
        reassessed every 6 months
        • Long waiting time

        Ranking, Priority and Waiting Times


        Donor Selection & Matching Criteria
        • Waiting lists for thoracic 
        organ transplantation grows 
        as a result of shortage of 
        donor organs
        • Medical centers are 
        expanding the criteria to 
        allow more organ donation


        Preoperative Rehabilitation (!!E).Lv3
        • Research supports significant training effects in 
        transplantation candidates
        • Most lung centers require participation of candidates in pulmonary 
        rehabilitation
        • Recommendation of cardiac rehabilitation is made on an individual 
        basis
        • Components of rehab include patient and family education, 
        cardiovascular endurance training, musculoskeletal strength 
        and flexibility training, breathing retraining


        Preoperative Rehabilitation (!!E).Lv1
        • Goal to improve or prevent deteriorations of candidate’s 
        physical condition, improve exercise tolerance
        • Level of participation in endurance activities may be limited 
        to minimal levels of exertion or just activities of daily living
        • Use of hemodynamic guidelines
        • Left ventricular assist device (LVAD) is used to “bridge” the 
        patient to heart transplant leads to improved performance
        • Most patients are able to participate in exercise 30 to 40 
        minutes three to five times per week


        .Preoperative Rehabilitation (!!E).Lv1
            Box 12-3 Pulmonary rehabilitation 
            recommendation
            Minimum of 20 sessions three times/week or two times/week plus 
            one home session
            Encourage high-intensity exercise when possible.
            Interval training may be useful to promote higher intensity levels of 
            exercise.
            Perform both upper extremity and lower extremity training.
            Combine endurance and strength training, especially in patients with 
            muscle atrophy
            Perform inspiratory muscle training as adjunctive therapy.
            Oxygen supplementation allows for high-intensity training.

            • Exercise benefits

            • Nutrition

        Preoperative Rehabilitation (!!E).Lv1
            • Building aerobic capacity during 
            inpatient pre-lung transplant 
            rehabilitation 
            A. Exercise bicycle in room on 20 L, 100% 
            FiO2 heated humidified high-flow nasal 
            cannula. 
            B. Patient walking in halls with a 
            combination of 15L nonrebreather 
            mask and 6L nasal cannula


        ECMO as a Bridge to Transplant
        • Some pre–lung transplant 
        patients who must avoid or are 
        failing ventilatory support 
        • Venovenous (VV) ECMO is 
        used for respiratory failure
        • Venoarterial (VA) ECMO is 
        used for circulatory collapse 
        due to pulmonary 
        hypertension


        Mobility and ECMO (!!E).Lv1
        • Able to mobilize patients on VV ECMO
        • ECMO cannula insertion site is 
        secured by head wrap and 
        supported by staff
        • Multidisciplinary approach is necessary:
        1. ECMO specialist supports cannula 
        and pulls ECMO machine
        2. PT supports patient with gait belt 
        and steadies rolling walker
        3. RN supports trach tube
        4. Tech pushes IV pole
        5. RT pushes ventilator


        Alternative Therapies to
        Transplantation


        Factors Related to Transplant Unsuitability
        • Patient did not meet criteria for organ system failure
        • Presence of contraindications limits potential for success
        • Decreased overall benefits for the patient from 
        transplantation
        • Patient opted for more conservative surgical or medical 
        management


        Alternatives to Lung Transplantation
        • Lung volume reduction 
        surgery (LVRS)
        • 20% to 30% of volume of each 
        lung is removed
        • Decreased lung hyperinflation 
        & improve elastic recoil


        Alternatives to Lung Transplantation
        • Noninvasive ventilation or BiPAP
        • Tightly fitting nasal mask 
        • Delivers positive airway pressure 
        during inspiration and 
        exhalation
        • Indicated for patients with signs 
        of respiratory failure despite 
        maximal drug and O2 therapy
        • Typically used at night to 
        decrease work of breathing, 
        daytime fatigue and improved 
        sleep


        Alternatives to Heart Transplantation -
        Mechanical Circulatory Support Devices (MCSD)
        • Ventricular Assistive Device (VAD)
        • Biventricular (BiVAD)
        • Right Ventricular (RVAD)
        • Left Ventricular (LVAD)
        • “Destination VAD”
        • Total Artificial Heart (TAH)
        • Able to resume ADLs and participate 
        in a cardiac rehabilitation program 
        in preparation for a heart 
        transplantation


        Left Ventricular Assistive Device (LVAD)


        Alternatives to Heart Transplantation
        • Cardiomyoplasty
        • Fatigue-resistant skeletal 
        muscle is wrapped around 
        the patient’s heart/stimulated 
        electrically
        • Intravenous pharmacological 
        management
        • Becoming more common to 
        manage chronic heart failure 
        in those waiting for transplant

    .('Thoracic Organ Transplantation Part 2.pdf')
        .Surgical Techniques

        .Four methods of cardiac transplantation 
            1. Heterotopic (HHT)
            2. Total transplantation
            3. Biatrial
            4. Bicaval


        .Heterotopic Heart Transplantation (HHT)
        • Piggyback
        • Native heart is not 
        removed
        • Donor heart is 
        connected to the native 
        heart via right/left atria
        • More associated 
        complications 


        .Total Heart Transplantation
        • Complete excision of the 
        recipient atria with complete 
        atrioventricular 
        transplantation, bicaval and 
        pulmonary venous 
        anastomoses
        • Not frequently utilized
        Mayo Foundation for Medical Education and Research (20221). https://www.mayoclinic.org/-
        /media/kcms/gbs/patient-consumer/images/2016/06/01/09/10/mcdc_heart-transplant-surgery-8col.jpg


        .Orthotopic Heart Transplantation
        A. Biatrial technique 
        • leaves recipient SA node intact, which 
        remains functional; donor heart SA is 
        denervated
        • Two separate P waves will be seen on 
        ECG
        • Donor and recipient atrial cuffs sewn 
        together 
        B. Bicaval
        • Sewing separate caval anastomoses
        • Most popular with less complications


        .Biatrial vs Bicaval
        Biatrial Versus Bicaval Anastomotic Surgical Technique for Heart Transplantation.

        .Lung Transplant Surgical Techniques 1
        • Harvest of donor lungs 
        • Pulmonary veins are detached 
        from heart with cuff of left 
        atrium
        • Pulmonary arteries are 
        transected
        • Lungs removed en bloc, divided 
        into separate right and left 
        lungs
        Completed preparation of a single left 
        lung transplant with anastomosis sites 
        designated by suture lines.


        Lung Transplant Surgical Techniques 2
        • Procedure for lung transplant
        • Use of mainstem bronchial 
        anastomoses, bilateral anterior 
        thoracotomies or transsternal 
        bilateral thoracotomy (clamshell)
        • Least functional lung is removed 
        and transplanted first
        • Chest tubes placed into each 
        pleural space
        • Single lung transplant—
        posterolateral thoracotomy


        Lung Transplant Surgical Techniques 3
        • Lung transplantation using bilateral 
        posterolateral thoracotomies
        • Image A: Diseased lung is 
        removed
        • Image B & D: Donor lung is 
        prepared for transplantation
        • Image C: Donor lung is inserted


        .Post-transplant Management 


        .Acute Complications 
        • Acute Rejection
        • Nonspecific graft failure
        • Infection
        • Reperfusion injury


        .Pharmacological Management 
        • Medications consist of:
        • immunosuppressive agents and drugs 
        targeting side effects of these agents
        • necessary to prevent rejection of 
        donor organ
        • Induction therapy
        • strong dose of immunosuppressives 
        at time of transplant
        • Acute rejection
        • Occurs when the immune system is 
        not adequately suppressed; 
        • treated with strong doses of 
        immunosuppressive meds


        .Signs and Symptoms of Acute Rejection
        Heart transplant Lung transplant
        Low-grade fever Fever over 100°F (38°C)
        Increase in resting blood pressure "Flulike" symptoms: chills, aches, headache, 
        dizziness, nausea, and/or vomiting
        Hypotension with activity Chest congestion
        Myalgia Cough
        Fatigue Shortness of breath
        Decreased exercise tolerance New pain or tenderness around the lung
        Ventricular dysrhythmias Fatigue or generally feeling "lousy"
        Dyspnea Decreased exercise tolerance
        Weight gain due to water retention Decrease in FEV1 and FVC

        .Cardiac Changes Post-Heart Transplant 1 Γ(new verison) (!!E).Lv1
            • Blood pressure monitoring 
            & control 
            • High risks associated with 
            hypertensive episodes
            • HTN is of significant concern 
            and must be avoided
            • Need to consider patient 
            positioning and exercise 
            prescription to reduce HTN 
            episodes from occurring

        .Cardiac Changes Post-Heart Transplant Γ(old verison) (!!E).Lv1
            HR at rest 
                Normal heart
                    60 to 100 bpm
                Denervated heart
                    Elevated as high as 90 to 110 bpm to achieve normal cardiac output
            Elevation of HR from rest
                Normal heart
                    -Up to 120 bpm: Regulated by parasympathetic withdrawal mediated by vagus nerveAbove 120 bpm: Activation of sympathetic system via sympathetic ganglia
                Denervated heart
                    -After 5 min of exercise: HR increases due to circulating catecholamines to contribute to increased CO
                    -Over time: denervation super sensitivity develops (increased sensitivity to endogenous catecholamines such as noradrenaline)
            HR response to activity
                Normal heart
                    Immediate increase in HR
                Denervated heart
                    HR increase has delayed response
            Initial CV response to exercise
                Normal heart
                    SV and HR provide immediate increase in CO 
                Denervated heart
                    HR does not change; SV increases to increase CO (Frank-Starling mechanism)
            Peak HR with exercise 
                Normal heart
                    With exercise HR increases 10 bpm per MET
                Denervated heart
                    Achieves 70% to 80% of normal
            Stroke volume 
                Normal heart
                    70 ml 
                Denervated heart
                     Lower than normal
            LVEF
                Normal heart
                    50% [50%] to 65% 
                Denervated heart
                    Lower than normal
            Systolic BP
                Normal heart
                    With exercise increases 7 to 10 mmHg per MET
                Denervated heart
                    -At rest: same or higher than before transplantation
                    -Exercise peak: reduced to 80% of normal
            Diastolic BP
                Normal heart
                    With exercise: rises gradually (<10 mm Hg), remains the same, or drops slightly (<10 mm Hg)
                Denervated heart
                    -At rest: elevated because of stiffness of left ventricle myocardium 
                    -With exercise: increases abnormally or may decline (20 mm Hg) as result of decreased peripheral resistance, causing patient to become hypotensive

        Cardiac Changes Post-Heart Transplant 2 (!!E).Lv1
            • Cardiac denervation initially occurs following heart 
            transplant; infrequent with isolated lung transplant
            • HHT—donor heart responds in same manner as denervated 
            heart; native heart still innervated, but attention should be on 
            donor heart response
            • Delayed reaction of denervated heart requires an adequate 
            warm-up and cool down
            • HR monitoring is NOT an accurate measure of exercise 
            intensity; use of RPE is better

        .Changes in Pulmonary Status after Heart & Lung Transplant (!!E).Lv1
        • Maximum O2 uptake and exercise capacity improve 
        significantly, but remain below predicted values
        • Exercise limitation in lung transplant recipients may be 
        related to HTN, muscle atrophy, pretransplant changes, 
        suboptimal nutrition, deconditioning


        .The Acute Postoperative Inpatient Phase (!!E).Lv3
        • PT evaluation is initiated in ICU within 12 to 
        24 hours
        • Protective isolation is observed 
        • Transplant recipients are initially 
        intubated and mechanically ventilated
        • Sternal precautions for median 
        sternotomy and clamshell incisions
        • Multiple medications, multiple 
        intravenous lines, chest drainage tubes, 
        endocardial pacemaker wires, urinary 
        catheter, multiple monitoring lines


        .The Acute Postoperative Inpatient Phase (!!E).Lv1
        • PT goals are to improve 
        function and QOL, 
        specifically functional 
        abilities in self-care and 
        mobility


        .The Postoperative Outpatient Phase (!!E).Lv1
        • Begins following hospital discharge and continues until discharge from formal 
        rehabilitation program—typically 6 weeks
        • Similar to phase II cardiac rehab
        • Cardiac rehab focuses on endurance; PT focused on functional mobility
        • 6 MWT is used to determine exercise prescription
        • Frequent complications as an outpatient
        • chronic rejection, infection, hypertension, steroid myopathy, osteoporosis…
        • Discharge goals
        • functional capacity improvement 
        • Achieved planned goals
        • competent with self-monitoring and independent with home exercise


        .The Postoperative Outpatient Phase
        • Reintegration into 
        community activity is the 
        final phase
        A. Finishing a 5K race 6 
        months after lung 
        transplant. 
        B. Conquering a hill on a 
        hiking trip 7 months 
        after lung transplant.


        .Physical Therapy Considerations Post-Heart Transplant (!!E).Lv1
            .Post-Operative Treatment Considerations
                ICU PT examination is 
                focused on impaired gas 
                exchange, airway clearance, 
                effects of prolonged static 
                positioning during surgery, 
                pain, mobility restrictions

                Goals: optimizing pulmonary 
                hygiene, strength, ROM, 
                exercise tolerance

                Exercise— low to mod 
                intensity, may begin in 
                supine, progress to sit to 
                stand, and ambulation; 
                appropriate warm up and 
                vital sign monitoring

                PT intervention is progress 
                as patient moves from ICU 
                to regular floor to outpatient 

                Education topics—safety, 
                correct performance of 
                exercise; Hospital stay for 
                about 7 to 10 days with 2-3 
                days in the ICU

                .Activity Recommendations
                Activity Level 1 
                • Breathing and relaxation 
                techniques
                • Exercises (15 to 20 repetitions, 
                supine or seated as 
                appropriate, emphasize 
                proximal muscles)
                • Shoulder AROM
                • Trunk rotation
                • Hip/knee flexion (seated 
                marching)
                • Bridging or hip extension
                • Knee extension
                • Ankle pumps
                • Gait: standing pregait activities 
                (minisquats, weight shifting, 
                single-leg stance)
                • Sitting in chair at least 30 - 60 
                min

                Activity Level 2
                • Exercises (15 to 20 repetitions, 
                standing, emphasize proximal 
                muscles)
                • Shoulder exercisesכ
                • Lunges
                • Marching in place
                • Minisquats, weight shifting, 
                single-leg stance
                • Toe raises
                • Gait: ambulate in room ad lib, 
                ambulate in the hall, as 
                tolerated
                • Up in a chair ad lib

                Activity Level 3
                • Exercises (15 to 20 repetitions, 
                standing, emphasize proximal 
                muscles)
                • Head and shoulder exercises: 
                progress to wrist weights (1 
                lb)כ
                • Toe raises (progress to single 
                leg as able)
                • Dynamic balance exercises
                • Gait: progress ambulation to 
                10 to 15 min continuously
                • Stair stepping
                • Add cool-down stretches for 
                lower extremities

                Activity Level 4
                • Exercise per Level 3
                • Progress ambulation to <20 
                min continuously
                • Stationary cycle: progress to 
                10 to 20 min at mild resistance 
                (include 2- to 3-min slower 
                warm-up and cool-down

                GUIDELINES AT REST GUIDELINES TO DETERMINE

                AND WITH EXERCISE

                HR>120 bpm HR that increases >40 bpm above the 
                resting level with exercise

                Dyspnea index >15

                SBP>190mm Hg SBP increases >40 mm Hg with exercise Excessive fatigue
                SBP decrease >10 mm Hg below the resting 
                level with exercise

                Vertigo

                DBP >110 mm Hg DBP increases >15 mm Hg above the 
                resting level with exercise

                Claudication

                ECG abnormalities that impair perfusion ECG abnormalities that worsen and impair 
                perfusion

                Metal confusion or dizziness

                RPE > 13/20 or 4/10 (somewhat hard) RPE that increases to 
                with exercise

        .Physical Therapy Considerations Post-Lung Transplant (!!E).Lv1
            .Post Operative Treatment Considerations
                • Rehab begins typically first 
                postoperative day 
                • Cardiopulmonary conditioning is 
                initiated
                • Problems and goals are like heart 
                transplant
                • Attention to changes in lungs caused by 
                pulmonary denervation including 
                decreased mucociliary clearance, 
                ineffective cough
                • Focus is on pulmonary hygiene, optimal 
                positioning, mobilization, cough effort


            .Physical Therapy Considerations
                • After ICU
                • Focus continues on ventilation and airway clearance for 
                optimal oxygen transport; thoracic mobility, breathing 
                exercise, multiple sessions of mobility training
                • Discharge goals:
                • Independence in self-care, secretion clearance, increased 
                thoracic mobility, general strength and endurance, ability 
                to participate in home exercise program


        .Future Trends in Transplantation Care
        • Increases in number and types of thoracic organ 
        transplantation are currently restricted by availability of 
        donor organs
        • Advances in donor allocation, selection, and support systems 
        must be enhanced
        • Alternative techniques are being used
        • Continued need for research and funding
        • Research ongoing to address immunological factors & 
        xenotransplantation

        .('PT 2202_Mod 7_Heart Transplant Case Study.docx') Heart Transplant Case Study 
            Read the following case and answer the discussion questions listed below:

            Patient:
            JJ is a 44-year-old man with end-stage congestive heart failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy. Cardiac risk factors include a positive family history and a 30-year history of tobacco use.

            Examination
            •   Tests: Cardiac catheterization showed 100% blockage of RCA, 90% blockage of left main coronary artery, and ejection fraction = 7%. Complication: pericatheterization MI.
            •   Activity: Unable to perform low-level activity without signs and symptoms of severe CHF.

            Pretransplant Period
            An attempt was made to manage JJ's CHF with pharmacologic support. Despite maximal pharmacologic support, JJ's CHF worsened. At this time an intra-aortic balloon pump was inserted to mechanically assist JJ's heart; the balloon pump was also unsuccessful. Following the failure of the balloon pump, a biventricular assist device (BiVAD) was implanted into JJ's chest. JJ was then referred to PT for evaluation and treatment.

            Physical Therapy Examination post-transplant
            •   Subjective: JJ was intubated, communicating with paper and pencil, following multistep commands. 
            •   Pulmonary: Crackles present in bilateral lower lobes. RR = 20, IMV = 8, 60% oxygenation, SpO2 = 95% 
            •   Cardiac: HR = 90 to 110 bpm. Rhythm: irregular. BP = 110/70 mm Hg BiVAD: pump flow 5-6 L/min. 
            •   Musculoskeletal: No abnormalities found in ROM, strength 2/5 UE's, 2/5 LE's, all mobility skills required moderate to maximal assist. 
            •   Impairments identified: decreased strength, decreased activity tolerance, ineffective secretion clearance.

            Post-Transplant Period
            JJ received an orthotopic bi-caval heart transplant 40 days after being placed on the transplant waiting list. Physical therapy was re-initiated 24 hours following heart transplantation.

            Discussion Questions:  
                1.What are the treatment interventions you would provide in the pre-transplant period?
                    Bronchopulmonary hygiene and suctioning, deep breathing exercises (DBE), coughing 
                    techniques, progressive mobility skills, strengthening exercises, and endurance training 
                    (stationary cycling and gait). Treatment was initiated with low-level skills and progressed as JJ 
                    was able to tolerate higher level skills and increases in intensity and duration. He was seen twice 
                    a day with a perfusionist present initially to ensure adequate cardiac output with changes in 
                    position and exercise. 

                2.As a PT working with a patient who has a BiVAD what would be some important considerations?
                    To work with a patient with a BiVAD the PT would need some specialized training, and knowing 
                    the pump type is an important consideration when monitoring vitals during exercise in a patient who has a VAD.  Working with a patient who has a LAD requires vast knowledge of the interworking of the device, including alarms and settings.

                3.What are the goals of PT treatment postoperatively during the acute stage?
                    Goals for this phase include (1) optimizing pulmonary hygiene and chest wall mechanics to 
                    facilitate weaning from the ventilator and supplemental oxygen, (2) improving strength and 
                    ROM in the upper extremities and thoracic area, and (3) improving exercise tolerance through 
                    ADLs and exercising at a low to moderate intensity.

                4.Devise a treatment plan on day 2 in the ICU, describe all components of the treatment session including, exercise, functional mobility training, education, and management of lines/tubes/drains.
                    The patient may still be on the ventilator, have chest tubes, have an A-line, CVP, and other 
                    invasive hemodynamic monitoring tools. On day 2 you would likely have a primary goal of 
                    getting the patient into the chair, therefore, functional mobility would include bed mobility and 
                    transfers. Exercises, which would occur prior to mobility training, would include supine lower 
                    and upper extremity active range of motion, like ankle pumps and heel slides. Education to the 
                    patient on breathing, pulmonary hygiene and sternal precautions would also be included.

                5.How would you monitor intensity during exercise in this phase of care and why?
                    Rate of perceived exertion, and heart rate is not an adequate indicator of exercise intensity due 
                    to the sympathetic denervated. 

                6.Describe the vital response with exercise that would warrant termination
                    HR>40 above rest, RPE >13/20, SBP >40mmHg or <10mmHg from rest, DBP >15mmHg above 
                    rest 

                7.What are the signs of organ rejection for the patient after heart transplant?
                    Fever, increase in resting BP, hypotension with activity, myalgia, fatigue, decreased exercise 
                    tolerance, ventricular dysrhythmias, dyspnea, weight gain 2/2 to water retention, decreased 
                    urine output.

                8.If the patient was independent with transfers and gait at discharge, what are the discharge options?
                    Cardiac rehabilitation phase II when ready.

        .('PT 2202_ Mod 7_ Posterolateral VATS Procedure Case Study.docx') Posterolateral VATS Procedure Case Study (!!Blind) 
            Read the following case study and answer the questions below for discussion.
            FM is a 56-year-old man who underwent surgical removal of his right lower lobe with a posterolateral thoracotomy after the diagnosis of lung cancer. FM had a 2.5 packs per day history of smoking for the past 38 years. FM works as an automobile mechanic and requires full use of both upper extremities and does a fair amount of lifting for his job.
            Postoperatively, the patient experienced moderate to severe pain and demonstrated a moist nonproductive cough; on the second day after surgery, he developed a 100.1° F temperature. Chest radiograph showed atelectasis in the right middle lobe and left lower lobe and infiltrates in the left lower lobe. The patient was started on incentive spirometry and respiratory breathing treatment of a bronchodilator every 4 hours. He continued to be very inactive, and by the fourth postoperative day, he was only getting up to the chair with assistance. Incisional pain remained severe and began radiating into the ipsilateral shoulder (with no prior pathology) by the fifth postoperative day. According to the nurse’s documented notes on day 6, the patient had difficulty feeding himself with his right arm and was observed using his left arm to assist his right. On the same day, nursing also noted that FM produced small amounts of thick, yellow-green sputum with much effort due to a weak cough. The surgeon was notified and wrote orders for physical therapy to evaluate and treat FM and specifically address the right upper extremity deficit and acute deconditioned state.

            Discussion Questions:
            1.Describe the procedure of a posterolateral thoracotomy via VATS
                VATS is a closed thoracic procedure, and unlike an open thoracotomy, it is performed by 
                making two small holes (ports) with an access incision of only 5 cm in length. This 
                procedure was performed in the posterolateral region of the chest. 

            2.What interventions should have been added right away in the early post-operative recovery to prevent complications that are present in this case?
                This case demonstrates the complications that can develop with a posterolateral VATS 
                when aggressive bronchial hygiene, frequent mobility, and range-of-motion activities are 
                not implemented early in the patient’s postoperative recovery. Radicular pain into the 
                shoulder after thoracotomy is quite common, but should be addressed as soon as possible 
                to avoid further complications such as range-of-motion limitations or, worse, adhesive 
                capsulitis 

            3.The onset of fever, radiographic changes seen in the lungs, weak cough, and now discolored sputum are consistent with what respiratory diagnosis?
                Hospital acquired pneumonia

            4.What lab values may be abnormal based on the current diagnosis (what you answered in question 2)?
                High WBC, abnormal blood gases 

            5.What PT examination techniques with proposed findings would you use to evaluate this patient’s lung consolidation, and how may you treat your findings?
                Auscultation with findings of crackles, and airway clearance techniques – postural drainage 
                and cough techniques to work on clearance of the mucus/consolidation in the areas where 
                crackles are heard.

            6.What PT examination techniques with proposed findings would you use to evaluate this patient’s atelectasis, and how may you treat your findings?
                Auscultation with findings of absent breath sounds, chest wall expansion with reduced 
                unilateral excursion on the right middle chest/lobe, and segmental breathing or inhalation 
                training (stacked breathing or inspiratory holds) would serve as the best intervention. 

        .('PT 2202_ Mod 7_Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Thoracic Surg.docx') Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Thoracic Surgeries Group Lecture Review Activity (!!Blind) 
            -Answer the following questions based on what you learned in the Module 7 video lectures, then we will discuss and review as a group.
            1.Describe the following surgical approaches, when they may be utilized and the PT implications involved:
                a.Posterolateral thoracotomy
                    The typical posterolateral thoracotomy incision extends downward from a point midway 
                    between the spine of the fourth thoracic vertebra and the scapula in a gently curving 
                    arch around the tip of the scapula to the fifth or sixth intercostal space at the anterior 
                    axillary line. The lower trapezius muscle is divided, as well as the entire extent of the 
                    serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi muscles in an effort to avoid the long thoracic 
                    nerve and to preserve motor function. However, with these muscles cut and ribs spread 
                    for exposure, risk of intercostal nerve damage is most frequently associated with this 
                    approach. Some PT implications would be pain in the surgical site, assessment for 
                    shoulder function post-surgery and long term, breathing retraining, pulmonary 
                    hygiene/airway clearance techniques 2/2 to possible chest wall pain that can disrupt 
                    breathing mechanics. 

                b.VATS (video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery)
                    Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery has become the standard procedure for 
                    minimally invasive surgery for the treatment of thoracic problems, including lung 
                    cancer, pleural problems, and esophageal and abdominal surgeries. The procedure is 
                    commonly performed under local anesthesia rather than general sedation, and unlike 
                    open thoracotomy, the ribs are not spread during VATS, which makes the VATS 
                    technique quite advantageous for the patient, Lobectomy via VATS has been 
                    demonstrated to be a safe and effective procedure to treat early-stage non–small cell 
                    lung cancer and is performed by making two small holes (ports) with an access incision 
                    of only 5 cm in length.  Some PT implications may be pain in the surgical site, but this 
                    surgical approach can significantly reduce hospital stay, possibly leading to little PT 
                    needs. 

                c.Median Sternotomy
                    The median sternotomy is probably the most frequently used incision for 
                    cardiothoracic operations.  The initial skin incision usually begins in the midline inferior 
                    to the suprasternal notch and extends below the xiphoid. The sternum is divided along 
                    its midline in a series of steps, and a sternal retractor is used to hold the incision open. 
                    At the end of the surgical procedure, the sternum is generally closed with stainless 
                    steel sutures either through or around the sternum, and the wound is closed in layers 
                    with the outer skin layer closed with either surgical adhesive or staples. An important 
                    role the PT plays in this approach is knowing and training and patient in sternal 
                    precautions, which may differ between facility and surgeon. Also, the PT will need to 
                    teach the patient functional training within those precautions, breathing retraining, 
                    pulmonary hygiene/airway clearance techniques 2/2 to pain with coughing and/or breathing mechanics 2/2 to pain in the chest form the surgical site. Also, education and assessment of the surgical site to ensure no infectious process is present.

            2.Define the following procedures and describe some of the implications for PT intervention after the following procedure(s):
                a.CABG
                    A CABG is indicated when there is multivessel occlusion present, and it is 
                    performed as an open-heart surgery with harvesting vascular grafts from the 
                    saphenous vein in the leg or an artery inside the chest wall such as the mammary 
                    artery.  A part of the graft vessel is cut off and anastomosed below the occlusion. 
                    The vascular graft then is used to bypass the occlusion in the coronary artery so that 
                    there is an alternate pathway for blood to transfuse the heart. A vessel is affixed to 
                    the aorta and anastomosed below the blockage. Some PT implications include 
                    sternal precautions though surgeons vary on the restrictions and time frames.  The 
                    acute are phase of PT also involves functional mobility training with monitoring of 
                    vital sign response, deep breathing exercise for lung expansion and patient 
                    education 

                b.PTCA (angioplasty)
                    Percutaneous revascularization procedures are interventions that are used to treat 
                    atherosclerotic disease or plaques, These procedures may be planned after 
                    outpatient testing reveals plaques or they may be scheduled more urgently in an 
                    individual that is experiencing an acute coronary syndrome. The angioplasty is 
                    performed when the lumen of a coronary artery is partially or nearly completely 
                    blocked by a plaque.  A balloon tipped catheter is inserted while deflated and 
                    positioned at the lesion site in the coronary artery.   The balloon is then inflated to 
                    compress the lesion against the wall of the artery to open the vessel. Due to the less 
                    invasive nature of this surgery, there may be little to no PT implications, but the 
                    patient may have an inpatient functional mobility and endurance assessment if 
                    indicated. An aerobic conditioning program may be indicated to retrain the patient 
                    who may have been deconditioned due to the vessel occlusion or other co-
                    morbidities.

                a.Lung transplant
                    A clamshell surgical approach is used the open the chest wall, and during the 
                    surgical procedure, the least-functional lung is removed and transplanted first, and 
                    the remaining contralateral lung is ventilated. After completion of both lung 
                    transplantations, two chest tubes are placed into each pleural space and the chest 
                    is closed. A patient post-lung transplant will have PT from ICU up until an outpatient 
                    setting. First and foremost, knowing the signs of rejection is key, and should be 
                    assessed by the PT at each visit with the patient. Attention to changes in lungs 
                    caused by pulmonary denervation including decreased mucociliary clearance and 
                    ineffective cough should be addressed right away and teaching the patient to cough
                    on a scheduled basis is very important. General functional mobility training, and 
                    aeronic exercise is indicated, and SPO2 (>90%) needs to maintain at a certain level 
                    as the new lung tissues are getting used to oxygenating the body.  Focus on 
                    ventilation and airway clearance for optimal oxygen transport; thoracic mobility, 
                    breathing exercise, multiple sessions of mobility training is all indicated. 

                b.Heterotrophic Heart Transplant
                    This is termed a piggyback procedure, and the native heart is not removed. The 
                    donor heart is connected to the patient’s native heart through a median sternotomy 
                    incision and the donor right and left atrium is connected to the recipient right and 
                    left atrium respectively. The four atria then function as two atria. Ascending aortas 
                    are anastomosed together, and pulmonary arteries are connected via a tube 
                    graft.  PT plays a large role post heart transplant from the ICU setting all the way to 
                    the outpatient exercise program they will engage in after DC. First and foremost, 
                    knowing the signs of rejection is key, and should be assessed by the PT at each visit 
                    with the patient. The PT will need to be aware that there may be 2 different ECG 
                    readings, due to the native and donor heart being present in the chest, but needs to 
                    take note of the donor heart only. The PT also needs to start with low level exercise 
                    and functional mobility training, be aware of all lines/tubes/drains, and educate the 
                    patient on pulmonary hygiene to prevent other complications. The exercise 
                    progressions will depend on the patient ability to progress, and intensity should be 
                    gauged by use of RPE scale vs heart rate. Also, a warmup and cool down that is 
                    extended is very important, and the sympathetic NS is less able to contribute to 
                    exercise response, and circulating catecholamines must take time to build then be 
                    uptake and the end of exercise.  If strength training it is also important to consider 
                    isometric mm activity, as this can lead to a severe rise in PT, which is a high risk for 
                    a heart transplant patient. There are 4 specific activity levels that are recommended 
                    with interventions listed in the lecture “Thoracic Organ Transplantation Part 2.” 

                c.Pacemaker Placement
                    This is a minimally invasive procedure and usually performed on an outpatient 
                    basis. It is important for the PT to be aware of when a patient has a pacemaker so 
                    vital signs can be monitored with exertion, especially in patients with newly 
                    implanted pacemakers.

                d.TAVR (least invasive)
                    The TAVR has 4 different surgical approaches, and the transfemoral approach is the 
                    least invasive. A percutaneous approach with a minimal groin incision occurs with 
                    transfemoral access, then a direct access to the valve for replacement can occur. 
                    Post-op the patient will require a functional mobility and endurance assessment, 
                    and a phase I cardiac rehab should be initiated. 

                e.Cardiac Ablation
                    Cardiac ablation is a procedure to correct cardiac arrhythmias such as atrial 
                    fibrillation.  In this procedure, a tube is guided into the heart to destroy small areas 
                    of tissue that may be causing the arrhythmias using either cryotherapy or 
                    radiofrequency energy.  This procedure is normally done in an electrophysiology lab 
                    where the patient can be monitored closely. The patient may be discharged on the 
                    same day leading to no real immediate PT needs post-procedure.

            3.Describe key differences between the following procedures:
                a.Traditional heart valve replacement surgery and TAVR
                    With a traditional heart valve surgery, a median sternotomy is required, while in a 
                    TAVR there is a minimal groin incision for transfemoral access and Delivers a fully 
                    collapsible replacement valve through the catheter

                b.Traditional coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG) and MIDCAB
                    The MIDCAB is less invasive with a smaller sternal incision and the patient is not 
                    placed on bypass during the surgery like they are with the traditional CABG. 

            4.  Patient Case: The patient is 45-year-old man who underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery for triple-vessel disease, using the left internal mammary and two saphenous vein grafts. A median sternotomy incision was used, as well as lower leg incision for saphenous vein grafts. The patient ended up back in surgery 6 hours after entering the surgical intensive care unit because of moderate to severe amounts of blood draining in chest tubes. The patient underwent subsequent repair of postoperative bleeding. ECG after surgery showed acute inferior wall injury when compared to preoperative ECG, and both troponin and CPK-MB levels were elevated. The patient was assessed as having a perioperative inferior myocardial infarction. The patient had a past medical history of smoking, hypertension, and above normal intake of alcohol prior to surgery. Postoperatively, the patient demonstrated moist cough, was slow to respond to functional activity because of difficulty bearing weight on left lower extremity (saphenous vein graft incisions caused pain and swelling) and showed decreased ability to bilaterally raise arms over head or use arms to push himself up and out of bed. 

            a.What portions of the chart review would be critical to check to see if this patient is appropriate or safe to initiate a PT evaluation/treatment?
                Lab values – troponins trending downward, HgB and RBC – bleeding risk, pain 
                levels, ECG changes, coagulation profiles

            b.What initial PT interventions would be indicated?
                The patient was started on a LE ROM program including ankle pumps and other 
                supine low intensity or anti-embolic exercises, bronchial hygiene with incentive 
                spirometer and splinted coughing program, and progressive mobility with 
                transfer/gait training.   The patient was educated on sternal precautions with 
                mobility and appropriate exercise/activity progression after surgery/MI.

            c.What may you do as a PT to address the patient’s difficulty in weightbearing to reduce pain and improve function?
                Suggest the use of an appropriate assistive device in order to progress ambulation 
                and WB activity, which is an important phase I rehabilitation intervention

..7.8. Module 7 Quiz

////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!Q)

    .Question 1
        Which of the following surgical approaches is MOST commonly used for cardiac procedures? 

        Posterolateral thoracotomy
        Median sternotomy
        Thoracoabdominal
        Subxiphoid

        Median sternotomy 
            Cardiac procedures are performed almost exclusively through a median sternotomy.

    .Question 2
        Which of the following musculoskeletal impairments is avoided by the surgeon sparing the long thoracic nerve during a lateral thoracotomy? 

        Scapular winging
        Shoulder adhesive capsulitis
        Shoulder external rotator weakness
        Rhomboid weakness

        Scapular winging 
            Postoperative scapular winging is avoided by careful preservation of the long thoracic nerve.
     
    .Question 3
        Which of the following vessels used in a coronary artery bypass graft is preferable due to its ability to resist atherosclerosis? 

        Saphenous vein
        Internal mammary artery
        External mammary artery
        Popliteal artery

        Internal mammary artery 
            The use of internal thoracic arteries (left internal mammary artery) is preferable for achieving a better long-term outcome, because these vessels have proved to be more resistant to graft atherosclerosis (a frequent problem with saphenous graft use).
     
    .Question 4
        Which of the following lung diseases is the MOST common lung pathology requiring lung transplantation? 

        Emphysema
        Chronic Bronchitis
        Asthma
        Pneumonia

        Emphysema
            The majority of lung transplants have been performed in patients who have emphysema. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the second most frequent indication for lung transplant. 
     
    .Question 5
        As part of the transplant evaluation team, which of the following evaluative procedures is MOST likely completed by the physical therapist? 

        Social history (smoking, alcohol, and drugs)
        Ideal body weight caloric intake
        Psychosocial assessment
        Mucociliary clearance evaluation

        Mucociliary clearance evaluation 
            As part of a patient evaluation for heart or lung transplant, the physical therapist completes an exercise tolerance test, exercise prescription, musculoskeletal assessment, and cough/mucociliary clearance. The other team members include a transplant coordinator, physicians and medical staff, dietician, social worker or pastoral care, and psychologist/psychiatrist.
     
    .Question 6
        Which of the following cardiac transplantation techniques is referred to as the “piggyback” technique? 

        Total transplantation
        Biatrial technique
        Bicaval technique
        Heterotopic heart

        Heterotopic heart 
            Heterotopic heart transplantation (HHT), referred to as the “piggyback” technique, is considered to be an alternative technique. This technique is performed without the removal of the native heart.
     
    .Question 7
        Which of the following monitoring tools is BEST to assess a heart transplant patient’s initial response to increases in activity? 

        Heart rate monitoring
        Rating of perceived exertion
        Pulse oximetry
        Blood pressure

        Rating of perceived exertion 
            Heart rate is not a good choice due to denervation. Blood pressure is important to monitor, but using a patient’s rate of perceived exertion or symptoms of fatigue are BEST to use initially for making decisions during treatment.
     
    .Question 8
        When the physical therapist is making decisions about treatment and activity tolerance, emphasis should be placed on the donor heart response.

        True
        False

        True
            It is best to monitor both responses by palpation of a peripheral pulse or ECG to see how the donor denervated heart and native innervated heart respond to treatment and activity. Emphasis should be placed on the donor heart when making decisions about treatment and activity tolerance.
     
    .Question 9
        Low intensity exercise is only permitted for a patient postoperative a lung transplant in a pulmonary rehabilitation program.

        True
        False

        False
            In a pulmonary rehabilitation program, high-intensity exercise is encouraged when possible. Interval training may need to be performed to promote higher intensity levels of exercise. 
     
    .Question 10
        Which of the following revascularization procedures is the BEST option when all three vessels of the coronary arterial supply are severely occluded? 

        Percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty
        Directional coronary arthrectomy
        Endoluminal stent
        Coronary artery bypass graft

        Coronary artery bypass graft 
            The Coronary Artery Surgery Study (CASS) concluded that surgical revascularization is the optimal choice for management of coronary artery disease when all three vessels are severely obstructed.

..8.0. Module Introduction
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    Module 8 will be presented in 2 units. In the first unit, you will be learning about cardiovascular and pulmonary monitoring and support as it relates to mechanical ventilation and oxygen therapy. In Unit 2 of this module, you will review cardiovascular and pulmonary interventions in preparation for your onsite lab immersion. In this unit, you will review the previous intervention lectures along with preparing for the lab immersion by reviewing the schedule and lab manual. 

    Learning Objectives
    Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to:

    Apply the use of the Hypothesis-Oriented Algorithm for Clinicians for evaluation selection, and re-examination in patients with cardiopulmonary dysfunction. 
    Give rationale for selection of evaluative tools and appropriate interventions in management of the cardiovascular and pulmonary patient.
    Develop a treatment plan and select appropriate interventions for patients with primary and secondary cardiopulmonary disorders reflecting the nature of the individual case based on client signs and symptoms.
    Identify the role of the physical therapist and other members of the health care team when recommending, selecting, and performing interventions on patients with cardiopulmonary impairments.
    Review and understand intervention plan including, but not limited to percussion, breathing exercises, positioning, strengthening, postural drainage, conditioning (aerobic exercise), relaxation techniques, energy conservation, suctioning, cough techniques, patient and family education.
    Identify, discuss the purpose, implications, and precautions of various life support monitoring equipment and oxygen delivery commonly used in the treatment of patients with cardiovascular and pulmonary disease.
    Discuss hospital-based coding systems, patient code status and emergency response in relation to monitoring a life support, and oxygen therapy.

..8.2. Unit 1 Background Materials
