    .Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Examination Techniques Skills Review: (page 275)
        Γ Same as: ('Student Immersion 2B Lab Handout.docx') I have added here the new stuff from this .docx 
        ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        -Practice the following examination techniques, as these techniques will be what you will be responsible for performing during your lab practical.
        -While performing the technique review
            when you may use them based on patient presentation and diagnoses, and also
            potential findings that would warrant intervention.
            Heart sounds
                -Heart sounds will be checked off by the instructors today, as they will not be on the lab practical but are a required skill to be checked off on.

        .Auscultation of Lung Sounds
            Position patient in the sitting position.
            Place diaphragm of stethoscope directly against the skin.
            Give proper instructions, i.e., "Breathe in and out through your mouth".
            Be sure that patient does not hyperventilate.
            Listen to lung sounds in at least 6 locations on both the anterior and posterior chest wall.
            Listen for quality of air exchange.
            Listen for one full breath in each location.
            Listen first at the apices, move stethoscope side to side, and compare each side.
            Note if sounds heard are normal (clear), abnormal or adventitious (noisy), diminished or
            absent (may be one-side only).
            Record findings.
            ------------------------------------------
            Instructs patient in procedure
            Uses stethoscope appropriately.
            Auscultates in appropriate areas.
            Compares lung sounds bilaterally.

        .Voice Transmission Tests
            Egophony- Patient says E, positive finding when A is heard (normal-muffled E sound)
            Bronchophony-Patient says 99, positive finding when sound heard loudly (normal-muffled /indistinguishable sound)
            Whispered Pectoriloquy-Patient whispers, positive finding when whisper heard loudly (normal-faint sound)
            ------------------------------------------
            Uses stethoscope appropriately.
            Auscultates in appropriate areas.
            Compares lung sounds bilaterally.

        .Chest Wall Expansion
            Patient in sitting
            Anterior at mid sternum - upper lobe
            Anterior at xiphoid (thumbs horizontal) - right middle lobe and left lingula
            Posteriorly at T8 level - lower lobe motion
            -------------------------------------------
            Instructs patient in procedure
            Places hands correctly on patient
            Notes normal vs abnormal motion

        .Diaphragmatic Breathing Assessment
            Patient in supine
            Palpate the diaphragm with thumbs over the costal margin and thumb tips meeting at the
            xyphoid while patient inhales deeply
            --------------------------------------------
            Instructs patient in procedure
            Places hands correctly on patient
            Notes normal vs abnormal motion

        .Auscultation of Heart Sounds & Check Off, you will be checked off on the below criteria before moving into the next section of this lab. This is out of 5 points for a lab grade.
            Locate the areas where you will listen to heart sounds.
            Position patient in supine
            Listen to the heart sounds with the diaphragm of the stethoscope.
            Bell is useful in picking up low pitched sounds (S3, S4, mitral stenosis).
            Assess your partner's heart rate by taking the apical pulse (auscultate and palpate)
            Assess if the heart rate corelates with the radial pulse.
            Normal sounds: Sl (lub-closure of mitral and tricuspid valves), S2 (dub-closure of aortic and pulmonic valves)
            Abnormal sounds: S3 (heart failure, diastolic dysfunction), S4 (noncompliant/hypertrophic ventricle)
            ----------------------------------------------
            Critical Criteria:
                Instructs patient in procedure
                Places stethoscope in correct locations on the chest wall and able to name the appropriate valve, lub vs dub, Sl vs S2
                Modifies need for placement accordingly
                Notes normal vs abnormal sounds
                Assesses apical pulse with stethoscope and palpation method

    .Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Intervention Techniques
        Practice the following intervention techniques, as these techniques will be what you will be responsible for choosing and performing during your lab practical. Each task is listed below with some points to consider along with check-off of critical criteria. Please refer to the Cardiopulmonary II lab manual for images and detailed instruction on each technique, as you will be responsible for all steps of the procedure. While performing the technique, review when you may choose them based on your examination findings.

        .Airway Clearance Interventions
            .Postural Drainage Positions
                Examination findings to determine treatment area
                Correct position to clear identified lung segment
                Instruct patient to assume position and perform cough when indicated to expectorate mucus
                Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                ------------------------------------------------------------------
                Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                Correctly places patient in position to target involved lung region
                Instructs patient in steps, time to remain in position, and coughing
                Re-assesses patient to determine if intervention is working

                .Add Manual Percussion
                    clapping with cupped hands over the affected lung segment
                    produces a hollow sound as the hand contacts the patient skin
                    performed at a rapid rhythm that may be 100-480 times per minute
                    ------------------------------------------------
                    Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                    Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                    Correctly places patient in position to target involved lung region
                    Instructs patient in steps, time to remain in position, and coughing
                    re-assesses patient to determine if intervention is working

                .Add Manual Vibration
                    -applies vibration to the chest wall over the affected lung segment by using the palmar aspect of their hand and overlapping that hand with the other hand
                    -The therapist will straighten their arms, and tense the muscles while creating a fine shaking motion over the chest wall
                    ----------------------------------------------------
                    Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                    Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                    Correctly places patient in position to target involved lung region
                    Instructs patient in steps, time to remain in position, and coughing
                    re-assesses patient to determine if intervention is working

            .Instructions for effective cough
                patient seated as best position
                patient performs maximal inspiration while performing slight spinal extension with cues to open the chest wall to bring air in
                At end range or maximal inspiration, the patient should then flex forward while performing a forceful cough at end range
                Addition of abdominal thrust
                Addition of pillow and splinting when indicated
                ---------------------------------------------------------------------
                Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                Correctly places patient in position to optimize effective coughing
                Adds the abdominal thrust at end range
                Adds the pillow to splint with post-operative state

            .Huff and Cough
                Patient in sitting
                Close the mouth and take a slow deep breath to fill lungs
                Hold breath for two or three seconds.
                Open the mouth and force the air out of your lungs with the mouth open as if trying to fog up a mirror
                -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
                Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                Correctly places patient in position to optimize effective huff and cough
                Adds the abdominal thrust at end range if needed

        .Breathing Strategies & Re-training
            .Pursed Lip Breathing
                -patient to inhale through the nose with the mouth closed for several seconds
                -patient to exhale slowly over 4 to 6 seconds through pursed lips, but be sure to not perform forceful abomination contraction with expiration
                -inhalation to exhalation ratio should start at 1 :2, then can progress to 1
                -Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                ----------------------------------------------------------------------
                Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                Correctly times patient inhalation to exhalation ratio
                Attempts to incorporate with functional activity or exercise

            .Diaphragmatic Controlled Breathing
                -Patient in a supine position with the trunk supported in slight flexion with the patient's knees bent over pillows or a bolster (posterior pelvic tilt facilitates the diaphragm, while anterior tilt will facilitate upper chest breathing)
                -Dominant hand over the upper abdominal region below the xyphoid process and the non-dominant hand over the mid-sternal region
                -Instruct the patient to breathe through the nose and direct the air so the dominant hand rises with inspiration
                -Little to no movement should be felt or observed in the non-dominant hand over the chest
                -----------------------------------------------------------------
                Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                Correctly places patient to optimize diaphragmatic activation
                Corrects patient when unable to perform correctly
                Moves onto a facilitation technique when the patient is having difficulty in self performance

                .Diaphragmatic Facilitation Techniques:
                    .Counter Pressure
                        Clinician then places their hand over the patient's dominant hand and applies resistance or pressure
                        Instruct the patient to breath into your while you continue to apply pressure
                        -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                        Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                        Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                        Correctly places patient to optimize diaphragmatic activation
                        Applies appropriate amount of pressure to facilitate diaphragmatic activation
                        Corrects patient when unable to perform correctly

                    .Quick Stretch
                        -Place your hand over the patient's mid abdomen, below the xyphoid process
                        -Instruct the patient to perform diaphragmatic breathing a few times so you may feel and assess the expiration and inspiration timing
                        -will inform the patient that you will be applying a quick stretch to the abdominal region during the next breath cycle
                        -Prior to inspiration apply a quick stretch or "Scoop" up and under the thorax with a subsequent instruction for the patient breath into your hand
                        -----------------------------------------------------------------------
                        Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                        Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                        Correctly places patient to optimize diaphragmatic activation
                        Applies appropriate amount of quick stretch, and timed correctly to facilitate diaphragmatic activation
                        Corrects patient when unable to perform correctly

                    .Lower Costal Expansion
                        Patient in sitting
                        Instruct the patient to place their own hands over the anterolateral rib cage
                        patient to breath into their hands to facilitate diaphragmatic motion as the rib cage moves up and outward
                        OR clinician to place hands OR use a belt/theraband as HEP or added resistance
                        --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                        Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                        Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                        Correctly places patient to optimize diaphragmatic activation
                        Correct placement of hands/belt/therband to facilitate diaphragmatic activation, HEP or added resistance
                        Corrects patient when unable to perform correctly

                    .Upper Chest Inhibition Technique
                        Patient is positioned supine (used it none of the above are working/last resort technique)
                        Clinician will place their arm over the upper chest and their other hand on the mid abdominal region
                        Patient performs a few respiratory cycles so you may feel and assess the expiration and inspiration timing
                        When the patient inhales, the therapist applies pressure to the upper chest to resist expansion
                        May apply a quick stretch to the diaphragm if needed prior to inhalation
                        Instruct the patient to breath into your hand on the abdominal region
                        Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                        ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                        Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                        Correctly places patient to optimize diaphragmatic activation
                        Correct placement of hands to facilitate diaphragmatic activation & inhibit upper chest activity
                        Adds other forms of diaphragmatic facilitation if needed
                        Corrects patient when unable to perform correctly

            .Segmental Breathing
                -Place the patient in supine, sitting, or sidelying to BEST access the area of treatment
                -Place your hand over the chest wall overlying the area of emphasis patient to breathe in deeply through the nose trying to direct airflow toward your hand while you apply a sight counter pressure with your hand
                -gradually decrease your pressure as the patient inspires to allow for expansion of that area
                -Instruct the patient to hold that breath for 2-3 seconds at the end of inspiration, then exhale
                -Patient can use their own hand or belt for HEP and to progress as added resistance
                --------------------------------------------------------------------
                Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                Correctly places patient to access treatment area
                Correct placement of hands/belt/therband to facilitate ventilation to treatment area
                Corrects patient when unable to perform correctly

            .Inspiratory Holds
                Patient is in suping, sitting or standing
                The patient is instructed to hold his or her breath at the height of inspiration for 2 to 3 seconds
                The patient then performs a relaxed exhalation
                ------------------------------------------------------------------------
                Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                Corrects patient when unable to perform correctly

            .Stacked Breathing
                Patient is in suping, sitting or standing
                The patient is instructed inspire once, hold that inspiration briefly, then inspire again on top of the previous inspiration
                The patient will continue this "stacking" or inspiration or breaths until maximum inspiratory levels can be reached and held for 2-3 seconds
                The patient then performs a relaxed exhalation
                ------------------------------------------------------------------------
                Sound reasoning for chosen intervention based on examination findings
                Instructs patient in intervention procedure
                Corrects patient when unable to perform correctly

    .Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Examination and Intervention Lab Cases
        Read the following cases from lab session 1, each case has added components which will allow you to propose findings with the chosen examination technique, and how to address those findings with an appropriate intervention. There are many correct answers, but sound rationale for findings and intervention must be included.

            1. The patient is a 75-year-old male with a history of restrictive lung disease due to exposure to asbestos. The patient is referred to outpatient PT given deconditioning and difficulty doing ADL's over the past year. He presents with shortness of breath with minimal exertion. He reports that he has been on 2 liters of supplemental oxygen for the past year and is wearing a nasal cannula. PMH: prostate CA, HTN, Hepatitis B, and CAD. Currently he is exhibiting an uncontrolled cough and high respiratory rate.

                -Based on the restrictive lung disease and patient symptoms you choose to perform lung auscultation (breath sounds and/or voice transmission testing):
                    Propose potential findings and propose a potential intervention for each of those findings.
                -Based on the restrictive lung disease and patient symptoms you choose to inhalation techniques and chest wall expansion:
                    Propose a potential intervention.

            2. The patient is a 65-year-old male 2 days s/p uncomplicated MI. The patient has been slow to mobilize and has had a weak cough. He was recently extubated and will soon be transferred from the ICU to the monitored cardiac unit. Physical therapy is ordered to evaluate and treat this patient. To date, the patient has only been out of bed to the bedside chair with nursing staff and required moderate assistance of one person. PMH: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, asthma, osteoarthritis of the left knee.

                Based on the recent MI, intubation, and period of immobilization you choose to perform chest wall expansion assessment:
                    Propose potential findings and propose a potential intervention for each of those findings.
                Based on the recent MI, intubation, and period of immobilization you choose to perform diaphragmatic breathing intervention:
                    Propose a potential intervention.

            3. The patient is a 55-year-old male presents who presents to outpatient PT with diagnosis of low back pain with pain into the abdomen, bilateral LE symptoms of pain and numbness. This pain has been bothering him for a about 8 days without relief. The PT discovered a (+) presence of AAA with auscultation and palpation, and sent the patient to the ED. The patient underwent a AAA repair that was complicated by a post-operative atelectasis. PMH: DM, hypertension, CKD Ill, and CAD.

                -Based on the recent AAA repair and post-operative atelectasis you choose to perform lung auscultation (breath sounds and/or voice transmission testing):
                    Propose potential findings and propose a potential intervention for each of those findings.
                -Based on the recent AAA repair and post-operative atelectasis you choose to perform breathing retraining and airway clearance:
                    Propose a potential intervention.

            4. A patient is admitted to the hospital with complaints of progressive dyspnea on exertion along with increased sputum production over the last week. He has a history of stage Ill COPD, emphysema and cor pulmonale. PMH: CAD, MI x2, CKD V on dialysis.

                Based on history of COPD and new onset productive cough you choose to perform lung auscultation:
                    Propose potential findings and propose a potential intervention for each of those findings.
                Based on history of COPD and new onset productive cough you choose to perform airway clearance:
                    Propose a potential intervention.

    .Lab Practical Review
        5 Points
            -Answers question and/or performs technique correctly with minimal delay in response.
            -Demonstrates appropriate patient approach including introduction, communication, preparation, and consent. No errors, or self-corrects errors without prompting.

    .Testing Format (Tin en conter açò cuan pegues la repasà al materia de este document)(!!)
        Each competency check is scheduled for 20 minutes. During the assessment one student will act as tester and one will act as patient. The tester will review the case description for a few minutes (2-3 minutes), conduct the testing scenario for 1-5 minutes, and then engage in a short debriefing session. You should be prepared to demonstrate all assessment and interventions covered in lab sessions 1 and 2 and provide an appropriate intervention to the patient based on examination findings/impairments. You will also be asked some discussion pieces included but not limited to:
            -TF1.Chart review information, like
                lab values
                    ECG strip findings
                    surgical history
                    medical history
                    imaging
                    medications
            -TF2.Identify key features of the chart review including history, and medications. Also discuss the current findings and possible patient diagnosis.

    .('PT 2202_Mod 8_Mechanically Ventilated Patient Case Study.docx') ('bPT 2202_Mod 8_Mechanically Venilated Patient Case_Ans Key.pdf')
        Mechanically Ventilated Patient Case Study 
            -The paramedics found this 59-year-old female with dyspnea and an oxygenation of 65% on room air and performed immediate tracheal intubation. Moderate ARDS with reduced lung compliance was diagnosed and treated with deep sedation with neuromuscular blocking agents. On day 3 in the ICU the patient was stabilized on mechanical ventilation and PT was ordered.

                Question set 1:
                    1.Prior to entering the patient:
                        a.What invasive monitoring may you expect the patient to have present and why, and how would you manage that when attempting to mobilize the patient?
                            Art line for MAP monitoring and continuous ABG draws, CVP, for medication 
                            administration and possible need for venous monitoring in light of ARDS and 
                            other organ involvement, swan ganz if pulmonary wedge pressures need 
                            measured. Careful montitoring and be sure of clearance for mobility esp if 
                            swan ganz present

                        b.What non-invasive monitoring would be present and why?
                            Continuous SPO2, BP, RR, ECG, possibly BIS if issues with LOC dur to ARDS 
                            and possible anoxic brain injury. BIS

                        c.What members of the inpatient medical team may you discuss the care, status or any history you may need for this patient inpatient medical team?
                            Nursing, MD, respiratory therapist, coordinate with OT to see the patient 
                            together. 

                    2.Which ventilator setting with do propose would be most appropriate for this patient based on her current state and why?
                        Due to deep sedation may be on CMV initially, but once stabilized and breathing 
                        could be on pressure support as she is able to initiate spontaneous breaths.

                    3.With the patient sedated how may you execute and what components of PT the examination can you complete?
                        Obtain history from social work or family. Patient may be able to answer yes/no 
                        questions or write to assist with history taking. Perform an evaluation on MSK, integ, 
                        pulmonary and cardiac examination, including observation techniques and passive examination techniques. You may perform some positional changes and PROM during exam and educate nsg or family on those as HEP to protect skin and joints.

                    4.Based on the patient’s diagnosis of ARDS what would be the primary intervention with prescription parameters you would prescribe to improve ventilation? Who would need to assist?
                        ARDS and the fluid overload would likely indicate performing proning, which would 
                        increase ventilatory ability in the dorsal lung region, and this would include dosing 
                        of up to 12 hours in that position. The PT would be the primary mobility specialize, 
                        but to perform the intervention would include a team of nsg, OT, RT and even the 
                        MD, along with continuous monitoring, then, dependent on the level of sedation and 
                        ventilator settings as the patient progresses, the patient would likely only be 
                        appropriate for mobility to initiate ventilation training, such as, performing 
                        positional change and observing the ventilatory responses via RR and o2 sats 
                        response. But, once the patient is weaning and becoming more independent 
                        specific interventions would include those aimed at inc lung capacity and 
                        inspiratory training. 

                        To ADD: Typically, in UH's ICUs patients who are proned while intubated are on paralytic drugs (we use 
                        cisatracurium) that paralyze the patient so they are unable to actively participate in the proning process--
                        different vs. a patient on less O2 support who can participate in rolling, edu, etc. Paralysis is helpful with severe ARDS because it reduces oxygen consumption from spontaneous muscle activity and allows ventilator to do 100% of respiratory work (also allows patient to be proned!). Side note--these paralytics, in my experience, have a high correlation with ICU acquired weakness

            -On day 14 the patient was no longer sedated but remained intubated and under pressure support ventilation. At this time you decided you could sit the patient edge of bed, which required 3 persons to maintain the position, but resulted in a significant increase in her level of consciousness and collaborative state. Her muscle strength indicated ICU-acquired weakness, still she continued with small but consistent improvements and started to participate actively in physical therapy sessions. 

                Question set 2:
                    1.Explain the SIMV settings.
                        Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation (SIMV) has a set RR  but the 
                        patient is able to breath spontaneously between ventilator breaths, and each 
                        spontaneous breath receives a tidal volume that depends on the patient’s effort. 
                        For examples the machine may be set at a RR of 10, but the patient may be 
                        breathing at a RR of 20, so the patient will have 10 machine supported breaths and 10 self-breaths.  This setting is a good mode for respiratory muscle exercise. The main disadvantage is that it may increase the work of breathing; therefore, may need to switch patient to A/C or pressure support if patient shows signs of fatiguing 

                    2.If the patient is in the weaning process what will the PT need to consider when it comes to treatment planning?
                        During weaning the patient will reduce ventilatory support until very little support is 
                        required for a patient to ventilate adequately. This is a very delicate process and 
                        takes all medical providers who interact with the patient during this time to take 
                        note of any changes in the patient status. During weaning continuous monitoring of 
                        ABG’s (arterial blood gases), Respiratory rate, depth and pattern, Pulse oximetry, 
                        HR and rhythm and Mental status changes. Physical Therapy treatment may need 
                        modification in POC during this time, and the patient may be fatigued during the 
                        weaning process, requiring lower frequency or intensity sessions over this time.

                    3.While sitting at the edge of bed what are some other interventions that you may be able to perform that would address the address impairments related to prolonged bedrest, immobility and respiratory weakness (be creative)?
                        DB exercises, postural exercises, insp/expiration with UE movements, LE exercises, 
                        balance/reaching while sitting EOB to work on seated balance and trunk 
                        strength/control  

                    4.Devise some home exercises that you would like for the family and/or nursing to encourage the patient to continue to prevent risks associated with immobility in the ICU.
                        PROM, anti-embolics, positional changes, delirium prevention

                    5.The patient is ready for transfers, and possibly to take some steps. Describe some examples of what would lead to a termination of treatment with the patient while they are performing this mobility progression.
                        Severe CP (chest pain) associated with EKG changes, HR above predicted MHR 
                        (max heart rate) or pre-determined limits set by medical team, Hypotension 
                        associated with dizziness, lightheadedness, and diaphoresis, Intolerable dyspnea, 
                        nasal flaring, or cyanosis, Unable to recover from or maintain SpO2 of 85% or more 
                        despite supplemental oxygen, Severe pain despite analgesia, Extreme fatigue, 
                        Patient or therapist safety, Patient wishes to stop

            -She was successfully extubated. The physical therapy team closely monitored her for secretion management and cough stimulation and continued her physical rehabilitation. On day 19, she started to walk with a walking aid, although at this point oxygen desaturation during exercise training became evident (89% with 3 L/min of oxygen).

                Question set 3:
                    1.What would the process of successful weaning look like in terms of weaning from SIMV to no mechanical ventilatory needs?
                        The SIMV setting would be weaned by gradually decreasing the number of breaths 
                        delivered to the patient until they can sustain a normal RR on their own, then the 
                        use of CPAP or BiPAP will give some airway support until the patient can breathe on 
                        their own without dropping in O2 sats or ABG changes.  One area of note is also 
                        careful monitoring of mental status to ensure no build up of CO2 over this time, 
                        which can affect brain function.

                    2.If the patient de-saturates to 89% with 3 L/min of oxygen with ambulation what would you do?
                        Stop, perform deep breathing and see if the patient recovers > 90%, if not increasing 
                        the supplemental oxygen would be indicated to see if the patient can recover. 
                        Discuss oxygen titration and standing orders, etc. here

                    3.Once extubated what would treatment sessions likely focus on?
                        Progressive mobility, pulmonary interventions to inc respiratory mm strength, 
                        coughing and general pulmonary hygiene. Working on higher level functional 
                        mobility with breathing re-training and relaxation techniques.

..8.10. Module 8 Quiz
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!Q)

    Question 1
        Which of the following arteries is the arterial line for hemodynamic monitoring MOST commonly inserted? 
          Femoral 
          Radial 
          Brachial 
          Axillary 

          Radial
        An arterial line is most commonly inserted through the radial artery, but can also be inserted through the femoral artery. Less commonly it can be inserted into the brachial, axillary, ulnar, or dorsalis pedis arteries.
     
    Question 2
        Low central venous pressure (CVP) indicates which of the following clinical abnormalities? 
          Fluid overload 
          Right ventricular failure 
          Dehydration 
          Tricuspid insufficiency 

          Dehydration
        Low CVP may be indicative of hypovolemia and dehydration. Elevations in CVP may result from fluid overload, right ventricular failure, tricuspid insufficiency, or chronic left ventricular failure.
     
    Question 3
        Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) measure all of the following EXCEPT: 
          Balance between oxygen delivery and oxygen demand 
          Amount of oxygen returning to the heart 
          Direct measure of venous oxygen reserve 
          Cardiac output per square meter of body surface area 

          Cardiac output per square meter of body surface area 
        Cardiac index is a measure of cardiac output per square meter of body surface area.

    Question 4
        The continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) ventilation system is the treatment of choice for which of the following pulmonary abnormalities? 
          Obstructive sleep apnea 
          Chronic ventilator failure 
          Acute respiratory failure 
          Pulmonary edema 

          Obstructive sleep apnea 
        CPAP is currently the treatment of choice in cases of obstructive sleep apnea syndrome. 
     
    Question 5
        Which of the following ventilation systems is MOST likely used when there is a need to disconnect the patient from mechanical ventilation for a prolonged period of time?
          Continuous positive airway pressure 
          Bilevel positive airway pressure 
          Manual resuscitator 
          Venturi mask 

          Manual resuscitator 
        The patient may require ventilator assistance by use of a manual resuscitator in an emergency response situation when there is a need to disconnect the patient from mechanical ventilator for a prolonged period of time or to stimulate or mimic a cough and/or augment tidal volume and supplement oxygen.

    Question 6
        Which of the following masks is typically used in conjunction with a nebulizer to humidify the gas being administered? 
          Nasal cannula 
          Simple mask 
          Aerosol mask 
          Venturi mask 

          Aerosol mask 
        Typically, aerosol masks are used in conjunction with a nebulizer to humidify the gas. This mask was originally designed for the administration of aerosolized medications.

    Question 7
        Which of the following oxygen delivery devices is generally intended for lower flow rates of oxygen between 1 and 6 L/min? 
          Nasal cannula 
          Simple mask 
          Aerosol mask 
          Ventruri mask 

          Nasal cannula 
        The nasal cannula is the most commonly used delivery device for oxygen. It is generally intended to be used with oxygen flow rates between 1 and 6 L/min for adults, and as low as 1/16 L/min in neonates.

    Question 8
        Which of the following invasive ventilator devices provides an airway and is LESS likely to stimulate a gag reflex in the semiconscious or alert patient? 
          Oral pharyngeal airway 
          Nasal pharyngeal airway 
          Endotracheal tube 
          Tracheostomy 

          Nasal pharyngeal airway
        The nasal airway is generally better tolerated because it is less likely to stimulate a gag reflex in the semiconscious or alert patient.

    Question 9
        Which of the following is an indicator for mechanical ventilation? 
          Protection of the airway and lung parenchyma. 
          Relief of upper airway obstruction. 
          Improvement of pulmonary toilet in patients with excessive secretions. 
          All of the above 

          All of the above 
        The use of ventilators allows for mechanical ventilator support in order to (1) meet physiological needs in acute respiratory failure, (2) protection of the airway and lung parenchyma, (3) relief of upper airway obstruction, and (4) improvement of pulmonary toilet in patients with excessive secretions or an inability to successfully clear secretions by coughing.

    Question 10
        Which of the following statements BEST describes how the intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) facilitates an increase in cardiac output? 
          -The inflated balloon creates a pressure forcing the blood to circulate into the coronary arteries. 
          -The deflated balloon creates a pressure gradient enhancing the flow of blood through the aorta during left ventricular systole. 
          -The inflated balloon creates a pressure enhancing the blood flow into the chambers of the heart. 
          -The deflated balloon enhances relaxation of the heart muscle.

          -The deflated balloon creates a pressure gradient enhancing the flow of blood through the aorta during left ventricular systole.  
        When the IABP is activated, the balloon is inflated during diastole as soon as the aortic valve closes. The increase in intra-aortic and diastolic pressures forces the blood in the aortic arch to flow in a retrograde direction into the coronary arteries. When the balloon is deflated during left ventricular systole, it lowers the left ventricular systolic pressure and the afterload by forcing the blood to move from an area of higher pressure to one of lower pressure enhancing the cardiac output.

..8.11. Cardiopulmonary II Lab Manual Quiz 2

////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!Q)

    Question 1
        Prior to performing a postural drainage technique targeting a particular lung region which examination procedure must be completed to determine the treatment area? 
          Diaphragmatic excursion 
          Chest wall mobility 
          Cough assessment 
          Lung auscultation

          Lung auscultation
            Begin any treatment session using auscultation techniques to determine area(s) of need.

    Question 2
        Manual percussion to the chest wall during postural drainage is performed at a rate of _________ per minute: 
          100 - 480 
          10 - 20 
          500 - 780 
          90 

          100-480
            Percussion involves clapping with cupped hands over the affected lung segment. This produces a hollow sound as the hand contacts the patient skin. This should be performed at a rapid rhythm that may be 100-480 times per minute.

    Question 3
        When instructing a patient in an effective cough, which of the following is the most optional position the patient should be placed? 
          Sidelying 
          Sitting 
          Prone 
          Supine 

          Sitting
          Sidelying
            Position patient allowing trunk extension and flexion, which is most preferable in a seated position, but you may use side-lying if required.

    Question 4
        The following image demonstrates when of the following interventions? 
        Patient in sitting position with hands on abdomen, leaning forward with mouth open
          Diaphragmatic controlled breathing 
          Segmental breathing 
          Lateral costal expansion 
          Huff and cough technique

          Huff and cough technique 
            The huff and cough intervention include the patient opening the mouth and forcing the air out the lungs with the mouth open as if trying to fog up a mirror. The patient may also preform abdominal thrust with the huff-cough.

    Question 5
        Pursed lip breathing is BEST performed in a supine position. 
          True 
          False

          False
        Pursed lip breathing can be performed in any position and can even be instructed during exercise or functional mobility. 

    Question 6
        When instructing the patient in self-diaphragmatic controlled breathing the non-dominant hand that is placed on the chest should ____________ with inhalation versus the dominant hand on the belly region:
          rise considerably 
          have no movement 
          have equal movement 
          slightly depress

          have no movement
            Instruct the patient to place the dominant hand over the upper abdominal region below the xyphoid process and the non-dominant hand over the mid-sternal region. Instruct the patient to breathe through the nose and direct the air so the dominant hand rises with inspiration and little to no movement should be felt or observed in the non-dominant hand over the chest.

    Question 7
        -In the following image the clinician is placing their hand over the patient’s dominant hand while the patient is performing diaphragmatic breathing. Which of the following BEST describes the action of the clinician’s hand during this intervention?
        -Patient is laying on back with left hand on upper chest near throat error, right hand flat on abdomen with physical therapist's hand resting palm down to patients back of hand.  

          Applies some resistance or counterpressure during inhalation for diaphragmatic biofeedback 
          Inhibits any movement during inhalation to block movement in the region 
          Provides vibration to the region to loosen up consolidation 
          None of the above are correct 

          Applies some resistance or counterpressure during inhalation for diaphragmatic biofeedback
            This image is of a diaphragmatic facilitation technique called counterpressure, in which, the clinician then places their hand over the patient’s dominant hand and applies resistance or pressure during inhalation as a form of biofeedback to the diaphragm for activation.

     
    Question 8
        Which of the following interventions would BEST facilitate direct airflow or ventilation to a known unilateral lower lobe atelectasis?
          Segmental breathing 
          Stacked breathing 
          Incentive spirometry 
          Diaphragmatic quick stretch

          Segmental breathing
        Segmental breathing encourages expansion of specific part of the lung that has been under ventilated due to lung collapse or shut down.

    Question 9
        A patient who is having difficulty performing a global maximal inhalation to produce an effective cough may be appropriate for which of the following interventions to work on increased inhalation and lung expansion prior to working on effective cough training?
          Inspiratory holds 
          Segmental breathing 
          Pursed lip breathing 
          Diaphragm counterpressure 

          Inspiratory holds
            Inspiratory hold is an intervention aimed at global lung ventilatory training and allows for ventilation to poorly ventilated areas, improved cough capabilities for airway clearance and is indicated for patients who are experiencing hypoventilation, atelectasis, or ineffective cough.

    Question 10
        During stacked breathing the patient will continue this “stacking” or inspiration or breaths until maximum inspiratory levels can be reached and held for ______  second(s).
          3 
          5 
          1 
          10 

          3
            The patient is instructed inspire once, hold that inspiration briefly, then inspire again on top of the previous inspiration. The patient will continue this “stacking” or inspiration or breaths until maximum inspiratory levels can be reached and held for 2-3 seconds.

..9.0 Module Introduction

    In this module you will be performing reviewing some of the cardiovascular & pulmonary examination procedures from immersion 2A, as well as, performing specific interventions that will be utilized to treat those examination findings. You will also be tested on your practical application of the examination and interventions performed during your time in the lab immersions. 

    Learning Objectives
        Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to:
            -Apply the use of the Hypothesis-Oriented Algorithm for Clinicians for evaluation, intervention selection, and re-examination in patients with cardiopulmonary dysfunction. 
            -Describe and administer the six components of the patient/client management model (Examination, Evaluation, Diagnosis, -Prognosis, Intervention, Assessment of Outcome) to patients with cardiovascular and pulmonary dysfunction.
            -Give rationale for selection of evaluative tools and appropriate interventions in management of the cardiopulmonary patient.
            -Modify physical therapy examination or intervention technique when a patient exhibits signs of intolerance.
            -Perform a screen for cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases and justify differential diagnosis based on cardiopulmonary data and assessment; identify the need for referral to other health care professionals as appropriate.

                QUESTIONS:

    -In lab immersion 2B you will be engaging in a lab practical. Please review the following guidelines prior to the lab practical to ensure full understanding of how you will be graded and what you may expect during the assessment.

    .Testing Format: 
        -Each competency check is scheduled for 30 minutes. During the assessment one student will act as tester and one will act as patient. The tester will review the case description for a few minutes (2-3 minutes), conduct the testing scenario for 20-25 minutes, and then engage in a short debriefing session. You should be prepared to demonstrate all assessment and interventions covered in lab sessions 1 and 2, as you will need to be ready perform them related to the case you receive. Read the following points carefully:

            -Chart review information, like lab values, ECG strip findings, surgical history, medical history, imaging, medications
            -Identify key features of the chart review including history, medications. Also discuss the current findings and possible patient diagnosis.
            -Discuss the lab value findings. Discuss the PT implications of the lab values and the EKG strip.
            -Consider the patient’s history of present illness and hospital course. Identify precautions that the patient may have based on his current state.
            -What would you include in your initial examination of this patient, including observation, inspection, and physical examination techniques?
            -You will be asked to perform one examination technique pertinent to that case
            -You will be asked to perform one intervention technique based on a single examination finding.
            -Information specific to the examination and/or intervention technique
            -Patient response & PT implications

    .Debriefing:
        -Your instructor will briefly discuss key points and provide you with areas that went well and areas where performance could be improved. This will be brief and provide insight on your strengths and weaknesses noted during the lab practical session. 

    .Scoring:
        -Each case will have 6 associated tasks/questions, and the total points for the exam will be 30 points. Students must score at least 75% or equal to or greater than 22.5/30 to receive a passing grade on the competency check. If a student does not receive a passing score, the instructor will contact them by email to schedule a re-take. Scoring will be based on 6 key criteria:

            1.Identify key features of the chart review including history and medications, laboratory values and tests, medications. If present and applicable, discuss imaging and final dx.
            2.Discuss the lab values and EKG findings. Discuss the PT implications of the lab values and the EKG strip
            3.Consider the patient’s history of present illness and hospital course. Identify precautions that the patient may have based on his current state, post-operative status, etc.
            4.Describe what you include in your initial examination of this patient, including observation, inspection, and physical examination techniques.
            5.Perform an identified and appropriate cardiopulmonary examination procedure
            6.Perform an identified and appropriate intervention based on examination findings

    .Rubric:
        Half scores may be awarded by instructor. For example: 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5 or 4.5

    .Schedule:
        -The tester will start at their designated start time. The assessment will take 20 total minutes. Once the assessment is complete the tester will remain in the room to be the patient for the next tester, and so on. Tester 1 will utilize the instructor as the patient, and the final tested will not have to remain to be a patient. See schedule example below.

..10.0. Module Introduction
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    In this module you will be learning about pulmonary rehabilitation. The module will include details regarding the structure and physical therapy considerations in a formal pulmonary rehabilitation setting.  

    Learning Objectives
        Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to:
            Give rationale for selection appropriate interventions in management of the pulmonary patient who is engaging in a pulmonary rehabilitation program.
            Modify pulmonary interventions and plan of care when a patient exhibits signs of intolerance. 
            Assess and develop plan of care for clients with pulmonary dysfunction in a pulmonary rehabilitation. 
            Perform a screen for cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases and justify differential diagnosis based on cardiopulmonary data and assessment; identify the need for referral to other health care professionals as appropriate.

        Pulmonary Rehabilitation (PR)
        • Pulmonary rehabilitation is 
        an evidence-based, 
        multidisciplinary, and 
        comprehensive intervention 
        for patients with chronic 
        respiratory diseases who 
        are symptomatic and have 
        decreased daily life activities 
        (ACS and ERS, 2006)


        Historical Perspective PR
        • Rehabilitation programs for patients 
        with COPD have existed for 30 years
        • Patient involvement in pulmonary care 
        started during WWI treating traumatic 
        respiratory complications
        • WW II—more patients in the United 
        States were instructed in airway 
        clearance techniques
        • Cardiovascular and pulmonary 
        residency was initiated in 2008 to 
        include intensive 1-year plan of didactic, 
        clinical practice, and research study


        Disease-Specific Aspects of PR

        PATIENT 
        ASSESSMENT AND 
        GOAL SETTING

        EXERCISE 
        PRESCRIPTION 
        AND TRAINING

        SELF-
        MANAGEMENT 
        EDUCATION

        NUTRITIONAL 
        INTERVENTION

        PSYCHOSOCIAL 
        SUPPORT


        Four Essential Areas of PR

        Symptom 
        improvement

        Functional and 
        exercise gains

        Improve health-related 
        quality of life outcomes Psychosocial status


        Choosing Goals and Outcomes in Pulmonary 
        Rehabilitation
        • Goals for pulmonary patient should be specific and pertinent 
        to his or her lifestyle, needs, and personal interests
        • Assist patient in identifying realistic goals described in 
        behavioral terms and measured as outcomes for 
        rehabilitation
        • Outcome measures assess the success of set specific goals
        • Essential areas include exercise capacity, symptoms 
        (dyspnea and fatigue), health-related quality of life


        Outcome Measures in PR
        Domain Outcome Measures 

        Exercise capacity and function Symptom-limited graded exercise test
        Submaximal exercise test
        6-minute walk test
        Shuttle walk tests (incremental or endurance)

        Symptoms (Dyspnea) Borg Scale [substitute with the word dyspnea]
        Visual Analog Scale (VAS)
        Pulmonary Function Status Scale (PFSS)
        Symptom domain of the St. George Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ)—evaluates dyspnea, cough, 
        sputum, and wheeze
        Activity domain of SGRQ—evaluates activity limitation resulting from dyspnea

        Fatigue Borg scale [substitute the word dyspnea with a comparable word of fatigue (e.g., tired, exhausted)]
        Visual Analog Scale (VAS) (with word substitution)
        Vitality dimension of the Short-Form 36 (SF-36)

        Health-related quality of life Medical Outcomes Study (MOS)—Commonly called the SF-36
        Chronic Respiratory Disease Questionnaire (CRQ)
        Seattle Obstructive Lung Questionnaire (SOLQ)


        Incremental Shuttle Test 
        • Externally paced maximal exercise 
        test where the speed of walking 
        increases with each level, controlled 
        by a series of pre-recorded signals
        • Test continues until the participant 
        can no longer continue or cannot 
        keep up with the required pace
        • ɀPLQOHQJWKZLWKWZRPDUNHUV
        LQVHWRIɀPIURPHLWKHUHQG
        • Patient walks around the cones, 
        thus avoiding abrupt changes in 
        direction


        Shuttle Protocol
        The incremental shuttle walk protocol
        Level Speed (m/s) Number of 
        shuttles per level

        Distance ambulated 
        at the end of each

        Structure of the PR Program
        • Structure and settings vary
        • inpatient rehabilitation or subacute facility, an outpatient program 
        in a hospital or freestanding clinic, or in the patient’s home
        • Accepted recommendations for qualifications of personnel, 
        program components, and patient candidacy exists


        The PR Team 

        • Patient and family
        • Medical director
        • physician with expertise in 
        pulmonary disease
        • Program director
        • coordinator of services
        • Other team members
        • exercise, breathing retraining, 
        respiratory care, education, 
        counseling, nutrition


        PR Patient Assessment Components
        Patient Interview Medical history, Review and interpretation of diagnostic tests, 

        Patient interview, Physical assessment, symptom assessment
        Exercise capacity and functional assessment MSK assessment, postural assessment, submaximal vs 

        maximal exercise testing 
        Educational assessment Education assessment assists with determining how well the 

        patient understands and manages disease

        Nutritional assessment Addresses alterations in nutritional status and BMI

        Psychosocial assessment Screening questionnaires


        Patient Candidacy

        • Patients with COPD, restrictive 
        lung disease, pulmonary 
        hypertension, musculoskeletal 
        disease, heart failure, peripheral 
        vascular disease, stroke
        • Other patients with risk 
        factors for pulmonary disease
        • PFTs not exclusively considered
        • Patients who continue to smoke
        • Patient’s financial ability and 
        transportation

        Box 19-1 Risk factors for the development of 
        obstructive pulmonary disease
        Smoking: cigarette, pipe, cigar, environmental tobacco 
        smoke
        Environmental exposures: air pollution, cooking over an 
        open fire in enclosed spaces
        Occupational dusts and chemicals: asbestos, grain farmers, 
        furance workers, vapors, irritants, and fumes
        Family history (genetic): Ž-antitypsin, cystic fibrosis
        Allergies and asthma
        Dietary: poor nutrition (e.g., low levels of vitamins A, C, and 
        E)
        Gestational and childhood factors: low birth weight, 
        respiratory infections
        Periodontal disease
        Simon H (ed). COPD Risk Factors, http://ww.healthcentral.com/copd/


        Reimbursement for PR

        • Moderate to severe COPD covered under bundled billing code
        • CMS will cover 36 one-hour sessions, with a maximum of two sessions per 
        day (use of KX modifier when >36 sessions)
        • COPD patient has a lifetime limit of 72 sessions

        Medicare Improvements for Patients and Providers Act  
        (MIPPA)

        Physician supervision is required 

        No component services may be billed separately

        Treatment Interventions 
        • Airway clearance
        • removal of excessive secretions that obstruct airways, to improve 
        cough, and decrease incidence of respiratory infections and 
        deterioration of lung function
        • Functional training
        • Especially important for patients with symptoms of weakness, 
        fatigue, dyspnea
        • Energy conservation
        • Relief dyspnea
        • Breathing retraining


        Dyspnea Scales 
        Table 19-3 Dyspnea scale
        Grade Degree
        None 0 Not troubled with breathlessness except with 
        strenuous exercise
        Slight 1 Troubled by shortness of breath when hurrying 
        on the level or walking up a slight hill
        Moderate 2 Walks slower than people of the same age on the 
        level because of breathlessness, or has to stop 
        for breath when walking at own pace on the level
        Severe 3 Stops for breath after walking about 100 yards or 
        after a few minutes on the level
        Very 
        severe

        4 Too breathless to leave the house or breathless 
        when dressing or undressing
        From Brooks SM: Survillance for respiratory hazards, ATS News 8:12-
        16, 1982.


        Oxygen Evaluation
        • Pulse oximetry 
        • APTA stance on decision 
        making re: O2 
        supplementation


        Oxygen Delivery 
        • Indications
        • PaO2 < 55 mm Hg or SpO2 < 88%
        • PO2 of 59 mm Hg or lower, or 
        SpO2 of 89% or less if evidence 
        of cor pulmonale, right heart 
        failure, or erythrocytosis
        • Typical Devices for Exercise:
        • Nasal cannula providing O2
        from 0.25 to 6 L/min
        • Oxygen masks
        • PT role in titration


        Physical Conditioning
        • Activity described by intensity, workloads, duration, 
        frequency
        • Advance functional training by:
        • increasing repetitions using lower weights
        • encouraging higher level of work within a given time
        • encouraging fewer rest periods
        • decreasing dependence on adaptive equipment
        • Goals 
        • increasing cardiorespiratory endurance, maximizing work capacity, 
        improving strength, flexibility, respiratory muscle function


        Endurance Training

        • Aerobic training—high or low intensity
        • Interval training is effective training option for 
        persons who cannot sustain extended periods
        • Frequency and duration—3 to 5 times/week, 
        60 to 120 min/session, over 4 to 72 weeks
        • Modes of exercise—walking, cycling, arm 
        ergometry, arm lifting exercises, step exercise, 
        rowing, water
        • Intensity of exercise—related to time, 
        workload, and physiological responses; 
        monitor oxyhemoglobin saturation; optimize 
        bronchodilator use
        • Upper and lower extremity training—direct 
        exercise to training of muscles involved in 
        functional living

        This Photo by Unknown author is licensed under CC BY-ND.


        Strength Training
        • Leads to improvements in muscle 
        strength, increased exercise endurance, 
        fewer symptoms during ADLs
        • Start with low resistance and progress 
        by increasing repetitions and then 
        weight
        • Monitor breathing pattern and pulse 
        oximetry
        • Objective methods to demonstrate 
        outcomes—lifting tests, dynamometry, 
        records of resistive loads


        Respiratory Muscle Exercise
        • Aerobic exercise training of UE 
        and LE provides stimulus to 
        improve respiratory muscle 
        endurance and strength
        • Inc work of breathing leading to 
        inc RR and TV = inc MV
        • Instruction in breathing 
        retraining exercise
        • Outcomes—increases in 
        training resistance and 
        maximal inspiratory pressures


        Exercise Considerations for Different Stages 
        of Lung Diseases
        • Global initiative for chronic obstructive lung diseased (GOLD) 
        is best method for identifying stages of obstructive lung 
        disease
        • 3DWLHQWVZLWKPLOGOXQJGLVHDVHȱ80% FEV1)
        • SOB only with relatively heavy exercise
        • Pulmonary rehabilitation usually not recommended
        • Recommend testing/training protocols used in normal population


        Exercise Considerations for Different Stages 
        of Lung Diseases
        • Patients with moderate lung disease (<80% FEV1)
        • SOB with usual ADLs and with a moderate to fast walking 
        pace (MET level 3-4)
        • Exercise tolerance assessments can be performed using 
        progressive exercise protocols
        • Aim—increase duration of workload resulting in 
        physiological adaptation


        Exercise Considerations for Different Stages 
        of Lung Diseases
        • Patients with severe lung disease (FEV1 below 50%)
        • Restricted by symptoms of SOB during most daily activities
        • May require modified approach to exercise testing
        • Lower workloads, interval training
        • Progressed gradually by increasing number of bouts, lengthening 
        bouts, decreasing length of rest periods
        • Monitor ECG, pulse oximetry, dyspnea, exertion scales, HR, BP

    .('PT 2202_Mod 10_Patient Case_Course Review.docx') Patient Case – Course Review
        .History:
            -A 56-year-old man with severe COPD is listed for lung transplantation. He is a disabled brick mason who lives alone. He is hypercapnic and oxygen dependent: 3 L/min via nasal cannula at rest, 4 L/min with exercise, and 2 L/min during sleep with bilevel PAP. He recently stopped smoking via the American Lung Association’s “Freedom from Smoking” administered by a pulmonary rehabilitation instructor. He has hypertension that is controlled with medication. His goals are to return to community activities, resume household chores, and become oxygen independent. The patient’s greatest physical difficulties are walking inclines, functioning in hot weather, showering, and vacuuming. The patient reports intermittent cervical stiffness with his worse pain level at 5/10. Medications include diltiazem, aspirin, inhaled formoterol, furosemide, inhaled levalbuterol, inhaled mometasone, omeprazole, lisinopril, and inhaled tiotropium

            -This patient underwent preoperative pulmonary rehabilitation (12/20/20 to 02/05/20). Bilateral lung transplant was performed on 7/5/20. Postoperative pulmonary rehabilitation started 17 days after surgery (07/22/20 to 09/15/20).

        .Rehabilitation physical evaluation:
            -height 6 ft., weight 190 lbs. Diminished breath sounds are present throughout all lung fields. His joint range of motion is within normal limits, and hamstring length is 80 degrees bilaterally. His strength is 4/5 throughout. His postural characteristics are a barrel chest with elevated shoulders. He demonstrates a fair diaphragmatic and good lateral costal expansion and a pursed-lips breathing pattern while supine with supplemental verbal and tactile cues. In the sitting and standing positions, he demonstrates accessory respiratory muscle use of bilateral sternocleidomastoid, upper trapezii, and scalene muscles. His gait is slow and steady.

        .Preoperative Data:
            Labs:
                Arterial Blood Gas: pH 7.38/ PCO2 72/ PO2 53/ HCO3 43/ on Fio2 30%.
                CBC panel: 
                    Red blood cells (RBC) or Hematocrit (HCT): 60%
                    Hemoglobin (Hgb): 12
                    White blood cells (WBC): 12,000
                    Platelets (Plt): 200,000
            At rest:
                SPO2 98%, RPE dyspnea scale: 0/10 at rest on 2 LPM
            6MWT @1300 ft with 2 wheeled walker: SPO2 93%, RPE dyspnea scale 8/10 on 4 LPM

        .Postoperative Data: 
            7 days after surgery (pre formal pulmonary rehabilitation, but working with PT in ICU to regular nursing floors)
            Labs:
                Arterial Blood Gas: PH 7.36/ PCO2 56/ PO2 64/ HCO3 32 Fio2 21%
                CBC panel: 
                    Red blood cells (RBC) or Hematocrit (HCT): 50%
                    Hemoglobin (Hgb): 10
                    White blood cells (WBC): 9,000
                    Platelets (Plt): 200,000
            At rest:
                SPO2 98%, RPE dyspnea scale: 0/10 at rest on 4 LPM
            6MWT @1400 ft with 2 wheeled walker: SPO2 94%, RPE dyspnea scale 8/10 on 8cLPM

        .Following 23 Pulmonary Rehabilitation Sessions:
            6-Minute Walk Test: walked 1600 feet without walker, without oxygen RPE of 5

        Discussion Questions:
            1.Define hypercapnia.

            2.Analyze the ABGs pre- and post-transplant

            3.Analyze the lab values, are any concerning or do any indicate need for further evaluation?

            4.What is the FiO2 value for each of the supplemental O2 readings above?

            5.Without medical intervention can this patient become oxygen independent by engaging in a pulmonary rehabilitation program? 

            6.The difficult tasks of walking inclines, showering, and vacuuming would be considered what intensity of activity based on MET level of each.

            7.If the patient as engaging in a preoperative pulmonary in the hospital what may be some potential interventions?

            14.Describe your aerobic training program for this patient in formal pulmonary rehabilitation setting.
